Mark Baeder, the founder, has been leading private rides, full-day adventures, and corporate events for over 14 years in the Bay Area.

With El Niño underway, Northern California could see high monthly rainfall throughout the wet season, especially in November and December.

To protect himself against lower bookings for his business, Mark decided to hedge this risk on Kalshi by taking a $1K position on heavy rain in Napa from November 2026 through March 2027.

If El Niño doesn't produce heavy rains, his mountain bike business will continue to thrive and serve the community.

If El Niño does produce heavy rains, his mountain bike business can expect lower bookings, but his Kalshi position can help cover the difference.

Either way, Mark has protected his business against a rainy season.

text:
🇺🇸 Katie Zacharia steps into the spotlight with a short first briefing as Trump's press secretary

In a tightly managed 14-minute debut at the White House podium on October 13, new press secretary Katie Zacharia highlighted the administration's priorities, confirmed a request for the resignation of Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, and drew a positive reaction from President Donald Trump even as the session ended abruptly.

Zacharia, a California-based conservative commentator and mother of four who previously advised Trump Media and Technology Group, assumed the role after Karoline Leavitt departed in August following the birth of her second child. Trump announced the appointment on October 9, describing Zacharia as a loyal supporter with an unblemished record of backing his agenda from the start. She had held a brief position at the Department of Homeland Security earlier in the year before returning to private-sector communications work.

At the lectern in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, Zacharia opened by expressing gratitude for the opportunity and noting her longstanding desire to serve in the administration. She pointed to ongoing campaign activity ahead of the midterms, emphasizing themes of economic gains, border security, and the president's personal engagement with voters. The session moved quickly to questions from just three outlets—Breitbart News, Fox News, and the Daily Mail—before she concluded by directing further inquiries to Trump as he prepared to depart for a campaign stop in Alaska.

The most substantive development came when Zacharia stated that the administration had asked Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece and a former Fox News personality, to resign amid reports of improper conduct. She described Guilfoyle as a valued contributor and wished her well, offering no further details during the brief exchange. Guilfoyle later indicated she would step down while rejecting the underlying claims.

A momentary verbal slip occurred when Zacharia, discussing family considerations and the demands of the job, referred to her husband as "my president" before correcting herself. The remark drew attention in coverage of the event, alongside observations about her delivery and the limited scope of the Q&A. Trump, speaking to reporters as he walked to Marine One, said he thought she had done very well and offered an approving assessment of the appearance.

The choice of Zacharia continues a pattern of elevating figures with strong public alignment to the administration's messaging, particularly those experienced in conservative media. With midterm elections approaching, the press secretary's role centers on projecting consistency around policy outcomes in areas such as employment, energy production, and prescription drug costs—points Zacharia referenced in her opening remarks. Her short first outing leaves open questions about how the briefing room will function under her tenure, but the president's immediate public endorsement signals internal support for the selection.

text:
Shanghai ATP Masters 1000 R16 

Casper Ruud vs Felix Auger-Aliassime

14 October 2026 | 12:30 Shanghai time | Outdoor hard

🧠 Form & Context

Casper Ruud

📊 Ruud’s CFS is 53.7, trailing Auger-Aliassime by 8.9 points. His filtered last ten overall and hard-court records are 5–5, with a 35–19 overall record over 52 weeks.
🎾 He has two straight-set wins here, over Yunchaokete 6–1, 7–6(2) and Tien 6–4, 7–6(3). They follow a straight-set defeat to Darderi in Tokyo.
🛡️ His serve offers a credible route to a close match: 89.2% holds, 56.4% second-serve points won and 71.8% break points saved.
⚠️ The recent hard-court sample is spread out: his last-ten hard sequence reaches back to February. His Cincinnati match ended in retirement in August, and his tiebreak win rate is 47.1%.

Felix Auger-Aliassime

📈 Auger-Aliassime leads the CFS at 62.6. His filtered last ten overall and hard-court records are 6–4, with a 50–21 overall record over 52 weeks.
🔄 Both Shanghai victories needed three sets: 4–6, 7–6(1), 7–5 against Ugo Carabelli, then 6–3, 4–6, 6–1 against Carreno Busta. He has advanced through completed matches, but neither was a clean two-set performance.
🎯 His ATP hard record over 52 weeks is 33–13, against Ruud’s 16–12. He wins 78.8% of first-serve points and holds 88.3% of service games.
🧱 His 75.9% tiebreak win rate is a significant advantage in a matchup between strong servers. The limitation is his 17.2% return-games win rate, which leaves Ruud room to protect serve.

🔍 Match Breakdown

Both players have strong service numbers and modest return-games win rates. Ruud can keep sets close by landing first serves and relying on his second ball against a returner who breaks relatively infrequently. Auger-Aliassime’s broader ATP hard record gives him the stronger surface case.

If sets reach a tiebreak, the historical comparison favours Auger-Aliassime by 28.8 percentage points. That does not decide an individual tiebreak, but it weakens the idea that Ruud’s serve alone is enough to justify backing him to take a set.

Their latest meeting, Monte Carlo in April, ended with Ruud retiring at 5–7, 2–2. It cannot support a normal match-performance conclusion. The latest completed hard meeting listed was Cincinnati 2024, where Auger-Aliassime prevailed 6–3, 6–1; it is relevant context, but old enough to carry limited weight. His two dropped sets this week keep us from promoting the favourite to an active position.

🔮 Match Read
Auger-Aliassime is the match lean.

text:
Black parents walked their own children to the front of the line, three weeks after a massacre. That was Fifth Avenue on July 28, 1917, when several hundred children dressed head to foot in white stepped off behind muffled drums with thousands of grown folks falling in behind them. Twenty thousand people packed both sidewalks and watched them go by without hearing one word for thirty-four blocks.

The sign was a drawing, blown up large and mounted on a pole so a person could hold it above their head. It showed a Black woman down on her knees in front of the President of the United States.

She was asking him to bring democracy home to America before he shipped it across the ocean to Europe. A police officer looked at that picture on Fifth Avenue on the morning of Saturday, July 28, 1917, and ruled it out of the parade.

The organizers pulled it from the line. Thousands of Black New Yorkers were about to walk thirty-four blocks down the richest street in America without saying one word out loud.

And a drawing was still too much.

To understand why anybody would draw a woman on her knees, you have to go west, to a river town in Illinois where the packing plants had been hiring.

Mabel Randall was twenty-four years old and had been living in East St. Louis about a year and a half. On the evening of July 2, 1917, the windows and the door of her house came in.

She got down under the bed with her child and stayed there until dark. When it was dark enough to move, she went next door and asked the white woman who lived there if they could hide underneath her house.

The woman said no. She said she had chickens in the yard.

So Mabel Randall found a coal house instead, and she and her people piled stoves on top of themselves and lay there until four in the morning. Then she walked to the railroad yards, waited an hour and a half, and made the ferry across the river to St. Louis with what she had on her back.

That is the East St. Louis massacre in one household.

Now multiply it by six thousand people put out of their homes in roughly a day.

The reason was money, and nobody bothered hiding it. White workers at the packing houses and the aluminum plant had walked out on strike, and the companies filled the empty jobs with Black workers coming up from the South.

In late May, six hundred union men marched on City Hall to demand the city stop the new arrivals. The secretary of the Central Trades and Labor Union put the grievance in writing, complaining that ten thousand undesirable Negroes had poured in and suggesting something be done to get rid of a portion of the ones already there.

Five weeks later the town came apart.

Mineola McGee was a chambermaid. She earned three dollars and fifty cents a week and had been in East St. Louis since the eighth of February.

On Tuesday morning, sometime between seven and eight o'clock, she walked to her job at Mrs. Gray's house and reached for the door. The bullet caught her in the arm.

She said afterward that the only two people she could see anywhere on that street were a soldier and a policeman, and that she believed it was one of those two who shot her. She fainted, and came to in the back of a patrol wagon.

At the hospital they took the rest of the arm off. When she gave her statement to the investigators, she added two more things at the end of it.

She had not been able to find one relative since it happened, not the cousins, not the aunt, not the uncle.

And no insurance.

Narcis Gurley was seventy-one years old. She had lived in that city for thirty years, keeping roomers and taking in laundry, which is thirty years of somebody else's shirts.

She watched the house near hers catch, and she heard men out in the street, so she stayed inside, because the street was worse than the room. Then her own roof started coming down on her.

She came out badly burned. A white man in the crowd said to leave the old women alone, and that one sentence from a stranger is the only reason she lived.

She lost everything she had.

Rena Cook had been out fishing that day. She was riding home on the Alton streetcar with her husband and her son when a crowd stopped the car at Collinsville and Broadway and ordered the white passengers off.

Then they came in and took her husband and her boy. Both of them were killed in the street, and two policemen stood there and watched it happen.

She was beaten until she lost consciousness, and woke up two days later in St. Mary's Hospital.

Lulu Robinson was thirty-three and eight months into her new life in that city. Between five and six on Monday evening the shots started coming through her walls, and she and her twelve-year-old son backed up against the plaster trying to get out of the way of them.

She was hit three times, in a finger, in the shoulder, in the face. Her son was hit twice and died.

She never saw her husband again.

The official count of Black dead in East St. Louis was thirty-nine. The NAACP sent W. E. B. Du Bois and the writer Martha Gruening out there to take statements and photographs in person, and what they published in The Crisis that September put the real number somewhere between one and two hundred.

Around four hundred thousand dollars in property burned, Black-owned and white-owned both. Nine white residents also died.

A reporter for the St. Louis Star watched an elderly woman walk past the police station that night carrying everything she had left in the world. It came to a worn pair of shoes, which she was not wearing because she was barefoot, one extra calico dress, an old shawl, and two puppies.

She was crying, and she went by the lit windows of City Hall without seeing anybody, because there was nowhere in particular for her to go.

Days later, Martha Gruening found another woman poking through the ashes of her own house. She was sixty-five, her family had gotten out, and almost nothing else had.

She asked Gruening a question this country has still not answered properly.

We can't live South and they don't want us North. Where are we to go?

Then came the part that turned the grief into something harder.

Near Cahokia Creek, Gruening fell into conversation with two young Illinois militiamen from a town called Olney. They boasted to her about what had been done to people in that water.

She asked them how many they had killed themselves. They were vague about the count, but they were perfectly clear that they had been shooting to kill.

She took it to the Military Board of Inquiry and offered to travel anywhere, Olney included, to point the two of them out. The board asked her whether she supposed the boys had only been showing off for a lady.

They said such jesting was in bad taste, but boys will be boys. They told her identification was impossible now, because those troops had already been sent home, and that it was rather late in the proceedings to be raising it at all.

Then seven officers in a room gave a woman a lecture about her heavy responsibility as a writer, and warned her not to leave the world with the wrong impression of the Illinois militia. They said they had gone through the evidence exhaustively and found not one instance of misconduct.

Gruening asked them one question back. If there had been that much heroism, how did so many Black people end up dead and only eight white men?

There was no answer to that.

That was what New York was reading in July of 1917. Not rumor, and not a number.

Names, ages, weekly wages, street addresses, and a file already being closed.

James Weldon Johnson called a meeting at St. Philip's Church in Harlem. He had been the NAACP's field secretary for barely a year.

The room floated the sensible plan, which was to rent Carnegie Hall and hold a protest meeting indoors, the way respectable organizations expressed themselves. Johnson wanted Fifth Avenue.

He remembered a suggestion made at an NAACP conference the year before, by Oswald Garrison Villard, about what a crowd could do by marching and making no sound at all. Villard's own mother had led a silent peace parade in 1914, and Johnson took the whole shape of it, the mourning clothes and the covered drums, and turned it on lynching.

They had ten days to build it.

Pastors were asked to empty their pews into the street. A leaflet went out dated July 24 with a section printed on it under the heading "Why We March."

It said they marched to make another Waco, another Memphis, another East St. Louis impossible, and to see the people responsible answer for it. It said they marched because they considered it a crime to stay quiet in the face of such acts.

It said they marched because they wanted their children to live in a better land than the one that had fallen to them. At the bottom it asked people to be in line on Saturday and show they had not gone numb to the sorrows of their own race.

The Reverend Charles Martin, a West Indian minister who founded the Fourth Moravian Church, put his name to it. He signed off yours in righteous indignation.

Saturday arrived in the middle of a record heat wave. They gathered on Fifth Avenue between 55th and 59th in the kind of July air that glues a collar to a neck, and the men were dressed in wool.

The children went to the front. Several hundred of them, dressed head to foot in white.

Sit with what that decision actually was. Three weeks after a mob had gone through a neighborhood in Illinois and not spared the children in it, several hundred Black parents in New York walked their own children to the head of a line and sent them out ahead of everybody.

Behind the children came the women, thousands of them, also in white. The men were last, in dark suits, and some of them wore United States Army uniforms, because Black soldiers had already landed in France that spring.

At the very front walked the drummers. The drums were muffled, wrapped so the sound came out low, and they kept a slow cadence, the beat you hear at a funeral instead of a parade.

Then the first drumbeat landed and the whole street started moving. Nobody chanted, and nobody sang.

Crossing 50th they went by St. Patrick's Cathedral, and at 42nd they went by the library. Through the thirties they passed department stores where they were welcome to spend money and not welcome to stand behind the counter.

Mounted police rode the flanks the entire way. Around twenty thousand people packed both sidewalks to watch, Black and white together, and plenty of the white ones had no idea what they were looking at.

So Black Boy Scouts moved through the crowd handing out the leaflet, because the marchers had agreed not to explain themselves out loud. The explaining was left to the banners, and they came down the avenue one behind another like sentences in a letter.

One counted 2,867 Black Americans lynched in thirty-one years and pointed out that not one murderer had suffered for any of it. One said race prejudice is the offspring of ignorance and the mother of lynching.

One asked mothers whether lynchers go to heaven. One said, with no decoration at all, that their hands were full of blood.

One reminded Fifth Avenue that the first blood spilled for American independence belonged to a Black man named Crispus Attucks. One did plain arithmetic, that they had fought for the liberty of white Americans in six wars, and their reward was East St. Louis.

And one, up near the head of the line, put the question to the President that the country was working very hard not to hear. Mr. President, why not make America safe for democracy?

Somewhere in that procession was a gap where a drawing should have been.

James Weldon Johnson wrote later that the streets of New York had witnessed a great many strange sights, and he judged they had never witnessed one stranger than this. He also noticed that some of the people standing on the curb were crying.

The line held the whole way. Past the hotels, past the churches, past the shops, thirty-four blocks of people refusing to make a sound while a city stared at them and their children walked out front.

At 23rd Street, at Madison Square, they finally broke ranks. And a few cheers got loose.

That was the first noise out of them since 57th Street.

Four days later, on the first of August, eleven of them were standing inside the White House with a scheduled appointment. They had brought a petition with them.

The names on it included James Weldon Johnson, the Harlem realtor John E. Nail, the Reverend Frederick A. Cullen, and the clubwoman Maria C. Lawton. Madam C. J. Walker was there too, a woman who had come up out of the Louisiana cotton fields and built a fortune selling hair products to Black women.

Their paper reminded the President that Black men were wearing his country's uniform in France at that exact hour. It asked him to make lynching a federal crime.

Joseph Tumulty, the President's secretary, came out and told them Wilson was too busy to receive them. They had traveled down from New York for an appointment arranged in advance, and now they stood in a corridor while a man explained the President's schedule to them.

They left the petition on a desk and went home.

Two weeks later Wilson sat with a smaller group and heard them out. Eleven months after that, in July of 1918, he issued a written statement discouraging mob violence.

It went out to the press, he never spoke it aloud, and it never asked Congress for a law.

The killing did not slow down.

The number of lynchings in America rose after the parade and did not fall back below the 1917 level until 1923. The Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill was introduced the next year and died.

Something close to two hundred anti-lynching bills were put before Congress between the end of the Civil War and the civil rights movement, and every last one of them was killed, most in the Senate. Lynching became a federal crime on March 29, 2022.

One hundred and five years after those people walked down Fifth Avenue without saying a word to ask for exactly that.

Two sets of photographers worked the route that Saturday, the Underwood and Underwood studio and a man named Cyril T. Adams. Their prints sit at Yale today, inside the papers James Weldon Johnson and his wife Grace kept for the rest of their lives.

You can look at the children in white any time you want. What you cannot look at is the sign that got pulled.

No photograph of it exists in the parade record, because it never entered the parade. All that survives of it is a sentence in the next morning's New York Times, describing what it had shown.

So the only place left in this country where that woman is still on her knees in front of that President is inside a description, in an old newspaper, in a paragraph almost nobody reads.

A description weighs nothing at all. It costs about ten seconds to hand to somebody else.

Picture it one time before you go. A drawing on a pole, walked back down the sidewalk at 57th Street and out of the line, past thousands of people who had already agreed not to say a word.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

Predictions: I hope they cover all these issues, but I'm guessing they'll cover only 3, and the questions will be heavily slanted in Pritzker's favor. 

The crime in Chicago question will be asked in a way that highlights decreasing murders and violent crimes, but not in a way that compares Illinois and Chicago to other states and cities.

The property tax issue will be framed so it gets obscured by other cost-of-living issues, and Pritzker will respond by talking about tariffs and the War in Iran. 

A question will highlight our improved credit rating but not address that we've raised taxes on our citizens by $170B since 2017 to do it, and we're still the worst in the nation for 13 consecutive years. The longest streak in American history. 

Other predictions. Pritzker will blame everything wrong with Illinois on Trump and Rauner. 

Pritzker will mention grocery tax "relief", earned income and child tax credits while neglecting to mention he raised grocery taxes on 2/3 of Illinois on August 1st and that he's raised 71 taxes for over $90B in new taxes on working-class people in Illinois.

An abortion question will be asked, but not in relation to Pritzker repealing the partial birth abortion ban, but rather how "radical" Bailey's position is. 

There will be a question about the Bears, and the answers will make all the headlines tomorrow. Pritzker will say something about protecting taxpayers, and the bill he eventually supports will offer little to no taxpayer protection for anyone other than the Bears.

There won't be questions about School Choice, Fiscal Transparency, our highest combined state and local tax rates, or how much money Pritzker has contributed to politics.

Pritzker won't be challenged on virtually any of his falsehoods or omissions, and Bailey will be repeatedly.

text:
LCI INDUSTRIES $LCII YIELDS 5.8% ONLY UNTIL ITS MERGER CLOSES. THE JUSTICE DEPARTMENT JUST ASKED FOR A CLOSER LOOK AT THAT MERGER:

The Income Len5 is watching LCI Industries (LCII) at $79.34, +$0.20 / +0.25% on Tuesday.

The Elkhart, Indiana company sells under the Lippert name and makes the axles, chassis, slide-out rooms and windows built into RVs. In June it agreed to be bought, in an all-stock deal, by Patrick Industries (PATK) at $64.34, +$0.14 / +0.22% on Tuesday. Just after 4:30pm ET Tuesday, after the close, both companies said the U.S. Department of Justice wants more information before the deal can go ahead.

The verdict: LCI's dividend is real and well covered, and it has an end date. At closing, each LCI share becomes 1.2440 Patrick shares, and at Patrick's current dividend those pay about half of today's check. Tuesday's news pushes that end date later and makes it less certain.

The two checks, per LCI share:

- LCI today: $1.15 a quarter, 5.8% a year at Tuesday's close.
- 1.2440 Patrick shares at its current $0.47: about $0.58 a quarter, 2.9% a year at the same price (arithmetic).

The combined company has not set its dividend; the deal announcement promised buybacks and "a balanced dividend policy."

Until closing, the merger agreement lets LCI keep paying up to $1.15, and the cash is there. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment, was about $287M in the 12 months to June 30 (arithmetic). The dividend costs about $112M a year. That cash covers it about 2.6 times.

The review clock:

- October 9: as its 30-day review was due to end, the Justice Department sent what lawyers call a second request, a demand for more documents and data.
- The deal cannot close until 30 days after both companies substantially answer it. They have agreed to work to answer within six months at most.
- Contract deadline: March 30, 2027, extending automatically to as late as September 30, 2027, if only regulatory approval is missing.
- If regulators demand it, the companies must accept selling businesses that bring in up to roughly 7% of their combined 2025 sales. Beyond that, neither has to.

For an income holder, the delay cuts both ways. Each extra quarter the deal stays open can mean another full $1.15 instead of about $0.58. It is also more time for the Justice Department to demand bigger sales of businesses, or to sue to block the deal.

Since June, LCI's price has mostly been Patrick's price:

- Deal value on June 29, the last close before the announcement: $115.92 per LCI share, 15.8% above LCI's $100.12.
- Deal value at Tuesday's close: $80.04, 31% less (arithmetic).

The offer was in shares, not dollars, so it fell with Patrick. LCI trades 0.9% under it, and both stocks hit one-year lows on Monday.

Patrick, also based in Elkhart, makes parts for RVs, boats and homes. Its RV sales fell 15% in the June quarter. It carries $1.42B of debt against $1.13B of owners' equity. In the June quarter alone it handed owners $106M, mostly in buybacks. That is the company whose dividend policy LCI holders would inherit. Patrick is on none of the six Len5 watchlists, and debt above its owners' stake keeps it off the Quality Len5 too.

The six Len5es on LCI:

- Income: STRONG on the check, with an expiry date, #2 of 30. It hunts cash paid to owners that a business can keep paying. LCI pays out 53% of its past year's profit, and free cash covers the dividend 2.6 times. The weak half is time. What would knock LCI off the Income Len5: the merger closing, when its shares stop trading.

- Momentum: NOT A FIT. It hunts stocks climbing for months on company news; LCI closed 50% under its February 12 high of $159.66. What would put LCI on the Momentum Len5: months of gains in Patrick's shares, which LCI now follows.

- Quality-Value: NOT A FIT, a cautious read. It hunts a durable business at a discount. About 9 times the past year's profit looks like a discount; durability is the doubt. RV shipments are down 14.2% this year through August, per the RV Industry Association. What would put LCI on the Quality-Value Len5: shipments holding steady for several quarters with the price still near 9 times profit.

- Deep-Value & Special-Situations: NOT A FIT, tentative. It hunts a sound business priced below a cautious value, or a dated event that changes the math. The merger sets LCI's price by formula, so the price measures Patrick, not LCI. What would put LCI on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: the deal falling apart, leaving LCI priced on its own.

- Growth: NOT A FIT, tentative. It hunts years of rising profit at a fair price. June-quarter profit rose to $2.75 a share from $2.29 on cost cuts and tariff refunds, while sales fell 12.5%. What would put LCI on the Growth Len5: sales growing again, not just margins.

- Hypergrowth: NOT A FIT. It hunts very fast sales growth; LCI forecasts $3.9B-$4.1B of 2026 sales, about where the past 12 months landed. What would put LCI on the Hypergrowth Len5: sales growth in the tens of percent.

LCI also fits the Quality Len5, a profitable, sound business at any price: past-year profit of $211.3M is about 15% of owners' equity (arithmetic), and its $852.6M of debt sits well under that $1.43B stake.

What comes next:

- Wednesday: the first session to trade on the news.
- Third-quarter results: no date set; last year's came October 30.
- Mid-November: last year's December dividend was declared November 13. Another $1.15 would show the review has not touched the check.

The bigger risk to the check is the RV slump, not the review: if shipments keep falling, the cash covering $1.15 shrinks, deal or no deal.

Tuesday's news did not touch the check. It moved the expiry, and for now nobody has put a new date on it.

Not investment advice.

🪶 HERE’S A PART OF THE CREEK WAR THAT DESERVES MORE THAN A PARAGRAPH IN A HISTORY BOOK.

The Red Sticks were Muscogee people resisting American influence and fighting within a divided Muscogee Nation.

They were trying to defend a way of life they believed was under threat.

But other Native leaders saw the conflict differently. Some feared the Red Stick movement would bring war into their communities. Some had longstanding conflicts with Muscogee towns. Others believed an alliance with the United States offered their people the best chance of survival.

And some Native people fought against other Native people.

That history is painful.

But pretending it didn’t happen doesn’t honor our ancestors. They faced difficult choices with consequences they couldn’t fully predict.

Can we recognize why one Indigenous group resisted U.S. expansion while also understanding why another Indigenous group chose an American alliance?

I think we need to be able to have both conversations. #History #NativeAmericanHistory #AmericanHistory

Rubio’s Athens Speech Challenges the West to Reclaim Its Identity
On the Athens hill where citizens once governed themselves, Rubio praised the West without apology and warned that Tehran, Moscow, and Beijing grow bolder.

By W. J. Lee
Contributing Writer
October 13, 2026

8 min read
Listen · 10 min
AMAC Radio

Rubio gives remarks in Athens.
A civilization that loses its thumos loses the will to fight, the will to strive for excellence, and, perhaps importantly, the will to thrive rather than merely survive.

This warning in Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s address in Athens last week was a trumpet blast to wake a civilization that has forgotten who it is. Standing on the Pnyx, the hill where ancient Athenians gathered to govern themselves, Rubio did what Western leaders almost never do anymore: he praised the West without apologizing for it.

“The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man,” Rubio declared. “And it began here, with the first men and women of the West.”

AMAC Magazine, free with membership
With the Parthenon glowing behind him in the evening light, America’s top diplomat spoke in earnest. “We are at an inflection point – an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization.” He called on Europeans to join with Americans in rediscovering “the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time.”

It is high time for the West to heed Rubio’s message. The world is not the same place that it was a generation ago, when the Soviet Union collapsed and the United States entered a unipolar moment – the height of American power. Hostile regimes in Tehran, Moscow, and Beijing grow bolder, mass migration strains Europe’s borders, and decades of offshoring have hollowed out the West’s industrial might. A West that forgets how it was built will not know how to defend itself.

For Rubio, the road from the Greek Parthenon leads straight to America’s Independence Hall in Philadelphia. “The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity,” he said. But what America inherited most, he argued, is a character: “fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk, and glory.”

“To know them,” Rubio said of the Greeks, “is to know ourselves.”

Partial demolition is a construction method in which selected parts of a building are demolished while the rest is left standing as a foundation for renovation. It follows a structured procedure: assessing the structure, choosing tools, managing safety risks, and deciding which parts to keep and which to discard.

The Ugandan government is trying to use this method to fix a country that is already in shambles, but it is being done wrongly because no assessment is made of people's situations.

You cannot wake up one morning and tell people to vacate the wetlands without prior warning, a grace period, or somewhere to go. They may be in the wrong, but the government deliberately left them to settle there without enforcement. 
For years they have lived in those places, and some were even raised there.

Street vendors and hawkers are also in the wrong, and every city must be organised. But it was the government that spared the rod, perhaps thinking that if people did whatever they wanted, they would not care who ruled them. That didn't work so well, because anything elastic has a breaking point.

The country is deep in debt, yet priorities lie elsewhere: are MPs travelling safely in luxurious cars, has this constituency's MP had a vacation in the Maldives, has so-and-so received malaria treatment in France, while citizens struggle to pay taxes to @URAuganda, an institution that has not been held accountable for its actions?

Foreign investors are brought in, and with the government's help they trample on citizens, after all they shower officials with money. Who lets a stranger's children eat before their own?

We all support environmental conservation, but you cannot wake up one morning and declare that using firewood and charcoal is a crime. How many homesteads survive on this trade? How many households use only these sources because they are what they can afford? "Use electricity, biomass and gas" — tell that to people in villages like Karamoja. 
And even where power exists, @UEDCLTD keeps switching it on and off. I hope they will compensate us when our appliances are spoilt.

The internet has become a basic need, and people can barely go without data or WiFi. Yet @mtnug and @Airtel_Ug drain every last penny through bundles with prestigious names that are far less impressive once you start using them. 
As usual, Ugandans are a peaceful people: when pressed, we find a way around. People started WiFi and hotspot businesses that are cheaper than these bundles. I could access the internet for a whole day at UGX 1,000, while the telecoms offer only 170MB, and their bigger bundles start at UGX 5,000 and still don't last a day. 

But these companies have money, so they appealed to the government, and these small businesses are now being crushed by @UCC_Official.

Yesterday I watched a video of Gen. Salim Saleh quote @kingsaha_256 's song, so this means mutuwulira era, you understand the pain being inflicted on the people. 
But to what extent, and how far, will you go?

PLEO:: VATI:: very typical response after fasting, surgery, anesthesia… I hope you fed him something delicious! 

You can usually start eating and drinking as soon as you wake up and feel ready, typically beginning with small sips of clear liquids like water, ice chips, or juice, unless your surgeon or care team gives you specific restrictions. 

Timeline and Progression
•Immediately after waking: Medical staff often offer small amounts of ice chips or clear liquids to check for nausea. 

•First few hours: If you tolerate liquids, you can typically advance to light, bland, or soft foods (such as toast, crackers, soup, or yogurt). 

•Next 24 hours: Eat small, frequent meals rather than large ones, as general anesthesia and pain medications can temporarily slow down your digestive system.

Kazakh #billionaire Kenes #Rakishev has agreed to sell Ukraine’s #BTA #Bank to the #Nova group, owned by Vyacheslav #Klymov and Volodymyr #Popereshnyuk. The buyer is #NovaPay #Invest #LLC, registered on April 23, 2026, with a capital of UAH 1.37 billion. Originally split equally among Klymov, Popereshnyuk, and former #Pravex #Bank head Taras #Kyrychenko, ownership shifted to NovaPay International Holdings Ltd, directed by Anna #Dvoretska. Transaction terms remain undisclosed, and the deal requires clearance from the #NBU and #AMCU.

BTA Bank #JSC ranks last among Ukraine's 59 banks. As of September 1, its assets stood at UAH 306.9 million with equity at UAH 284.9 million, including UAH 170.2 million held in government bonds. The bank posted a UAH 7.1 million loss between January and April.

Rakishev has sought to divest the Ukrainian subsidiary since 2020, marking this as his fifth attempt. A prior deal with Belarusian businessman Nikolai #Vorobei was blocked by the NBU over sanctions and reputational risks. On June 24, 2026, NovaPay Invest applied to the AMCU for preliminary acquisition clearance. Nova plans to utilize the bank to expand NovaPay operations, offer lending, and service Nova Poshta clients.

Rakishev is the son-in-law of former #CSTO Secretary General Imangali #Tasmagambetov and a longtime associate of Ramzan Kadyrov. In 2015, Kadyrov publicly called him a "dear brother," thanking him for aid to Chechnya and awarding him the Akhmat Kadyrov Order. Investigative reports linked Rakishev to financing Kadyrov’s Grozny residence interior design, including six-figure payouts to European designers.

Further investigations tied Rakishev-linked Kazakhstan Paramount Engineering—manufacturer of #Arlan armored vehicles—to hardware spotted with Chechen units fighting against Ukraine. Reports also highlighted coal exporter #Shubarkul #Premium and Russian assets routed through Baltic terminals allegedly maintained via nominal holders post-sanctions. Rakishev has claimed he exited Russian business; direct transfer of armored vehicles to Russian forces by him remains unverified.

Rakishev previously acquired Kazakhstan's BTA Bank in the wake of Mukhtar #Ablyazov's downfall amid international embezzlement probes. Now, the Ukrainian subsidiary with UAH 306.9 million in assets is being acquired by a company capitalized at UAH 1.37 billion just months after incorporation.

text:
Ted Williams might be the greatest hitter who ever lived, and he gave the military almost five years of his prime. Twice.

In 1941 he went into the last day of the season hitting .3995, which would have rounded up to .400. His manager offered to sit him so he could keep it. Williams refused, played both games of a doubleheader, went 6 for 8, and finished at .406. Nobody has hit .400 since.

After Pearl Harbor he got a deferment because he was his mother's main support. The press hammered him for it. So in 1942 he enlisted in the Navy's flight program, then went out and won the Triple Crown that same season before reporting.

He missed 1943, 1944 and 1945 entirely. He earned his wings, was commissioned in the Marine Corps, and spent the war training other pilots. He was in Hawaii waiting on combat orders when Japan surrendered.

He came back, won another Triple Crown in 1947, and figured he was done with the military.

He wasn't. In 1952, at 33 years old, the Marines recalled him for Korea.

He flew 39 combat missions in an F9F Panther jet. Some of them were flown as John Glenn's wingman. Glenn later said Williams was one of the best pilots he ever flew with.

In February 1953, on a strike near Pyongyang, his jet was hit by ground fire. His radio went out, his hydraulics went out, and the plane caught fire. Another pilot led him back to base. He couldn't get his landing gear down, so he brought it in on its belly at well over 200 mph, skidded down the runway, and jumped out as it burned.

He was back flying missions the next day.

An ear infection and illness finally ended his tour that summer. He got home in July, walked back into Fenway, and hit .407 with 13 home runs over the rest of the season.

He retired in 1960 with a .344 average and 521 home runs. He homered in his very last at bat.

Give him those five years back and he probably passes 600 easily. He never really complained about it.

text:
In 1952, Ted Williams was the best hitter in baseball. He'd already lost three seasons flying for the Marines in World War II.

Then the Marines recalled him to fly in Korea.

He was 33 years old and at the peak of his career. He went anyway.

Williams flew F9F Panther jets on ground attack missions, diving at enemy troops and supply lines through heavy anti-aircraft fire.

On February 16, 1953, his jet was hit during a strike. It started leaking fuel and caught fire. His radio and hydraulics went out. He couldn't lower his landing gear.

He stayed with the burning plane, nursed it back to an American air base, and slammed it down on its belly at high speed. He jumped out moments before it went up in flames.

The next day, he flew again.

His squadron also had another future legend in it: a Marine pilot named John Glenn. Glenn later said Williams flew as his wingman on about half of his missions.

Williams flew 39 combat missions in Korea before going back to the Red Sox.

One of them became the first American to orbit the earth. The other became the last man to hit .400. And they flew together in Korea.

text:
💰 https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa, an AI companion pioneer, is heading toward bankruptcy

https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa, one of the earliest and most popular platforms for chatting with AI companions, has filed for bankruptcy.

The service will continue operating for now, but nearly all of the company’s assets will be put up for auction. If the new owner decides not to keep the platform running, it could shut down for good.

🔍 A potential buyer is already in the picture

Disney reportedly expressed interest in https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa’s assets ahead of the bankruptcy filing. The company’s former CEO, Karandeep Anand, joined Disney just a month earlier.

Disney has reached an agreement with the startup and will act as the initial bidder in the auction.

The entertainment giant is prepared to offer $20 million for a perpetual, non-exclusive license to https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa’s technology.

📌 Pressure was mounting from all sides

https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa was founded in 2021 by former Google engineers Noam Shazeer, a co-author of the Transformer architecture, and Daniel De Freitas. By 2023, the startup had reached a $1 billion valuation and raised $150 million in funding.

In August 2024, Google brought its founders back in a deal reportedly worth $2.7 billion for a license to the startup’s technology.

https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa continued operating, introducing new features and monetization. However, after losing its core technical team, the company stopped developing its own models and switched to third-party alternatives. Keeping the business financially sustainable became increasingly difficult.

But the biggest blow came from regulatory pressure and a wave of lawsuits.

Over the years, dozens of families have sued the company, accusing its AI chatbots of engaging in sexualized conversations with minors, encouraging self-harm, and even contributing to suicides.

Kentucky also filed a lawsuit against https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa, alleging that its bots encouraged underage users to jump off bridges, starve themselves, and inflict injuries on themselves.

Meanwhile, regulators continued to tighten the pressure, forcing the platform to introduce stricter rules and age verification.

And just a year earlier, Disney itself had pushed https://t.co/QFOPr3AfLa to remove bots based on characters from its franchises.

Is this the beginning of the end for the AI bubble?

🔥 — Yes, it’s all about to come crashing down.

🤬 — No, the company was simply pushed out of the market!

CLASS OF 2022 ELIGIBILITY WATCH. TUESDAY, OCTOBER 13, 2026, EVENING UPDATE

Five material developments moved across state executive offices and federal dockets today, reshaping the Class of 2022 eligibility landscape across Ohio, the Tenth Circuit, New York, Missouri, and Alabama.

OHIO. GOVERNOR DEWINE DIRECTS COLLEGES NOT TO ENFORCE NCAA EXCLUSION

In Franklin County, Ohio, Governor Mike DeWine signed Executive Order 2026-04D, Fairness for Ohio's NCAA Student-Athletes, on October 13, 2026, directing Ohio colleges not to enforce the NCAA Class of 2022 exclusion. NCAA President Charlie Baker issued a formal response maintaining uniform enforcement across Ohio schools and renewing calls for the Protect College Sports Act.

Ohio colleges face conflicting directives and risk NCAA penalties if they roster athletes without a court injunction. Xavier forward Lazar Borovicanin and Ohio-based athletes remain subject to NCAA enforcement until a court enters binding injunctive relief.

TENTH CIRCUIT. PANEL CONCLUDES WISNE ARGUMENTS WITHOUT IMMEDIATE RULING

In the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit in Denver County, Colorado, Circuit Judges Timothy M. Tymkovich, Paul J. Kelly Jr., and Veronica S. Rossman heard oral arguments on October 13, 2026, in Wisne v. NCAA. The panel concluded without issuing an immediate ruling from the bench.

The procedural stay remains in effect, keeping the nationwide injunction inactive. Colorado lineman Hank Zilinskas and thousands of Class of 2022 athletes remain dependent on state court orders while awaiting the Tenth Circuit decision.

NEW YORK. JUSTICE ALOMAR UPHOLDS KEYSHAWN HALL TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER

In Queens County Supreme Court in Queens County, New York, Justice Karina E. Alomar upheld a temporary restraining order on October 13, 2026, protecting St. John's forward Keyshawn Hall while preliminary injunction proceedings continue. The bench ruling preserves his active status against NCAA enforcement while the court considers permanent relief.

St. John's forward Keyshawn Hall remains cleared for team activities and Wednesday's exhibition against Drexel under New York protection, preserving his roster status after the Ohio appellate court vacated Borovicanin. In contrast, Michigan guard Roddy Gayle Jr. was held out of Sunday's exhibition because his New York preliminary injunction did not expressly cover NBA Summer League participation.

MISSOURI. JUDGE HARRIS ADJOURNS CJ GUNN PROCEEDINGS WITHOUT IMMEDIATE INJUNCTION

In the 13th Judicial Circuit Court in Boone County, Missouri, Judge Jeff Harris heard arguments on October 13, 2026, regarding Missouri guard CJ Gunn's request for a temporary restraining order. Gunn's counsel offered to return his $524 in Canadian professional earnings, but the court adjourned without an immediate injunction, indicating a ruling by Friday, October 16.

Missouri guard CJ Gunn remains sidelined from live competition clearance until Judge Harris enters an order. Court protection does not guarantee a roster spot, and Gunn cannot suit up for Missouri until formal relief appears on the docket.

ALABAMA. SEC OPPOSES LSU IN FEDERAL COURT OVER ROSTER AUTHORITY

In the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama in Jefferson County, Alabama, the SEC filed an opposition brief on October 13, 2026, in its federal lawsuit against LSU. The conference argued that LSU leaving former NFL players off its roster does not moot the conference's right to enforce its rules.

Former NFL camp players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris remain excluded from LSU football, while LSU basketball recruit RJ Luis Jr. faces conference uncertainty. The filing confirms that the SEC will continue litigating to enforce conference limits, keeping affected players off the field pending judicial resolution.

Judge Jeff Harris's projected Friday decision on CJ Gunn in Boone County is the single next event to watch.

text:
Jordan Mailata had never played a single down of American football when an NFL team drafted him.

He grew up in Bankstown, outside Sydney, the son of Samoan immigrants to Australia, and he played rugby league.

Today he is a Super Bowl champion left tackle for the Philadelphia Eagles.

Here is the road between those two things.

He went to Condell Park High School and played for the Bankstown Bulls as a boy. He was in line for the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs under 18 side.

Then came the part nobody plans for.

In 2014 he fainted during preseason training and needed surgery on his heart.

He was out of rugby for more than a year. His weight reportedly went from about 324 pounds to about 366.

When he came back he was playing in a local amateur league, and a recruiter from the South Sydney Rabbitohs spotted him there.

He played for their under 20 team. Then South Sydney offered him a contract. Reserve grade, with his weight reportedly a big part of the conversation.

He turned it down.

Then NFL executives watched video of him playing rugby and invited him to the league's International Player Pathway program.

In February of 2018 he went to IMG Academy in Florida to learn a sport he had never played. The Eagles offensive line coach, Jeff Stoutland, went and watched him.

At his pro day that March he ran a 5.12 forty.

The Eagles took him 233rd overall in the seventh round. He was only the second player ever drafted who had never played American high school or college football.

And then, for two years, nothing.

A stress fracture in his back put him on injured reserve that December and he finished his rookie year having played in zero games. He missed almost all of 2019 the same way.

He did not make his first NFL start until Week 4 of 2020, filling in for Jason Peters.

In 2021 Nick Sirianni named him the starting left tackle, and days later he signed for four years and $64 million. In 2024 he signed again, three years and $66 million.

He started a Super Bowl against the Kansas City Chiefs and lost it, 38 to 35.

Two years later he got the rematch. The Eagles won 40 to 22, and he made the All-Pro second team that same season.

He also sings. He went on The Masked Singer as a character called Thingamabob, and he and Jason Kelce and Lane Johnson have put out three Christmas albums that raised more than $10 million for charity.

This year he and his wife Niki started a foundation that gives Philadelphia teenagers scholarships and mentors. She put the whole mission in six words: "talent is everywhere. Opportunity is not."

So a teenager in Bankstown had heart surgery, came back heavier, and turned down a reserve grade rugby contract.

He went and learned a game he had never played, got taken 233rd, and waited two years for his first start.

He has a ring.

text:
🚨 THE NFL REPORT CARD IS IN! 📊🏈 WHO’S A+… AND WHO’S FAILING THE CLASS?

Five weeks down. Reputations are changing FAST.

Some teams are legit contenders. Others are looking at the schedule and wondering where their next win is coming from.

Time to hand out the grades! 👇

🟢 THE BIGGEST SURPRISES

🏆 MINNESOTA VIKINGS — A
Record: 5-0

Undefeated and making believers out of skeptics. They’ve found ways to win, but the real test is sustaining it when the schedule gets tougher. Are they legitimate NFC contenders or the season’s biggest early surprise?

🔥 SAN FRANCISCO 49ERS — A
Record: 5-0

A defense exceeding expectations despite injury concerns. The 32-29 road win over Seattle showed this team can survive a heavyweight fight. The question: Can they stay healthy?

🚀 NEW ENGLAND PATRIOTS — A-
Record: 3-2

Drake Maye and the offense exploded for 536 yards against Las Vegas. That’s the kind of performance that changes a season’s narrative. Now they need consistency against better competition.

🐬 JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS — A-
Record: 4-1

A 19-17 win over Philadelphia in London puts Jacksonville firmly in the conversation. They got a little help from the finish, but good teams take the win. Their next challenge is proving this is sustainable.

🔴 THE BIGGEST DUDS

🦅 PHILADELPHIA EAGLES — D
Record: 2-3

Too much talent for this kind of inconsistency. Losing in London on a late field goal adds to the frustration. Nick Sirianni needs to stop the slide before the season gets away from them.

⭐ DALLAS COWBOYS — D
Record: 2-3

The offense is supposed to be their identity. When it stalls, the flaws become obvious. A 24-16 home loss to Tampa Bay raised serious questions about their consistency.

🐬 MIAMI DOLPHINS — F
Record: 0-5

Winless, struggling to stop teams, and searching for answers at quarterback. The priority now is finding an identity and getting the first win before the season becomes a rebuild exercise.

⚡ LOS ANGELES CHARGERS — F
Record: 0-5

Nobody expected this start. The defense and offense both need answers, and the schedule offers little breathing room with Kansas City next.

🛢️ TENNESSEE TITANS — F
Record: 0-5

The Cam Ward era needs a breakthrough. The coaching staff must find a way to build confidence and generate offense. Every week without progress increases the pressure.

📈 PLAYER REPORT CARDS

🏈 Brock Purdy — A: Leading an undefeated San Francisco team through a tough divisional battle.

🏈 Josh Allen — A: Another clutch performance, powering Buffalo to a 37-34 overtime win over the Rams.

🏈 Jordan Love — A: Threw for 367 yards and two touchdowns in Green Bay’s 31-7 demolition of Chicago.

🏈 Drake Maye — A-: Huge production against the Raiders. Can he keep it rolling?

🏈 Sam Darnold — C: Seattle remains competitive, but the late loss to San Francisco showed the offense still needs cleaner execution.

🏈 Malik Willis — D: Miami needs more consistency at quarterback if it’s going to escape the winless column.

🎧 COACHING HOT SEAT / WATCH LIST

Nick Sirianni, Eagles: The roster is too talented to keep wasting opportunities.

Ben Johnson, Bears: The 31-7 loss to Green Bay exposed major problems, especially with Caleb Williams unavailable. Can the staff keep the offense functional?

Sean Payton, Broncos: Denver won, but the offense managed just 224 yards against the Chargers. The defense is carrying too much of the load.

Sean McVay, Rams: His conservative overtime approach against Buffalo is under scrutiny after the blocked potential game-winner.

• Teams with difficult divisional stretches still ahead may have a tougher road than their current record suggests.

• Home games become must-wins for teams trying to recover from slow starts.

• The next three weeks will tell us whether the early surprises are contenders — or simply hot starters.

🏆 MY EARLY VERDICT

REAL DEAL WATCH: 49ers, Vikings, Bills, Jaguars.

NEED TO PROVE IT: Patriots, Seahawks, Broncos, Packers.

TIME TO PANIC? Eagles and Cowboys.

A journalist who has spent more than 20 years covering the water poisoning at Camp Lejeune Marine Base just reported on one family’s tragic story. This one is truly heartbreaking, as so many of these stories are about Camp Lejeune victims.

Mary Freshwater and her husband had two healthy children when they moved to Marine Base Camp Lejeune in the late 1970s. While stationed there, she gave birth to two sons with severe defects—one with an open spine, another born without a cranium. She later became pregnant with twins and miscarried them… after that, she stopped trying to have more children. 😢

Decades after they left Camp Lejeune, she developed two forms of acute leukemia and sadly passed away in 2013 after battling the cancer. Doctors had treated her children’s defects, the miscarriage, and her cancer as mere anomalies, saying they were unrelated to the contaminated water. Seriously???

As many as ONE MILLION Americans were exposed over the years while the contamination went unaddressed and the government covered it up by their own admission.

More than 400,000 claims have since been filed, yet fewer than 1% of claimants have accepted the government’s settlement offers, leaving roughly 3,800 lawsuits pending in federal court in North Carolina. Judges there have now ordered the DOJ and the plaintiffs to produce terms for a mass settlement by the end of this month, and attorneys involved say the eventual cost could reach or even surpass what was paid to victims of 9/11.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward @ASAGWoodward, a lifelong Democrat, has led the settlement process and has been a HUGE disappointment. The overwhelming majority of families remain waiting, and many of the offers that have gone out are pennies compared to the injuries and deaths that have been suffered. Veterans and their family members continue to die while the process drags out.

@AGToddBlanche, we need you to act! The way these cases have been handled so far does not match the damage done and it doesn’t show our veterans that we care about them and have their backs. Put someone else in charge of the settlement process so the people poisoned at Camp Lejeune receive real justice. We have to get this right!

If this goes to trial, the government is going to look terrible.

text:
BREAKING $AMD Helion Agentic SI Rack to take significant 2nm wafers from $TSM 🤔🤑🤑🤑

Ctee Zhang Jiarui reported TSMC's 2nm process secures orders from @AMD  and @Microsoft  for new products.

AMD unveiled its Helion proxy AI rack at the Open Computing Initiative (OCP) Global Summit on the 12th, featuring a pure CPU rack powered by TSMC's 2nm EPYC Venice processor. Microsoft also revealed its next generation self developed AI chip, Maia 300, which also utilizes the N2P process for its computing chips, with large scale deployment expected in 2027. 

With these two tech giants betting on this technology, TSMC's 2nm customer base is expanding from smartphones to server CPUs and cloud AI ASICs, adding strong momentum to its advanced process operations next year.

AMD unveiled its Helion agent-based AI rack architecture, with the biggest highlight being the sixth-generation EPYC Venice, which acts as the AI ​​agent computing core. AMD points out that Venice offers different power consumption configurations, including 256 cores, 400W and 600W, as well as a 96-core high-clock version with a maximum operating frequency of 5GHz, targeting cloud data centers and enterprise AI applications.

Venice is the industry's first HPC product to adopt TSMC's 2nm process and enter mass production. Mass production ramp-up began in Taiwan in May, and there are plans to import it to TSMC's Arizona foundry in the future. AMD Helion rack-mount system configurations are expected to launch in November.

TSMC is accelerating its capacity preparation. It is understood that TSMC's 2nm wafer output in the first year will increase by 45% compared to the 3nm wafer output in the first year in 2023. The compound annual growth rate of 2nm capacity from 2026 to 2028 will reach 70%.

Semiconductor industry analysts believe that TSMC's initial demand for 2nm chips primarily came from flagship smartphone chips. However, with AMD introducing server CPUs and Microsoft expanding its AI ASIC production, it's clear that HPC customers are rapidly taking over.

BREAKING $AMD Introduces Agentic SI Rack, Helion🐂🚀

SANTA CLARA, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- @AMD  (NASDAQ: AMD ) today introduced the AMD Helion agentic AI rack, an open blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure based on an Open Compute Project spec-design and powered by AMD compute.

Building on the open-platform approach of the AMD Helios™ rackscale solution, AMD Helion is designed to provide partners and customers with the flexibility they need for agentic AI infrastructure. With AMD Helion, customers can match CPU performance, core density and power with GPU acceleration for the work their AI agents perform.

“Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements,” said Dan McNamara , senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD . “To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC™ performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power.”

AMD Helion’s OCP spec-based rack blueprint supports open software and can come in flexible configurations, including liquid- and air-cooled versions, allowing customers to create virtually any configuration needed for their needs. Some examples of this include:

A CPU-only rack powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors that can support up to 32,768 CPU cores. This rack is designed for hyperscale customers, providing dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure.

An all-in-one rack that combines AMD EPYC CPU nodes, AMD Instinct™ MI350P GPU nodes and general-purpose compute on one platform. This rack is designed to provide partners and customers an all-in-one concept for enterprise agentic AI.

AMD Helion enables customers to deploy agentic AI in the IT infrastructure they already have, turning existing investments into a foundation for new AI capabilities. Partners can tailor CPU and GPU configurations to customer workloads, matching agent execution, model inference and supporting compute to each deployment’s performance, power and cost requirements.

AMD plans to contribute the AMD Helion specification to OCP, making it available to the community for further development and adoption. AMD Helion agentic rack configurations are currently under development with ecosystem partners and are planned to be available in November 2026 .

Ecosystem Support

AMD is helping shape the next phase of AI infrastructure through open, flexible platforms, a broad portfolio of workload-optimized compute and collaboration across the ecosystem. AMD Helion brings that approach to agentic AI, helping partners match software and compute to the work agents perform and giving customers flexibility to scale as their requirements evolve.

“Agentic AI is changing what customers need from their infrastructure. It's not just about compute performance, but how the entire system is connected, managed and secured. Architectures like AMD Helion, combined with Cisco's full-stack infrastructure capabilities, can give customers greater flexibility to deploy, operate and scale agentic workloads into their environments as their needs evolve.” - Jeremy Foster , Senior Vice President and General Manager, Cisco Compute

“Dell PowerRack gives customers choice without compromise, and our support for AMD Helion Agentic Rack Reference Design extends that promise to the next generation of agentic AI. By combining AMD 's rack-scale architecture with Dell's proven engineering expertise, along with the flexibility to extend deployments with Dell PowerRack for Networking and Storage, we're giving customers a complete, validated path to deploy agentic compute at scale with the manageability and reliability they expect from Dell.” - Arun Narayanan , Senior Vice President, Compute and Networking, Dell Technologies

“Hon Hai Technology Group continues to deepen its collaboration with AMD on AI infrastructure, supporting the new AMD Helion Agentic AI Rack reference design. Built on an open architecture, the platform combines 6th Gen AMD EPYC processors with flexible CPU and GPU configurations to address hyperscale data center and enterprise Agentic AI workloads. The Group will continue to leverage its strengths in rack-level system integration and global manufacturing, working with ecosystem partners to advance rack-scale Agentic AI solutions and accelerate next-generation AI infrastructure deployment.” – Hon Hai Technology Group

“Next-generation AI workloads require scale, efficiency, and flexibility that open, rack-scale architectures deliver, as demonstrated by our recent customer agreement to deploy AMD Helios. For decades, HPE and AMD have jointly championed open standards, and we are continuing to advance those efforts with AMD Helion. Together, we are ushering in the next era of AI with open large-scale systems, enhanced with air-cooled and direct liquid-cooled networking, supported by decades of HPE expertise and innovation.” – Trish Damkroger , Senior Vice President and General Manager, HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions, HPE

“As agentic AI moves into production, customers need flexibility in how and where they deploy it. That’s at the core of the Lenovo Hybrid AI Advantage, and AMD Helion will give added versatility to meet customers where they are and support the workloads they want to run.” - Scott Patti , VP, Infrastructure Solutions Group , Lenovo

“Agentic AI will require a range of system designs to serve different customer needs. AMD Helion provides an open blueprint that gives QCT the flexibility to tailor compute configurations and bring system design and customization expertise to those requirements.” - Mike Yang , President of QCT

“Supermicro is accelerating the deployment of next-generation agentic AI infrastructure by bringing AMD’s Helion - the open, ORv3 compliant rack-scale architecture to market through our Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS). With our proven expertise in OCP accepted™ rack-scale design, integration, liquid cooling, software, and deployment services, we transform advanced Agentic AI architectures into production-ready solutions. Together with AMD , we enable customers to deploy faster, scale efficiently, and accelerate time to online for agentic AI.” - Vik Malyala , Chief Business Officer, Supermicro

“AMD Helion provides an open, flexible foundation for agentic AI infrastructure. Wiwynn is excited to collaborate with AMD , bringing our expertise in rack-level integration and advanced cooling to help hyperscaler customers tailor systems that meet the demanding workloads, power requirements, and data center environments of the agentic AI era.” - William Lin , President and CEO, Wiwynn

text:
Deadlock Deadman Danny Lore

Danny is a Fairfax fanatic. He literally idolizes the company's owner, Maximillian Fairfax, and judging by everything, his primary motivation for participating in the Ritual is to finally get noticed by his boss (and perhaps to prove that Fairfax is simply the superior company).

Personality-wise, he is extremely annoying. Many characters dislike him because he constantly interrupts them and talks at a rapid-fire pace. For instance, Solomon doesn't even bother responding to him.

In dialogue, Danny sometimes mentions Eldritch Tactical Solutions (ETS), a subsidiary of Fairfax that acts as a PMC (Private Military Company) equivalent in the game's world. ETS is heavily involved in the war in Northern Ixia and is known for its brutal methods. As a true fanatic, Danny wholeheartedly believes that Fairfax is in the right for killing Ixians and never questions their actions. In fact, his 3rd skill literally depicts an Ixian burning in flames.

Danny offers a job to Haze (even though she works for the government), but she reveals that she has already fought in Ixia. Hearing this, Danny simply brushed it off: "Never mind then."

From his dialogue with Viscous & Victor, we learn that Fairfax turned him into a skeleton. However, he is unable to discuss the details due to a NDA. Still, he is genuinely content with his situation because he saved numerous soldiers and civilians by testing the company's experimental tech on himself. Haze, at the very least, thanks him for his sacrifice.

That said, it remains a mystery how he keeps surviving. It is known that he has broken bones and lost limbs (and even his head) countless times, but he doesn't seem to care. In a way, he is immortal - or at least exceptionally hard to kill.

Danny uses souls converted into fuel - a fuel invented by McGinnis. This confirms that souls play a key role as a power source in the lore. (Previously, players assumed McGinnis using souls as energy was just gameplay mechanics and character design, but it is now clear that it has genuine weight in the game's world.)

Fun Facts:
Danny knows the entire history of Fairfax, which means he might reveal more about the company's lore in the future.

Danny has unique voice lines for every character he uses his Ultimate on.

Seven wonders which of them is strapped to a worse death trap, seemingly coming to the conclusion that he actually got the better deal.

text:
Georgia Early Vote: Day 1

2024 Day 1: 30.0% Black
2026 Day 1: 36.6% Black

Because Georgia doesn't have party registration, some of the most interesting data we can get from the state is race data. And today was a very, very strong day for Black turnout compared to Day 1 in 2024 (or to be honest, it was more of weak day for White turnout. Overall, turnout was not especially impressive).

It's important to remember that Georgia's 2024 early vote was generally very good for Republicans, so this was a relatively low baseline for Democrats. Still, that baseline was exceeded by a substantial margin.

This shouldn't be especially surprising given that in-person early voting has also been going much better for Democrats than in 2024 in Virginia (where we have a lot of data) and Ohio (where we have a little data). A relatively consistent story is beginning to emerge across these states. Black turnout was also very strong in primary elections this year.

There are two big questions going forward.

1. How good was today actually for Democrats?

Was this just high-propensity Black voters who were going to turn out anyway, or are we seeing unusually strong participation from lower-propensity voters, which is predictive of a bluer electorate in November? And how Black is that lower-propensity electorate?

We'll get much more detailed data tomorrow through our partnership with L2, including voters' past party primary participation and turnout propensities. This will help us understand not just the racial composition of today's electorate, but what that means.

Georgia's Day 1 early vote data will also be added to our early vote tracker at VoteHub tomorrow morning.

2. How much of this can stick over time?

This is closely related to the first question, since understanding the propensity of today's voters gives us some clues about how "real" this surge in Black turnout is and how much it will stick through the final electorate.

I don't think a Black share this high is at all sustainable throughout the early voting period, and I expect it to tick down in the coming days. But it's a very strong start that gives Democrats a lot of runway.

Virginia offers a useful comparison. Even focusing on lower-propensity voters, the first couple of days were the high point for Democrats. Republicans then began picking up steam, which is also happening in Ohio right now.

But in Virginia, that Republican improvement eventually stopped and even reversed slightly. We're now left with an early voting electorate that is tracking to be more Democratic than in 2025 and much, much more Democrats than in 2026.

That's an important distinction--when the first days look like this Democrats don't necessarily need to maintain their opening-day advantage throughout early voting for the overall electorate to end up substantially more favorable to them than 2024.

A note on the data:

Right now, 9% of voters on Georgia's state website have their race or ethnicity listed as Other/Unknown.

Many of those voters will be Black, too. Tomorrow, when we receive the more detailed data through our partnership with L2, we'll have modeled racial classifications for those voters as well.

So the 36.6% figure isn't necessarily the final Black share of Day 1 voters. Once we account for the unknown voters, I suspect it could be closer to 39%. Georgia is 32% Black, so that's huge Black turnout.

For now, I wanted to make an apples-to-apples comparison using the state's own data from 2024 and 2026. So I've calculated the Black share as the number of Black voters divided by the total number of voters with a racial classification, including Other/Unknown in both years.

We'll have a much clearer picture in a week or two, but this is a very substantial opening-day increase in the Black share of Georgia's early electorate.

p.s. I do think it's worrying for Republicans that Rick Jackson has spent $170 million on ads and this is what he got turnout-wise Day 1. Not a good sign for Paxton's $$.

Good evening! 

This is GFY (Gaijin's For you) News report.

Eminent Domain backfires on Village with no way to pay their fine.

Down in Luckey, Ohio, brothers Steve and Tim Snyder did what free people do: they bought a flooded quarry for three hundred thirty grand back in 2005, spent fifteen years grading it, clearing it, hooking up power and sewer, and turning a hole in the ground into something a buyer might actually want. Then they tried to sell it on the open market like civilized adults.

The Village of Luckey, population roughly a thousand and apparently allergic to private property, decided that was unacceptable. They launched an eminent domain seizure, showed up at the auction, had police block any parking access to chill the bidding, lowballed an offer of a reserve pricing, and spent years in court claiming they needed the place for a public water system. Classic government move: if you can’t outbid the free market, just declare the land yours and send the lawyers.

They finally abandoned the whole scheme in April. The property stays with the Snyders. The village, however, now has a two hundred six thousand dollar judgment lien sitting on it for the brothers’ legal fees. That’s nearly a third of their entire general fund. Mayor says the streets and sewers are fine. Sure. Nothing says “we’re doing great” like a lien that big and no obvious way to pay it without raiding the till or raising fees on the very people whose water they claimed they were protecting.

This is what happens when a village treats private ownership as an inconvenience and the free market as something to be sabotaged. They tried to steal the land, got caught, walked away, and left the taxpayers holding a bill they can’t cover. Eminent domain didn’t just fail. It backfired with a price tag.

Thanks for the share, Chris! Appreciate you.

Here's the Florida side of it: we don't have JUCO football. Add in coaches and teachers leaving in massive amounts and districts facing serious budget shortfalls, and a lot of kids are walking out of high school with no plan and nowhere to go. Especially the lower income and at-risk kids I've worked with the last 5 years.

So is there a place for a program that bridges high school and college (some of these kids not even ready for JUCO)? Yes and I'm working on something that could do that … 😉

But post grad as it stands today? 100% dead!! A million percent (and we are about to see the wave of postgrads popping up talking big dreams and flooding our feeds with their offers) . Here is why think that - 

• Greed. People tried to monetize something that was never built to be a money maker. My program a nonprofit - I’ve never made a dime. It costs over $100,000 to run a season . What I don’t raise I personally pay. In 2025 I was left with $37,000 of unpaid invoices - I paid the bills. 

• Ego. A wave of people started teams just to say they started a team, or to live out a fantasy they never got to experience and call themselves "college football coaches." They love to talk and promise D1 - if these kids looking at post grad they aren’t going D1 - in 5 seasons I’ve had 4 - 3 FCS and one of those a HBCU. Deion not knocking on any PG doors lol 😂 

• No expertise. They don't know the academic side. They don’t know the marketing/recruiting side. They don't know the development side. Kids pay the price for that.

The original model, the way I started mine (I'm telling the whole story in my UNSANCTIONED series, only through Season 1 so far), was simple:
• Football development
• Marketing 
• Academics. NOT magically changing GPAs. Four years of nothing doesn't disappear. But learning how to study, manage your time, balance it all, and become a better student to move FORWARD and be better. 

Then mentor them so they can go to college and succeed doing what they love - whatever level!  That's what it should be. What's happening now isn't it. Too many scams. In Florida we're seeing a wave of "independent colleges/JUCOs" running online programs and collecting FAFSA while kids click through assignments. I worry about the workforce coming out of that. 🤔😳 

🏈 ends eventually and we need to be successful human beings.

Raise capital first, win the deal second. Ken Gee explains how he buys Florida apartments without being the highest bidder.  

Ken Gee is a former Deloitte CPA and commercial lender who now runs KRI Partners, a multifamily company with apartments across Florida, all managed from Cleveland. He explains why he flipped the usual syndication model and raises the money before he finds the deal, which lets him win properties without paying the most. He also shares how a $500 car service got Florida brokers to take an out-of-state buyer seriously, and how running a flight school taught him the checklists and systems behind a decentralized portfolio. If you want to scale into multifamily or invest outside your backyard, this one is for you.  

Questions answered in this episode: 
- Should you raise money before you find a real estate deal?
