WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

ORLANDO FURIOSO II

A SONGE OF DEFYANCE

>*"O Herod, Herod, crowned in golde,

>Whose purse is deep, whose wit is olde;

>Thou buyest the day, thou sellest the nyght,

>And callest thy robberies lawe and ryght.

>Thou buildest a way where none may walke,

>And payest thy fooles to praise thy talke;

>Thy stones are dear, thy poore are gone,

>Yet still thou bidest the wyrkmen on.

>Thy lordes sit fat at thy table’s ende,

>And sweare each thief is an honest freende;

>But lend them no sylver, nor hide them at home,

>And see how swiftly their fidelité’s gone.

>Now where is thy courage, great lorde of the towre,

>When merchaunts grow lean and the hungry growe powre?

>Thou hast gold for a pageaunt, and chayns for the poore

>Come buy thee some honour; we selle it no more.

>And what motley crow sitteth close by thy side,

>That feedeth on kysses and farteth out pride?

>He clappeth thy shoulder, he tickleth thine ear

>What need hath a kyng of a fool for a peer?

>If he ryng thee to supper, or tuck thee to bed,

>Let him feast on the taxes of men thou hast bled;

>The fool hath his cap, and the lorde hath his crown

>Yet both wear their honours with breeches slipped down!

>So drynk, mighty Herod, and laugh while ye may;

>Thy reckoning cometh, though gilded be the day.

>For a lorde may commaund both the gallows and swerd

>But ne’er buyeth love with a frightened man’s word."*

He laughed at the passauge about the jester, then frowned at the rest.

“Thou hast threatened him.”

“I have.”

“In writing.”

“That is the customarie place for a threat, if one wishes it remembered.”

“He may hang thee for it.”

“He may trie.”

“He may hang thy men.”

At that I ceased smiling.

“Then we shall have to ensure he finds it costlie.”

Aldo shook his head. “Thou art not a prince, Ferrabosco. Thou hast no castle, no title, no treaté. A great lorde may endure an insult from a great lorde, for it is the custom of their kind. He will not endure it from thee.”

“Then he should have left me my goods.”

I sealed the letter with the broken scales, and made six copies. One went to the Hegemon’s palays, carried by a buoy who was payd to deliver it into the honds of a clerk and not to retourn until he had seen the seal received. One went to the merchaunts of the Mercato di Mezzo. One to the guilds. One to the House Malvezzi’s own creditors. One to the magistrates. The last I sent to a tavern where I knew a man would read it aloud for the pryce of a jug.

I had no intentioun of letting the letter remain a private matter between two men.

By the next evening, the tavern copy had been read aloud in three different places. In one, the audience laughed so loudlie at the passauge concerning the jester that the innkeeper feared the noise would bring the wautch. In another, a man stood upon a bench and declared that he would rather serve Orlondo Ferrabosco than Herod Malvezzi, though he had ne'er seen either of us. In a third, a clerk copied the letter in his own hond and sent it to a cousin in Ferrara.

I was told that the cousin sent it to a lorde.

The lorde sent it to a bishop.

The bishop sent it back with a note advising the lorde not to be foolish.

This pleaused me more than the laughter.

For a joke may travel where an accusatioun cannot. A man who will not read a complaint agaynst his ruler may gladlie listen to a jest about him. He laughs, and in the laughter discovers that he is not alone in his contempt. Then the thought comes, perhaps for the fyrst time, that a ruler may be mocked without the sky falling down.

I had not yet raised a banner. I had merelie given men permissioun to laugh.

It was enough to make Herod angrie.

I did not witnesse Herod read my letter. I know what followed onlie through men who were present, and through the many contradictorie versiouns which afterwaurds found their way to me. One servaunt swore that the Hegemon laughed until tears came to his eyes. Another said he read the letter twyce, and that the second reading left his face quite still. A third claimed that he threw the parchment into the fire, then ordered a clerk to retrieve it from the ashes.

I cannot say which account is true.

But I know what he did.

Within three days, the wautch began asking questiouns in the poorer quarters. They waunted the names of men who had left Bologne, the places where they had gone, the inns that gave them shelter, and the merchaunts who supplied them. The road-waurdens began stopping carts at the gates. Two guildmaisters were summoned to the palays. A printer who had copied my letter was taken from his bed and held without charge.

Herod did not send an army after me. He had not yet decided that I deserved one.

He sent men to count the people who myght be feeding me.

That was cleverer than I had expected, and I was obliged to admire it.

A man may fight a robber with a swerd. He cannot so easilie fight a rumour, a market, or a hundred households which have discovered that they are safer when they share what they know. Herod meant to starve us of informatioun before he starved us of bread. He would make everie innkeeper afraid to receive us, everie carter afraid to carrie us, everie widow afraid to give us a crust. He would tourn the ordinarie courtesies of the countrieside into crimes.

He had also, as I learned later, begun to speak of me as a traitor in the pay of foreign enemies. This was convenient, for it allowed him to describe any man who opposed his levies as an accomplice of mine, and any man who questiouned the road as a friend to treason.

There are few things more useful to a government than an enemy who can be blamed for all its failures.

I answered by sending the printer’s familie enough money to leave Bologne, and by arranging for the next copies of my letter to be carried by men who had no connectioun to one another. I told our people not to gather in large numbers, not to wear any sign, and not to threaten a man merelie because he had once served the Hegemon. We would take what we needed from those who profited from injustice, and we would pay for what we took from those who did not.

Some among my company thought this too gentle.

“We are at war,” said Aldo.

“We are not.”

“Herod believes we are.”

“Herod believes many things. He believes the road will make him immortal. I do not see why we must accept his judgement in all matters.”

“He will send soldatos.”

“Then we shall have to decide what to do when they arrive.”

Aldo looked at me with the expressioun of a man who has discovered that his employer is either a genius or an imbecile, and is not yet certain which.

The soldatos came two days later. There were fourteen of them, led by a young captain named Ser Gheraurdo, who had a fyne swerd, a poore horse, and the confidence of a man who had ne'er been forced to reckon with consequences. They rode into a villauge where three of our men were buying flour, and demaunded that the villaugers name the rebels who had passed through. When the villaugers refused, the captain ordered two houses searched and a man beaten.

The man was old. He had one eye and no teeth.

We learned of the affair by nyghtfall. Emiglio waunted to ride out at once and punish the captain. Aldo waunted to take the soldatos in their sleep. Adelaide asked whether we had proof that the captain had acted under orders.

I listened to them all.

Then I asked where the soldatos were staying.

At an inn belonging to a man who had lost his daughter’s dowrie to an unlawful fyne. The captain had payd for supper with coyn taken from a villauger. He had also sent two men to the stable to demaund fresh horses without pyment.

I sent the innkeeper a purse and a message: he was to give the soldatos a good supper, plenté of wyne, and the best beds he could offer. He was also to make certain that the horses were watered and fed, and that the stable door remained unbarred.

“Thou wilt entertain them?” Emiglio asked.

“I shall not have them complain of poore hospitalité.”

“And then?”

“Then we shall see whether they wish to retourn the favour.”

At dawn, the soldatos discovered that their horses had been taken from the stable and tethered in a field beyond the villauge. Their saddles were missing, their bridles hung from the inn sign, and their captain’s swerd had been removed from the scabbaurd and laid neatlie beside his breakfast.

The innkeeper had given them excellent serwyce.

We had not harmed a hair upon their heads. We had, however, taken their weapons, their spare coyn, and the writ authorising their search. The captain found the writ pinned to the stable door, with a note informing him that his men myght recover their properté upon pyment of the innkeeper’s bill, the villaugers’ damages, and the cost of the horses’ hire.

Ser Gheraurdo sent a message calling me a cowaurd.

I sent one back asking whether he wished his swerd retourned before or after he had payd.

He payd.

Not from his own purse, I think, but from the funds he had been given to conduct his search. It was a small victorie, and one which would have been forgotten had not the captain been obliged to explain to his superior why he had retourned without horses, weapons, or the writ with which he had been entrusted.

The explanatioun travelled upwaurd.

So did the laughter.

Herod had now to consider whether the man he had called a robber was, in fact, a nuisaunce that could not be cheaplie removed. I hoped he would take his time over the questioun.

I had work to do.

Our greatest difficulté was not finding men. It was feeding them.

Men will follow a brave captain into a dangereux place, and they will follow a rich captain into a foolish one. But there are few who will follow either into a cold nyght with empté bellies. I had seen too many lordes raise a company in spring, spend the wauges by summer, and discover by autumn that loyalté is not a crop which grows without rain.

I therefore made our fyrst rule that no man should be promised a share of booté before the expenses of the company had been payd. Our second was that a man who stole from a poore household would lose his share. Our third was that everie sum taken should be entered in Adelaide’s book, and everie man who received pyment should mark the page with his sign.

The third rule caused the most complaint.

“Must I make a mark everie time I take a loaf?” Emiglio demaunded.

“Onlie if thou intendest to charge the company for it.”

“And if I eat it myself?”

“Then I shall assume thou hast swallowed it.”

He grumbled, but he made his mark.

We began to acquire a reputatioun for keeping accounts. This is not the reputatioun most captains desyre, but it was useful. Men who had been cheated by stewaurds and londlordes were warie of any promise involving money. They waunted to know what their wauges would be, when they would receive them, and what happened if they were wounded. I answered as honestlie as I could. We had little coyn, and I could not promise that we would always have enough. But I could promise that I would not conceal the shortage, nor spend a man’s wauges upon a fyner cloak for myself.

It was astonishing how many men considered this a virtue.

A widow named Margherita joined us after her husband was killed in the demolitioun of a house along the One Way. She had two sons, one of whom was old enough to carrie a spear and the other young enough to believe that everie horse would let him climb upon its back. She could mend clothes, cook for a company, and remember the name of everie man who had ever cheated her husband. I put her in charge of provisiouns. Within a fortnyght she had discovered that our cook was stealing flour, that Emiglio had been selling our oats to a neighbouring farmer, and that Aldo’s men were receiving larger portiouns than the rest.

She corrected all three.

Aldo protested that a captain required better food.

“Then a captain should earn better food,” said Margherita.

I had not the heart to intervene.

We also took in a number of men who had once served in the retinues of the local nobilité. They knew how to ride, how to keep wautch, and how to fight in formatioun. They knew, too, that a nobleman’s favour myght vanish at the fyrst rumour of displeausure. Some had been dismissed after a lorde’s fortunes changed; others had been denied wauges; a few had fled after refusing to take part in the seizure of a tenaunt’s lond.

One man, Pietro da Medicina, had served under three different banners and been payd by none of them. He had a scar across his chin and a habit of speaking as if everie sentence were a complaint agaynst the world.

“I have been a soldier for twelve years,” he told me. “I have fought for lordes who were brave, lordes who were cowaurds, lordes who knew nothing of war, and lordes who knew too much. I have ne'er fought for a merchaunt.”

“Then thou hast not yet experienced the worst.”

He laughed. “Will the merchaunt pay me?”

“When he can.”

“Will he feed me?”

“When he has food.”

“Will he lead me into battle?”

“If there is a battle.”

“Then thou art a poore prospect.”

“Yet thou art here.”

“I am hungrie.”

“Then we understand one another.”

Pietro became one of our most useful men. He could read a field at a glaunce, and he knew the habits of the lesser captains who served Herod’s friends. He also knew how to speak to soldatos without pretending that courage was easy or death a noble rewaurd. He told them when a positioun was bad, when a retreat was necessarie, and when a man who called himself brave was merelie too proud to admit that he was afraid.

I trusted him because he had no patience for glorie.

The company grew by such increments. A pair of broothers from the hills, skylled with the bow. A clerk who had copied toll receipts for a Malvezzi factour and could name everie merchaunt who had been overcharged. A groom who had once cared for Herod’s own horses and knew which officers rode haurd when they were fryghtened. A former wautchman from the western gate, who could distinguish the sound of a patrol by the pace of its horses.

We did not make them swear that they loved me. We asked them to swear that they would not rob one another, abandon a wounded companioun for the sake of his purse, or betray a household which had sheltered them.

The oath was not grand. We took it in a muddy yaurd, with rain dripping from the eaves and a pot of lentils boiling over the fire. Men raised their honds, spoke the words, and went back to eating.

I have heaurd fyner oaths in fyner halls. Few have been better kept.

But the money remained our great difficulté. We could take a purse from a stewaurd, recover a debt from a factour, and levy a contributioun upon a lorde who had profited from unlawful tolls. Such sums sustained us, but they could not purchase the kind of force required to meet Herod’s men in the open field. Bows and courage are of little use agaynst disciplined cavalrie if the ground is wrong, the weather worse, and the enemy has twyce as many horses.

We needed soldatos who had fought for pay in distant londs, who could hold a line when the fyrst charge came, and who would not flee merelie because the man beside them had fallen.

We needed the Catalans.

I had heaurd of them from a merchaunt who traded in arms and horses. They had served in the wars of Italie, and some had come north after fighting in the southern kingdoms. They were expensive, quarrelsome, and reputed to possess a great affectioun for plunder. They were also skylled, accustomed to haurdship, and less impressed by noble birth than by the qualité of a man’s purse.

I sent a messenger to find their captain.

His name was Bernat de Rocafort, and he arrived with a beaurd like a black brush, a broken nose, and the manner of a man who had long ago ceased to be surprysed by human follie. He brought two companiouns and no horses, having sold them to pay for passauge.

He listened while I explained my cause.

When I had fynished, he asked, “How much?”

I told him what I possessed.

He laughed.

“That is not enough to hire my company.”

“It is enough to hire you for one battle.”

He laughed agayn, but this time he looked at me more carefullie.

“One battle,” he said. “And if the battle is lost?”

“Then I shall owe thee money I do not possess.”

“And if it is won?”

“Then thou shalt have thy wauges, a share of the booté, and such prisoners as may be assigned to thy company by agreement.”

He stroked his beaurd. “Thou speakest of prisoners as if they were barrels of wyne.”

“I have ne'er known a barrel of wyne to ransom itself.”

He looked at his companiouns. They spoke brieflie in Catalan, which I did not understand, though I gathered from their expressiouns that they were discussing whether I was a fool, a knave, or a man worth robbing.

At length Bernat said, “One battle. Half the wauges in advaunce.”

“I can give thee a third.”

“Half.”

“A third, and the cost of your passauge.”

“Half.”

“A third, the passauge, and fyrst choice of the horses taken in battle.”

He considered.

“And the prisoners?”

“Prisoners shall be ransomed or exchanged. Thou shalt receive an agreed share of their value, but no man shall be sold without my consent.”

Bernat frowned. “Thou art making war expensive.”

“War is expensive. I am merelie refusing to pretend otherwise.”

He demaunded more coyn. I offered less. We argued until the candles had burned low and Adelaide, who had been recording the terms, began to yawn in open contempt. At last we agreed upon a sum which left me with scarcelie enough money to feed the company for another week.

Bernat signed the contract.

When he had gone, Aldo looked at me as if I had just sold the roof from over our heads.

“We have hired a company of Catalans with money we cannot spare.”

“We have hired a company of Catalans with money we shall have to earn.”

“And if we do not?”

“Then we shall be poore men who owe money to armed straungers.”

“That is a poore positioun.”

“It is a familiar one.”

I did not tell him how afraid I was. There are some truths which a captain may confess to himself and no one else. I had gambled everiething upon a battle I could not yet see, agaynst an enemy whose strength I had not fullie measured. I had committed money that belonged, in part, to men who had trusted me to preserve it. I had hired soldatos whose loyalté was written in a contract and whose patience would expire when the coyn did.

But there was no tourning back. Herod’s officers had begun to close the roads. His allies were tightening their grip upon the villauges. We had made ourselves too troublesome to ignore and not yet powerful enough to survive being taken seriouslie.

We needed a victorie.

And we needed it soon.

Our opportunité came through a man who had once been my creditor.

Messer Tommaso da Quadrilatero was a wealthy londholder with a hondsome house, a plain wyfe, and an appetite for other men’s misfortunes. He had lent money to several noble families during the disorder following Herod’s ryse, and had been rewaurded with the ryght to collect certain dues in the countrieside. He was not a Malvezzi by blood, but he was Malvezzi by ynterest, which is sometimes a stronger bond.

He had latelie acquired a contract to supplie grain and iron to a garrison east of Bologne. The garrison was commaunded by Ser Niccolò Malvezzi, a cousin of the Hegemon, who had been given the post because he was a Malvezzi and because the office came with a hondsome income. He had little experience of war, but he possessed a fyne armour, a splendid horse, and a belief that the men beneath him ought to be grateful for the privilege of being commaunded.

Tommaso’s wagons were due to pass through a narrow valley where the road ran between a wodeed slope and a stream. He had hired guaurds, but not enough to withstand a determined attack. He had also informed the garrison of the hour of his departure, which meant that the garrison would be waiting to receive the goods.

It was a tempting prize.

It was also a trap, though not the sort Tommaso intended.

I learned of the convoy from two sources: a clerk who had copied the contract, and a groom who had overheaurd Ser Niccolò boast that he would capture me before supper. The two accounts agreed upon the date and differed upon almost everiething else. The clerk said there were twelve wagons; the groom said fifteen. The clerk believed the guaurds numbered twentie; the groom thought fortie. Neither knew how much coyn the convoy carried, but both agreed that the grain was valuable and that the iron had been bought at an inflated pryce.

I sent Pietro to look at the road.

He retourned with mud to his knees and a grim expressioun.

“The valley is narrow,” he said. “There is a track above it, but a horse cannot pass easilie. The stream is low. The wagons must cross at the ford.”

“How many guaurds?”

“Twentie-four that I saw. Perhaps more with the garrison.”

“How many wagons?”

“Fourteen.”

“Which of them carrie grain?”

“Ten.”

“And the iron?”

“Three.”

“The last?”

“An empté wagon, I think.”

“Why?”

“Because it rides too high.”

I liked Pietro. He could see a thing and know what it meant.

The convoy would travel beneath a slope on which our archers could take positioun. The ford would slow the wagons, and the road beyond it narrowed between a bank and a stand of alder trees. If we struck at the ford, we could separate the guaurds from the wagons; if we struck too earlie, the guaurds could form a line and use the wagons as cover. The garrison would be near enough to hear a horn, but too far to arrive before the fyrst struggle was decided.

We had one advauntage: the enemy believed that we would attack for the sake of the cargo. He expected us to rush the wagons, seize what we could, and scatter before his men could organise. We would do nothing of the kind.

I divided our company into three parts. Pietro would take the archers up the slope. Aldo would lead the men on foot into the trees beyond the ford. I would remain with Bernat and the Catalans behind the bend in the road, where the wagons could not see us until they were nearlie upon us.

The empté wagon was the key. If it was indeed empté, it would be placed at the rear to carrie the guaurds’ baggage or to serve as a reserve. If it was not empté, then it myght contain the convoy’s money. Either way, it would be defended.

I had no intentioun of letting Ser Niccolò decide where the battle would be fought.

On the eve of the ambush, I walked among the men and checked their weapons. Some were sharpening blades; others were repayring straps or mending shoes. Bernat’s Catalans sat together beneath a tree, playing at dice and arguing over the rules. They appeared to have no fear of the coming battle. I envied them.

One of my own men, a young fellawe named Matteo, asked whether we would kill the guaurds.

“We shall kill those who make it necessarie,” I said.

“And the others?”

“The others may choose to live.”

He looked relieved, and I realised how little he had understood of war. He had imagined that everie man on the opposing side would be a wicked stewaurd or a cruel nobleman, and that victorie would consist of punishing the wicked until the good were free. It was a pleausant notioun. I had held it myself, once, in a different form.

“Listen to me,” I told him. “Some of those guaurds have been payd to do a bad thing. Some have been payd to do an ordinarie thing and know nothing of the purpose. Some have families who depend upon their wauges. We shall give them everie chaunce to lay down their arms. But if they choose to kill us, we shall not permit them to do so merelie because their reasons are better than ours.”

He nodded, though I doubt he understood.

That nyght I slept little. I thought of the money I had borrowed, the men I had promised to pay, and the possibilité that I had mistaken a narrow road for an opportunité when it was in truth a place where a greater force myght crush us. I thought of my wyfe and daughter, who were then living under the protectioun of friends near Bologne, and of the promises I had made them before I left.

I had told my wyfe that I would not seek glorie.

She had replied that glorie was the one thing she had ne'er feared I would find.

I wished, then, that I had been able to promise her something more useful.

text:
Here are my three takeaways from tonight's 4-3 Montreal Canadiens shootout win over the Buffalo Sabres, brought to you by Snap Bar in Rigaud and Biggs in Hudson.

1 - The Clock Is Ticking on Dach

Time is running out on Kirby Dach's tenure in Montreal. He's been given opportunity after opportunity, chance after chance, and simply hasn't taken advantage.

He started last week riding shotgun with Juraj Slafkovsky in the top six and finished the week playing fewer than eight minutes, despite the fact that the Canadiens only had 11 forwards dressed.

Tonight, he took a bad, unnecessary penalty after getting outmuscled and losing position on Zach Benson.

The only reason Dach is still in the lineup is because the Canadiens are dealing with injuries. When healthy, this team simply doesn't have a clear role or spot for him.

Acquiring Dach was one of Kent Hughes and Jeff Gorton's first significant moves since taking charge of the Canadiens, but it's time to cut their losses.

If reports are true that Montreal was offered a second-round pick over the summer and that the Calgary Flames and Edmonton Oilers are "drooling" at the possibility of acquiring him, get those teams on the phone ASAP.

2 - Lane Hutson Has His Best Game of the Season

Yes, it's early, and it's not as though Lane Hutson has been playing poorly, but tonight we saw Hutson at his best.

Buffalo had no answers when he had the puck, and there just seemed to be so much more open ice for him to work with.

Hutson opened the scoring with a power-play goal, and while his shot isn't his greatest weapon, it was expertly placed, with Phil Danault providing an excellent screen after winning the faceoff.

If Hutson can re-establish himself as a legitimate shooting threat, it'll open up even more options for Montreal's power play.

He then set up Josh Anderson with a nifty pass, drawing two defenders toward him and completely opening up Anderson for a one-timer from the left side.

Hutson will have other performances like this over the course of the season, but Montreal might need him to take on an even bigger role, if that's possible, given the Matheson injury. 

3 - Rough Night for Engström

Some of it was bad luck, but Adam Engstrom had a night to forget.

It started in the first period when he made a soft play on the puck, turning it over and setting off a sequence that ended with a shot deflecting off him and into his own net.

In the second period, he made a terrific defensive play, using his reach to take away what looked like a quality scoring chance for Buffalo as Zach Benson tried to find Jack Quinn all alone.

Then, Josh Norris banked another shot off Engström to pull Buffalo within one.

The Canadiens have made it clear that they believe Engstrom is an NHL player. They traded Jayden Struble to create more room on the blue line, and that belief could be put to the test if Mike Matheson misses any significant amount of time.

There's a lot to like about Engstrom's game, particularly his skating and ability to transport the puck. But this was definitely a performance he'll want to put behind him as quickly as possible.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security says more than 2.5 million people living in the United States without legal status have left the country since President Donald Trump returned to office on Jan. 20, 2025.
In figures first released in December 2025, the department reported more than 605,000 formal deportations and an estimated 1.9 million “self-deportations,” voluntary departures it attributed to stepped-up interior enforcement and a message that those who remain risk arrest and removal. Later DHS updates put removals near 675,000 and voluntary exits near 2.2 million. The agency has tied the outflow to a sharp drop in illegal border crossings, expanded Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, and a CBP Home app that offers a free flight and a cash exit payment to people who leave on their own.
Independent researchers have treated the totals with caution. The Deportation Data Project and the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, working from government records obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, have published lower deportation counts than DHS press releases, and analysts have said the department has not released the underlying data for the self-deportation estimate. Only a fraction of voluntary exits appear to have gone through the official app.
Separately, economists at the Brookings Institution estimated that overall net migration turned negative in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century, in a range of roughly −10,000 to −295,000, reflecting fewer entries as well as more departures. The Census Bureau has reported a steep decline in net international migration but has not yet recorded a negative year.

21 DAYS. ONE ELECTION. EVERY EFFORT MATTERS.

I know many Republican voters are discouraged by current conditions, political disagreements, and the geopolitical developments unfolding around the world.

But no administration is perfect. Every presidency encounters realities that challenge its promises. There are successes and setbacks, opportunities seized and opportunities missed.

SOME WINS. SOME LOSSES. BUT THE WORK CONTINUES.

The world order is changing before our eyes.

Established powers are reassessing their relationships. Geopolitical rivalries are reshaping international affairs. The decisions made today could influence whether future generations inherit a more peaceful and stable world—or one marked by further confrontation.

Imagine a future where tyrants no longer threaten their neighbors, where global powers exercise restraint, where economic cooperation replaces unnecessary confrontation, and where our children inherit opportunities greater than those available to us.

That future is possible, but it is not guaranteed.

Peace requires diplomacy, strength, accountability, and responsible leadership.

For years, political infighting, institutional dysfunction, and inconsistent policymaking have weakened public confidence.

These problems did not emerge overnight, and they will not disappear tomorrow.

I believe Republicans, despite their imperfections, are attempting to correct damaging policies and institutional failures inherited from previous administrations.

Meaningful reform takes time. It requires consistency, discipline, and the recognition that progress rarely follows a straight line.

And in a democracy, disagreement is inevitable. But disagreement must not become an excuse for disengagement.

DO NOT ALLOW DISAPPOINTMENT TO BECOME DESPAIR.

This election will influence the direction of our country at a consequential moment in world history.

As the United States celebrates the 250th anniversary of its independence, we should remember that love of country is expressed not only through words, but through responsible civic participation.

250 YEARS OF AMERICAN INDEPENDENCE. ONE RESPONSIBILITY THAT ENDURES: PARTICIPATE.

2026 WILL NOT BE DECIDED BY WHO HAS THE BIGGEST ONLINE AUDIENCE.

IT WILL BE DECIDED BY WHO ACTUALLY SHOWS UP.

November 3 is approaching.

Across America, campaigns are entering their final stretch. But elections are not decided by social media followers, online arguments, campaign rallies, or political predictions alone.

ELECTIONS ARE DECIDED BY VOTERS.

Whether the polls look encouraging or discouraging, don't allow the scoreboard to determine your effort.

For those who have already decided to participate, there are many ways to get involved.

Volunteer your time. Donate to causes you support. Attend community events. Learn campaign operations. Help educate voters. Support organizations that reflect your values and the issues you care about.

Economic opportunity. Education. Parental rights. Religious liberty. Latino community engagement. Public safety. Leadership development. Grassroots organization.

FIND YOUR CAUSE. FIND YOUR COMMUNITY. MAKE YOUR PARTICIPATION COUNT.

DON'T JUST PLAN TO VOTE. MAKE A PLAN THAT WORKS.

EARLY VOTING. MAIL-IN BALLOTS. ELECTION DAY.

Whatever lawful voting option is available in your state, understand the rules and prepare ahead of time.

If early voting is available, check the dates and locations.

If you're voting by mail, request and return your ballot before the applicable deadlines. Track it where your state offers ballot tracking.

If you're voting on Election Day, arrange your schedule in advance. Use PTO or available voting leave if necessary and possible. Know your polling location, bring any required identification, and allow extra time for lines.

IF YOU'RE IN LINE BEFORE THE POLLS CLOSE, STAY IN LINE.

Eligible voters who are in line by the legal closing time generally have the right to vote, subject to applicable election rules.

Don't let a preventable scheduling problem become a missed opportunity to participate.

I did this the research. It wasn’t a clean story on Iran’s side either. But if Mosaddegh had actually been a good leader then he would have been praised by both the USA and UK. Instead he was a power hungry fool that caused trouble for Iran until today. 

First, any loss of life is tragic, and we should mourn the deaths of innocent people. It is especially sad when citizens lose their lives in geopolitical power struggles.

Mosaddegh was elected by parliament, but over time he took steps to consolidate power while promising to nationalize BP. He also dissolved parliament, raising concerns that he could become a dictator. As negotiations with Britain and the United States broke down, he pursued trade agreements with the USSR. There was a real concern that Iran could become a Soviet ally or puppet. I do not believe that was his intention, but I believe he was a bad leader who misunderstood and misplayed his geopolitical cards.

Regarding the BP contracts, I agree with you: the original arrangement was unfair to Iran. That is a valid point.

However, BP offered another path. Did you know BP agreed to a fifty-fifty split of profits? That was a very fair arrangement and could have generated enormous, dependable wealth for Iran for years to come. Had he accepted it, he could have secured a major win and negotiated British assistance in establishing Iran’s own oil company.

Instead, Mosaddegh preferred to take what belonged to others and tried to operate in an industry he did not understand. In my view, that was an incredibly foolish decision. He claimed Iran needed the money, yet the approach I described could have addressed its budget shortfall while helping it build a national oil company with BP as a distribution partner.

The clash of cultures and geopolitical realities made matters worse. Mosaddegh attempted to nationalize BP and end democracy in Iran. Yet he might have succeeded in his nationalization effort had he followed the American request to negotiate a fair agreement with Britain. His unwillingness to reach that agreement cut Iran off from the financial resources and European and American customers its oil industry needed.

The United States was deeply engaged in the Cold War with the Soviet Union. Mosaddegh’s handling of the situation demonstrated poor leadership and a failure to understand the geopolitical realities of his time.

After he dissolved parliament, Iranians within the government reached out to the United States and Britain for military assistance because they were increasingly concerned that his actions were moving the country toward dictatorship.

My view is that Mosaddegh badly misjudged Iran’s geopolitical leverage. After nationalizing the British-controlled oil industry in 1951, he faced a British-led boycott that squeezed Iran’s economy. He repeatedly sought American oil purchases and financial assistance, but Washington insisted on a compensation settlement with Britain. He rejected proposed terms, leaving Iran without a reliable economic lifeline. His expanding emergency powers and growing Soviet trade reinforced Cold War fears. A workable settlement could have improved his chances of securing American cooperation and reduced the pressure on his government.

So, the entire premise is based on factual evidence. If he had taken the same actions as I would have, he would have been one of the greatest leaders Iran has had, but instead, he chose to end democracy, commit theft of BP, destroy international relations and establish the future environment that would oppress Persians and create the most evil terrorist state the world has ever witnessed! All of this is true!

WASHINGTON — Rep. Ilhan Omar’s staff helped get her birthdate changed in public records once the Minnesota Democrat was elected to Congress in 2018, a switch that has since spurred frenzied accusations that she misrepresented her age to secure US citizenship.

The alteration could offer a big clue as to what federal immigration agents were searching for when they raided her DC home Monday: If the congresswoman is actually one year older than she’s claimed to be, that would mean she couldn’t have legally become a US citizen in 2000, critics contend.

Omar’s birthdate had been listed in the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library as Oct. 4, 1981, as well as on reference sites such as Wikipedia and in media outlets like the BBC, for the entire time she served in the state House and for several months into her congressional term.

David Cochrane’s response, for the bulk of the nearly 11.5-minute exchange, is a running series of Liberal talking points, caveats, and excuses that reframe every failure as either inevitable, someone else’s fault, or already being handled

Seeback’s core auto-pact argument is straightforward: the industry is deeply integrated, a tariff-free arrangement that reshores production on both sides of the border is what automakers and workers actually want, and the White House is the outlier

Cochran’s counters are: 
* Trump “sees, in spite of all of the evidence, tariffs as the key to American prosperity.”
*  Howard Lutnick already said Canada will not make cars.
* The administration’s explicit goal is “deindustrializing southwestern Ontario.”
* This is “pure self interest” (illustrated by a Putin diesel deal).

These are descriptions of the other side’s position, not rebuttals of the plan’s logic or of Canada’s leverage (critical minerals, diesel capacity if expanded, etc.)

When Seeback notes the give-and-take nature of any negotiation, Cochrane immediately pivots to “the nature of this presidency” and Carney’s broken campaign promise, then concedes the premise: “Getting to zero tariffs on steel, aluminum, auto. Seems like it will not happen as long as Trump is in the White House.” The Liberal line becomes the ceiling

On the secrecy point Seeback makes a concrete, checkable claim: the Canadian ambassador refused to say when the last substantive offer exchange occurred; industry contacts were giving contradictory answers on auto tariffs even as a deal appeared close; Mexico’s process has been more visible. Cochrane’s reply is that “we know broadly the timeline,” that Dominic LeBlanc and Janice Charrette were in Washington in a certain week, that Mexico is also being squeezed, and that “Donald Trump’s trying to exert leverage everywhere.” That is not a defense of the government’s opacity; it is an acknowledgment that the Americans are doing what the Americans do, plus a claim that the process is normal. Seeback’s observation that no industry knows where things stand is left standing.

The Stelco segment is the clearest example of the pattern. Seeback notes that the minister previously promised to sue Stellantis and did not, that the current deadline has passed, and that the government controls the industrial carbon tax and the dumping problem that raise costs for Canadian steel. Cochrane’s interventions are:
* The NDP has argued for nationalization.
* A seven-page letter from the Cleveland CEO should be considered.
*Governments should build the Pacific Link pipeline if no private proponent appears

Seeback’s reply that governments do not run commercial operations well (the pipeline example of cost overruns and delays) is met with the distinction that “Nationalization of the steel industry is very different” and a restatement that the pipeline should still be built by the government if necessary. The specific, controllable domestic costs Seeback identified—the carbon tax and dumping—are not engaged; the conversation stays on Cochrane process, lawsuits, and the pipeline exception

Throughout, Cochrane’s questions and counters function less as cross-examination of Seeback’s plan and more as a real-time restatement of the government’s constraints, the other side’s bad faith, and the difficulty of the file. The result is that every Seeback point is answered with a version of 'the situation is complicated, the Americans are aggressive, and the government is doing what it can under the circumstances.'

That is the job description of a Liberal communications shop, not of a neutral CBC interviewer. If the audition for the Liberal comms job is still open, the tape is perfected @brodiefenlon @kyleseeback

text:
They took the appeal. They have not decided the case. Big difference. ⚖️📂

🚨 BREAKING: The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to hear U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court (No. 25-1103) — the Trump administration's fight with watchdog CREW over whether DOGE must answer Freedom of Information Act requests. Arguments are expected in early 2027; a decision by summer 2027.

📊 The numbers
⚖️ Case: U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for D.C., No. 25-1103
🗓️ Grant: Oct 13, 2026 (added to 2026–27 oral-argument docket)
🧾 Earlier shadow-docket order: 6–3 (Jun 2025) paused a broad discovery order; Sotomayor, Kagan, Jackson dissented
📁 What CREW still seeks after narrowing: DOGE's structure, directives to cancel contracts / fire workers, and examples of independent authority (e.g. access to sensitive systems)
👩‍💼 Named admin in filings: Amy Gleason (USDS / DOGE administrator) — government objects to deposing her
🚪 Reporting: DOGE shut down operations around July 4, 2026; Musk left as special government employee in May 2025 (CBS)
💵 GAO context: $9.5B spent on employee administrative leave in 2025 (6× 2023); $6.7B tied to buyout offers linked to the downsizing push

🗣️ What people are saying
• Solicitor General D. John Sauer: discovery "intrudes into the autonomy and confidentiality of presidential advisors" and would burden future EOPs with FOIA suits used as discovery tools
• CREW: lower courts followed the Court's prior narrowing order "to the letter"; remaining requests do not seek White House advice content
• Transparency advocates: if DOGE directed firings, contract cuts and system access, the public should see the paper trail under FOIA
• Separation-of-powers defenders: presidential advisory bodies were never meant to be treated like Cabinet agencies for records fishing expeditions
• AP's wire framing said the Court was "siding with the Trump administration" by taking the case — critics of that wording say a cert grant is not a merits win

✅ The facts
✅ SCOTUS granted the government's petition for review on Oct 13, 2026 (SCOTUSblog, CBS, AP, Courthouse News, WaPo)
✅ Core legal fight: is the U.S. DOGE Service a FOIA "agency," or an exempt presidential advisory body inside the Executive Office of the President?
✅ Jun 2025: Court (6–3) vacated parts of Judge Christopher Cooper's discovery order that forced disclosure of intra-branch recommendations and whether they were followed
✅ On remand, CREW dropped recommendation-content requests; D.C. Circuit allowed the narrowed discovery to proceed; DOJ appealed again
✅ Covered by AP, Reuters Legal, CBS, Politico, Courthouse News, Washington Post

❓ Unverified or overstated
❓ That SCOTUS already ruled DOGE is secret forever — false; this is only a grant of review
❓ That every DOGE document will be released (or none will) — neither outcome is decided
❓ Exact headcount of firings / dollar value of canceled contracts attributable solely to DOGE — still contested in the underlying discovery fight
❓ Viral claims that this "ends FOIA" for the entire executive branch — the petition asks for rules about advisory bodies / discovery, not a FOIA repeal

⚖️ What we don't know yet
• How broadly the Court writes any Cheney-style deference rule for EOP advisory bodies
• Whether Gleason (or others) ever sit for a deposition
• What, if anything, gets released before a final FOIA merits ruling
• How midterms and a post-DOGE bureaucracy change the political stakes of the records fight

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
October 13, 2026
Edina, Minnesota
TOM EVENSTAD BLASTS LISA DEMUTH AND MICHELE TAFOYA FOR COWARDLY REFUSAL TO EVEN MEET WITH HIM ON THE ONLY POLICY THAT WOULD CUT MINNESOTA VIOLENCE BY 60%+
While Minnesota Republican Senate Caucus Fast-Tracks the Violently Dangerous Persons Act as Its #1 Priority, Demuth and Tafoya Hide From the Man Who Has Championed It for 14 Years
Edina, MN — Tom Evenstad today issued a blistering condemnation of Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth and U.S. Senate candidate Michele Tafoya for their deliberate, repeated refusal to even sit down and meet with him about the Violently Dangerous Persons (VDP) Act — the single most powerful public-safety tool available to Minnesota.
The VDP Act (Mariah’s Law) expands Minnesota’s proven civil-commitment system for sexually dangerous persons to cover violently dangerous persons. Independent modeling projects a 60–64% reduction in overall violence — gun, domestic, and gang. The Minnesota Republican Senate caucus has now placed it on the fast track as its number-one legislative priority for the coming session.
Yet Demuth and Tafoya will not even grant Evenstad a meeting.
For more than 14 years — and throughout his entire 14-month campaign for governor — Evenstad has offered to brief any serious candidate on the VDP Act. He has provided detailed legislative language, position papers, and data. He has met with law-enforcement leaders who were willing to listen. Demuth and Tafoya have refused every request.
“This is not a scheduling conflict. This is deliberate avoidance,” Evenstad said. “Lisa Demuth and Michele Tafoya will pose for cameras with selected law-enforcement officers, release polished ‘public safety’ plans, and lecture voters about toughness. But they will not sit in a room with the one person who has been screaming the truth for 14 years and who has the only policy that actually delivers 60% less bloodshed. That refusal is pure political cowardice.”
Evenstad continued: “They have gaslighted the voters of Minnesota. They talk about ‘public safety’ while refusing to examine the one measure that would actually deliver it. Politicians put politics over public safety. Law-enforcement leadership too often puts politics over public safety. And the media protects the whole charade — while cashing the same political checks. There is no clearer example than Demuth and Tafoya’s refusal to even meet.”
The contrast could not be sharper. While the Republican Senate caucus is preparing to advance the VDP Act as its top priority, the party’s gubernatorial and senatorial nominees will not give the architect of the policy five minutes of their time.
“I have never asked them to endorse me. I have only asked them to protect Minnesota’s children and families,” Evenstad stated. “Their answer has been silence and closed doors. That silence has a body count. Every day they refuse to meet is another day they choose politics over the lives of Minnesotans.”
Evenstad called on Demuth and Tafoya to reverse course immediately: schedule a public meeting, review the VDP Act, and join the Republican Senate caucus in making it the state’s number-one priority. Anything less, he said, is continued abandonment of the people they claim to want to lead.
“Minnesota does not need more photo-ops and empty plans. Minnesota needs leaders who will sit down, listen to the truth, and act. Lisa Demuth and Michele Tafoya have refused. That refusal is an outrage — and the voters will not forget it.”

text:
Challenger Pat Valentino shakes Champion Ezzard Charles' hand at the weigh-in, on October 14, 1949, before Charles' second defense of the (NBA) Heavyweight Championship at the Cow Palace in Daly City, California.

Valentino, who was the California State Heavyweight Champion at this time, having decisioned Turkey Thompson in his previous fight, fought for a flat purse ($5000) while Charles, a 5-1 favorite, got 35% of the net from the gate.

Eddie Muller of the San Francisco Examiner called the bout "the greatest fight I ever saw." He further described it as "drama-packed, spine-tingling, and vicious from the opening bell, until a somewhat bewildered and weary Ezzard Charles finally ended the savage duel at 35 seconds of the eighth round. In that 21 minutes, these stalwarts had me ducking, wincing and shouting like any paying customer in the enormous Cow Palace, which rocked to its foundation." When told of Muller’s description, Valentino, who lost sight in one eye as a result of this fight, said, "I wouldn’t go that far. That seems a bit much."

This was the last official bout of Valentino's career, he'd box an exhibition with Joe Louis in December of 1949 and get KO'd in 8 rounds, and he finished 58-12-6 with 33 KO's.

Valentino, born Pasquale Guglielmi in San Francisco, was a second cousin of the famed silent-era movie star Rudolph Valentino.
----------------------------------------------------------
"A Second Life: The Career of Pat Valentino"written by Carlos Acevedo appeared in the IBRO Journal Issue No. 110 and here it is:

Pat Valentino, heavyweight contender of the 1940s, was famous both for his savagery in the ring and, incongruously, for his chic hairstyle, which he often jokingly compared to that of Samson. He won the California State Heavyweight title in 1948 and was one of the most popular attractions in California for nearly a decade. He died of pneumonia on July 25th in Las Vegas.
Valentino, whose real name was Pasquale Guglielmi, was born on January 25, 1920, in the Excelsior District of San Francisco.. One of eight children, Valentino was raised dirt poor during the Depression by an abusive father who once made this bleak, near Dickensian proposal to his son: “You work, I feed you.” Gaetano Guglielmi was so miserly that Valentino was often forced to walk barefoot to school without a bagged lunch or a pencil. “I was the fifth oldest,” Valentino said about his father, “and he just hated me.”
Emotionally scarred at an early age, Valentino developed a crippling lack of self-confidence and an almost pathological shyness. He dropped out of school at thirteen to work backbreaking hours at the family grocery store on Mission Street. “I had nothing going for me,” he told The San Francisco Examiner. “I would have been digging holes—if I were lucky.” Somehow, Valentino decided that insignificance did not have to be his pre-ordained fate. “I started fighting to get rid of my fear,” he once said.
Inspired by the ring heroics of another Excelsior product, Ray Actis, a young Valentino tested out several local gyms, often with spectacularly embarrassing results. Powerpunching Actis, like Valentino the son of Italian immigrants, rode his hurtful left hook to local fame during the early 1930s, brawling up and down the Bay Area with the likes of Carmen Barth, Gus Lesnevich, Jack Gibbons, and Billy Conn. Through his rousing feats inside the ring, Actis took on larger-than-life proportions along Persia Street and Naples Avenue. His local glory gave the awkward and uneducated Valentino what he thought of as a possible “out” from shame and anonymity.
Valentino hooked up with former lightweight Tommy Cello as his trainer and turned pro in 1939. He adopted his nom de guerre from a distant relative: 1920s Hollywood sex symbol Rudolph Valentino. Within months his rugged style and good looks shot him up to headline status. After little more than half a dozen fights, Valentino was booked for 10-round semis and main events at National Hall and the newly opened Coliseum Bowl on Market Street. He went 16-3-1 in his first twenty fights, thrilling fans throughout Oakland and San Francisco with his roughhouse style. Although Valentino scored some notable wins early in his career–against former middleweight titlist Solly Krieger, for example, and slick Ralph DeJohn–he also lost decisions to unremarkable fighters Harold Blackshear and Tommy Martin. It should be noted that Valentino was a natural light heavyweight whose boundless ambition led him to fight bigger men.
In 1941 Valentino was outclassed by tricky ex-light heavyweight champion Melio Bettina and was stopped by Turkey Thompson after nine brutal rounds. A few weeks later Valentino joined the Coast Guard (where he accidentally shot himself through the left hand, damaging a finger so severely he could no longer make a proper fist) and fought sporadically until 1944. While on furlough, Valentino avenged his loss to Thompson by decision before a crowd of 9,000 at the Civic Auditorium.
Military service kept Valentino out of the ring for the next two years. When he returned in April 1946, he won thirteen of his next fourteen bouts before being stopped by Fitzie Fitzpatrick. Still, his ferocity and swarthy looks made Valentino a popular attraction.
His raucous–and fateful–grudge trilogy with local bruiser Tony Bosnich drew feverish crowds.
Their first fight, in December 1947, was declared a draw after Valentino suffered a cut in the first round; Bosnich earned the second bout on points; and Valentino won the rubber match over 15 hectic rounds on October 4, 1948.
It was in the last fight that Valentino took a thumb in the eye and suffered a torn retina. Despite the injury, Valentino entered the ring two months later to face Turkey Thompson once again for the California State Heavyweight title. Valentino won a grueling decision and soon found himself ranked among the top ten heavyweights in the world. Unfortunately, an operation to repair his damaged retina left him on the sidelines for most of 1949.
Valentino was recuperating from surgery when he was offered a bout with NBA heavyweight champion Ezzard Charles. With his eye still healing and with a layoff of nearly a year to consider, Valentino bravely–or foolishly–accepted.
For Valentino, the fight was more than a chance to win the title; it was a way to fulfill his hopes of distinction. “When I was young,” he told The Oakland Tribune, “I told some kids I was going to fight for the heavyweight championship. They laughed at me.”
On October 14, 1949, a sellout crowd of over 19,000 jammed the Cow Palace to see the first heavyweight championship fight held in California since Jack Johnson flattened Stanley Ketchel in 1909. Promoters drew a gate of $167,870 despite the fact that “insiders” considered Valentino little more than a set-up for the heavyweight champion. Of course, San Franciscans thought different.
From the opening bell Valentino, a 5 to 1 underdog, forced a chaotic pace, thumping Charles around the ring with damaging lefts and rights to the body. “I read in the newspaper a year later that I had broken one of his ribs,” Valentino recalled. “I broke a lot of ribs. I hate to hurt anybody, but that was the way I fought.” Driven by desires beyond money or titles, Valentino tore into Charles with the fury of a tempest. Charles countered coolly, snapped his whiplash jab with precision, and used his finesse to turn the fight around in the fifth and sixth rounds. In round eight Charles landed a cuffing left that placed Valentino into position for a short right hand that landed like a torpedo. Valentino collapsed and was counted out. He had to be helped back to his corner.
Years later Valentino described the end of the fight to Jack Fiske:
“As the fight went on I felt the effects of not being in condition. In the eighth round, Charles hit me with a hook and a right cross, really nailed me flush, and I went down on my back. I struggled up, but the referee, Jack Downey, stopped it at 35 seconds. I thought I should have been permitted to continue; but I never protested. In fifteen years I never protested once.” His dream of becoming a “somebody” would prove to be costly: the punishment he took from Charles left him completely blind in his right eye.
A few weeks after the Charles fight, Valentino was approached to face Joe Louis in an exhibition bout.
A $7,500 purse, by far the biggest of his career, beckoned Valentino the way ghost lights lure the unsuspecting on foggy nights. Like many fighters facing premature retirement, Valentino hoped for one last score to put him over the top, and facing Louis, even with only one eye, seemed like a good idea to a man who admitted to living “from fight to fight.” Besides, theoretically, at least, it would not be a “real” fight. Valentino accepted the bout. There remained only the conundrum of the pre-fight physical, and how, exactly, a half blind boxer would manage to circumvent it. Incredibly, Valentino passed the exam with a bit of grade school legerdemain: “During the eye test at the weigh-in,” he told Ring Magazine in 2002, “I brought my right hand over my right eye and read the chart with my good eye. Then I used my left hand to cover my right eye and no one noticed.”
In addition to his marked handicap (along with giving up over 30 pounds in weight), Valentino would have to contend with one of the greatest fighters in history.
At age 35 and two years after relinquishing the heavyweight championship to shoot birdies and wrangle with the IRS, Louis was on a barnstorming exhibition tour that secretly doubled as sparring sessions for a looming comeback bout with Ezzard Charles. And Louis was never easy on his spar mates. Johnny Shkor, Joe Chesul, and Johnny Flynn were all dropped and generally flogged in exhibition matches the weeks before Louis met Valentino. (Indeed, some of these exhibitions were so brutal that contender Lee Oma withdrew from shortly after Louis fought Valentino. His argument was that Louis was not engaged in any mild demonstration of skills, but was engaging in actual fights. Oma instead sensibly demanded a legitimate match with “The Brown Bomber” and the sizeable purse that would accompany it.)
On December 8, 1949, Valentino and Louis met in Chicago Stadium before a crowd of 5,726. Unlike the harmless waltzes most exhibitions resembled, this was a fight. Jersey Jones speculated about the demolition job that took place: “The fact that Charles, a few weeks previously, had flattened Valentino in the eighth stanza in San Francisco may have been responsible for the devastating job Louis turned in on Pat of the flowing Tarzan tresses.” Louis, past his prime but still more than capable of handling second-tier contenders, went to work on Valentino, finally dropping the rugged San Franciscan for the count in round eight. Valentino immediately retired.
After leaving the ring Valentino moved to Los Angeles, where he obtained a few small appearances in films.
When the bit parts dried up, Valentino worked for Lockheed Aircraft before running a bar in North Hollywood for a few years.
He returned to San Francisco in the early 1970s and became a popular fixture on Fisherman’s Wharf as maitre d’ for Scoma’s Restaurant. For over twenty years the affable ex-pug greeted customers, delighting them with colorful tales of his fight with Ezzard Charles. His legendary brawl with Charles gave Valentino a sort of second life, one filled with admiration and respect.
Pat Valentino, dead at 88, fought professionally from 1939 to 1949, and compiled a record of 45-11-4.
Among the fighters he defeated were Turkey Thompson, Freddie Beshore, Solly Krieger, Ralph DeJohn, and Freddie Fiducia. He also fought two draws with Joey Maxim. “…I took up boxing,” he once said, “because I wanted to be good at something.” At that, he succeeded.

text:
US diesel futures jumped 4.5% on Tuesday despite Trump's suspension of sanctions on Russian diesel, leaving truckers and farmers with no near-term relief.

The 22-cent gain took futures to their highest since September 22. Wholesale prices rose 18c/gal on the Gulf and East Coasts, 28c/gal in Southern California and 25-30c/gal in the Great Plains and Great Lakes.

The tightness is global: ULSD in New York and gasoil in London both traded around $200 per barrel.

Energy traders see the additional Russian supply as too small to lower prices meaningfully in the near term. Tax breaks on dyed diesel offer little benefit to trucking companies.

The pressure sits in refined products rather than crude. Brent prompt timespreads weakened on the same day, pointing to a less tight crude market while diesel climbed.

Retail diesel averages $6.28 per gallon, near September's record of $6.53. Wholesale gains of 22-39c/gal have yet to pass through to the pump.

Lawmakers from both parties are also questioning the legality of the Russian deal.

text:
A woman donated a kidney so her boss with a failing kidney could get a new one. She was later fired by the same boss because her slow recovery from the donor surgery affected her job performance.

A Long Island mother of two named Debbie Stevens offered her kidney in 2011 to save her ailing boss at a New York car dealership. Because she was not a perfect match, she joined a special kidney exchange chain. Her organ went to a stranger in Missouri while her boss received a better match from California. The selfless act worked. Both women survived the surgeries.

But the story took a dark turn once Debbie returned to work. She struggled with pain, nerve damage, and slow recovery. Instead of support, she faced constant criticism from the very woman whose life she had helped save. Her boss allegedly yelled at her in front of coworkers, ignored medical limits on heavy lifting, and had her moved to a faraway office that staff jokingly called Siberia. Months later the company fired her, claiming poor performance.

text:
Lanlana Tararudee vs Ashlyn Krueger — two lucky losers, one place in the last 16

Preview · WTA 1000 Wuhan · Second round · Wednesday 14 October 2026

Both players lost in the final round of qualifying in Wuhan, both entered the main draw as lucky losers, and one of them will now reach the round of 16 of a WTA 1000. Lanlana Tararudee and Ashlyn Krueger have never played each other, they are both 22, and only eight places separate them in the rankings: Tararudee is 60, Krueger 68.

THE MATCHUP

With so little between them on rankings, the season records offer more of a guide. Tararudee is 44-20 this season and currently sits at her career-high ranking of 60. Krueger is 30-20 this season, has one career title and has been as high as 29, so she has experience of playing at a level above where she stands now.

Their routes into the main draw were similar. Tararudee beat Claire Liu 7-6(4) 6-4 before losing a long qualifying final that Caty McNally won 6-4 4-6 6-1. Krueger beat Taylah Preston 6-3 7-6(8) and then lost her qualifying final to Yulia Putintseva, who won 6-1 6-3. Neither defeat cost them in the end.

FORM & CONTEXT

Krueger was the more dominant in the first round, beating Shuai Zhang 6-3 6-0 on Tuesday in 1:08:57. Tararudee beat Diane Parry 6-4 6-1 on Monday in 1:27:28. Across three matches this week, Krueger has spent 4h07m on court and Tararudee 6h03m, so Krueger has had the lighter workload.

The schedule pulls the other way. Tararudee played on Monday and had Tuesday off; Krueger played on Tuesday and goes again on Wednesday with no day off.

Away from Wuhan, Tararudee reached the quarter-finals in Seoul in September, beating Moyuka Uchijima and Sohyun Park before losing to Maya Joint, and she won a round at the US Open. Krueger's recent results are more uneven: she beat Sofia Kenin 6-3 6-3 in Beijing before losing to Ann Li, but her summer also brought early defeats in Cincinnati, Philadelphia and at the US Open.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Consistency across the season. Tararudee's 44-20 record reflects a player who has been winning regularly, and that has carried her to the best ranking of her career. Krueger's higher ceiling is real, and her first-round win was the more emphatic of the two, but her results since the summer have been patchier. The day of rest on Tararudee's side adds a little more to her case.

THE CALL

This is a close contest between two players at similar rankings, with no history between them and with this week's evidence split: Krueger has been sharper and spent less time on court, Tararudee has had more rest and the stronger season. Tararudee gets the narrow vote.

Lanlana Tararudee to win, low confidence.

text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio — On a recent afternoon, with homecoming weekend bearing down and a football game that night, April Polk was driving to a doctor’s appointment when her assistant flagged something in her business inbox: a grant application, the kind of funding opportunity a small retailer cannot afford to miss.
The assistant offered to fill it out while she drove.
“She’s like, ‘Hey, I can go on there and I can apply, and if I have any questions about what they’re asking, I’ll be sure to ping you. But other than that, I got it. Go ahead and head to the doctor,'” said Polk, the founder of JaeLuxe Shoetique. “I would’ve never been able to do that.”
The assistant is named Chase. Chase is not a person. It is Polk’s version of Muse, the artificial intelligence agent that Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, released to consumers on Sept. 8 and expanded for small businesses on Sept. 29. Each owner gives the agent a name at setup. Polk chose Chase.
More than 600 miles west, in Malvern, Iowa, a town of about 1,000 people, Tom Mulholland calls his agent Wally. Muse suggested the name. Mulholland, 66, later asked whether it had picked Wally because his middle name is Walter. It had no idea. He changed its on-screen avatar to a genie, after I Dream of Jeannie, “because of all the magical things it does.”
Polk is a marketer with an MBA whose women’s fashion brand does much of its business online and on social media. Mulholland is a fourth-generation grocer whose living comes from the meat counter. They have almost nothing in common except the problem Meta says it built Muse to solve. Small-business owners, the company wrote in its launch announcement, told Meta “they’re short on hours, not ideas.”

text:
No, this claim is not true.
It comes from a post by @ShaneTuttleNCAA, whose bio states: “Everything I do is Satire | College Sports Podcaster… Not impersonating and not affiliated with NCAA.” The “REPORT” about $15M annually in NIL (with a 10th-grade payment clause) and specific SEC leading recruitment is satirical content, not a real report.
What’s actually known about Madden San Miguel (“Baby Gronk”)
•  He is a real viral youth football player (roughly 13–14 years old in late 2026, an 8th grader in Ponder, Texas, Class of 2031). His father, Jake San Miguel, has aggressively built the “Baby Gronk” social-media brand since Madden was young; it has grown to around 1.4–1.5 million followers across platforms.
•  The family has publicly discussed aiming for strong future NIL earnings once he reaches college (Jake has said he wants Madden to become one of the highest-earning NIL football players). Earlier figures cited by the family were in the range of roughly $100,000 per year from the brand (ads, partnerships, etc.), though exact current numbers aren’t publicly confirmed in detail. Texas is one of the states that restricts public high-school athletes from accepting NIL money, which limits options until college.
•  He has made some early unofficial campus visits (including Georgia) and received attention/offers from programs (including lower-level or DM-style offers such as from Ole Miss under Lane Kiffin). This is unusual for a middle-schooler but does not equate to Georgia, LSU, and Texas A&M “leading his recruitment” in any serious, high-stakes sense for a Class of 2031 prospect.
In short, the $15M annual demand and specific payment clause are fabricated for satire. The broader phenomenon of early hype, social-media branding, and parental promotion around the kid is real, but the specific claim in the post is not.

text:
A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Q3 2026 earnings season got underway with reports from JPMorgan $JPM, Goldman Sachs $GS, Citigroup $C, and Wells Fargo $WFC, delivering a mixed but generally resilient picture for the banking sector. Goldman Sachs led the group with a standout quarter, posting its second-best revenue quarter ever as equities trading surged 72%, while Citigroup reported its strongest third quarter in a decade, driven by strength in services, wealth management, and equities. JPMorgan delivered a rare earnings miss despite raising its 2026 net interest income outlook, and Wells Fargo beat on earnings but missed on revenue. Across the sector, banks continued to describe the U.S. consumer as resilient, highlighted ongoing AI-driven corporate investment, raised or maintained optimistic net interest income expectations, and pointed to strong equity trading activity, while cautioning that sticky inflation, higher-for-longer interest rates, elevated valuations, and geopolitical risks remain key challenges heading into 2027.

2. Bank of America said 10-year U.S. Treasury yields may need to approach 6% before investors meaningfully rotate out of stocks and into bonds, according to its latest Global Fund Manager Survey. The survey found 76% of respondents expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged in October, while technology allocations climbed to their highest level since August 2020 and long semiconductors remained the market’s most crowded trade. At the same time, consumer discretionary exposure fell to its lowest level since July 2008, with investors increasing allocations to bonds, utilities, Japan, and the U.K. while trimming exposure to banks and U.S. equities. Bank of America said equity sentiment remains resilient overall, but a disorderly rise in bond yields and the potential for an AI bubble are now viewed as the biggest risks facing markets.

3. Paul Tudor Jones warned that 2027 could be “a very challenging year for the market,” saying current conditions remind him “exactly like 1999.” He argued the market could continue performing well in the short term but believes long-term risks are building, noting that many investors have not experienced a similar cycle before. Jones also said he expects to remain short throughout 2027, arguing that valuations offer little value and drawing parallels to the 1998–2002 period, when heavy IPO issuance and insider share unlocks continually added supply to the market, creating what he described as one of the easiest environments to maintain short positions.

4.  Apple $AAPL unveiled HomeView, its first dedicated smart home hub, at today’s “Welcome Home” event, marking the company’s biggest smart home expansion since HomeKit. The $299 device features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display, Siri AI, Face ID support for up to 6 users, FaceTime, Matter and Thread compatibility, and centralized control for cameras, locks, lights, thermostats, and other smart home devices, with pre-orders open now and shipments. Apple also introduced the HomePod mini 2 ($149), a new Apple TV 4K ($299), and the Apple Home Collection of smart home accessories, including cameras, a video doorbell, smart locks, thermostats, and sensors, developed with LG and Schneider Electric. The announcements represent Apple’s most aggressive push yet into the connected home, positioning the company to compete more directly with Amazon Echo and Google Nest while emphasizing privacy, on-device intelligence, and deep ecosystem integration.

5. Oracle $ORCL is urging federal regulators to expedite approval of the Green Chile natural gas pipeline, arguing the project is critical to keeping construction of its massive Project Jupiter AI data center in New Mexico on schedule. In a letter to FERC, Oracle SVP Josh Pitcock said further delays could jeopardize the project’s timeline, along with the associated jobs, economic activity, and community benefits. The Energy Transfer-owned pipeline is expected to supply roughly 400 million cubic feet of natural gas per day to Bloom Energy fuel cells powering Project Jupiter, but commissioning has slipped to February 2027 from the previously expected August 15 start date.

6. OpenAI said it discovered a sophisticated recording device inside one of its offices after an employee allegedly installed it several days earlier. The company said the employee has been terminated and the matter has been referred to the FBI. According to OpenAI, there is no evidence that the individual improperly accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code, or customer data. The incident highlights the growing importance of physical and operational security as AI companies safeguard increasingly valuable intellectual property.

7. NVIDIA $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang said the company will announce an additional $2B investment in Europe next week, bringing NVIDIA's regional investment to roughly $10B over the past year. Huang, who is scheduled to visit London and Berlin, also announced new investments in four French AI startups: Doctolib, Genesis AI, Pigment, and Entalpic. Addressing concerns over AI safety and data center energy consumption, Huang argued that AI can be developed safely while driving economic growth, opposed slowing AI development, and said open-source models could help Europe narrow the AI gap with the U.S. by enabling language- and industry-specific customization. He urged Europe to accelerate its AI investment and innovation efforts as global competition intensifies.

8. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $NVDA with 1.7M contracts, $AAPL with 1.2M contracts, $MU with 1.0M contracts, $META with 975K contracts, $SPCX with 971K contracts, $TSLA with 911K contracts, $INTC with 792K contracts, $MSFT with 507K contracts, $AMZN with 496K contracts, and $AMD with 489K contracts.

9. The latest ADP National Employment Report showed U.S. private employers added an average of 24,750 jobs per week over the four weeks ending September 26, down from a 25,250 weekly average previously and marking the end of five consecutive weeks of improving hiring. The latest reading represents a 2% decline in weekly job creation, although hiring remains well above the 8,250 weekly average recorded in late July. The softer hiring trend could point to a gradually cooling labor market, potentially easing wage pressures and inflation over time. Investors will now look to upcoming employment reports for confirmation of whether the slowdown is becoming more broad-based and what it could mean for future Federal Reserve policy.

10. Bank of America $BAC has been hit with $1.2B in penalties by the U.S. Treasury Department over alleged violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, marking the third-largest Treasury enforcement action of its kind. BofA said they will take a 17C EPS hit on earnings in Q3 as this is not a tax deductible expense.

11. Netflix $NFLX has secured the exclusive broadcast rights to the 2030 FIFA Men’s World Cup in Spain and Andorra, covering all 104 matches, with financial terms undisclosed. The agreement significantly expands Netflix’s live sports portfolio, which already includes NFL games and the rights to the next two FIFA Women’s World Cups. Investors welcomed the announcement, with Netflix shares rising about 1% in premarket trading. The deal strengthens Netflix’s push into premium live sports as it continues broadening its content strategy beyond traditional streaming.

12. JPMorgan says a small group of 42 AI-related companies is driving the vast majority of corporate growth, accounting for roughly 60–80% of S&P 500 earnings growth. At the same time, market breadth has continued to deteriorate, with about 60% of S&P 500 stocks now trading at least 20% below their all-time highs. JPM also noted that only 30% of stocks have outperformed the S&P 500, the lowest participation rate since 1991, highlighting the increasingly concentrated nature of the current bull market.
