Strategic contests change in two ways: through their rules and through what those rules reward. MindCast’s Mozart-Nietzsche series finds that a contested valuation moves payoffs only when an authority that can attach consequences writes it into binding terms. Wide circulation does not move payoffs. Of five live controversies, only artificial intelligence (AI) data centers show that change today, through large-load cost allocation tariffs.

Predictive Behavioral Economics + Dynamic Game Theory Foresight Simulation predicts: the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) final event-contract rule keeps the casino-style exclusion and defines at least one class of event contracts as swaps (80–88%, given a final rule by June 30, 2027).

1. At least four of six grid operators propose large-load cost-shifting protections to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) by November 30, 2026 (78–86%).
2. Kalshi’s Supreme Court brief in opposition distinguishes its event contracts from the excluded casino-style products by November 30, 2026 (82–90%).
3. Washington’s Department of Licensing takes no public disciplinary action under Substitute Senate Bill 6091 against Compass or an affiliated broker through June 30, 2027 (72–82%).
4. At least one of the ten largest U.S. commercial property and casualty carriers offers AI liability coverage conditioned on documented governance controls by June 30, 2027 (45–55%).

Each call carries a disconfirmation condition and resolves against CFTC rulemaking, FERC dockets, Supreme Court filings, Washington licensing actions and carrier announcements.

The actor who opens a valuation contest rarely decides it. Compass opened the listing fight and Washington’s legislature set the terms. Kalshi litigated and the CFTC moved to write the rule. Behavioral economics explains how framing shifts choices among unchanged options, and game theory explains when an authority converts that framing into payoffs. Data centers moved first because ratepayers felt a local, visible burden and 33 states wrote it into tariff terms.

🏛️ Policymakers: Draft definitions as if they were the rule, because a classification moves payoffs once enforcement attaches to it.
💼 Executives: Model the authority that can make a rival classification operative, not the firm that opened the contest.
⚖️ Counsel: Treat the CFTC’s interim final rule and proposed rule separately, since only the interim rule binds on publication.
📊 Investors: Treat data center cost allocation as a project input, since 33 states already carry approved large-load tariffs.

🇵🇰|Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: The Puppet Regime Declares War on Its Own People

October 14, 2026 | Peshawar / Bara

The Killing of a Protester in Bara

A young man stood in Bara Bazaar, in the Khyber district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He was protesting the suspension of his elected provincial government, the imposition of emergency rule, and the arrest of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. He was not armed. He was not rioting. He was exercising the most basic right of any human being: to object to the dismantling of his own democracy.

Police opened fire. Live rounds. He was shot. He died.

By sunset on Bara that day, at least one protester was dead and three civilians lay injured from police gunfire. PTI lawmaker Iqbal Afridi confirmed that eleven party workers had been injured and one had been killed. The state's response was not an investigation. It was denial. The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government's Fact Check account declared the news completely baseless and fake.

A man is dead. His blood is on the asphalt of Bara Bazaar. And the regime calls it fake news.

The Takeover: Governor's Rule and the Death of an Elected Government

This did not begin yesterday. It began on October 11, 2026, when President Asif Ali Zardari signed a summary approving the imposition of emergency and Governor's Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under Articles 232 and 234 of Pakistan's Constitution. The elected provincial government, led by Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, was dissolved. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, provincial ministers, advisers, and the advocate general ceased to hold office immediately. Afridi was placed under what the government called protective custody, a euphemism for house arrest.

The justification offered by Islamabad was deteriorating law and order and the provincial government's alleged deliberate indifference in the war against terrorism. The federal government accused the PTI administration of colluding with militants. The same government that had been elected by the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was branded a terrorist accomplice and stripped of power by decree from Islamabad.

The army was deployed under Article 245 to assist the civil administration. The message was unmistakable: the people's vote is meaningless. Power flows not from the ballot box, but from the barrel of a gun.

The Streets: Live Rounds, Tear Gas, and Torched Government Buildings

The people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa did not accept this quietly. They marched. They protested. They raised their voices. And the puppet regime answered with force.

On Tuesday, police fired live rounds and tear gas at PTI supporters in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The provincial administration, through information official Samar Haroon Bilour, denied that police fired live rounds, calling allegations baseless and frivolous and claiming footage was AI-generated. Yet PTI officials documented injuries. Five people were injured, the most serious in Bara, 15 kilometers from Peshawar.

The protesters did not submit. In Bara Bazaar, they set fire to the National Database and Registration Authority center and a portion of the Rescue 1122 building. Government buildings went up in flames. It was a response, an act of fury from a people who had just watched their elected leaders arrested and their democratic rights suspended by a federal government that answers not to them, but to its masters in Washington.

The Information Blackout: A Regime That Fears the Truth

The regime's crackdown on information was as swift as its crackdown on protesters. According to Netblocks, there was major disruption to internet connectivity in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Mobile phone and internet services were slowed or shut down in selected areas of Peshawar and other cities. Schools were closed. Shipping containers and razor wire blocked roads to Peshawar's administrative zone.

The regime also imposed Section 144 in districts across the province: Shangla, Buner, Hangu, Chitral, Lower and Upper Dir, banning all gatherings, rallies, processions, and protests for thirty days. Displaying weapons was prohibited. Gatherings of five or more persons were outlawed. Zero tolerance was promised for violations.

The regime shut down the internet. It banned public assembly. It deployed the army. It fired live rounds at unarmed protesters. Then it announced that nothing was happening.

The Puppet Regime: Who Does Islamabad Actually Serve?

This is not a Pakistani government. This is a US vassal state run by a military establishment that answers to Washington, not to the Pakistani people. Field Marshal Asim Munir, the Chief of Defence Forces, has consolidated more power than any Pakistani general since Zia-ul-Haq. He speaks directly with Donald Trump. The London Plan report laid bare the architecture of the regime change that removed Imran Khan and installed a pliant military establishment at the pinnacle of power. Washington orchestrated the removal of a democratically elected prime minister. The man it installed, Munir, was not the king. He was the pawn.

This is the same pattern we see in Lebanon, where the Western-backed government admits it cannot afford reconstruction while Hezbollah delivers $14,000 to families. It is the same pattern we see in Yemen, where the legitimate government provides diplomatic cover for Saudi bombing campaigns. Puppet governments that perform sovereignty while exercising none. That beg for aid that never comes. That exist to absorb Western pressure and maintain the fiction of a functioning state.

The Blood of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

A young man is dead in Bara. His name may never appear in Western media. His death will be classified as fake news by the regime's fact-checkers. But his blood is real. It is on the hands of police who fired shots, generals who gave orders, and the American empire that sustains them.

The people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa are not rioting. They are resisting. They are resisting a regime that has declared their votes meaningless, their leaders criminals, their protests illegal, and their lives expendable. They are resisting the same architecture of colonial subjugation imposed on the Global South from Palestine to Yemen to Pakistan.

The regime can impose emergency rule. It can deploy the army. It can shut down the internet. It can shoot its own citizens in the streets. But it cannot kill the idea that has taken root in the hearts of a people who have decided that they will be free.

Do not consider their silence as their defeat. Do not consider this blood that is flowing as useless.

Long live the resistance in Pakistan. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

October 13th, 2026

Spotlight Player OTD: Lee Nailon 

Taken by Charlotte No. 43 overall in the same 1999 draft class as Baron Davis, Nailon’s career got off to a… rough start, to say the least.

He didn’t play a lot at all as a rookie; Davis himself didn’t even start in his first season. 

Nailon’s lack of PT was for a different reason, though. Davis was just stuck behind PG David Wesley, who was Mr. Reliable, and SG Eddie Jones in his best year as a pro.

Nailon, on the other hand, went to play over in Italy for one year after being drafted. 

An arrest at a Fort Worth Hotel for drug possession (was later dropped, his agent said it was just wrong place wrong time) contributed to Nailon’s decision to play one more year overseas before playing with the Hornets.

Returning to Charlotte to make his NBA Debut in 2000-2001, Nailon’s first actual NBA year after being drafted in 1999 saw Paul Silas bench him for, long story short, not trying hard enough.

Nailon played in 42 games in ‘00-01, none as a starter, while averaging just 11 minutes and 3.2 shot attempts per game.

He was forced in the summer of 2001 to either take a small offer from Charlotte to stay in the NBA, or head back overseas.

So Nailon bet on himself, for less money than his overseas offer mind you, and came back to Charlotte.

It turned his NBA career outlook from the fringes of overseas ball again, into blossoming a nine-year NBA career because of his 2nd, and last year in Charlotte.

His last year comes around, Charlotte’s last before N** O****** (Nailon would later play 1 more year with the fake Hornets), and the beginning of Nailon’s career change all started when Mash went out.

Nailon didn’t start his first NBA game until November of 2001 against Washington and MJ; starting due to the aforementioned Jamal Mashburn abdominal injury.

Mash missed just over half of the 2001-2002 season (42 games).

With Mash out, and the crowds in Charlotte dwindling, Nailon helped keep the guys who had no choice but to show up afloat alongside Baron Davis.

This ‘01-‘02 team really struggled offensively without Mash, and the progression that Nailon made kept that team chugging along. 

Nailon was a big reason this team actually got to go out with their head’s held high by making the playoffs and finishing over .500. in 2002.

The few Nailon highlights on YT were too random/low quality to be worth showing, unfortunately.

text:
👼🏻👼🏽👼🏿🤰🏻🤰🏽🤰🏿 Baby Cherub Angel Ara Sings Phonic Songs, Week One: Prenatal Development
👶 Pregnancy Days 1 to 7 (Week 1)
Your baby is not here yet. Not one tiny cell. So why is a little cherub named Ara already flying down from heaven with four songs in Ara's hands, ready to sing baby music over a home with no baby in it? Here is the secret God whispered to Ara.

🩺 What Week One Really Is
Doctors count week one from the first day of your last period. Conception comes about two weeks later. So this week there is no baby yet. There is a home God is getting ready, and a child He already knows by name.

🌌 Before the Stars
Once upon a time, before one star, before the oceans learned to sing, there was God. His heart was full of a song He had been singing forever. He smiled and said, "I want to make someone to love. Someone brand new. And I will know them before anyone else does."

👼 The Angel Ara, Who Could Not Wait
High above the clouds, where the air hums like lullabies, lived Ara, the smallest angel in the choir. Ara had wings like spun sugar and a voice like a silver bell. Every morning Ara pressed an ear to the shelves of heaven's golden library, where God keeps every name.

One morning Ara heard a name no one had ever spoken. "God, whose name is that?" God leaned close. "That is a baby I am preparing. I knew that little one before the world was made." Ara's wings trembled. "Can I go see them?" "Soon," said God. "And you will carry songs."

📖 God Knew You First
✝️ "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. And before you went forth from the womb, I sanctified you." (Jeremiah 1:5, CPDV)

This is God's plan. He knows your child before your child is formed. That is why GLAL School starts singing before the baby is even here. Phonic songs are not for a test. They are a love song from God, sung over the home He is preparing.

🎶 The Four Songs of Heaven
God placed four songs in Ara's hands. The Song of Recognition says, "I see you." The Song of Attachment says, "You belong." The Song of Curiosity says, "Wonder with Me." The Song of Comfort says, "You are safe." All the lullabies, nursery rhymes, and kids music on earth echo one of them.

🏡 Angel Ara Finds an Empty Cradle
Ara flew down on a beam of morning light to a little house with a garden. A mother was sleeping. Ara looked everywhere for the baby. No baby. "God," Ara whispered, "did I come too early?" And God laughed softly. "No, Ara. You came right on time."

"This is the week I prepare the home. Sing over the mother. Sing over the house. Sing over the cradle that is still empty." So Angel Ara sang baby music over the whole house, soft as nursery rhymes at bedtime, kids music for a child who is not here yet.

💭 Why Sing Before There Is a Baby?
Because God does. He sang over creation before there was anyone to hear. When you sing this week, you are not performing for an audience. You are joining the oldest song there is, the one God has been singing over your child since before time began.

🎧 This Week's Song from Angel Ara
Play this week's song from Angel Ara. It is baby music in little Ara's voice, full of phonic songs: the soft "m" of mama, the long "ooh" of lullabies, like nursery rhymes from heaven. Hum along. If Dad or Grandma puts on the headphones and sings along too, even better.

📝 Week One Journal
Write one line this week: "God, You already know my child's name." Then write down any sound from the phonic songs that stays with you. Kids music starts here, not in a classroom, but in a mother's heart that sings first.

🙏 Week One Prayer
🕊️ "Father, You knew my child before the stars. Prepare my body, my home, and my heart. Let our house be full of Your song. In Jesus' name, Amen."

👼🏻👼🏽👼🏿🤰🏻🤰🏽🤰🏿 Pregnancy Deep Dive: Week 1 (Days 1 to 7): Baby Cherub Angel Ara Sings Phonic Songs, Prenatal Development

📚 The Library of Names
In the golden library of heaven, the shelves stretch farther than any eye can see. Each shelf holds a book, and each book holds a name. Not a nickname. The true name, the one God has for that person and no one else in all of history.

Ara had spent a thousand years reading those shelves. Ara found Abraham, who left everything because God called him. Ara found Moses, who argued with God at a burning bush and still said yes. Ara found Ruth, who chose loyalty over comfort, and Esther, who found courage she did not know she had.

But the new name was different. Reading a name in a book is one thing. This was like hearing a song for the first time and knowing, somehow, that the song was about you. Something stirred in Ara's little chest that Ara had no word for. "God," Ara said, "I want to meet them."

"You will," God said. "But first you must understand what you are carrying." Then God opened His hand, and four notes of light lay in His palm, each one humming a different tune. This is where the four songs of heaven begin.

👀 The Song of Recognition
The first note was no bigger than a snowflake. When Ara looked closely, Ara saw it was made of thousands of tiny sounds woven together. "This is the song of recognition," God said. "It is the sound a soul makes when it is finally seen. Every child is waiting to be known."

In heaven, this song is made of consonants, the little sounds that say "I know you." Ara practiced until Ara's bell voice could sing every one, from the soft "m" of mama to the strong "b" of beloved. These are the building blocks of phonic songs, the sounds a child will one day read.

"On earth," God went on, "there are mothers who sing to a child they cannot see yet. They do not always know why. They hum. They sing nursery rhymes. They say a name out loud. That is this song. That is recognition. That is the sound of 'I see you.'"

Ara thought of Elizabeth. When Mary, carrying Jesus, came to visit, the baby John leaped inside Elizabeth's womb. Even before he was born, John recognized the presence of the Savior. Elizabeth could not keep it in. She cried out:

✝️ "For behold, as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy." (Luke 1:44, CPDV)

"The child knows," God said. "Spirit to spirit, the child always knows." That is the heart of GLAL School. Long before a baby understands words, God's song can reach their spirit. Recognition comes first. Reading comes later. This is God's plan.

🎀 The Song of Attachment
The second note was long and soft. It stretched out like a ribbon of gold. "This is the song of attachment," God said. "It is the sound of belonging. It is what a mother hums when she rocks her baby. It says, 'You are mine, I am yours, and nothing will change that.'"

This song is made of vowels, the sounds that stretch out long and warm, "oooh" and "aaah," wrapping around a baby like a blanket. Ara held the note close and heard lullabies from every corner of the earth, in languages Ara did not speak, from places Ara had never been.

And under all those lullabies, one steady rhythm: the heartbeat. God showed Ara how, months from now, when the baby's ears are ready around the middle of pregnancy, a mother's heartbeat becomes one of the first sounds her child hears. The first music. The sound of home.

Mary knew this song. While she carried Jesus, she visited Elizabeth, and her heart overflowed into a song the Church still sings today. Her long, warm vowels carried her love for God and for the baby she was carrying:

✝️ "My soul magnifies the Lord. And my spirit leaps for joy in God my Savior." (Luke 1:46-47, CPDV)

Ara also thought of the mother of Moses. She hid her baby for three months, then placed him in a basket among the reeds and trusted God with him. We can only imagine the lullabies she hummed as she let him go. God heard her heart, and Pharaoh's daughter found the basket.

Moses grew up to lead a nation out of slavery. "Even when a mother cannot see the way," God said, "the song goes on." Attachment is not only holding on. Sometimes it is trusting the One who holds your child even better than you can.

✨ The Song of Curiosity
The third note sparkled. It jumped and danced in Ara's hand like it could not sit still. "This is the song of curiosity," God said. "It is the giggle, the coo, the 'da da da' a baby makes when they find their own toes. It is the hundredth 'why?' It is a mind waking up."

This is where kids music begins. Not in a classroom. Not on a stage. In the wonder of a small voice discovering sound. And it began with God. In the garden, He brought every animal to Adam to see what Adam would call it.

Picture it. God holds up a feathered little creature. "What will you call this one?" Adam laughs and says, "Bird!" And God laughs too, because naming things is one of the greatest joys there is. Naming was not a chore. It was an invitation to explore, to wonder, to ask.

✝️ "And God saw everything that he had made. And they were very good." (Genesis 1:31, CPDV)

Ara thought of the disciples, who walked with Jesus for three years and still asked questions every single day. Teach us to pray. Who is the greatest? How many times should I forgive? Jesus never grew tired of them. He answered with stories, with silence, and with questions of His own.

"Curiosity is holy," God said. "It is the sound of a soul reaching toward Me." That is why GLAL School fills a child's world with nursery rhymes, kids music, and phonic songs. Each new sound is a door, and God loves to watch His children walk through it.

🕯️ The Song of Comfort
The fourth note was the quietest. It did not sparkle or dance. It simply glowed, steady and warm, like a candle in a window. "This is the song of comfort," God said. "It does not fix anything. It does not explain anything. It simply stays."

It is the steady beat, the "shhh, shhh, shhh" that says you are safe, you are held, you are home. Young David sang it in the fields while he watched his sheep. And on the night before He died, Jesus sang a hymn with His disciples before He walked into the dark:

✝️ "And after a hymn was sung, they went out to the Mount of Olives." (Matthew 26:30, CPDV)

Ara thought of Job, who lost his children, his wealth, and his health, and sat in the ashes. His friends came to comfort him, but their long explanations only made things worse. Then God spoke out of the whirlwind, not with answers, but with wonder:

✝️ "Where were you, when I set the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding." (Job 38:4, CPDV)

Job had demanded answers. What he found instead was presence. God Himself had come close. And Job's whole heart changed in one sentence:

✝️ "By paying attention with the ear, I have heard you, but now my eye sees you." (Job 42:5, CPDV)

"Comfort is not the absence of trouble," God told Ara. "Comfort is the presence of love in the middle of trouble." Ara thought of Jesus praying in the garden of Gethsemane, in such agony that His sweat became like drops of blood. God did not take the cup away. But He sent help:

✝️ "Then an Angel appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him." (Luke 22:43, CPDV)

Presence. Not rescue. Presence. "That is the song," God said. "That is the one a child needs most." It is why the quiet lullabies at bedtime matter so much. They are not just baby music. They are a mother saying, "I am here, and God is here too."

🌱 How God Grows a Person
Now you might wonder: if God already knows everything about us, why does He take so long to grow us? Why not make us grown-ups from the start? Because God is not in a hurry. God is a gardener, not a factory. King David knew it. He sang:

✝️ "For you have possessed my temperament. You have supported me from the womb of my mother." (Psalm 138:13, CPDV)

A gardener knows a seed does not become a tree in a day. A seed becomes a sprout. A sprout becomes a sapling. And only after many seasons of sun and rain and wind does the tree bear fruit. Week one is the soil being made ready. God is patient with the soil.

🧥 Joseph
God grew Joseph slowly. Joseph was the next-to-youngest of twelve brothers, and they were jealous because their father loved him so much. They threw him into a pit and sold him to traders headed for Egypt. But God was not finished with Joseph.

In Egypt, Joseph worked hard and stayed honest. Even when he was thrown into prison for something he did not do, he kept trusting God. Then Pharaoh had a dream no one could explain, and Joseph, who had learned to listen to God in the dark, told him what it meant.

Pharaoh made Joseph the second most powerful man in Egypt. When famine came, Joseph had food stored up, and he saved his own family, the very brothers who had betrayed him. He forgave them, and he told them the truth about what God had done:

✝️ "You devised evil against me. But God turned it into good." (Genesis 50:20, CPDV)

That is character. That is what God grows in us. Not just strength, but forgiveness. Not just success, but mercy. And it grows slowly, one season at a time, like a song a mother sings over and over until her child knows every word.

🐑 David
God grew David slowly too. He was the youngest of eight sons, so small that when the prophet Samuel came to anoint a king, David's own father did not even call him in from the fields. Samuel looked at the tall older brothers. But God said no to every one.

✝️ "For man sees those things that are apparent, but the Lord beholds the heart." (1 Samuel 16:7, CPDV)

God chose David's heart. A heart that sang. A heart that danced before the Lord. A heart that wrote songs people are still singing three thousand years later. The shepherd boy's psalms became some of the most loved songs in history, and they began alone in a field with sheep.

🌸 Mary
God grew Mary slowly too. She was a young woman in a small town, nobody famous by the world's standards. But when the angel Gabriel told her she would bear a son and call His name Jesus, she did not say, "I am too young." She did not say, "I am not ready."

✝️ "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord. Let it be done to me according to your word." (Luke 1:38, CPDV)

That is trust. That is what God grows in us: the courage to say yes even when we do not understand the whole plan. Every mother in week one is standing where Mary stood, at the start of a story she cannot see the end of, saying yes to God.

⭐ The Baby Who Changed Everything
And then there is the baby at the center of it all. Jesus did not come as a king in a palace. He came as a baby in a manger, with animals breathing warm air around Him and shepherds hurrying in from the hills. And the angels sang over Him that night:

✝️ "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." (Luke 2:14, CPDV)

Think of that. The very first song sung over the newborn Jesus came from angels. Heaven's choir, the same choir where little Ara sings, filled the sky over Bethlehem. Ara and the angels have been singing over babies from the very beginning.

And that baby grew. He learned to walk and to talk. He learned the songs His mother sang. At twelve He stayed behind in the temple, listening to the teachers and asking questions, and everyone who heard Him was amazed.

✝️ "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and in age, and in grace, with God and men." (Luke 2:52, CPDV)

Even the Son of God grew up slowly. Even He learned. Even He had a mother who sang to Him and a father who taught Him to work with wood. God does not rush. God grows.

🤱 The Mothers Who Sang
As Ara flew down through the clouds, Ara saw the mothers. Ara saw Hannah, who prayed for a child for years. When God gave her Samuel, Hannah brought her little boy to the house of the Lord to dedicate him, and she sang a song of praise so strong it is still in the Bible today.

Ara saw Mary singing her Magnificat while Jesus grew inside her. Ara saw Elizabeth rejoicing as her baby leaped. And Ara saw mothers in every time and every place, singing lullabies and nursery rhymes to babies they could not yet see, humming melodies they did not know they knew.

"They are all singing My song," God said. "They just do not always know it." Mom, that includes you. Every time you hum this week's phonic songs, you are joining a choir of mothers that stretches all the way back to Hannah and Mary.

🔨 The Fathers Who Built
Ara saw the fathers too. Ara saw Joseph the carpenter teaching the boy Jesus to measure wood and drive nails. Ara saw Joseph wake in the night when an angel warned him in a dream, and take Mary and the baby to Egypt to keep them safe from King Herod.

Ara saw Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist. Zechariah did not believe the angel's message, so he could not speak for months. But when his son was born and named, his very first words poured out as a song:

✝️ "Blessed is the Lord God of Israel. For he has visited and has wrought the redemption of his people." (Luke 1:68, CPDV)

Silence turned to song. That is what God does. Dad, this week is your week too. Put on the headphones and sing along with Angel Ara's song. A father's voice is part of the home God is preparing, long before the baby arrives.

🧒 The Children God Chose
And Ara saw the children, chosen by God while they were still small. Ara saw the boy Samuel, sleeping in the temple, hearing a voice call his name in the night. Three times he ran to old Eli. The fourth time, he answered God Himself:

✝️ "And Samuel said, 'Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.'" (1 Samuel 3:10, CPDV)

Ara saw David, a shepherd boy with a sling and five smooth stones, facing a giant because he trusted God more than he feared Goliath. Ara saw Josiah, who became king at eight years old and grew into a king who turned the whole nation back to God.

And Ara saw the little boy who offered his five loaves and two fish to Jesus, and watched them feed five thousand. God does not wait for people to be grown. God calls them while they are still small. Even before they are born.

📝 Your Week One Practice
This is God's plan for week one: sing first. Play Angel Ara's song once a day this week. Let it be baby music for a home that is getting ready. Hum the vowels. Say the consonants out loud. Do not worry about getting it right. Heaven is not grading you.

Teach it three ways, the way the best preschool teachers do. First, listen. Second, hum along. Third, sing it with someone: your husband, your mom, your older children. Kids music is meant to be shared. The same song three different ways is how a lesson truly lands.

Journal prompts for this week: Which sound in the song stayed with me? What do I want my child to know about God first? Which Bible mother do I feel closest to right now: Hannah, Elizabeth, Mary, or the mother of Moses? Write one line for each.

One practical gift: doctors recommend a daily prenatal vitamin with folic acid before and early in pregnancy to help protect the baby's developing brain and spine in the earliest weeks. Ask your doctor or midwife which one is right for you. The songs are a spiritual gift. They are not medical care.

💛 The Promise
At last Ara reached the little house with the garden. The mother was still sleeping, and the cradle was still empty. Ara was not worried anymore. Ara understood now. Ara opened those little wings, and the four notes of light rose from Ara's hands and began to sing.

The song of recognition. The song of attachment. The song of curiosity. The song of comfort. The notes filled every room. They settled on the mother like sunlight. They settled on the empty cradle like a blanket, so that when the baby comes, the songs will already be there.

"Before you were formed," Ara sang into the quiet, "God already knew your name. You will be wrapped in peace before you ever open your eyes. Ara and the angels will stay near. You will never be alone. You are already loved." And far above, God rejoiced:

✝️ "He will rejoice over you with gladness. In his love, he will be silent. He will exult over you with praise." (Zephaniah 3:17, CPDV)

In the great golden library, a new book appeared on the shelf. It had no pages filled in yet. Just a name, and a song, and a promise. God was not finished. God never is.

🌅 The End, or Rather, the Beginning
Because that is the truth of it, little one. Your story will not start the day you are born. It will not start with your first breath or your first word. Your story started before the stars, before the oceans, before time itself, in the heart of God.

He looked at all that light and all that love and said, "I want to make someone to love." And He is making you. He is preparing your home right now. He is not done. Next week, Ara has a new song to carry, so keep the baby music playing.

🕊️ "Father, thank You for knowing my child before the world began. Fill our home with Your four songs: recognition, attachment, curiosity, and comfort. Grow us slowly and grow us well. In Jesus' name, Amen."

text:
#dailywisdom4me #TreePlanting #Discipleship

The Shade We Owe

A young tree is an act of patience disguised as landscaping.

You dig a hole, loosen the roots, settle the tree into the earth, and water something that may look almost unchanged for years. The trunk is thin. The branches offer little shelter. Whatever beauty the tree may someday possess exists mostly in anticipation.

Plant one when you’re young and there’s a reasonable chance you’ll watch it mature.

Plant one when you’re old, and the gesture means something different.

You begin with the knowledge that the fullest branches may belong to a season you’ll never see. Someone else will hear leaves moving overhead. Someone else will rest against the trunk. Children not yet born may climb its limbs. Families you will never meet may spread blankets beneath it on hot summer afternoons.

And they may never know who put it there.

That’s why I’ve always been drawn to the old saying:

“A society grows great when old men plant trees whose shade they know they shall never sit in.”

The older I get, the more I realize the wisdom isn’t really about trees. It’s about learning to care deeply about a future that doesn’t include us.

We’re accustomed to connecting effort with reward. Work hard and enjoy the result. Save money and spend it later. Build something and take pride in what you’ve built. There’s nothing wrong with that. But some of the most consequential things we do operate on a timetable longer than our own.

Someone taught us to read.

Someone poured concrete for a sidewalk before we lived on the street.

Someone preserved an institution, paid off a debt, built a church, established a scholarship, protected a piece of land, kept a promise, or raised a child who eventually became the person who helped us.

We live every day beneath shade we didn’t plant.

Christianity gives this idea even deeper roots for me. Scripture is filled with people building toward promises they wouldn’t live long enough to see completed. Abraham looked toward generations still unborn. Moses led Israel toward a land he would only glimpse. David gathered materials for a temple Solomon would build. Paul described ministry in similarly agricultural terms: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”

That’s a remarkably freeing way to understand a life.

I don’t have to finish everything I begin. I don’t have to be present when every seed becomes something substantial. I don’t even have to be remembered.

Maybe that’s one of the harder lessons of getting older. A meaningful life isn’t measured only by what I manage to gather before I leave. Part of maturity is learning to invest myself in things whose benefits will arrive after I’m gone.

What am I leaving stronger than I found it? What am I maintaining because someone else will need it? What am I teaching that may outlive me? What am I willing to build without receiving the satisfaction of completion?

A great society depends on people willing to think beyond the borders of their own lifetime. So does a great family. A great church. A great community.

The planter accepts a small patch of bare ground while believing in a canopy.

He waters what cannot repay him.

Then, eventually, he leaves.

Years later, someone steps out of the heat and finds shade waiting for them.

They may never know his name.

That doesn’t make the shade any less real.

text:
Day 4 of Navratri: the Goddess who created the universe with a smile ☀️

Day 1 gave you a foundation. Day 2 gave you discipline. Day 3 gave you courage.

Day 4 shows you what all of that is for: creating something from nothing.

Read this once. You will never underestimate a small beginning again. 👇

🔥 The story nobody tells you
➤ Before creation, there was nothing. No sun, no stars, no sound, only endless darkness
➤ Then the Goddess smiled
➤ From that one gentle smile, a tiny cosmic egg of light appeared
➤ From that egg came the sun, the planets, the stars and every living being
➤ She then made her home at the very centre of the sun
➤ Only she can live there, because she is the source of its heat and light
➤ The lesson: the biggest things in the universe began with one small spark

🙏 How to recognise her
➤ "Ku" = a little, "Ushma" = warmth, "Anda" = cosmic egg
➤ Also called Ashtabhuja Devi, the Goddess with eight arms
➤ Rides a lion - strength that protects creation
➤ Holds kamandalu, bow, arrow, lotus, amrit kalash, chakra, gada and japa mala
➤ The japa mala is said to hold all the siddhis and riches
➤ Her face shines like the sun and her smile is warm

🎃 The secret of the name
➤ "Kushmanda" is also the Sanskrit word for ash gourd (petha)
➤ Ash gourd is her favourite offering in many traditions
➤ The deeper meaning: one small seed holds a whole field inside it

🌱 Why she comes fourth
➤ She governs the Anahata chakra, the heart
➤ Anahata = love, warmth, compassion and balance
➤ She rules Surya, the Sun, the giver of energy and life
➤ Root, discipline, courage. Now the heart opens and energy flows outward
➤ Strength without warmth turns cold. She brings both power and light

🪔 Puja vidhi: step by step
➤ Bathe early and wear clean royal blue clothes
➤ Check the Akhand Jyot and water the jau, which should be sprouting now
➤ Offer red or yellow flowers, kumkum, akshat, sandalwood and green cardamom
➤ Offer the bhog with a smile, as she created the world with one
➤ Chant her mantra 108 times
➤ Close with aarti and pray for health, energy and growth

💙 Colour of the day: Royal Blue
➤ Depth, calm and boundless energy, like the endless sky she filled with light

🥞 Bhog: Malpua
➤ Offered for intelligence, good decisions and a sharp mind
➤ Share the prasad at a temple or with Brahmins and the needy

🌼 Flowers
➤ Red flowers or yellow marigold and jasmine

📿 Mantra (108 times)
ॐ देवी कूष्माण्डायै नमः
Om Devi Kushmandayai Namah

🕉️ Dhyan mantra
सुरासम्पूर्णकलशं रुधिराप्लुतमेव च।
दधाना हस्तपद्माभ्यां कूष्माण्डा शुभदास्तु मे॥

🍎 If you are fasting
➤ Halfway mark is close. The body has adjusted, so stay steady
➤ Yes: fruits, milk, sabudana, kuttu, singhara, makhana, sendha namak
➤ No: grains, onion, garlic, regular salt, alcohol, non-veg
➤ The real fast today: no negativity, no complaining, no dimming someone else's light

✨ What Day 4 is really asking you
➤ What are you waiting to start because it looks too small?
➤ The universe began with a smile. Your big thing can begin with one step
➤ Where in your life is it still dark? Bring the light there first
➤ Warmth is a strength. Kindness is not weakness
➤ Smile more today. It is how the Goddess began creation

🗓️ Where we are
➤ Day 1 Shailputri ✅ → Day 2 Brahmacharini ✅ → Day 3 Chandraghanta ✅ → Day 4 Kushmanda ☀️ → Day 5 Skandamata → Day 6 Katyayani → Day 7 Kalaratri → Day 8 Mahagauri → Day 9 Siddhidatri

Type "Jai Mata Di" 🙏 if you are starting something new this Navratri.
Save this for your puja. Share it with the one person whose smile lights up your home.

Shubh Navratri 🌺

text:
Danantara Wants to Revive Sritex. Good Luck Competing With China.

I have been following the latest development surrounding Danantara’s plan to establish a state-owned textile company and potentially acquire the assets of bankrupt textile giant Sritex, and while I fully understand the motivation to revive domestic manufacturing, restore employment and rebuild Indonesia’s textile supply chain, I have serious reservations about the commercial economics of this investment, particularly when the proposed sector-wide funding commitment could reach US$6 billion, equivalent to roughly Rp100 trillion, in an industry where Indonesia is already struggling to compete with China, Vietnam, Bangladesh and other established manufacturing hubs.

According to the latest reports, Danantara is considering consolidating several textile businesses, including Sritex, into a vertically integrated state-owned platform spanning upstream materials, spinning, weaving, dyeing, finishing and downstream manufacturing, with the idea that combining existing industrial assets, introducing modern machinery and improving coordination across the supply chain could restore Indonesia’s competitiveness.

The industrial logic is understandable, but my first question is much simpler: What exactly is Indonesia’s sustainable competitive advantage in textiles, and why would acquiring a bankrupt company suddenly create one?

Sritex was not an insignificant manufacturer that failed because it lacked scale or market recognition, because it was once among Southeast Asia’s largest integrated textile producers, had extensive manufacturing infrastructure, supplied international customers and operated across several stages of the textile value chain, yet even with those advantages it eventually entered bankruptcy in October 2024 and ceased operations in March 2025.

According to ANTARA, creditor claims in the bankruptcy proceedings reached approximately Rp29.8 trillion, while other contemporary reports put its assets at around Rp10 trillion, although those figures should not be interpreted as a final liquidation valuation or as liabilities that any asset purchaser would automatically assume.

That distinction is important because buying machinery, land and buildings through a properly structured bankruptcy asset sale is fundamentally different from taking over the old corporate entity together with its debts and legal obligations, and at a sufficiently distressed purchase price, some of Sritex’s assets could genuinely represent an attractive industrial opportunity, but acquiring assets cheaply and operating those assets profitably are two completely different things.

A bankrupt factory does not become competitive simply because its new shareholder has a much larger balance sheet.

The fundamental issue is that textile manufacturing is an extraordinarily competitive, relatively low-margin and capital-intensive business in which the winners are determined not simply by access to funding, but by a combination of manufacturing productivity, raw-material costs, energy efficiency, product quality, procurement scale, logistics, inventory management, technological capabilities, buyer relationships and the ability to deliver enormous volumes consistently at internationally competitive prices, and this is where China enters the conversation.

According to China’s customs statistics, the country exported approximately US$293.8 billion of textiles and apparel in 2025, comprising roughly US$142.6 billion of textiles and US$151.1 billion of apparel, and although exports declined modestly that year, China remains the world’s dominant textile manufacturing ecosystem, supported by decades of accumulated investment, deeply integrated supply chains, advanced machinery, extensive industrial clusters and enormous supplier networks.

Indonesia is not simply competing against a few Chinese factories that happen to employ cheaper workers, because Indonesia is competing against an entire manufacturing ecosystem that has spent decades optimizing almost every component of the production process, with China possessing enormous capacity in synthetic fibers, yarn, fabrics, dyes, chemicals, textile machinery, automated manufacturing, packaging, logistics and export infrastructure, while the real competitive advantage comes from the interaction among those industries, because a fabric manufacturer can source inputs from nearby suppliers, access specialized machinery, obtain technical assistance, scale production rapidly and move products through established export channels with fewer frictions.

China’s advantage is therefore not merely cheap labor, and anyone still analyzing its industrial competitiveness primarily through wages is missing the structural transformation that has taken place over the past two decades, because China’s labor costs have risen substantially while the country has remained dominant through higher productivity, automation, scale and supply-chain efficiency, all of which can more than compensate for higher wages.

That is precisely the challenge Indonesia faces, because building a new textile SOE does not automatically replicate China’s network of suppliers, engineers, machinery manufacturers, industrial clusters, logistics providers and international customer relationships, and those capabilities cannot simply be purchased by injecting Rp100 trillion into a holding company, since they take years, and sometimes decades, to develop.

The competition does not stop with China, because Vietnam and Bangladesh have also developed substantial garment export industries, with Vietnam benefiting from extensive foreign direct investment, manufacturing integration and trade relationships, while Bangladesh remains highly competitive in several labor-intensive garment categories, meaning that Indonesia would be entering an already fiercely competitive market where established producers are continuously improving efficiency, investing in automation and fighting aggressively for orders.

Good luck beating China in textiles by simply becoming another large producer.

The second issue is that Indonesia’s existing textile industry is already suffering from weak capacity utilization, which should immediately raise questions about the rationale for committing substantial additional capital before understanding why existing capacity is not being fully utilized, because in June 2026, industry representatives estimated that textile utilization remained below 50%, citing weak demand, imported competition and rising input costs, and although this was an industry estimate rather than a complete census of every factory, it illustrates the problem rather clearly.

If substantial manufacturing capacity is already idle because producers cannot sell their output competitively, then injecting more capital into additional production capacity does not necessarily solve the underlying problem, and it could simply create more underutilized assets, because what matters is not how many factories Danantara eventually controls, how many machines it purchases or how much nominal production capacity appears on the balance sheet, but whether those factories can secure profitable orders at internationally competitive prices while maintaining sufficient utilization to cover depreciation, labor, maintenance, energy and financing costs.

A factory operating at 50% utilization can have materially different unit economics from the same factory operating at 85%, because fixed manufacturing overheads are spread across substantially fewer units, and if the new state-owned platform expands capacity without first securing incremental demand, it risks worsening the very economics it is supposed to repair.

The third issue concerns the proposed investment size, because US$6 billion is an extraordinarily large amount of capital to deploy into a mature, competitive industry with inherently challenging margins, even if that figure represents the broader textile-development program rather than the specific Sritex acquisition, and if Danantara eventually deploys the entire US$6 billion while expecting a 10% return on invested capital, the investment would need to generate roughly US$600 million of sustainable annual after-tax operating profit, assuming that amount represents the relevant incremental invested-capital base.

At a hypothetical 5% NOPAT margin, that would require approximately US$12 billion of annual revenue attributable to that capital base, while even at a substantially stronger 10% margin, it would still require around US$6 billion of annual revenue, and although these are illustrative calculations rather than forecasts, with the actual economics depending on how much capital is deployed, how it is structured, the mix of businesses acquired and the profits generated, they demonstrate why the size of the proposed commitment deserves serious scrutiny.

Textile manufacturing is not software, it is not a hyperscaler and it is not a semiconductor designer with extraordinary intellectual-property economics, because it is a physical manufacturing business requiring continuous spending on machinery, facilities, working capital, maintenance, environmental compliance and modernization, while customers possess considerable bargaining power and can often move orders between countries when pricing becomes more attractive elsewhere.

That combination makes sustained high returns on invested capital difficult to achieve without a genuine cost advantage, differentiated products or unusually strong customer relationships, meaning that the capital invested may be large, but the resulting economic moat could still be very small.

I am also interested in the government’s earlier ambition to increase a reported textile export base from US$4 billion to US$40 billion within ten years, because that would imply approximately 26% compound annual growth, and before such a target becomes an investment assumption, the exact export categories and starting base need to be reconciled with Indonesia’s broader textile and apparel export statistics.

A tenfold increase over a decade is an extraordinary commercial ambition for an established manufacturing industry, and achieving it would require far more than building factories, including securing large international orders, gaining market share from entrenched competitors, maintaining quality and delivery standards, expanding working capital, developing technical capabilities and potentially competing aggressively on price, which brings me to the fourth issue, one that is particularly relevant to our current global macro view.

We are long oil, and we believe energy prices could remain elevated or move even higher.

Textile manufacturing is significantly exposed to energy and petrochemical input costs through synthetic fibers such as polyester, electricity-intensive spinning and weaving, thermal energy used in dyeing and finishing, chemicals, transportation and shipping, and although individual producers have different energy mixes, the broader industry is vulnerable to sustained increases in energy prices.

A stronger dollar and weaker rupiah compound that pressure because imported machinery, chemicals, synthetic inputs and other intermediate products become more expensive in local-currency terms, creating a difficult environment for a newly established textile manufacturing platform, particularly if global customers remain unwilling to accept meaningful selling-price increases because they can source comparable products from multiple countries.

The company could therefore find itself facing rising input costs precisely when it needs to offer aggressively competitive prices to win back export orders, while higher global interest rates introduce an additional problem because working-capital financing becomes more expensive in an industry where companies often need to fund raw materials, inventories, production and receivables long before customers make their final payments.

So even if reported EBITDA eventually looks respectable, investors would still need to examine whether that EBITDA converts into operating cash flow after changes in working capital, and whether the resulting cash flow is sufficient to cover maintenance capital expenditure and earn an acceptable return on the original investment, because revenue growth without free cash flow would not constitute a successful turnaround.

The fifth issue is the tension between modernization and employment creation, because part of the stated rationale for rebuilding Indonesia’s textile industry is understandably to preserve and create jobs, particularly after Sritex’s collapse affected more than 10,000 workers, and that is a legitimate economic and social consideration whose consequences for workers, their families and surrounding communities should not be underestimated.

But commercial competitiveness in modern textile manufacturing increasingly depends on automation, better machinery, greater output per worker and more efficient production processes, meaning there can be tension between maximizing short-term employment and maximizing productivity, and although the two objectives are not necessarily incompatible because a sufficiently competitive factory could expand output and employment simultaneously, they cannot simply be assumed to reinforce each other.

If the investment succeeds primarily by replacing outdated, labor-intensive processes with automated production, the resulting operation may employ fewer workers than the previous industrial structure, while if employment is maintained regardless of commercial productivity, the business may struggle to achieve internationally competitive unit costs.

This is why the investment needs two clearly differentiated performance measures: commercial returns on the capital deployed and separately measured economic benefits from employment, technology transfer and industrial development, because blurring those objectives would make it difficult to distinguish a genuinely profitable industrial investment from an expensive employment-support program.

The Sritex situation is especially sensitive because the welfare of former employees, settlement of outstanding labor entitlements, recovery for creditors and commercial viability of the productive assets are interconnected but distinct questions, and a properly priced asset transaction might preserve economically viable operations and help creditors receive recoveries through the legal process, while a broader corporate rescue could involve a very different allocation of risks and liabilities.

Before any acquisition, I would therefore want an independent assessment of the machinery, property, environmental obligations, legal encumbrances, maintenance backlog, working-capital needs, customer contracts, potential liabilities and estimated replacement cost of the productive assets, while also requiring management to demonstrate precisely why Sritex’s production facilities would become competitive under new ownership when the old operating structure could not sustain itself.

If the explanation is simply stronger capitalization and better management, that is not enough.

Where is the measurable cost advantage? Where are the customers? Where is the productivity improvement? And where is the sustainable return on capital?

This also matters for Danantara’s broader mandate, because Danantara is not merely a restructuring vehicle for troubled state and private enterprises; it is expected to become a sophisticated allocator of Indonesian capital, capable of investing domestically and internationally while generating commercially acceptable financial returns and contributing to long-term national development.

We have already discussed the challenges surrounding Garuda, where a very substantial capital injection has not eliminated the airline’s structural vulnerability to fuel costs, and the same capital-allocation questions arise when evaluating large investments in mature industries with weak profitability and substantial competitive pressure, because capital committed to one opportunity is capital unavailable for another.

If US$6 billion is invested in textile manufacturing and ultimately earns only a 3% return, that would represent US$180 million of annual operating earnings on that simplified capital base, whereas the same amount invested at a hypothetical 10% return would produce US$600 million, implying an annual opportunity-cost gap of approximately US$420 million, and that is before considering the possibility that the textile business requires additional capital injections during difficult operating cycles.

The point is not that every investment must generate software-like margins or that a labor-intensive industry lacks economic value, because manufacturing jobs, export income and industrial know-how can provide significant broader benefits, but those benefits do not eliminate the need to measure capital efficiency, particularly when the institution deploying the capital also has financial obligations and competing investment opportunities.

There is, however, an important distinction that should not be overlooked, because Indonesia does not need to beat China across the entire textile industry to develop commercially successful textile businesses, and there may be viable opportunities in specialized technical textiles, industrial fabrics, uniforms, functional materials, selected export niches and manufacturing segments where Indonesia can offer quality, speed, traceability, dependable delivery or favorable trade access.

The global movement toward supply-chain diversification could also create opportunities for manufacturers able to satisfy international buyers’ requirements, particularly if they can operate within competitive industrial clusters and maintain attractive landed costs, while the acquisition of selected Sritex assets at genuinely distressed valuations could be commercially attractive if those assets are modern enough, legally transferable, supported by credible customer orders and capable of generating sufficient returns without relying on indefinite financial support.

But that is a very different investment thesis from assuming that consolidating several struggling textile companies under a new state-owned holding structure will somehow create the scale economies required to compete with China, because scale is valuable only when it improves unit economics, vertical integration is valuable only when it reduces total delivered cost, improves quality or strengthens reliability, modernization is valuable only when the productivity gains justify the capital expenditure, and consolidation is valuable only when the combined business becomes economically stronger than the companies were separately.

Combining several weak businesses does not automatically create one strong business.

Ultimately, the financial test should be quite straightforward: whether the final business plan can demonstrate competitive unit costs, contracted or credibly forecast demand, adequate capacity utilization, positive operating cash flow, sustainable free cash flow and an acceptable ROIC under conservative assumptions for energy prices, exchange rates and selling prices, while a particularly important stress test would be whether the business remains commercially viable without preferential financing, artificially favorable input prices or guaranteed purchases that merely shift the economic burden to another part of the state sector.

The acquisition price matters enormously, but so does the amount of additional capital needed to make the acquired assets productive, because a factory purchased for a very low price can still become an expensive investment if it requires substantial modernization, suffers prolonged operating losses or cannot secure adequate demand.

So my concern is fundamentally about the economics of the proposed industrial platform rather than the desirability of preserving textile employment or domestic manufacturing capacity, because the objective of rebuilding Indonesia’s textile competitiveness is understandable, but there is a very large difference between creating a globally competitive textile industry and recapitalizing companies that previously failed to compete.

The first requires enduring improvements in productivity, technology, infrastructure, energy efficiency and customer access, while the second requires money, and money alone is not a competitive advantage.

China’s textile industry was not built merely by injecting capital into factories. It was built through decades of developing industrial capabilities, supplier networks, technology, infrastructure, productivity and export relationships.

That is the benchmark against which any ambitious Indonesian textile expansion ultimately needs to be tested, and if Danantara can acquire selected assets cheaply, introduce commercially meaningful technology, rebuild an efficient production network and demonstrate satisfactory returns on invested capital, there could be a viable investment case.

But if the commercial thesis rests mainly on buying distressed factories, combining them into a large state-owned group and assuming that financial scale will somehow overcome the industry’s structural disadvantages, the risk of disappointing returns and recurring capital requirements would be substantial.

You can acquire Sritex’s factories. You cannot acquire China’s manufacturing ecosystem.

And if the plan is to compete with China in mass-market textiles primarily through a larger balance sheet, my closing question is simple:

Good luck beating China. What exactly is the competitive advantage?

text:
📌 RVN: From outage to empty shelves

Sunday afternoon. Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall. First an IT incident. Then a cybersecurity incident. Systems switched off as a precaution.

Monday. App, site, customer service, delivery down. Bonus card stutters. Shelf labels show last week’s offer. Distribution centres at a standstill.

Tuesday. The shelves. Fresh is gone. Ahold: no indication that customer data was stolen. Some of the centres are running again. Site and delivery not yet. Experts: almost certainly an attack. A company of this size does not just switch the chain off.

Wednesday. Still no name. No ransom note. The shift stands. From outage to empty shelves in three days.

📌 The same week, a different method

France. Hackers take over the cooling in hundreds of supermarkets. 50 degrees. Food gone, fires here and there. Intermarché speaks of tens of millions in a single day. Software partly without updates. Paris has opened a criminal investigation. NCSC: no link with Ahold.

Japan. A wave, not a decree. Suppliers, cloud, rail. Tens of millions of records. This week Arcadia as well, up to 3.1 million possible leaks at a service for municipalities. A party official called it a state of emergency in cyberspace. It is not a decision. The leaks are.

Russia, a little earlier. Drones on three Yandex data centres. The hall itself wrecked. Taxis and banking gone.

📌 What it shows

Food, data and transport hang on systems you can switch off, take over or hit. The backup took over nowhere.

At Ahold the word is the story. Incident. Switched off as a precaution. Empty shelves. The word attack comes from outside. The company does not say it hard yet. The tomato does.

📌 OIM way out

Do not turn every outage into a war.  
Do not leave “IT problem” standing when distribution has stopped.

Do: what was down, for how long, what came back.  
Three countries, three methods, one lesson. Whoever does not have the second line, does not have the shelves.

𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐲𝐨𝐮

From outage to empty shelves in three days…  
how much backup did the shop where you get your food have?

text:
Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 And since honesty is rare in my politics, allow me to confess a few things.

The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that the war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything, and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me up in refugee camps for generations, so that I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I'm still stateless. Turns out rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said, "Let's give it a try." It gave me autonomy. Guns for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in almost 20 years. Hamas kills dissidents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother."

But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurd. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological powerhouse, desert farms, dusty cities. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said, "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of showcasing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I displayed only the culture of the sword.Anger, extremism, and bloodshed. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to the Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I feign surprise when the Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced that I don't want coexistence at all.

Accountability. I blame Israel for everything. Always. Do my leaders steal billions? Blame Israel. Does Hamas fire rockets from hospitals? Blame Israel. Do I glorify death more than life? Blame Israel. Accountability is not my strong suit.

I am Palestinian. I could have built a nation, many times over. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

text:
Part 4 

Families already living in the mining towns also paid a price. As Wismut expanded, local residents were sometimes compelled to vacate homes for the company’s use. Complaints to the Soviet management brought little relief. German officials handled many of the resulting disputes, and some protesting residents faced intimidation. The state eventually organized thousands of relocations to accommodate the growing industry. Compensation arrangements existed for some property owners, but that did not mean residents could freely refuse displacement.

These abuses were not completely hidden from German political leaders. Reports describing forced recruitment, deadly accidents, violent Soviet supervisors, and workers fleeing the mines reached the leadership of the Socialist Unity Party. Karlsch identifies Wilhelm Pieck, Walter Ulbricht, Fritz Selbmann, and other senior officials among those who had access to information about the conditions. One report from August 1949 described assignment to Aue as among the worst punishments a worker could experience and accused official newspaper and radio commentary of misrepresenting reality.

That evidence establishes knowledge of serious abuses. It does not prove that Pieck, Ulbricht, or Selbmann personally ordered every beating, arrest, or dangerous assignment. Soviet management retained dominant authority over Wismut during the occupation years, and German leaders had limited direct control over its operations. Nevertheless, the surviving reports undermine any suggestion that the political leadership was simply unaware of the conditions under which uranium was being extracted.

Maltsev also exercised authority over labor discipline. On March 25, 1949, he issued Order No. 66, directing stricter action against workers accused of absenteeism or pretending to be ill. The order belongs to a broader pattern in which production targets and discipline were prioritized even as workers complained about health risks and dangerous conditions. In a mining industry already suffering from inadequate medical safeguards, the distinction between a worker avoiding duty and a worker genuinely becoming ill could have grave consequences.

Yet the history contains an important complication. Wismut was not staffed entirely by men forced into the mines. As the company expanded, it offered unusually high wages, additional food allocations, and privileges that attracted voluntary workers, including refugees, displaced people, and returning soldiers. By the early 1950s, wages were substantially higher than those in many other East German industries. Some workers developed lasting careers and strong occupational identities within the enterprise. The early coercive recruitment system and the later attraction of better-paid employment were both real.

By 1950–1951, the workforce had reached approximately 200,000 people, according to Wismut’s official historical chronology. The scale was staggering for an enterprise whose output was directed toward a foreign state’s strategic requirements. Entire towns and regional economies became dependent on the mines. Shops, housing, transport, medical facilities, and local administrations were reshaped around the company’s demands. Wismut became what historians describe as a Staat im Staate a state within a state.

The secrecy was central to its power. Information about uranium production, security arrangements, workplace conditions, and environmental hazards was restricted. Soviet security services exercised influence within the enterprise, while East German state security later became deeply involved in personnel screening and surveillance. Ordinary residents had little ability to investigate the consequences of the industry transforming their communities. Even some East German officials lacked access to basic information about Wismut’s operations.
