text:
If Paul had intended to replace Jesus Christ with himself, we would expect his writings to encourage believers to establish their faith around his personal identity.

But Paul repeatedly condemned that very conduct.

1 Corinthians 1:13 (KJV)

«Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?»

Paul's question leaves no room for confusion.

He was not crucified for the Church.

Jesus Christ was.

Paul did not want believers identifying themselves as belonging to him instead of the Lord.

He also explained the proper place of ministers within the Church.

1 Corinthians 3:5–7 (KJV)

«Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?

I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.

So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.»

Paul described himself and Apollos as ministers through whom people believed.

He attributed the spiritual increase to God.

He did not claim that ministers were the source of salvation.

And he expressly reminded the Corinthians that they belonged to Christ.

1 Corinthians 3:21–23 (KJV)

«Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours;

Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours;

And ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's.»

"Ye are Christ's."

Those words summarize Paul's understanding of the Church.

The believers did not belong to Paul, Peter, or Apollos as competing religious possessions.

They belonged to Jesus Christ.

The testimony of the other apostles must also be considered.

James, Peter, and John extended fellowship to Paul and Barnabas, recognizing the grace given to them.

The Jerusalem Council recorded cooperation concerning the Gospel among Gentile believers.

And Peter's second epistle called Paul a beloved brother.

These passages do not suggest that every apostle always agreed on every matter of conduct. Galatians 2 records a genuine confrontation between Paul and Peter.

But the existence of a disagreement does not prove that the men preached different saviours.

Paul's confrontation concerned conduct that was inconsistent with the Gospel's recognition of Gentile believers.

His concern was that the truth of the Gospel be reflected in the conduct of those who professed it.

Jesus taught that false prophets would be recognized by their fruits.

When we examine Paul's ministry, we should therefore ask what his life and teachings actually produced.

He preached Jesus Christ crucified and risen.

He called people to repentance and faith.

He instructed believers to love and forgive one another.

He condemned idolatry, fornication, greed, hatred, drunkenness, and division.

He warned against false teachers.

He defended the resurrection.

He suffered imprisonment, beatings, rejection, and persecution.

He cared for the churches and encouraged believers to remain faithful through tribulation.

None of this means that Paul was a sinless man. He never claimed to be.

But the New Testament presents a consistent testimony of a man transformed by the mercy of Jesus Christ and devoted to His Gospel.

Near the end of his ministry, Paul wrote:

2 Timothy 4:7–8 (KJV)

«I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:

Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.»

Paul's hope remained in Jesus Christ.

He did not claim that the Church should worship him after his departure.

He looked toward the Lord, the righteous judge.

And the crown he anticipated was not reserved for himself alone, but for all who love the appearing of Jesus Christ.

That is the testimony of a faithful servant.

Several passages deserve closer examination because they are frequently used to accuse Paul of contradicting the original apostles or abandoning the Scriptures of Israel.

We must begin by recognizing that Paul did not reject Moses and the prophets.

He repeatedly appealed to them as witnesses concerning Jesus Christ.

Acts 24:14 (KJV)

«But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:»

Paul openly confessed that he believed the Law and the Prophets.

He did not declare that the Scriptures were false.

He proclaimed that their testimony concerning God's saving purpose was fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

Romans 3:21–22 (KJV)

«But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets;

Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference:»

Notice that Paul described righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ as being witnessed by the Law and Prophets.

He did not present it as something disconnected from the earlier Scriptures.

Jesus Himself taught that Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms testified concerning Him.

The distinction is between recognizing the divine testimony of the Law and requiring Gentile believers to keep the entire Mosaic covenant as a condition of salvation.

This distinction is especially important in Acts 21.

James and the elders told Paul that reports were circulating concerning his teaching about Jewish customs.

They proposed that he participate in purification arrangements to demonstrate that those reports did not accurately represent his conduct.

Acts 21:23–24 (KJV)

«Do therefore this that we say to thee: We have four men which have a vow on them;

Them take, and purify thyself with them, and be at charges with them, that they may shave their heads: and all may know that those things, whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing; but that thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law.»

Paul agreed to participate.

But the elders immediately reaffirmed the decision concerning Gentile believers.

Acts 21:25 (KJV)

«As touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled, and from fornication.»

The distinction remained.

Paul's participation in a Jewish purification practice did not mean that Gentiles were required to observe the entire Mosaic Law.

Nor did his teaching concerning Gentile liberty mean that Jewish believers were forbidden from observing every ancestral custom.

Paul explained his missionary approach elsewhere.

1 Corinthians 9:22–23 (KJV)

«To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.

And this I do for the gospel's sake, that I might be partaker thereof with you.»

Paul adapted his conduct to different audiences for the sake of the Gospel.

His purpose was not to deceive people about salvation, but to remove unnecessary obstacles while proclaiming Jesus Christ.

Galatians 2 is another passage frequently used against him.

Paul recorded confronting Peter at Antioch because Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers when certain men arrived.

Galatians 2:11–14 (KJV)

«But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.

For before that certain came from James, he did eat with the Gentiles: but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision.

And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation.

But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?»

Paul did not confront Peter because he rejected Jesus Christ or wanted to establish a competing Gospel.

He confronted Peter because his conduct was inconsistent with the truth they had already recognized concerning Gentile believers.

Peter himself had testified in Acts 15 that God purified Gentile hearts by faith.

The disagreement concerned conduct that undermined fellowship.

It is also important to examine Paul's teaching concerning marriage in First Corinthians 7.

Paul distinguished between a command already given by the Lord and his own apostolic instruction concerning particular circumstances.

1 Corinthians 7:10–12 (KJV)

«And unto the married I command, yet not I, but the Lord, Let not the wife depart from her husband:

But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife.

But to the rest speak I, not the Lord: If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away.»

Paul recognized the Lord's teaching concerning marriage.

He then addressed a circumstance involving a believing spouse married to an unbeliever.

When he said, "But to the rest speak I, not the Lord," he was distinguishing the Lord's recorded teaching from the instruction he was providing for that situation.

He was not declaring that Jesus had been wrong.

He was applying Christian instruction to circumstances arising within the Church.

These passages demonstrate the importance of reading the Scriptures carefully.

An accusation may appear persuasive when one sentence is isolated, but the surrounding context often reveals a very different meaning.

And throughout these accounts, Paul remains devoted to the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

Paul's distinction between a direct command of the Lord and his own judgment appears elsewhere in First Corinthians 7.

1 Corinthians 7:25 (KJV)

«Now concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord: yet I give my judgment, as one that hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful.»

Paul did not pretend that every instruction he offered was a direct quotation from Jesus' earthly ministry.

He carefully distinguished between what the Lord had expressly taught and the apostolic counsel he was giving concerning particular circumstances.

That transparency should not be transformed into an accusation of deception.

He was addressing practical questions involving marriage, remaining unmarried, and the circumstances facing believers.

Another disputed passage appears in First Corinthians 14.

1 Corinthians 14:34–35 (KJV)

«Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.

And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church.»

These verses occur within a chapter addressing order in congregational worship.

Paul discussed tongues, interpretation, prophecy, and conduct within the assembly.

Earlier in the same letter, however, he acknowledged women praying and prophesying.

1 Corinthians 11:5 (KJV)

«But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven.»

Therefore, the instructions in chapter 14 should not be examined as though chapter 11 did not exist.

Christians have differed concerning whether the restriction in chapter 14 addresses disruptive questioning, particular forms of congregational speech, the evaluation of prophecy, or a broader restriction.

There are also textual questions discussed by scholars concerning the placement and transmission of these verses.

These matters deserve careful examination rather than careless assumptions.

But Paul's recognition of faithful women throughout his ministry is undeniable within the biblical record.

He commended Phoebe, acknowledged Priscilla, and recognized women who laboured in the Gospel.

His instructions concerning congregational order should not be used to erase those testimonies.

First Timothy 2 is another frequently disputed passage.

1 Timothy 2:11–14 (KJV)

«Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection.

But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.

For Adam was first formed, then Eve.

And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression.»

Paul grounded his argument in the creation account.

Christians differ concerning the precise application of these instructions to teaching and authority within the Church.

But the passage does not establish that women are excluded from salvation, spiritual inheritance, prayer, or faithful service.

Paul also wrote:

Galatians 3:26–28 (KJV)

«For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.

For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.»

Paul affirmed the unity of believers in Jesus Christ.

That unity must be considered alongside his instructions concerning responsibilities and order within the Church.

The fact that a passage requires careful interpretation does not establish that its author was a false apostle.

Another accusation concerns Paul's teaching about the return of Jesus Christ.

In First Thessalonians 4, he used the expression "we which are alive and remain."

1 Thessalonians 4:15–17 (KJV)

«For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep.

For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.»

Paul was comforting believers who were concerned about those who had died.

He assured them that the dead in Christ would rise and that believers would be gathered to the Lord.

He did not provide a calendar date for that event.

And in Second Thessalonians 2, he warned against being deceived concerning the Day of Christ.

A distinction must therefore be maintained between expectation, readiness, and an explicit prophetic deadline.

Paul's message was to remain faithful and prepared for the coming of Jesus Christ.

The resurrection and the gathering of believers to the Lord remained the foundation of that hope.

The future resurrection is one of the clearest examples of Paul's agreement with the teachings of Jesus Christ.

Jesus promised that He would raise believers at the last day.

Paul proclaimed the resurrection of the dead at the coming of the Lord.

1 Corinthians 15:20–23 (KJV)

«But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.

For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead.

For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming.»

Paul did not teach that the resurrection was merely a past spiritual experience.

He proclaimed a future resurrection associated with the coming of Jesus Christ.

He also warned against those who claimed that the resurrection had already occurred.

2 Timothy 2:17–18 (KJV)

«And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;

Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some.»

Paul recognized that denying the future resurrection endangered the faith of believers.

His teaching preserved the hope proclaimed by Jesus Christ.

Another accusation concerns grace.

Some suggest that Paul taught believers they could continue living in sin because salvation was not earned through the works of the Mosaic Law.

But Paul expressly rejected that conclusion.

Romans 6:1–2 (KJV)

«What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?

God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?»

Romans 6:15–16 (KJV)

«What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.

Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?»

Paul did not excuse unrighteousness.

He taught that believers must turn away from sin and walk according to the Spirit.

He proclaimed salvation through faith in Jesus Christ while insisting that genuine faith must not become an excuse for the works of the flesh.

This is not a contradiction.

It is the distinction between attempting to earn salvation through works of the Law and living a transformed life through the grace and Spirit of God.

The Jerusalem Council concluded that Gentile believers were not required to receive circumcision and keep the entire Mosaic Law as a condition of salvation.

Paul defended that same liberty.

Galatians 5:1 (KJV)

«Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.»

But Paul immediately warned that Christian liberty must never be used for sinful conduct.

Galatians 5:13–14 (KJV)

«For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.

For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.»

The Gospel of grace and the commandment of love belong together.

Paul did not preach freedom from righteousness.

He proclaimed freedom in Jesus Christ, accompanied by a life of love, holiness, and obedience through the Spirit.

And when we examine the entire testimony concerning Paul, from his former persecution of the Church to his final declarations of faithfulness, a consistent picture emerges.

Paul was a persecutor who received mercy.

He encountered the risen Jesus Christ.

He was identified by the Lord as a chosen vessel.

He received fellowship from believers who had previously feared him.

He preached Jesus Christ in synagogues and among Gentiles.

He participated in the life of the Church.

He was sent forth through the work of the Holy Ghost.

He proclaimed repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ.

He defended the resurrection.

He instructed believers to love and forgive one another.

He warned against false apostles and deceptive doctrines.

He upheld holiness and righteousness.

He recognized the ministries of other apostles.

He suffered persecution and imprisonment.

And he continued proclaiming Jesus Christ.

1 Corinthians 15:10–11 (KJV)

«But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.

Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed.»

Paul gave the glory to God.

He attributed his ministry to grace.

And he recognized the shared Gospel proclaimed by the apostles.

This was not a man attempting to establish another foundation for the Church.

He continually pointed believers toward Jesus Christ.

I want to conclude this study by returning to the purpose for which it was written.

I am not defending Paul because I believe that he was above correction, above examination, or greater than the other apostles.

I am defending Paul because the Scriptures present him as a faithful servant of our Lord Jesus Christ.

His former persecution of the Church was a terrible wrong, and Paul never attempted to conceal it.

Instead, he testified concerning the mercy that Jesus Christ had shown him.

His conversion did not produce a man who exalted himself above Jesus.

It produced a man who surrendered his former religious standing, endured persecution, and devoted his life to proclaiming the very Lord he had once opposed.

And what did Paul gain from this ministry?

He gained suffering, imprisonment, rejection, hardship, and the responsibility of caring for the churches.

Yet he continued.

Not because he believed himself to be the foundation of the Church, but because Jesus Christ was the foundation.

1 Corinthians 2:2 (KJV)

«For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.»

1 Corinthians 3:11 (KJV)

«For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.»

2 Corinthians 4:5 (KJV)

«For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.»

These declarations summarize the very heart of Paul's ministry.

He preached Christ.

He served Christ.

He suffered for Christ.

And he called believers to follow Christ.

We should not confuse difficult passages with evidence of deception. We should not isolate a sentence from its surrounding context and use it to condemn an entire ministry.

We must examine the whole testimony of Scripture.

And when we do, we find a man whose life was transformed by the mercy of Jesus Christ and whose ministry was devoted to proclaiming Him.

Paul was not the Saviour.

Jesus Christ is the Saviour.

Paul was not the foundation.

Jesus Christ is the foundation.

Paul was not the head of the Church.

Jesus Christ is the head of the Church.

And Paul himself taught these very truths.

Galatians 2:20 (KJV)

«I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.»

This was Paul's testimony.

His life belonged to Jesus Christ.

And as he approached the end of his ministry, he could write:

2 Timothy 4:7–8 (KJV)

«I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:

Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.»

Paul finished his course looking toward the Lord Jesus Christ.

And that is where our attention must remain.

We do not worship Paul.

We do not place his name above the name of Jesus.

We recognize him as a brother who was called by the Lord, transformed by His mercy, and used to proclaim His Gospel among the nations.

May we learn from his faithfulness, his humility, his endurance, and his love for the Church.

And may we never forget the Lord whom Paul preached.

Jesus Christ is our Saviour, our foundation, our hope, and our coming King.

text:
As Paul's ministry continued, he became increasingly aware of the dangers facing the churches. His concern was not merely that believers would remember him, but that they would remain faithful to the Gospel after his departure.

In Acts 20, Paul addressed the elders of Ephesus and reminded them of his conduct among them.

Acts 20:20–21 (KJV)

«And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,

Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.»

Paul identified repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ as central to his preaching.

He also warned the elders that false teachers would arise.

Acts 20:28–30 (KJV)

«Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.

For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.

Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.»

Notice the seriousness of this warning.

Paul described the Church as belonging to God. He warned against men who would draw disciples after themselves.

That is the very conduct Paul is sometimes accused of practicing. Yet his own teaching condemned it.

When Paul returned to Jerusalem, he met with James and the elders. They heard what God had accomplished among the Gentiles and glorified the Lord.

Acts 21 also records concerns about reports circulating among Jewish believers concerning Paul's teaching about Moses and ancestral customs. The elders proposed a course of action intended to answer those reports, and Paul participated.

But the same discussion reaffirmed the decision concerning Gentile believers.

Acts 21:25 (KJV)

«As touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled, and from fornication.»

The distinction remained. Jewish believers could continue certain ancestral customs without making those practices conditions of salvation for Gentiles.

Paul's participation in a purification practice did not mean he had abandoned the Gospel of grace.

His arrest followed amid accusations and unrest. But imprisonment did not silence his testimony.

Paul appeared before governors and kings, including Felix, Festus, and Agrippa.

Before Felix, he declared:

Acts 24:14–15 (KJV)

«But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:

And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.»

Paul did not proclaim another god.

He identified the God he worshipped as the God of his fathers. He affirmed the Law and the Prophets and testified concerning the resurrection.

Before Agrippa, he explained that his preaching fulfilled the testimony of Moses and the prophets.

Acts 26:22–23 (KJV)

«Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come:

That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles.»

Paul's defense was rooted in the Scriptures.

He proclaimed the suffering and resurrection of Christ and the light of salvation reaching the Gentiles.

His journey toward Rome was also marked by hardship. Acts 27 records a dangerous voyage and shipwreck, yet Paul continued to testify concerning God's promises.

When Acts reaches its conclusion, Paul is in Rome, receiving those who came to him and proclaiming Jesus Christ.

Acts 28:30–31 (KJV)

«And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,

Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.»

Consider the significance of this conclusion.

The book of Acts does not leave us with Paul preaching his own kingdom.

It leaves us with Paul preaching the kingdom of God and teaching concerning the Lord Jesus Christ.

That was his message throughout his ministry, and that was the message he continued to proclaim in Rome.

The testimony concerning Paul does not end with the historical account recorded in Acts. His epistles provide further evidence of what he taught, how he understood the Gospel, and what he expected from believers.

When examining these writings, we must remember that they were addressed to churches and individuals facing particular circumstances. Paul often answered questions, corrected errors, confronted sin, and encouraged believers to remain faithful.

His letter to the Romans presents the universal problem of sin and the righteousness revealed through Jesus Christ.

Romans 3:23–24 (KJV)

«For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;

Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:»

Paul did not teach that certain people could earn salvation through their own righteousness while others required grace. He declared that all had sinned and that redemption was found in Jesus Christ.

But he also rejected the suggestion that grace gave permission to continue in sin.

Romans 6:1–2 (KJV)

«What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?

God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?»

Paul's Gospel did not excuse unrighteousness. It called believers to a new life.

In his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul confronted divisions within the Church. Some believers identified themselves with Paul, others with Apollos, and others with Peter.

Paul challenged that conduct directly.

1 Corinthians 1:12–13 (KJV)

«Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ.

Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?»

What an extraordinary answer to those who accuse Paul of seeking his own followers.

He asked whether Paul had been crucified for them.

Of course not. Jesus Christ was crucified for them.

Paul did not encourage the Church to divide itself into factions bearing the names of ministers. He condemned that behavior.

The same letter contains his teaching concerning love in chapter 13 and the resurrection in chapter 15. These subjects demonstrate his concern for both the conduct and hope of believers.

In Second Corinthians, Paul described the hardships of ministry and the sufficiency of Christ's grace.

2 Corinthians 12:9–10 (KJV)

«And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.»

Paul did not present himself as a man whose natural greatness made him worthy of worship. He acknowledged his weakness and attributed his strength to Jesus Christ.

His letter to the Galatians addresses attempts to impose circumcision and the Mosaic Law upon Gentile believers as requirements for salvation.

Paul defended the liberty believers had received through Christ.

But he also declared that his own life belonged entirely to Jesus.

Galatians 2:20 (KJV)

«I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.»

Paul did not describe himself as the source of salvation.

He declared that Christ lived in him.

He also warned believers not to misuse their liberty.

Galatians 5:13–14 (KJV)

«For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.

For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.»

The Gospel of grace was never a license for selfishness, hatred, or unrighteousness.

Paul taught that believers were to serve one another through love.

And when we examine Romans, Corinthians, and Galatians together, the same pattern emerges. Paul proclaimed salvation through Jesus Christ, condemned sin, rejected religious pride, defended the resurrection, and commanded believers to walk in love.

That is the substance of his ministry, not the invention of another religion.

Paul's letter to the Ephesians continues the same testimony concerning salvation through Jesus Christ and the unity of His Church.

Ephesians 2:8–10 (KJV)

«For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

Not of works, lest any man should boast.

For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.»

Notice that Paul did not end his teaching with salvation by grace. He continued by declaring that believers are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.

Salvation is not presented as the achievement of human pride. It is the gift of God, producing a life transformed through Jesus Christ.

Paul also emphasized unity within the Church.

Ephesians 4:4–6 (KJV)

«There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;

One Lord, one faith, one baptism,

One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.»

Paul did not proclaim competing bodies, competing lords, or competing gospels. He called believers into unity through Jesus Christ.

In Philippians, he encouraged believers to demonstrate the humility of the Lord.

Philippians 2:5–8 (KJV)

«Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:

Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:

But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:

And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.»

Paul directed the Church toward the example of Jesus Christ, who humbled Himself and became obedient unto death.

That is not a message of self-exaltation.

It is a call to humility and service.

Colossians provides another important testimony concerning the identity and supremacy of Jesus Christ.

Colossians 1:18–20 (KJV)

«And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.

For it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell;

And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.»

Paul expressly declared that Jesus Christ is the head of the Church.

He did not claim that position for himself.

The preeminence belongs to Jesus.

And in his first letter to the Thessalonians, Paul encouraged believers to remain faithful while awaiting the return of the Lord.

1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 (KJV)

«For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:

Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.»

Paul proclaimed the return of Jesus Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and the gathering of believers to Him.

He did not teach the Church to anticipate Paul's return or to place its hope in another saviour.

Throughout these letters, the same truths appear repeatedly: salvation through Christ, unity within His body, humility, holiness, love, and hope in His coming.

The more carefully we examine Paul's writings, the more clearly we see the Lord whom he served.

Paul's second letter to the Thessalonians is especially important when examining his teaching concerning the return of Jesus Christ.

Some have accused Paul of making a failed prophecy, while others have used his writings to establish interpretations that overlook the warnings he gave concerning deception and events preceding the Day of Christ.

But Paul explicitly instructed believers not to be troubled by premature claims.

2 Thessalonians 2:1–3 (KJV)

«Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him,

That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.

Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;»

Paul connected the coming of Jesus Christ with the gathering of believers to Him.

He also warned that the Day of Christ would not come before the events he described.

This agrees with Jesus' warnings in Matthew 24 concerning deception, tribulation, and His coming.

Paul was not encouraging believers to accept every prophetic claim. He was warning them to remain grounded in the truth.

His pastoral letters demonstrate the same concern for sound doctrine and faithful conduct.

In First Timothy, Paul instructed Timothy concerning prayer, teaching, the qualifications of ministers, and the responsibility of setting a godly example.

1 Timothy 4:12–13 (KJV)

«Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.

Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.»

Paul did not instruct Timothy to establish authority through intimidation or personal pride. He told him to be an example in conduct, love, faith, and purity.

He also warned against those who would depart from the faith and follow deceptive teachings.

In Second Timothy, Paul emphasized the importance of remaining faithful to the Scriptures.

2 Timothy 3:14–17 (KJV)

«But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;

And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:

That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.»

Paul did not tell Timothy to abandon the Scriptures or replace them with his personal opinions.

He declared their value for doctrine, correction, and instruction in righteousness.

And he connected their saving testimony with faith in Jesus Christ.

His letter to Titus likewise emphasized sound doctrine and godly living.

Titus 2:11–14 (KJV)

«For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,

Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;

Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;

Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.»

This passage directly challenges the accusation that Paul's Gospel encouraged lawlessness.

Paul declared that grace teaches believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.

He called them to live soberly, righteously, and godly while awaiting the appearing of Jesus Christ.

Notice also how he identified Jesus as our great God and Saviour.

Paul was not preaching a lesser saviour or another god.

His testimony concerning Christ remained central even while addressing practical responsibilities within the Church.

Taken together, these letters reveal a minister concerned with preserving the Gospel, protecting believers from deception, instructing ministers to live faithfully, and encouraging the Church to remain prepared for the coming of Jesus Christ.

Paul's message was not centered upon the authority of man.

It was centered upon the Lord Jesus Christ and the Scriptures that testify concerning Him.

Paul's short letter to Philemon provides another revealing example of his character and teaching.

The letter concerns Onesimus, whom Paul describes as having become dear to him in the Lord. Rather than simply demanding obedience, Paul appealed to Philemon through love.

Philemon 8–10 (KJV)

«Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient,

Yet for love's sake I rather beseech thee, being such an one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds:»

Paul urged Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother.

Philemon 15–16 (KJV)

«For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever;

Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?»

This letter demonstrates Paul's concern for mercy, reconciliation, and the transformation of relationships through Jesus Christ.

It also provides a useful example of how he exercised influence. He could appeal to his apostolic authority, but in this situation he deliberately appealed through love.

And love is one of the clearest areas of agreement between Jesus and Paul.

Jesus called people to believe in Him.

John 3:16 (KJV)

«For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.»

Paul proclaimed justification through faith in Jesus Christ.

Romans 5:1 (KJV)

«Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:»

There is no competing object of faith.

Jesus called people to believe in Him, and Paul proclaimed salvation through Him.

Jesus also called people to repentance.

Mark 1:15 (KJV)

«And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.»

Paul proclaimed the same necessity.

Acts 20:21 (KJV)

«Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.»

Paul did not teach that repentance was unnecessary or that believers could continue living in rebellion against God.

He called both Jews and Gentiles to repentance and faith.

Jesus connected love for Him with obedience.

John 14:15 (KJV)

«If ye love me, keep my commandments.»

Paul likewise instructed believers to reject the works of the flesh and walk according to the Spirit.

Romans 8:12–14 (KJV)

«Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh.

For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.

For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.»

Paul did not teach that faith in Jesus removed the responsibility to live righteously.

He taught that believers must be led by the Spirit of God.

We must distinguish between attempting to earn salvation through the works of the Mosaic Law and obeying Jesus Christ through faith and the power of the Holy Ghost.

These are not identical questions.

Paul opposed justification through the works of the Law, but he did not oppose holiness, righteousness, or obedience to Christ.

When the teachings of Jesus and Paul are examined together, we repeatedly find agreement concerning faith, repentance, obedience, mercy, and love.

The Gospel calls sinners to Jesus Christ, and those who receive Him are called to walk in newness of life.

California-based Harbor Associates bought it in 2018, later refinanced with an ~$18.6 million loan from Thorofare Capital (2022). When the loan matured, the owner could not pay it off, refinance, or sell at a high enough price (offers received were only in the $2.3–5 million range). A judge ruled it in default; Thorofare foreclosed and acquired it at auction for $6 million. The planned conversion to ~116 apartments (which had conditional city/DDA financing of $17 million that was never disbursed) collapsed as a result.

100% vacancy in a severely depressed downtown office market. 
The last Symes tenant left around March 2026. Downtown Denver office vacancy has been extremely high (around 38%+ in the CBD in recent quarters, far above suburban or Class A figures), driven by remote/hybrid work, tenant downsizing, and limited demand for older buildings. Values across many downtown offices have fallen sharply; this is a market-wide issue, not unique to Symes.

Dog in need of rescue:
Edmond, OK

Neighbors, I am urgently seeking your help and advice...  There is a pregnant, female dog tied up near Enoon Cafe (207 SW 25th St). She is newly pregnant, just started showing. I bring food every so often. There is a homeless group there and one person claims to own her. That dog never leaves that leash. I don't have a picture, but she closely resembles a mixed breed, possibly 40 pounds max. I visited on Saturday and offered to help the dog when she gives birth, to help find a rescue, etc.   The homeless person said, "if you help me, I will help her." This dog was INFESTED with flies. I am not exaggerating when I say she had at least 30 flies swarming her. She cries when you approach. She was laying in her own filth. I gave her a bone, and she tried to find any clean place to sit in her small radius to enjoy that bone. I genuinely do not know what to do. The woman who owns her claims to have had her since she was young. I am witnessing animal abuse.   I hesitate to call animal control because I do not want her to be euthanized. I am willing to pay the homeless person to take her away, to a foster, but I know how insulting that can be to someone, when all they have is their dog. When you drive by, you can hardly see her. She is tied up right next to a shopping cart, which is sitting right next to their couch. If you are standing outside of Enoon cafe, look to your left (like your 10pm). That's where she is. Please, I need advice. How can we help her?

text:
My post about France went viral. Thousands of likes. Many Americans told me: "Democrats aren't socialists. America will never be France." I want to answer that seriously, step by step.

Start with a simple observation. Look at what has gotten cheaper in America over the last 25 years: TVs, phones, software, clothes, toys. Now look at what has exploded: college tuition, healthcare, childcare, housing.

What separates the two lists? The first lives in competitive markets. The second is exactly where government is most involved: subsidies, mandates, licensing, zoning, regulation.

College. Washington lends students almost unlimited money. Universities know the money will always come, so they raise tuition and hire more administrators. The student pays the bill for twenty years. More government money, higher prices.

Housing. Why can't a nurse buy a home in the city where she works? Not because of capitalism. Because of zoning laws, permits, environmental reviews, years of procedure to build a single building. The most expensive places to live in America are the places where it's hardest to build. When building is nearly illegal, prices explode.

Healthcare. The patient almost never sees the price. A third party pays, regulations limit who can compete, and costs climb year after year with no one able to say no.

So here is the trap. The problems you suffer from are not the failure of free markets. They are the places where the market has already been replaced by the state. And the solution you're being offered is more of the same.

That's the Trojan horse. It always works the same way. A real problem. A generous-sounding promise. A program that makes things worse. Then the failure of that program becomes the argument for the next one. People who lived under communism in Poland learned to recognize the lie and the mask the lie wears. The lie never presents itself as a lie. It presents itself as compassion.

In France we are at the end of that road. Debt we can never repay. Young people who can't afford a home. Our best people leaving. And every few years our cities burn. Nobody voted for this. They voted for one more generous promise, fifty years in a row.

If you're a Republican, share this with the Democrat in your life. Not to win an argument. To start a conversation.

If you're a Democrat, I'm not asking you to switch teams. I'm asking you to look at the pattern. Wherever the state took over, life became unaffordable. Don't fix the failures of government with more government.

Stay American. Ask for less state, not more.

text:
I’m French. I want to talk to Americans who are about to vote Democrat. Not to insult you. To warn you.

I come from your future.

In France we did everything your progressive politicians promise. Free healthcare, free college, generous welfare, strong unions, heavy regulation, high taxes on the rich, a state that takes care of everything. Public spending close to 57% of GDP, one of the highest on the planet. On paper, it’s the dream.

Here’s what it looks like from the inside. France hasn’t passed a balanced budget since 1974. Our debt is above 3,300 billion euros. Interest on that debt is becoming one of the biggest items in the national budget. Our hospitals are collapsing despite record funding. Our schools rank lower every year. Young people with degrees can’t afford an apartment in the city they were born in. Our best engineers leave for London, Zurich and San Francisco. And the rich you wanted to tax? They left too, and took the jobs with them.

The promise was protection. The result is stagnation.

The worst part is that nobody in France voted for decline. Every single step sounded generous, compassionate, reasonable. One more program. One more regulation. One more tax to fund it. Each step alone makes sense. Fifty years of them, and you wake up in a country that can no longer build a nuclear plant on time or keep its streets safe.

I love America because it’s the one place on earth where people still believe they can build something from nothing. I came to Silicon Valley as a self-taught kid and it changed my life. That spirit is the most precious thing your country has.

Before you vote, ask yourself one question: is the program you’re voting for making America more like America, or more like France?

Trust me. You don’t want to be France.

text:
When you're an old soul, and a hopeless romantic, living in a world that expects you to be everything you're not some days it feels like a curse.
Sometimes you're forced to be a loner because no one really understands you and the more you hang out with people, the more you ask yourself if you're an alien living with humans or if you're a human living with aliens.
It feels like you can't fall in love. Because you can't find it, and when you do, people don't want it from you. They don't want the kind of love you want to offer, they don't want the deep connection that comes naturally to you, they don't want the old-fashioned romance. They don't want your love because it's outdated, it's not cool, it's not casual, and now it feels like the more you fall in love, the more you get your heart broken.
It feels like you're alive but you're not actually living because you wake up every day and you don't know if you're happy, if you're in the right generation. You dream about another era, another time when life was more about peace rather than stress, when less was more, when beauty wasn't so hard to find. You talk to people but you don't connect, the communication is shallow, the words are meaningless and the bond is weak. You long for conversations that never end, for words that are real and heartfelt, for a connection between souls.
But some days, it's a blessing.
Because you're a dreamer among realists, you hope when all hope is lost, you love when the love is gone, you dig deeper when no one even wants to scratch the surface, you give when everyone takes, you radiate warmth, honesty and sincerity when people are only seeking power.
You try to find meaning in an empty world, you try to find the best of both realities and fuse them together and even though most of the time it feels like a struggle, at the end of the day, I do believe you'll win. 
I believe you'll prevail. Because when you're an old soul and a hopeless romantic, you don't give up. You don't settle. You keep fighting. You keep dreaming. You believe that somehow, you'll find the home you're looking for. You'll find where you belong.

-From one old soul to another. ❤️

🇸🇦😂| The Saudi Regime Bombs Its Own Mercenaries: The Khash’a Desert Massacre, the Betrayal of the Sixth Giants Brigade, and the Fate of Nasser al-Ka’lul

October 14, 2026 | Al-Sabiha / Ras al-Ara

The Saudi regime did not content itself with killing the sons of the South in the Khash’a Desert at the beginning of this year. It pursued those who remained even those who had come to fight in its mobilizations, even those who had taken the Saudi riyal and sworn loyalty to Riyadh. Its air force launched dozens of airstrikes over the past month, targeting the herds of the sons of al-Sabiha, Yafi’, and Dhala’ in Ras al-Ara, the outskirts of Dhahab, and parts of al-Sabiha.

On September 26, Saudi aviation bombed what is called the Sixth Giants Brigade, led by the mercenary Nasser al-Ka’lul, in the Mansura area of al-Sabiha. Dozens of raids. Hundreds dead and wounded. Not a word of apology. Not a single Saudi official acknowledged the dead. The dead were Yemenis. The dead were southerners. The dead were the men Riyadh had paid to fight its war. And Riyadh bombed them anyway.

💥 The Khash’a Desert: The Massacre That Started It All

The Saudi treachery did not begin in September. It began in the Khash’a area of Hadramawt, where the Saudi-led coalition launched a wave of attacks targeting the Al-Khasha military camp. At least 20 people were killed, according to the separatist Southern Transitional Council. A tank belonging to the STC was set ablaze by a Saudi airstrike. Reports indicated airstrikes targeting the 37th Armored Brigade camp, followed by a mass exodus of STC fighters. Seven Saudi airstrikes were carried out in the opening minutes, with the total number of strikes reaching approximately 300 by Sunday.

The STC military official’s admission was blunt: “We carried out a complete withdrawal from the areas of Al-Khasha... as a result of pressure from Saudi air strikes on us”. The men Riyadh had armed and funded were now fleeing the bombs Riyadh was dropping on them.

⚔️ September 14: The “Erroneous” Airstrikes That Were Anything But

On September 14, 2026, Saudi warplanes carried out intensive airstrikes in the Al-Mudharabah and Ras Al-Arah districts of Lahj Governorate. The targets were gatherings of the “Giants” and “Shield of the Nation” factions on the outskirts of the Kahbub Mountains northwest of Al-Mudharabah. The result: deaths and injuries, including prominent field commanders, with the final toll withheld. A number of vehicles and armored personnel carriers were completely destroyed.

Field sources described the airstrikes as “erroneous.” But they were not erroneous. They were repeated. And they sparked widespread anger among recruits and field commanders, with escalating accusations of deliberately targeting people from the southern governorates—and demands for an urgent investigation into these strikes.

🎯 The Sixth Giants Brigade: Nasser al-Ka’lul and the Price of Betrayal

Nasser al-Ka’lul was not an unknown figure. He was the commander of the Sixth Giants Brigade, a formation that had been deployed to the Bab al-Mandab area at the height of the Saudi-Emirati campaign on Yemen’s western coast. He was a man who had marketed illusory victories for the Saudis in Bab al-Mandab the strategic strait that the Saudi regime and its Western masters coveted as a chokepoint for global shipping, the gateway between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

Al-Ka’lul’s brigade was part of the Giants Brigades, the UAE-backed and Saudi-funded formation that fought alongside the Saudi-led coalition. They were the men who captured Mokha and swept up the coast through Dhubab and the Bab el-Mandeb strait. They were the men Riyadh relied upon to secure the western coast, to prevent Ansar Allah from controlling the strait, to protect the flow of oil and goods through the Suez Canal. They were the men who died for Saudi Arabia’s strategic interests.

And then Saudi Arabia bombed them.

The September 26 airstrikes on the Sixth Giants Brigade in the Mansura area of al-Sabiha were not a mistake. They were a message. And the message was received: over 400 members of the Giants Brigades were killed or wounded in Ras al-Ara, including field commanders. A senior Yemeni military source confirmed the staggering toll, which sparked a wave of dissatisfaction among the Saudi-formed forces and deep concern among the fighters deployed on the battlefield.

Riyadh continued to mobilize its ground forces despite the losses, pursuing victory on the ground regardless of the human cost. The decision to press ground mobilization was reportedly driven by the failure of Saudi Arabia’s air defense systems to intercept the threat from the Yemeni side the Saudi military was caught off guard by the volume and accuracy of the Yemeni missile waves.

📜 The Mercenary’s Fate: Cheapened, Then Discarded

Look at Nasser al-Ka’lul. Look at what became of him and his men.

He marketed illusory victories for the Saudis in Bab al-Mandab. He led his brigade into battle on behalf of a regime that saw him not as an ally but as a tool. He took the Saudi riyal. He wore the uniform. He raised the banner of the coalition. He fought against Ansar Allah, against the Yemeni people, against his own countrymen all in the service of Riyadh.

And when the moment came, when the Yemeni Armed Forces pressed forward and the Saudi air defense failed, Riyadh’s response was not to protect its mercenaries. It was to bomb them.

The Saudi enemy’s raids on the Sixth Giants Brigade in al-Sabiha left hundreds dead and wounded. No apology was offered. No compensation was paid. No investigation was launched. The dead were not even acknowledged. Riyadh does not mourn its mercenaries. Riyadh does not honor its proxies. Riyadh discards them like spent ammunition.

He who cheapens himself ends up priceless. He who sells his honor for a foreign paycheck ends up buried in a mass grave with no name, no apology, and no justice. He who fights for the riyal of a tyrant ends up bombed by the tyrant himself.

🔻 Conclusion: The Enemy of the South Is Not Sana’a

The Saudi regime has revealed its true face in the Khash’a Desert and in Al-Sabiha. It has shown the people of the South that it does not care whether they live or die, whether they fight for it or against it. The Saudi enemy has killed the sons of the South, pursued those who remained, and bombed its own mercenaries when they became inconvenient. It has dropped hundreds of tons of American-made ordnance on southern tribes al-Sabiha, Yafi’, Dhala’ without a word of remorse.

The mercenaries who fled from Taiz to Aden under Ansar Allah’s safe passage should take note. The Sixth Giants Brigade should take note. Every southern fighter who has been paid to fight for Riyadh should take note. The Saudi regime does not protect its allies. It consumes them. It spends their blood like currency and discards their bodies like waste.

Long live the people of the South. Long live Yemen. Long live Ansar Allah. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
Objections: Getting the Verdict Right

By Sharan Kumar

International practices offer valuable lessons on interference, stewards’ decisions and the need for better video evidence.

Few decisions on a racecourse provoke as much argument as an objection. For owners, trainers and jockeys, it can mean the difference between victory and defeat. For racegoers, it can affect betting returns and confidence in the sport. For racing authorities, it tests their ability to interpret evidence and apply rules consistently.

Interestingly, some international betting operators, including Bet365, settle certain bets on the horse that crosses the finish line first, irrespective of a subsequent disqualification. Such provisions depend on the operator’s rules and the type of bet. Unfortunately, this practice is not generally available in India, where bettors may have to wait for the official result before their wagers are settled.

The fundamental distinction, however, is that interference does not automatically warrant reversal of the result. The crucial question is whether the incident affected the finishing order and what remedy the applicable rules prescribe.

Horses do not always run straight. They may jump sideways from the stalls, drift under pressure or shy away from another horse. Stewards must establish which horse caused the interference, how seriously another runner was disadvantaged and whether the incident altered the result.

Britain, Australia and France broadly follow the principle known as Category 1. The central question is whether the affected horse would have finished ahead of the horse responsible had the interference not occurred. If so, the offending horse can be placed behind the affected runner. If the interference did not alter the finishing order, the result may stand, although the jockey can still face a separate penalty for careless or improper riding.

The United States has traditionally followed a different approach, commonly described as Category 2. Under the model rules of the Association of Racing Commissioners International, a horse may be disqualified when the stewards determine that a foul altered the finish. Actual rules vary between states.

The controversial 2019 Kentucky Derby illustrates the debate. Maximum Security crossed the line first but was disqualified after stewards ruled that the horse had interfered with rivals on the final turn. Country House was declared the winner. The decision provoked widespread disagreement and highlighted the difficulties of judging interference in a major race.

Another important distinction concerns the nature of the offence. A horse may be demoted for interference, while its jockey may separately face disciplinary action. In Britain, whip-rule breaches can also attract suspensions and, under specified circumstances, disqualification. These are separate regulatory questions and should not be confused with the test applied to interference.

What, then, should stewards examine when an objection is lodged? First, they must establish the sequence of events. Which horse moved first? Did it continue into another runner’s path? Was the affected horse forced to check, lose momentum or change course? Could the jockey reasonably have avoided the incident? Most importantly, did the interference affect the finishing order under the applicable rules?

The winning margin is relevant but not conclusive. A horse beaten narrowly may have lost a winning chance through interference, but the margin alone cannot establish that it would have won. Equally, a horse that recovers from a severe check and finishes strongly should not automatically be considered unaffected. The evidence must determine the decision.

Video coverage is vital to this process. British stewards have access to multiple camera angles, including head-on, side-on and close-up views, to help examine incidents. Racing authorities elsewhere should aspire to comparable standards. High-definition cameras, high-frame-rate slow-motion replays, clear views of the starting stalls and synchronised recordings from different angles would substantially improve the quality of evidence available to stewards.

Technology cannot eliminate human judgment, nor should it. But better footage can reduce uncertainty, expose mistaken interpretations and make decisions more transparent. The objective should be to ensure that stewards interpret the evidence rather than struggle to establish what happened.

Transparency is equally important. After a contentious objection, racegoers should be told why it was upheld or dismissed. The explanation should identify the interference, establish responsibility, describe its consequences and explain how the applicable rule was applied. A verdict without adequate reasoning may settle the result, but it does little to settle the debate.

Disagreement among officials is inevitable. What matters is that each examines the evidence independently and that the final decision follows a consistent application of the rules.
Objections are not merely disputes between jockeys or rival connections; they are an essential safeguard for the integrity of racing.

Ultimately, the question is not simply whether one horse interfered with another. It is whether that interference compromised a rival’s legitimate chance and what the rules require the stewards to do about it.

Racing’s credibility depends not only on getting the decision right, but also on demonstrating why it is right.

text:
AI detection is getting a lot more interesting. Instead of looking at how something is written, researchers are starting to look at the ideas behind it.

A new paper called IdeaLens, from researchers at the University of Maryland, Google DeepMind, and Simon Fraser University, takes exactly this approach.

It strips away the writing style, breaks the text down into its core arguments, and tries to figure out whether the ideas came from a human or an AI.

And the results are pretty surprising.

Pangram 4, one of the strongest traditional AI detectors, identifies 92% of AI-written text.

But when a human takes an AI-generated outline and writes the article themselves, its detection rate drops to just 8%.

IdeaLens still catches 68%.

Now reverse the situation.

Give AI a detailed outline written by a human, and Pangram flags 92% of the resulting text as AI-generated. IdeaLens flags only 7%, because the underlying ideas came from a person.

That’s a pretty big difference.

What I found most interesting is how the researchers describe the differences between human and AI-generated ideas.

After analyzing 90,000 predictions, they found that human ideas tend to include verifiable sources, specific details, and an acknowledgment of what’s still uncertain.

AI-generated ideas are more likely to be generic, make broad claims, use questionable numbers, and offer solutions that seem a little too complete.

There’s something interesting about that.

Real thinking often involves uncertainty. People question their assumptions, recognize what they don’t know, and sometimes leave problems unresolved.

AI tends to produce a confident, polished answer, even when the underlying reasoning isn’t particularly strong.

Of course, IdeaLens has limitations. Its training labels came from an existing detector, and its performance already drops with newer AI models. It’s still research, not a finished product.

But I think the direction matters.

We’ve spent years trying to detect AI writing by looking at words and sentence patterns. Maybe it’s time to pay more attention to where the ideas actually come from.

And there’s an interesting problem ahead.

If AI detectors start looking for uncertainty and imperfect reasoning, what’s stopping AI models from learning to imitate those things too?

We might eventually end up training AI to sound less certain just to appear more human.

That’s a strange direction for this whole AI detection race to take.

🛑✋✋✋ AMERICAN DEMOCRACY AT A CROSSROADS: HAVE WE LOST OUR WAY?

🛑✋ Before you continue, ask yourself: Are we truly living up to the democratic principles America claims to represent?

As we approach the 2026 midterm elections, that question deserves serious attention. America presents itself as a guardian of free and fair elections, where the people—not money, manipulation, or intimidation—determine the nation’s future. Yet our political culture increasingly appears driven by wealth, misinformation, rumors, and personal attacks rather than ideas and solutions.

🛑✋ When elections become contests of money, character assassination, and hostility, the public interest becomes the casualty.

Campaign spending can amplify certain voices while pushing meaningful discussions about the economy, healthcare, education, immigration, and everyday struggles aside. In states such as Texas and Georgia, the issue is not only how much money enters politics, but whether it informs voters or overwhelms substantive debate.

Misinformation and false accusations further weaken democratic accountability. When winning matters more than truth, voters cannot fairly evaluate candidates, and public trust erodes. Candidates should explain their platforms, defend their records, and offer practical solutions—not rely on attacks and division.

Criticism is a legitimate part of democracy, but it must be based on evidence. In Michigan, for example, candidates of Muslim heritage have faced intense scrutiny. Questioning their policies or qualifications is appropriate; targeting their religion, ancestry, families, or identity is prejudice, not political accountability.

🛑✋ The same standards of fairness, evidence, and accountability must apply to everyone, regardless of party, wealth, religion, or political affiliation.

Democracy is more than the right to cast a ballot. It requires informed voters, honest candidates, responsible media, transparent donors, and citizens willing to hold leaders accountable for their promises and actions. Political disagreement is inevitable, but it does not justify dishonesty, hatred, or personal attacks.

America can continue allowing money, misinformation, and prejudice to drown out serious debate, or it can demand a political culture centered on truth, fairness, public service, and accountability.

🛑✋ The future of American democracy will be shaped not only by the candidates we elect, but also by the values we defend, the standards we demand, and the truth we are willing to uphold.

text:
Mailing your passport to Texas is one of four ways to file a W-7. It is the one with the most exposure.

The IRS wants either the original document or a copy certified by the agency that issued it. For a passport that usually means the real one travels to the ITIN Operation in Austin and stays there while the application is worked. Seven weeks, or nine to eleven between 15 January and 30 April.

Two of the alternatives hand it straight back.

A Certifying Acceptance Agent reviews the document for authenticity and returns it immediately. What goes to the IRS is the application plus the agent's certificate, not your passport.

An IRS Taxpayer Assistance Center does the same. They can verify original documents and certified copies from the issuing agency, and what they verify is returned to you on the spot. Appointments are by phone only, on 844-545-5640, and not every centre offers the service. The ones that don't will mail your originals to Austin.

The fourth route is a plain Acceptance Agent, without the C. That one has to submit originals or certified copies with the application.

Nothing in the two titles tells you which is which.

Christopher Lloyd just teased the Tesla Roadster reveal, streaming live Thursday. Here's what you need to know.

Lloyd, who played Doc Brown in Back to the Future, posted "Almost time to see some serious shit…" on Oct 14. It passed 282K views. Fans read it as a nod to the Roadster's rocket thrusters and a time-travel style launch.

Tesla confirmed the event will be livestreamed Thursday, Oct 15, at 8:55 PM ET (7:55 PM CST). It was first set for Oct 1, then moved after severe weather was forecast in Waco, Texas. Tesla's first Roadster reveal was Nov 16, 2017.

The event is at SpaceX's test site in Texas. The Roadster is expected to offer a SpaceX option package with about 10 small cold-gas thrusters, which push out pressurized nitrogen. Earlier reports said the car may be remotely operated in the demo because of the noise and force. The listed 0-60 mph time with the rocket option is 1.1 seconds.

Musk said: "It'll be a banger. Excitement guaranteed. Success is not guaranteed, but excitement is. We actually need an audience to vouch for the fact that this is not AI."

Eric Larchevêque says he paid $250,000 cash five years ago for a Founder Edition, limited to 1,000 units. He got no email, just took the payment, and is flying to Texas for the event. Tesla also took $50,000 deposits, and has never announced a final price.

Markets are watching too. Someone bought 3,999 Tesla $430 calls expiring April 2027 at $27.40 each, about $10.96M in premium. Tesla needs to hit about $457 for them to pay off.

- Event: Thursday Oct 15, 8:55 PM ET
- Original date: Oct 1
- Founder Edition: $250,000, 1,000 units
- Other deposits: $50,000
- Thrusters: about 10
- 0-60 mph: 1.1 seconds with rocket option
- Options bet: $10.96M premium

text:
Have been saying it for quite a while now and will die on this hill, that owners vs owners is the problem and nobody put a gun to each owners head and told them to spend the way they do. 

They want the players to fix the problem(s) for them. “Stop taking our money we offer you I say!” Each team chooses to spend the way they see fit and build the way they see fit. Can they spend more if they choose to? Yes, but does that ensure winning and long term success? No! It’s about choosing to put your resources in scouting, player development and tech. It’s always been that way. But because of some rogue owners who can’t stop reaching into their pockets and throwing money into the air and then others who decide to bank all the profits for themselves on the flip side, it leaves the one’s in the middle who in most cases are doing it right to just look to their right and say “what are you doing, and look to their left and say what are YOU doing?”

If you are elite at all three, yes you won’t have to pay prices you are uncomfortable with. Hence the Brewers and 3-4 others. 

Because the game is so cloak and dagger with player evaluations and keeping any and all information close to the vest, why would the ones doing it the right way, want to expose their secret sauce? But if the ones scratching their heads, like the Reds owner said: “Why can’t we be more like the Brewers?” Well if the Brewers let everyone in to see what they are doing, yes it would help the industry and they would say “So that’s how it’s done!” But if successful teams did that to cure the ills of the game, they would be chopping off their nose, to spite their face and lose their competitive edge. 

But then there are the scouting departments out there who say when a scout from a successful org comes along with his own success, “we are going to fill this or that position internally.” Well you don’t even know if that so-called rookie scout can actually evaluate or scout. Which are two different things! 

It’s because the departments are run by non baseball people who are threatened by those who are not like them and so when they find the internal candidate at the xerox copier who thinks like they do, that’s the winner of the prize, the position. They aren’t a threat and will be grateful for the opportunity and won’t push back or have an opinion, because they know they weren’t qualified for the job and so they become company and yes men.

text:
Remembering Geof Fletcher, the Scottish man who loved Kiwoko Hospital 

In the first weeks after taking up the communications officer job at the Commonwealth Secretariat in London in June 2006, I was on the train from Finsbury Park, the home of @Arsenal when a Muzungu/middle aged white man walked over to me and said "gyebalekko Ssebo. "

Stunned, I raised my head,looked at him closely, and replied, " Webale Ssebo, nawe gyebale. "

The man introduced himself as Geof Fletcher, and that he had heard me speaking on phone in Luganda and wanted to take the opportunity to speak and practice his Luganda with me. 

Curious to know how he had come to know the language  he told, me that he had been to Uganda several times to visit his daughter Alison, who was a health worker working at Kiwoko Hospital in Nakaseke District, as part of volunteers sent by the Church Missionary Society. 

He then sat opposite me and we started a conversation, him telling me more about Kiwoko and I telling him how I had only been to London for two months and was trying to learn my ways around. 

Geoff asked if I had already found a church to attend, to which I reality that I was still hoping from one church to another trying to find one that suited me.
 He then introduced me to St James New Barnet Church and invited me the following Sunday to join the service. 

Inside the church and pinned on the walls were several photos and stories from and about Kiwoko hospital, taken by his daughter, Alison. 

He introduced me to the congregation and asked me to greet the people which I did. 

I had never been to Kiwoko. My only knowledge about Kiwoko hospital was from the book by Dr Ian Clarke, formerly of International Hospital Muyenga, the Irish Muzungu who came to Uganda after the war in mid 1980s and helped establish Kiwoko hospital. 

In the book, The Man With the Key Has Gone, Dr Clarke writes about the Uganda of the 1980s where everything was scarse, to the extent that whenever he went to shops to buy cement, nails, and other construction materials, shop keepers wanted to be bribed before selling him those items. 
Apparently, they would first claim that the man with the key to the store has gone, so that you give them money to take a bicycle to look for him. 

On giving them money for transport to bring the man with the key, they would move around the corner and return with the key. 

In the 10 years that followed, St James New Barnet became our family church. When I joined, I found that there were special Sundays where the congregation would be asked to put some money in the basket to support Kiwoko hospital. 

Working with Geoff, his daughter Alison and other Ugandan families in the church, we decided to elevate the arrangement and started organising a 'Ugandan Night' where we would invite friends to join in an evening at which we would raise money and send it to the hospital. The main focus was supporting staff training and provision of equipment. 

The Ugandan night became a highly anticipated day on the calendar of the Church.  We would prepare different dishes of Ugandan food, from matooke, karo, firindi, malakwang, katogo, gnuts, dodo, omugoyo and many other items. 
What started as a simple event for Kiwoko became a Uganda promo. 

Through the Uganda Night, a number of British people pickrd interest and made trips to Uganda to visit national parks and enjoy the beauty of the people, culture and all it has to offer. 

Then some time towards the end of 2014, we got devastating news. Geoff who had been looking healthy and athletic was diagnosed with cancer. On January 29th 2015, he succumbed to it. 
It was a big shock and blow to everyone who knew him, and especially to the people of Kiwoko. 
At his funeral in Edinburgh, the family asked asked for donations to Kiwoko in his memory, bringing close to a chapter of a man who was so committed to supporting such a worthy cause.
