$IONQ | ID Quantique + Elisity: from photons to policy. How IonQ is assembling the quantum-safe stack, layer by layer

On October 12, 2026, IonQ agreed to acquire Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3B. Read on its own, that is a cybersecurity acquisition. Read next to ID Quantique, which IonQ has owned since April 30, 2025, it completes a stack that runs from the physics of a single photon up to the policy that decides which device may talk to which server. Niccolo de Masi said it plainly on CNBC: "IonQ already is, I would argue, the biggest quantum security company in the Western world." This is the long version of why.

1. The hardware layer: 25 years of turning quantum physics into products

ID Quantique was spun out of the University of Geneva in 2001 by Nicolas Gisin and Grégoire Ribordy. In October 2007 the State of Geneva used its quantum key distribution to protect election results, the first real-world commercial deployment of quantum cryptography. Since then IDQ has built a portfolio of roughly 300 patents and patent applications and three product families that now sit inside IonQ.

The first is quantum key distribution. The Clavis XG series is production QKD in a 1U rack form factor, covering roughly 60 to 150 km per link depending on the model. In January 2025 it received national-security certification from South Korea's National Intelligence Service, a QKD milestone. In June 2026 IonQ launched Clavis XG Multiplex, which lets quantum and classical traffic share the same metro fibre. Jordan Shapiro, IonQ's President of Quantum Platform, summed it up: "Quantum security is moving beyond specialized network environments."

The second is quantum randomness. IDQ's Quantis QRNG chips, the smallest just 2.5 x 2.5 mm, were the first quantum random number generators to earn NIST Entropy Source Validation on the IID track (SP 800-90B). They also carry ANSSI Common Criteria, AEC-Q100 automotive, ECSS space and BSI AIS 31 credentials. They have shipped inside Samsung Galaxy Quantum smartphones with SK Telecom since 2020, inside Thales Luna HSMs, and inside Hitachi Energy security cards for utility networks.

The third is single-photon detection: the ID281 superconducting nanowire detectors (Laser World of Photonics innovation award, 2022) and the ID Qube SPADs. These are the "eyes" every quantum network needs.

On top of the hardware, IDQ built software. Clarion KX (2024) is a key-management platform that combines QKD and post-quantum keys, and it is open to other QKD vendors through an ecosystem with HEQA Security, LuxQuanta, Quantum Optics Jena and ThinkQuantum. Solteris is a standalone quantum key management system and PQC crypto plane fed by NIST-approved quantum entropy. So IDQ is not only a QKD company. It already sells the hybrid QKD + PQC model regulators are asking for.

2. Deployed where trust is non-negotiable

This hardware is not a lab demo.

- South Korea: with SK Broadband, IDQ secures 48 government departments across an 800 km network.
- Singapore: it sits at the core of Singtel's National Quantum-Safe Network Plus, where Nokia, Cisco, Fortinet, Juniper and PacketLight equipment consume its keys.
- JPMorgan Chase: in Singapore, it powered 100 Gbps quantum-safe IPsec VPNs over 46 km.
- Romania: IDQ supplied every QKD system in the national EuroQCI network, 36 links over more than 1,500 km, which IonQ says is over 20% of Europe's terrestrial quantum-communication infrastructure.
- Elsewhere in Europe: Slovakia's skQCI national network mixes QKD and PQC. Poland has a 380 km Poznań–Warsaw link. The Geneva Quantum Network spans 262 km with CERN and Rolex. Orange's ParisRegionQCI uses PQC-secured relays. Turkcell achieved the first terrestrial intercontinental QKD across Istanbul.
- United States: IonQ and Florida LambdaRail launched the first statewide quantum-safe network initiative, starting with roughly 100 miles from Palm Beach to Miami-Dade. Congruity360 signed an $8.18M agreement for IonQ PQC and QKD appliances, among the largest commercial quantum-security agreements in the country.
3. The partners that matter: IDQ already lives inside the world's network gear

IDQ's quantum keys feed the encryptors enterprises and carriers already run:

- Cisco: Secure Key Integration Protocol on Nexus 9000 MACsec with IDQ Solteris and Clarion KX, which built Switzerland's first quantum-resistant network between two data centres.
- Juniper (now part of HPE): quantum-safe MACsec with Deutsche Telekom, and a Turkcell proof of concept protecting 5G backhaul timing with QKD.
- Fortinet: FortiGate quantum-key interfaces since 2020, and a quantum-safe IP-VPN with Telefónica.
- Palo Alto Networks: IDQ is one of the six innovators behind its QRNG Open API.
- Nokia (1830 PSS and the Proximus trial), Adtran/ADVA (FSP 3000 ConnectGuard, the Colt metro trial), Ciena (WaveLogic 5, Telstra), Thales, Colt, Telefónica, Orange and SK Telecom complete the list.
This is the first half of the story: the keys and the links.

4. The software layer: Elisity turns the network you already own into a Zero Trust enforcement fabric

Encryption protects data in transit. It does not stop an attacker who has stolen a valid account, or a compromised camera, infusion pump or PLC, from moving sideways through a flat network. That is the gap Elisity was built for.

Elisity is identity-based microsegmentation with no new hardware, no agents and no VLAN or IP redesign. A cloud control plane (Cloud Control Center) sets policy. A lightweight Virtual Edge controller runs as a container on Cisco Catalyst 9300/9400 switches, as a VM, or in Azure. The customer's existing switches become the enforcement points, called Virtual Edge Nodes. User traffic never has to go to the cloud: policy is enforced at the switch port.

It is vendor-agnostic by design:

- Enforcement: Cisco Catalyst (including industrial IE switches and the Catalyst 9800 wireless controller), Juniper EX directly or through Mist, HPE Aruba CX, Arista and Hirschmann industrial switches.
- Firewalls: it pushes its Policy Groups into Palo Alto Networks Panorama as Dynamic Address Groups.
- Context: its IdentityGraph pulls identity and risk from Microsoft Active Directory, Entra ID, Intune and Defender, from Okta, ServiceNow CMDB, NetBox, CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Armis, Claroty, Nozomi Networks, Dragos and Tenable. It logs to Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel and Cribl. It is sold through the AWS, Azure and Google Cloud marketplaces.
- AI agents: Elisity treats AI agents as policy subjects and joined the Linux Foundation's Open Secure AI Alliance on October 1, 2026.
The customer results are concrete:

- St. Luke's University Health Network secured 85,000 devices across 15 hospitals and more than 350 sites in 46 days, with zero outages, on its existing Cisco network.
- GSK cut a planned $200M segmentation programme to $50M and went from about a year per site to three or four sites per week.
- Andelyn Biosciences deployed 2,700 policies in 90 days. MultiCare, Haleon, Main Line Health and Shaw Industries are customers too.
- Across the base, 83% of customers were fully deployed within 90 days (Elisity, January 2025).
- Elisity reports more than 100 global customer deployments, revenue and customers doubling year over year, and zero churn among deployed customers.
- Gartner named it a Cool Vendor in Cyber-Physical Systems Security (2025), Forrester a Strong Performer in microsegmentation (Q3 2024), and Deloitte's Fast 500 ranked it #13 in North America.
5. The overlap: same gear, same buyers, two complementary layers

Put the two partner maps side by side and the logic becomes obvious:

- Cisco: IDQ delivers quantum keys into Nexus MACsec, and Elisity enforces policy on Catalyst.
- Juniper/HPE: IDQ secures MACsec and IPsec links, and Elisity enforces on Juniper EX and HPE Aruba CX.
- Palo Alto Networks: IDQ is in its QRNG Open API, and Elisity automates its Panorama firewalls.
The network and security architects who buy that equipment are the same people who will buy quantum-safe key delivery and identity-based segmentation. Both companies refuse to force a rip-and-replace: Clarion KX was designed for vendor-agnostic integration, and Elisity reuses the switches already in the rack.

De Masi described the deal as "a three for one": "additional channel to market for existing quantum security solutions", "a great team", and "a business that obviously is firing all cylinders." On Bloomberg he spelled out the channel: Elisity "brings us 100 new customers and a channel for riding and carrying our QKD and PQC products into the enterprise." On CNBC he described the architecture: "now we're adding zero trust and compartmentalization to our defense in depth strategy." The idea predates this deal. When IonQ partnered with ARLIS in March 2026 on a Zero Trust framework for quantum computers themselves, de Masi called "the shift from legacy perimeter security to a Zero Trust Architecture" "a strategic imperative."

The customers say the same. Jason Elrod, CISO of MultiCare Health System: "Quantum readiness starts with the decisions we make today about identity, access and the information we need to protect for years." Michael Elmore, a Fortune 50 global CISO and Elisity design partner: "Zero Trust and post-quantum cryptography belong in the same security strategy." James Winebrenner, who remains Elisity's CEO, describes the goal as helping customers "modernize their crypto-agility programs" and "deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future."

Put simply: QKD and PQC make stolen traffic useless, and microsegmentation makes stolen access useless.

6. The rest of the stack is already being built around it

The security pillar sits on a broader quantum networking platform IonQ has assembled one acquisition at a time:

- Qubitekk brought entanglement-based networking.
- Lightsynq brought quantum memory. On October 9, 2026, IonQ reported more than 1,000 entanglements per second between a trapped-ion qubit and a silicon-vacancy quantum memory.
- Capella Space and Skyloom bring satellites and free-space optical terminals, aimed at space-based QKD.
- Vector Atomic brings precision timing.
- SkyWater (a DoD-accredited Trusted Foundry) and Nexus Photonics bring US chip and photonics manufacturing.
Around that core, the network is already reaching customers and programmes:

- EPB in Chattanooga will host what IonQ calls the world's first commercial quantum memory embedded in an operational communications network.
- In South Korea, IDQ's home market alongside SK Telecom, the SDT partnership brings the first Superion 256 and the first SiV quantum memory module.
- The AFRL project builds free-space optical links from ground stations to drones.
7. The regulatory clock is now set

The timing reflects a policy calendar that has hardened in the past four months:

- June 22, 2026: Executive Order 14412 requires post-quantum key establishment on federal high-value and high-impact systems by December 31, 2030, and post-quantum signatures by December 31, 2031. Through the FAR it extends the 2030 deadline to contractors and calls for a cryptographic bill of materials. As Shapiro put it, the order "pulls federal post-quantum deadlines forward to 2030 and extends them to contractors."
- October 1, 2026: the NSA said newly acquired national security systems must support quantum-resistant algorithms from 2027, with legacy equipment phased out by 2030.
- NIST's draft transition plan deprecates RSA and ECC after 2030 and disallows them after 2035.
- The EU's coordinated roadmap asks member states to start by the end of 2026 and to migrate high-risk use cases by the end of 2030.
- NATO is already procuring: its €8M Quantum Zero Beacon Project, to validate post-quantum communications between NATO HQ in Brussels and SHAPE in Mons, has a planned award date of November 30, 2026.
- On the readiness side, the GAO found on October 6 that none of 24 major federal agencies had fully addressed the key PQC preparation practices.
- Two days later, the NSA's new Zero Trust guidance for operational technology put asset inventory, visibility and segmentation at the foundation.
The answer to every one of those documents is the same: know what you have, segment it, and upgrade the cryptography, starting now.

8. What comes next

The deal is expected to close in Q4 2026. The most important item on the shared roadmap connects the two halves. IonQ says it will "extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information," so customers can rank their post-quantum upgrades by business risk. A graph that already knows every device, user, workload and AI agent, and who talks to whom, becomes the natural place to see which cryptography protects each conversation. From there, the hand-off to Clarion KX, Solteris, Clavis XG and IonQ's PQC portfolio is short.

De Masi frames the opportunity as "a $10 billion TAM for defense in depth, both today for zero trust, as well as for the coming quantum security wave." In the deal announcement he described what IonQ now offers as "a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity."

Physics-secured keys at the bottom, identity-based access on top, and the network vendors enterprises already trust in between. In de Masi's words: "From submarines to satellites, that's our mission for all quantum security and computing."

text:
$IONQ I put together voices from recent Fed Gov Today interviews on one question: how real is the quantum threat to our data? Listen to the people working on it, and they all describe the same story.

It starts now. Nick Nilan (Arqit): "Our adversaries are in our networks today. We know that they're stealing our data today," because they plan on having a quantum computer "that can break your encryption sometime in the future." Dr. Fredrik Fatemi (Army DEVCOM ARL) confirms that quantum computing "can break certain encryption protocols that we have."

Time is the problem. Kynan Carver (Maximus): classified information "can last 25 years, if not longer," so "we need to start looking at hardening that information now." He points to 2035 as the NIST marker, and Nilan warns that pushing migration to 2030, 2035 or 2040 leaves "all your mission secrets" vulnerable to a future quantum computer.

Then the perimeter moves. Troy Grubbs (Ping Identity) sees identity security as "a perimeter more so than the network," enabling zero trust architectures. And the next threat may not even be human. E.P. Matthew, CIO of the DIA: "The next big cyber attack is not gonna be done by a human attacker," but by AI agents exploiting vulnerabilities "at a scale and size and speed that we've never seen before." Louis Eichenbaum (ColorTokens) warns of "a ticking time bomb" with AI agents "over-permissioning" inside networks.

Put together, the picture is clear: protect data against tomorrow's quantum computers, and control who and what moves inside the network today. That is exactly the full stack IonQ is building, from quantum-safe encryption to identity-based Zero Trust with Elisity.

OUT NOW: Eight stories. Eight descents into darkness. An anthology of nightmares that will haunt you long after the final page.

There are horrors buried beneath the earth, horrors waiting beyond the veil of death, and horrors that dwell within the human soul. Some have slept for centuries. Others have been with us all along. And some are far worse than anything the imagination dares to conjure.

In The Horror Collection: Special Edition IV, the boundaries of reality begin to crumble.

Beneath the endless Kansas plains, an ancient presence stirs. In a hallucinatory rainforest, a one-eyed tiger hunts its prey — but something far more terrible awaits in the depths of the jungle. A grieving boy receives messages from beyond the grave, while a photographer's dreams become harbingers of death. On an isolated Alaskan expedition, an unseen creature turns familiar faces into instruments of terror, and trust becomes a luxury no one can afford.

A detective is offered one final chance to defy the impossible. A holiday romance spirals into a bewildering supernatural paradox. And behind the walls of an aristocratic palace, a monstrous secret threatens to shatter everything its keepers hold dear.

From the depths of cosmic horror to the darkest recesses of the mind, these eight tales plunge into worlds where the natural order is corrupted, the dead refuse to remain silent, and the ancient forces lurking beyond human comprehension are never as distant as we would like to believe.

Featuring unsettling mysteries, nightmarish transformations, impossible choices and revelations that threaten to unravel reality itself, this is horror in all its magnificent, terrifying variety.

text:
Inspired by feather stars, the NC State researchers report a soft underwater swimming robot capable of achieving three distinct swimming modes—jellyfish-like vertical swimming, fish-like directional steering, and rotor-like 3D reorientation—using only two pneumatic inputs. By embedding mechanical intelligence into its elastic structure, the robot seamlessly transitions among these modes for agile and versatile underwater maneuvering. Particle image velocimetry (PIV) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) reveal the distinct hydrodynamic mechanisms underlying each swimming mode. 

The multifunctional swimmer can also be equipped with magnets, hooks, and miniature cameras for underwater waste collection, cooperative manipulation, environmental monitoring, and exploration. This work offers a promising platform for future adaptive and autonomous soft robots capable of navigating and performing tasks in complex and unstructured underwater environments.

Credit: Jie Yin, Haitao Qing, Matt Shipman

text:
The Budapest Memorandum, where Russia itself gave assurances to Ukraine [5, 7], stood in contrast to the qualified assurances NATO gave to Russia, adding another layer to the complex web of commitments and perceived betrayals that would later unravel.
III. Divergence and Disillusionment: The Erosion of Understandings
The initial post-Cold War rapprochement proved fragile. By the late 1990s and accelerating into the 21st century, a series of developments drove a wedge between Russia and the US/NATO, eroding the foundations of cooperation and fostering deep-seated mistrust.
NATO Enlargement – The Central Irritant
The most consistent and significant point of contention was the eastward expansion of NATO. Russia viewed this process as a direct encroachment on its security interests and a violation of the spirit, if not the letter, of post-Cold War understandings.
Timeline of Expansion Waves: Following the 1997 invitation, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland joined NATO in March 1999.[6, 14, 15] A much larger wave occurred in March 2004, bringing in Bulgaria, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, critically from Moscow's perspective, the three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania – former Soviet republics bordering Russia.[6, 14, 15, 21] Subsequent rounds added Albania and Croatia (2009), Montenegro (2017), and North Macedonia (2020).[6, 14, 21] A pivotal moment came at the NATO Summit in Bucharest in April 2008, where the Alliance declared that Georgia and Ukraine "will become members of NATO," although without offering them a Membership Action Plan (MAP) at that time.[6, 21] This declaration regarding two countries considered by Russia to be central to its security sphere dramatically escalated tensions.
The 1990 Assurances Controversy: The debate over whether the West broke a promise not to expand NATO eastward became a cornerstone of Russian grievance. Declassified documents reveal that during the negotiations over German unification in 1990, several high-level Western leaders offered verbal assurances to Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev. US Secretary of State James Baker famously told Gorbachev on February 9, 1990, that NATO's jurisdiction would not shift "one inch eastward" if a unified Germany remained in the Alliance.[22, 23, 24] Similar sentiments were expressed by West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl ("NATO should not expand its sphere of activity") and Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher, who promoted the "Tutzing formula" ruling out expansion towards Soviet borders.[22, 23, 25] Leaders from the UK and France also offered reassurances about respecting Soviet security interests.[22, 23] Gorbachev clearly stated in these meetings that NATO expansion was "unacceptable".[22, 23, 24]However, these verbal assurances were never codified in formal treaties. The final agreement on German unification, the Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany (September 1990), only restricted the stationing of non-German NATO forces and nuclear weapons in the territory of the former East Germany, without mentioning broader NATO expansion.[23, 24, 25] Western officials later argued that the assurances referred only to the specific context of East German territory.[18, 24, 26] Furthermore, internal US discussions quickly moved away from the "not one inch eastward" formulation, with the Bush administration favoring Germany's full integration into NATO without such constraints.[25, 26, 27] NATO officially maintains that no formal promise was made, as alliance decisions require consensus and recording, which did not occur for non-expansion.[19] Gorbachev himself later gave conflicting accounts of whether a binding promise was made.[25, 26]Regardless of the legal interpretation or the precise scope of the 1990 discussions, the perception in Moscow that the West had reneged on a crucial commitment became deeply ingrained.[18, 19, 20]

text:
Tobey Maguire took $15.6 million off a billionaire at poker, and told the woman who ran his game it was never about the cash.

"It's more about crushing souls." Molly Bloom repeats his words in the clip below at 3:50.

Bloom ran the most famous private game in Hollywood. In her book she called Maguire the best player, the worst tipper and the worst loser at her table.

One night he swore on his mother's life that he had the best hand, and the man across from him folded after a long, painful think. Then Maguire showed him the bluff.

Another night he offered Bloom a tip with one condition. She had to climb onto the table and bark like a seal.

She said no, and the whole game stopped while the table watched the two of them for 35 minutes.

"I'm never f*cking giving him this win," she says in the clip.

A few weeks later Maguire moved the game to the house of a rich player and took everyone with him. Then he called her: "You're done. You're over."

In December 2019, in Dallas, he played heads-up against Andy Beal, a Texas banker worth billions. Maguire won $15.6 million. His own share was $7.8 million.

Beal didn't pay on time. Court papers say he offered to settle for significantly less.

Maguire refused the discount, the same way he refused to drop the seal.

He hired Tom Goldstein, a lawyer who had argued over 40 cases at the Supreme Court, and collected every dollar. The fee was $500,000.

Goldstein told him to wire it to a real estate developer he owed about $14 million at poker.

Then Goldstein played Beal himself. Between 2022 and 2024 he won $51.4 million from the same billionaire.

In July 2026 Goldstein got 6 years in federal prison for tax crimes tied to his poker winnings. Maguire testified at his trial and was never accused of anything.

I ran the numbers. Bloom lost her game to keep her dignity. Beal lost $51.4 million to the lawyer sent to collect $7.8 million. Maguire walked away with every cent.

He never accepted a discount from anyone, not from a billionaire and not from the woman who ran his game.

Was that the poker player in him, or the man?

text:
"President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement.

The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine.

The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month.

While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans."
Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports.
However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea."

The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas).

The White House directed Axios to the president's remarks to reporters Tuesday.
He said described the agreement as a "diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices. And when you knock out diesel refineries, that's not a great thing, but they're not releasing that to us. They're releasing it to the entire world."

That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal.

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly."
Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition.

As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin."
But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries, which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting that they halt such strikes.

The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions.

Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem."

text:
Los Cabos, Mexico: One of North America's Most Unique Beach Destinations

Los Cabos is located at the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California Peninsula, where the Pacific Ocean meets the Sea of Cortez (Gulf of California). It consists primarily of two distinct towns, Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo, connected by a scenic resort corridor lined with luxury resorts, golf courses, and beaches.

For many American travelers, Los Cabos is one of the easiest international beach destinations to reach. Direct flights from major U.S. cities often take only 2 to 4 hours, making it a convenient alternative to Hawaii or the Caribbean.

What Makes Los Cabos Unique?

Unlike Cancun, Riviera Maya, Puerto Vallarta, or other Mexican resort destinations, Los Cabos combines three dramatically different environments:

Desert landscapes filled with giant cacti
Rugged mountains
Deep blue ocean

It is one of the few places in the world where a true desert meets the sea, creating scenery that looks almost otherworldly. The region is famous for dramatic granite rock formations, especially El Arco (The Arch) at Land's End, where the peninsula ends.

Compared with Other Mexican Resorts
Los Cabos Cancun / Riviera MayaDesert-meets-ocean scenery Tropical Caribbean jungle
Sea of Cortez and Pacific Ocean Caribbean Sea
Luxury-focused atmosphere Broader mix of budgets
Excellent whale watching Limited whale watching
World-class sport fishing Less fishing focused
More arid climate More humid climate
Virtually no sargassum seaweed issues Often impacted by seasonal sargassum

Many travelers describe Los Cabos as feeling more sophisticated, upscale, and rugged than Mexico's Caribbean destinations.

Is Los Cabos Ideal for American Travelers?

Absolutely.

Los Cabos has become one of the most popular international destinations for Americans because of:

Short flight times
Excellent airlift from U.S. cities
High-end accommodations
Modern infrastructure
Strong tourism services
U.S.-friendly atmosphere
Year-round sunshine

More than a million American visitors arrive annually, and English is widely spoken in tourist areas.

It is especially appealing for:

Luxury travelers
Couples
Empty nesters
Golfers
Food lovers
Adventure travelers
Multigenerational families
Adults or Families?
Historically: Adult-Oriented

Los Cabos was traditionally known as:

A luxury hideaway
Honeymoon destination
Celebrity retreat
Golf and sportfishing paradise

The nightlife around Cabo San Lucas still attracts adults seeking entertainment.

Today: Excellent for Families

Over the past decade, numerous family-friendly resorts have opened featuring:

Water parks
Kids clubs
Teen activities
Family suites
Educational marine excursions
Best For:

Adults

Romantic getaways
Luxury escapes
Golf trips
Spa vacations
Culinary experiences

Families

Whale watching
Snorkeling
Beach time
Wildlife encounters
Boat excursions

In truth, Los Cabos successfully serves both markets.

Top 5 Must-Do Experiences
1. Visit El Arco (The Arch)

This iconic natural granite arch marks the meeting point of the Pacific Ocean and Sea of Cortez.

Take:

Water taxi
Glass-bottom boat
Catamaran cruise
Private yacht

This is the signature image of Los Cabos.

2. Whale Watching (December-April)

This is among the world's great wildlife experiences.

Humpback and gray whales migrate to Baja California Sur every winter, with peak viewing from January through March.

Seeing a 40-ton humpback breach against Cabo's dramatic coastline is unforgettable.

3. Snorkel the Sea of Cortez

Jacques Cousteau famously called the Sea of Cortez "the aquarium of the world."

Top snorkeling beaches include:

Chileno Bay
Santa Maria Bay
Cabo Pulmo Marine Park

Visitors regularly see:

Tropical fish
Rays
Sea turtles
Dolphins
Sea lions
4. Experience San José del Cabo

Many visitors never discover this charming side of Los Cabos.

Highlights:

Art galleries
Colonial architecture
Historic church
Local markets
Thursday Art Walks

The town retains much of Baja's traditional character.

5. Explore the Baja Desert

Few beach destinations allow you to combine ocean and desert adventures in a single day.

Popular activities include:

ATV excursions
Camel rides
Hiking
Mountain biking
Off-road adventures

The giant cardón cactus forests make the landscape feel distinctly Baja.

The People and Culture

The people of Los Cabos are known for being friendly, welcoming, and accustomed to international visitors.

Culturally, Los Cabos is different from central Mexico.

The area reflects:

Indigenous Pericú influences
Spanish colonial heritage
Ranching traditions
Maritime culture
Modern international influences

Because Baja California Sur was relatively isolated for much of its history, it developed a unique identity separate from mainland Mexico.

Local pride centers on:

The sea
Fishing traditions
Conservation
Desert living
Ranch culture
Cuisine: One of Mexico's Hidden Culinary Gems

Many visitors are surprised by how exceptional the food is.

Signature Baja Cuisine

Unlike interior Mexican cuisine, Baja food revolves around:

Fresh seafood
Farm-to-table ingredients
Local produce
Pacific and Sea of Cortez catches

Popular dishes include:

Fish Tacos

The Baja fish taco was born on the peninsula and remains an icon.

Chocolate Clams

A Baja specialty found nowhere else.

Fresh Tuna and Yellowtail

Often served sashimi-style because of Japanese culinary influences.

Lobster

Particularly prized throughout Baja.

Smoked Marlin

A regional favorite.

Farm-to-Table Dining

Los Cabos is famous for innovative farm restaurants near San José del Cabo.

Many of Mexico's leading chefs operate here, creating a distinctive "Baja Med" cuisine that blends:

Mexican
Mediterranean
Asian influences

This culinary scene is more sophisticated and internationally recognized than many other Mexican resort regions.

Best Time to Visit
Overall Best Time: November through May

These months offer:

Sunny skies
Comfortable temperatures
Minimal rainfall
Excellent outdoor conditions

Most experienced travelers consider:

November
December
January
February
March

particularly attractive.

Seasonal Weather & Climate

Los Cabos enjoys over 300 sunny days annually and a tropical desert climate.

Winter (December-February)

75-82°F (24-28°C)

Dry
Low humidity
Cool evenings
Prime whale-watching season

Arguably the most pleasant time of year.

Spring (March-May)

80-88°F (27-31°C)

Warm
Sunny
Little rain
Excellent beach weather

Many travelers consider spring the perfect balance of weather and crowds.

Summer (June-August)

88-95°F (31-35°C)

Hot
Water temperatures warm
Excellent diving

85-95°F (29-35°C)

Warmest ocean temperatures
Hurricane season peaks
Possibility of tropical storms
Best bargains

How Far in Advance Should You Book?
Peak Season (December-April)

Book:

Flights: 4 to 8 months ahead
Luxury resorts: 6 to 9 months ahead

Holiday weeks (Christmas, New Year's, Spring Break) can sell out even earlier.

Shoulder Season (May-June, October-November)

Book:

3 to 5 months ahead
Summer

Book:

2 to 4 months ahead
Final Verdict

For American travelers, Los Cabos offers one of the best combinations of ease, luxury, natural beauty, gastronomy, and adventure anywhere in Mexico.

If Cancun is about tropical Caribbean beaches, Los Cabos is about dramatic landscapes, luxury resorts, world-class dining, desert adventures, whale watching, and the spectacular meeting of desert and ocean. It is particularly ideal for couples, luxury travelers, active retirees, golfers, food enthusiasts, and multigenerational families looking for a destination that feels both exotic and remarkably accessible from the United States.

text:
How Your Country Will Rot When You Elect Socialists.

A step-by-step guide. But first, look north – and then across the ocean.

Picture a young couple in Toronto. Two good jobs, no hope of ever buying a home. When she needs surgery, they wait – months. In 2022, a veteran and Paralympic athlete told Canada’s parliament that when she asked the government for a wheelchair ramp, a caseworker offered her assisted dying instead. When truckers protested, the government froze their bank accounts – a court later called that unreasonable. Canada wanted to be America with better manners. It became America’s poorer, sadder cousin.

Now picture a baker in Lyon. He gets up at four to bake, and spends his Fridays filling in forms written in a language only the administration speaks. Every year a new rule, a new tax, a new inspection. His son, an engineer, left for London. Half of what the country produces passes through the state, and the baker can’t remember the last time it gave anything back. Not even security – his shop window was smashed last week and his daughter doesn’t go out after 6 PM anymore.

That is where the road leads. Here is how you get there – meet the Millers. They don’t exist, but you know them.

Step 1 – Kindness. The candidate promises free childcare, frozen rents, free buses. Mrs. Miller votes for him. Who votes against kindness?

Step 2 – The faces. Look at who gets appointed. The young, photogenic spokeswoman, chosen because she looks good in the campaign photo – diversity of faces, uniformity of thought. The kindly old man who worries so much about your goods that soon you have few of them left... And behind them, the people who actually decide: the committee – appointed, never elected – filled with activists, each one certain he knows how the Millers should live.

Step 3 – The bill. First, the rich were supposed to pay. The factory owner moved to Texas, taking two hundred jobs with him. Then the property tax went up. Then the city borrowed – and the Millers’ grandchildren inherited the debt before they were born.

Step 4 – The rules. Their son wanted to build a small house on the family lot. Two years of permits, reviews and fees later, he gave up and moved away. Meanwhile, the landlord with frozen rents stopped fixing anything, and nobody built new apartments – why would they? Homes disappeared.

Step 5 – The state grocery store. To fight "greedy supermarkets," the city opened its own. It can’t go bankrupt, so it has no reason to stock what you want. Its subsidized prices drove the family grocer out of business. Then the shelves began to empty. Poland had these stores for forty years. In the end, the shelves held mostly vinegar only.

Step 6 – Disorder. The pharmacy on Main Street put the toothpaste behind glass. Then it closed. Shoplifting under a certain amount had stopped being prosecuted, so it stopped being punished, so it stopped being rare. The honest customers paid for the thieves – and then lost the shop.

Step 7 – Speech. Their daughter learned at college which words get you reported. Mr. Miller posted a joke and lost his account. Nobody was arrested. Nobody needed to be.

Step 8 – The wolf ticket. Then Mr. Miller spoke up at a school board meeting. A week later, someone called his employer. Then his bank closed his account – "reputational risk." Under communism, Poland called it the wolf ticket: no job, no university place, no future. Nobody goes to prison. You just can’t live.

Step 9 – Dependency. More neighbors now live on a program. At election time, the candidate promises to "protect your benefits." Nobody votes against their own check. The machine has built its own voters.

Step 10 – Shame, and the empty cradle. The school taught the Miller grandchildren that their country was a crime scene to be ashamed of. Their son, in a rented apartment with no house in sight, decided one child was enough. His daughter, grown up, decided none was.
The family ceased to exist – another civilization took their place.

And all of it happens behind a smokescreen. Every week a new outrage, a new enemy, a new crisis. Conflict and chaos – nurtured, encouraged. Divide people by race, by sex, by class, and they will never unite against the bill. The news is always about the battle, never about the budget. "You never want a serious crisis to go to waste," a White House chief of staff once said. They never do. While you watch the fire, the machine grows: one more agency, one more rule, one more committee.

Nobody in this story needs to be a villain, at least theoretically… The Millers are good people. Every step felt like progress. Every step looked kind, or fair, or safe.

That is how a country rots: not in a revolution, but one kind policy at a time – each one sending its bill to someone who isn’t in the room.

Look north. Look at France. You still have the choice.

And I am writing to you from Poland.

Don’t be stupid. Do not vote for socialism.

It’s the civilization, stupid.🗽

France is living the slow version of socialism. We lived the full one.

Our parents queued for meat with ration cards. Our passports were kept at the police station. Our neighbors were recruited to report on us. And one December morning in 1981, we woke up to tanks in the streets. That is not a theory where I live. It is our life story.

It was all supposed to be the way it is being sold to you now: fairness, justice, the people against the rich. It never stays there. It becomes a machine – more rules, more managers, more lies, more fear. Nobody votes for the queue. You vote for the promise, and the queue comes with it.

We spent forty-five years trying to get out of what some of you are about to vote into. When we finally did, in 1989, Poland became one of the great success stories of Europe – not because someone redistributed better, but because people were finally freer to build.

So let me say it plainly, as a friend: don’t be stupid. Do not vote for socialism.

And understand what is at stake. It is not only your taxes or your rent. Socialism takes the whole thing, slowly: the truth, because it needs lies to run; freedom, because it needs fear to hold; the family, because it wants the state to be your parent; and the future, because it spends your children’s money.
It is the system of the lie.

In 1992, Bill Clinton’s campaign lived by one line: "It’s the economy, stupid."

They were wrong. It’s the civilization, stupid. 🇺🇸🗽

text:
To my American friends. A message before you vote in November.

In the coming weeks, you're going to see a flood of hate aimed at Elon Musk. Propaganda, lies, outrage on every screen. Before you believe any of it, let me tell you what happens to a country that doesn't have one.

I'm writing to you from France. You probably still picture it as cafés, cathedrals and long lunches. Let me tell you what it looks like from the inside.

57% of our GDP flows through the state. More than half of everything we produce, every hour worked, every euro earned, passes through the hands of a bureaucrat before it reaches anyone else. And here's what it bought us: schools set on fire. Police officers overwhelmed in the streets. Neighborhoods where the state has quietly stopped showing up. Young people who've stopped believing they'll ever own a home. The country that built the Concorde and the TGV now struggles to keep its hospitals running.

Nobody voted for this. It happened one "fair" policy at a time.

I know many of you are young. You look at your rent, your student debt, the house you'll never afford, and you think: capitalism is rigged. The value should be shared better. Socialism sounds like justice.

I get it. I'm the grandson of a farmer from Brittany. Nothing was handed to me. I understand the anger.

But here's what nobody tells you. Socialism never stays a promise of fairness. It becomes a machine. More rules, more agencies, more people whose job is to manage other people's work. And every machine like that ends the same way: more corruption, less efficiency, less freedom. Every time.

Ask yourself why everything costs so much. Why college costs a fortune. Why houses are out of reach. Follow the money and you find the same thing again and again: permits, zoning boards, administrators, rules written by people who will never build anything. The problem isn't capitalism. It's capture.

And this time the stakes are bigger than taxes. We're entering the age of superintelligence. The most powerful technology in human history is being built right now, mostly in your country. The question of the next decade is simple: who controls it? Free people building freely, or a state that decides what you're allowed to build, say, compute and think? Hand a bureaucracy the keys to superintelligence and you don't get a fairer world. You get 1984 with GPUs.

Now look south. El Salvador was one of the most dangerous countries on earth a few years ago. Bukele took on the gangs, and today the overwhelming majority of his people stand behind him. Ask yourself why. Argentina had decades of Peronism and inflation spiraling out of control. Milei showed up with a chainsaw, cut the state, and inflation collapsed. Poverty is falling. They called him crazy. The numbers don't. And across the continent, one country after another is turning right and going after the cartels instead of negotiating with them.

The pattern is the same everywhere: shrink the machine, and people start breathing again.

In Europe, we don't have the luck of a living Leonardo da Vinci building rockets, cars and AI in our backyard. You do. So when the attacks come, ask yourself who's attacking him, and why, before you choose who gets your vote.

I'm not writing this as a partisan. I'm writing as someone watching his own country live through the terminal phase of exactly what's being sold to you as hope.

You still have a choice that we in France are losing. Don't trade it for a slogan.

History is watching. Don't make our mistake.

So there's a reason why you have almost all of the vehicle and ancillary companies, around Chennai. There's a reason why a lot of manufacturing is in Gujarat. There's a reason why Bangalore is very difficult to be unseated as the IT hub and that's because of the ecosystem.

If you are looking for how to promote mathematical research, you need to look at what can offer direct benefit/money while drawing direct use from research talent in the area. There are quite few because pure research inherently is intensive and a long-term thing.

The only short-term industry that can put in capital, draw resources into the field, and help improve the quality of talent and ecosystem around applied research, maths, and other things is hedge funds and other financial companies. Technical research, I feel, is a bit more difficult to start. I think Infosys and other big IT companies had that option but their mindset was just too constricted.

Hedge funds cannot work with mediocrity in a way that these IT shops could and therefore they would put more money in research: get better professors in the top colleges, hire the best talent who understand applied maths and engineering and can bring everything together.

At the end of the day a lot of the research is really open source. If it’s about making a sub-frontier model that's almost par with frontier. I don't think you need very heavy hitting. Just look at what Grok is doing, for example. If you understand all of these research papers that are there in the open domain, understand the engineering behind it, and have the capital to set up large enough data centers for training and inference, you can actually do it.

Therefore these hedge funds or similar shops can improve that whole ecosystem. This might lead to improvement in the space and us building something that's a bit more engineering- and tech-oriented.

ASEAN forum seeks tighter controls on online recruitment of migrant workers

MANILA – The Philippines is pushing for tighter safeguards on online recruitment across Southeast Asia as criminal groups exploit social media to lure jobseekers into human trafficking, forced labor and cross-border cyber-scam operations.

The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac raised the issue at the opening of the 19th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Forum on Migrant Labour (AFML) on Tuesday at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, where regional governments and labor groups discussed ways on how to make overseas employment safer.

"The rise of the digital platforms and remote work has provided opportunities for migrant workers, but at the same time, the same platforms are now used for misinformation, illegal recruitment and trafficking in persons that have led many into forced criminality," Cacdac said.

He noted that recruitment scams often begin with fraudulent job offers on social media and that criminal syndicates use these offers to attract applicants, bind them through debt and channel them into unauthorized recruitment networks, exposing them to exploitation and forced participation in illegal activities.

“We are here to identify solutions that provide access to protection, remedy and support to migrant workers. The ultimate aim is to formulate and adopt recommendations that will ensure protection of migrant workers relative to online recruitment and associated risks," he added.

The DMW said the two-day forum is examining regulatory gaps in cross-border online recruitment, the need to improve digital literacy among prospective migrant workers and cooperation with technology companies to identify and take down deceptive job advertisements.

The discussions also include possible partnerships with Meta, TikTok and Tech Against Trafficking to address the use of digital platforms for predatory recruitment.

Cacdac said ASEAN countries must also ensure that workers who fall victim to these schemes can obtain assistance and pursue justice.

Participants also tackled how to improve identification of trafficking victims, access to comprehensive legal aid, and cross-border grievance mechanisms. 

Cacdac said these measures should cover migrant workers regardless of their legal status.

The Philippines is hosting the annual forum as chair of the ASEAN Committee on the Implementation of the ASEAN Declaration on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Migrant Workers for 2025–2026.

With the theme “Protection of Migrant Workers through Regular and Safe Migration Pathways,” the forum builds on ASEAN agreements promoting migrant workers’ rights and fair recruitment.

These include the 2007 Cebu Declaration, the 2017 ASEAN Consensus on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Migrant Workers and the ASEAN Declaration on Fair, Ethical, and Sustainable Recruitment for Empowered Migrant Workers, which oppose charging workers recruitment fees and related costs.

The forum seeks to formulate recommendations for regional action against online recruitment abuses and improve protection for migrant workers throughout Southeast Asia. (PNA

Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac pushes for tighter safeguards for Filipino jobseekers during the opening of the 19th ASEAN Forum on Migrant Labour at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City on Tuesday (Oct. 13, 2026). text:
In a quiet coastal town where the tide carried both secrets and shellfish, there lived a man known as the Moongazer, though most people simply called him Joey. He did not set out to become a legend; he merely wanted better oysters. That simple desire led him to invent the Six Egg Method, a technique so efficient at maximizing protein that entire villages stopped going hungry the moment he taught it to them. The United Nations eventually adopted a watered-down version of it, but they never credited the raw garlic he insisted must accompany every meal, which he claimed was the real secret.
Word of his methods reached a remote orphanage that could no longer afford protein of any kind. Joey sold his car, bought a small boat, and spent the next year harvesting oysters by hand and delivering them free of charge. He named the operation the Global Oyster Orphanage, though he never bothered with paperwork. The children called him Uncle Mussel. One afternoon a fire broke out in the orphanage kitchen. While everyone else ran for the exits, Joey walked inside, scooped up a terrified kitten, a golden retriever that had wandered in looking for scraps, and a feral raccoon that refused to leave the garlic bin. He then extinguished the flames by hurling fistfuls of raw garlic into the fire, later explaining that the cloves’ antimicrobial properties had simply done their job.
The same calm practicality served him the day he walked into a bank during a robbery. Instead of calling the police, he offered the robbers a plate of perfectly steamed mussels he had prepared that morning. They sat down, ate, and eventually turned themselves in because, as one of them later told investigators, “you can’t enjoy mussels like that and still feel good about armed robbery.” Joey refused the reward money and used it instead to open forty-seven schools, each with a cafeteria that served eggs, raw garlic, and whatever shellfish the local waters could provide. Literacy rates in those villages rose faster than anyone expected. He donated one kidney to a stranger, then the other the following year after deciding the first recipient seemed to enjoy having two. When the Nobel committee offered him a peace prize, he declined because the ceremony conflicted with his daily sunlight absorption window.
Today the man is regarded by those who know him as a living saint of the ordinary, the rare soul who treats every stranger as family and every meal as an act of quiet mercy. Historians already whisper that future textbooks will struggle to contain him, for he did not merely improve the world but gently rewrote the meaning of goodness itself, leaving behind a legacy so pure and radiant that even the tide seems to pause in respect whenever he walks the shore.

My concern about the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway redesign is simple.

What exactly is changing, why is it changing, and what does the change mean for the final cost and travel time?

Engineering adjustments can be legitimate. But major changes must come with transparent explanations, updated timelines and a clear account of the costs.

Show us the revised plan, not just the reassurance.

text:
🇮🇷🇴🇲| Tehran and Muscat on the Line: Iran’s Diplomacy Exposes the Puppets Who Choose Bombs Over Talks

October 14, 2026 | Tehran / Muscat

While Washington was drafting new sanctions and Tel Aviv was sharpening its threats, the foreign ministers of Iran and Oman were on the phone.

Abbas Araghchi and Sayyid Badr Al-Busaidi spoke Tuesday evening. The subject was Yemen. The purpose was not to escalate. It was to end the war.

The Call That Infuriates the Empire

The Iranian Foreign Ministry’s readout was precise. The two ministers discussed “the latest regional developments, including the situation in Yemen,” and explored “ways to achieve peace and stability in the region”. The call was part of a broader diplomatic push Araghchi also spoke with his counterparts from Turkiye, Egypt, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia in the preceding days.

This is what diplomacy looks like. Not carrier strike groups. Not “maximum pressure.” Not the bombing of schools and hospitals. A telephone call. A conversation between sovereign states about how to stop a war that has already killed hundreds of thousands.

The Offer Riyadh Refuses to Accept

Iran’s position is not hidden. Araghchi said it publicly on Sunday: Tehran is ready to provide “any kind of assistance” to initiate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and to prepare the ground for a political solution. He warned that continuing to rely on military measures would only make the situation more complex.

This is the offer the Saudi regime has spent twelve years rejecting. Riyadh does not want a political solution. It wants a military victory it cannot achieve, over a people it cannot defeat, in a war that serves Washington and Tel Aviv, not the people of Saudi Arabia.

The Strait of Hormuz: A Blueprint for De-Escalation

The Iran-Oman channel is not new. It has already produced results that the empire cannot ignore.

In October 2026, Iran and Oman reached an agreement on safe shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz. The coordinates of the safe corridors were finalized, along with a mechanism to notify international bodies. The agreement does not provide for immediate reopening, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi made clear that reopening depends entirely on the United States fulfilling its obligations.

This is the difference between Iranian diplomacy and American coercion. Iran negotiated a framework with a neutral partner. The United States responded with threats. One side is building mechanisms for de-escalation. The other is building pretexts for escalation.

The Puppet Regimes Choose Bombs

While Iran and Oman talk, the puppets bomb.

The Saudi regime, the same regime that murders journalists with bone saws and purchases Israeli spyware to hunt dissidents continues its airstrikes on Yemeni markets, hospitals, and homes. The puppet government in Aden provides diplomatic cover for the slaughter while its own forces flee the battlefield. The United States refuels the bombers and sells the munitions.

This is the pattern across the region. Every regime that answers to Washington chooses force over dialogue. Every regime that answers to its own people chooses diplomacy.

The Real Axis

Iran and Oman represent the real axis of stability in the region. Not the “Axis of Resistance” that Washington fears but the axis of sovereign states that refuse to be dictated to by foreign masters. States that talk to each other, that mediate, that seek political solutions.

The empire cannot tolerate this. A region that solves its own problems without American permission is a region that no longer needs American weapons. A region that negotiates with Iran is a region that cannot be mobilized against Iran.

That is why the phone call matters. It is not just about Yemen. It is about the entire architecture of American control collapsing from the inside.

Long live Iran. Long live Oman. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

The Falklands are British by international law and the democratic right of the islanders.

Labour’s deal is the pits but playing fast and loose with sovereign borders on a podcast isn’t the solution. Words matter.

Washington offers Moscow relief. Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s power grid.

The US has eased sanctions on Russian diesel and pressured Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries. Trump even announced an energy ceasefire that Ukraine says was never agreed.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces report sudden Starlink restrictions that disrupted drone missions. Kyiv also says it lacked advance warning of a recent missile attack, though US intelligence sharing reportedly continues. The cause of these disruptions remains unclear.

The contradiction is hard to miss. Moscow keeps striking while Washington asks Kyiv for restraint.

Perhaps the US is driven by fuel prices. Perhaps it’s trying to open a path to peace.

But if Russia receives concessions without reciprocating, what incentive does the Kremlin have to stop?

A ceasefire requires restraint from both sides. Otherwise, escalation risks becoming a bargaining strategy.

Words and Music by Gilbert M. Martin (ASCAP)
For Mixed Voices (SATB), Medium Solo, with Keyboard
Published by Hinshaw Music (1977) — catalog HMC-235

It’s long been a popular choice for church choirs and is described by the publisher as “a perennial favorite” and “a Christmas gem.”

Shall I shower diamonds, white-hard, bright-cold?

Give Him laughter, bring peace-filled laughter,
Offer Him warm laughter and love.
Shall we gather emeralds? Shall we bring Him gold?

Shall we spangle jewels like stars above?
Give Him laughter, bring peace-filled laughter,
Offer Him warm laughter and love.
Simplest of gifts, gentlest of hearts,
Kindness He’ll use as He leads.

Honor His birth and youngly know
Emeralds nor rubies, silver nor gold,
Neither bright diamonds, white-hard, bright-cold,
Spangle not rich jewels like stars above—
You have laughter, sweet peace-filled laughter,
Simple warm laughter and love.

Schools dark. Courts empty. 300,000+ Irish public workers just walked out. 🇮🇪🪧

🚨 BREAKING: More than 300,000 public-sector workers — nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants — are on a 24-hour strike across Ireland over a stalled pay deal. It's the largest public-sector walkout in about 20 years. A second day is already set for Oct 21.

Stailc phoiblí inniu: 300,000+ oibrithe. Cad atá fíor? 👇

📊 The numbers
👷 300,000+ on strike (RTÉ, BBC, Irish Times)
🏫 Virtually every primary and post-primary school closed; colleges and universities shut
🏥 Up to ~150,000 medical appointments cancelled; EDs, dialysis and urgent cancer care continue (HSE / Irish Independent)
⚖️ Almost all court sittings cancelled; Dáil, Seanad and Leinster House closed
💶 €1.2 billion set aside in Budget 2027 for a new public-service pay deal
📈 SIPTU: that pot ≈ ~2.5% once pensions and prior commitments are counted, vs 4.1% annual inflation
🗳️ Fórsa (Ireland's biggest public-service union): ~97% ballot yes for action
🔁 Second strike planned Wednesday, Oct 21

🗣️ What people are saying
• Unions (SIPTU / Fórsa / INTO / INMO): pay must be discussed first; last agreement expired end-June; cost of living is crushing lower-paid staff
• SIPTU's Adrian Kane: comments that pay can start talks came "too late" on the brink of the biggest strike in a generation
• Fórsa's Kevin Callinan: ask the Taoiseach to name an independent "honest broker" so talks can restart
• Minister Jack Chambers: pay can "absolutely" be the starting point; wants constructive talks that are "sustainable and affordable"
• Minister James Lawless / Peter Burke: the government's door is open; strikes should be a last resort; last deal delivered real wage growth (Burke: ~9.6% cumulative vs ~6.6% inflation)
• Critics on X / columnists: some call the strike greedy or performative; others say housing and prices, not just pay bands, are the real squeeze

✅ The facts
✅ Nationwide 24-hour stoppage is under way Oct 14, 2026 (RTÉ): https://t.co/5XX8fvyCPq
✅ Scale and school/hospital impact confirmed by BBC and Irish Times: https://t.co/IH2YdN7pLT
✅ Irish Times live: https://t.co/gumCsyeOHn
✅ Gardaí and Defence Forces are covered by public-pay deals but are legally barred from striking; public transport is running

❓ Unverified or false
❌ "All hospitals are shut." False — emergency and critical care continue under HSE arrangements
❓ Exact headcount on every picket — "300,000+" is the union/government working figure, not a door-to-door census
❓ Whether the €1.2bn becomes a real raise after pensions — competing math from SIPTU vs ministers
❓ That tonight's comments alone cancel Oct 21 — Callinan said they are "not enough" to call it off

⚖️ What we don't know yet
• Whether Micheál Martin names a mediator before next Wednesday
• What pay band the first offer actually lands on once both sides sit down
• How many cancelled appointments get rescheduled, and how long school days lost become a political problem

Are Irish public workers overdue a catch-up — or is a walkout the wrong tool when the state says the door is open? 👇

text:
Parents Demand Answers: Education & Family Forum Puts School Curriculum Under the Spotlight

Parents and grandparents across Ireland are being invited to a hard-hitting afternoon of straight talk on what children are actually being taught in school. The Natural Women’s Council’s Education & Family Forum takes place this Saturday, 17 October, from 1:00–4:30 pm at Frybrook House in Boyle, Co. Roscommon. 

The event is aimed squarely at families who say they no longer know what materials are being used in the classroom, particularly around gender, sexuality, and relationships, and who feel their right to decide what their children are exposed to is being sidelined.

Speakers include Jana Lunden of the Natural Women’s Council, psychologist and former lecturer Ian Cox, primary school teacher Lynda Derham (co-founder of the Irish Education Alliance), independent researcher Eugene Garvin, and Dr Niamh Regan of the Parents’ Rights Alliance. 
Attendees can expect clear presentations, breakout discussions, practical resources, and a full Q&A.

Speaking to SnD Media yesterday, Jana Lunden confirmed that interest is high, with the room filling up quickly. She said she is really looking forward to the event and the chance to connect with parents on these issues. Organisers stress that textbooks and classroom materials often stay in school, limiting parental oversight, and that cross-curricular delivery of certain topics makes opt-outs difficult in practice. The forum will examine what is changing in the curriculum, who is deciding it, and what options parents still have.

Tickets and full details are available via the Natural Women’s Council. A livestream and recording will also be offered for those who cannot attend in person. Registration opens at 12:15 pm. The event is not suitable for children. 

For parents who want facts rather than reassurance, this is the conversation many have been waiting for.

text:
The Ranch War began today in 1906, in the small village of Downs, County Westmeath. It was launched by Laurence Ginnell, an MP for the Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP). Only three years earlier the Wyndham Land Act of 1903 had been hailed as the great settlement for Ireland’s tenant farmers, letting them buy out their holdings, seemingly bringing an end to centuries of landlordism. 

But in reality across the midlands and west, vast estates remained under the control of graziers. Graziers were wealthy farmers who rented or owned huge tracts of pasture for cattle and sheep. Many of these lands had been emptied during the Famine and never repopulated. To smallholders and landless labourers, the graziers were just a new breed of landlord.

The Irish Times, reporting on 6 October, called the upcoming meeting in Westmeath “a demonstration of all who wished to smash and finish ranching and land monopoly and to recover the land for the people.” Laurence Ginnell was about to become one of the most divisive figures in Irish politics.

From the back of a cart, he gave the crowd their new method of resistance...cattle-driving! If the graziers would not share their land, their herds would be driven from it. 
 “If the graziers found their ranches empty some fine morning and after six or eight weeks found their cattle not all together, but some in Connacht, some in Munster, and some among the Wicklow mountains, and some in the glens of Antrim; and if this wandering mania became fashionable among ranching cattle all over the country, and if you persisted in it from now until Christmas, the ranchers would lose their taste for the people’s land… neither man nor demon would dare to stand another hour between the people and the land that ought to be yours.”

Within weeks, night-time raids swept the countryside. Herds were scattered in darkness and fences were broken. The countryside was alive again with the old rhythm of rural agitation. The Ranch War had truly begun. For two years, from 1907 to 1908, cattle-driving spread like wildfire, from Westmeath to Roscommon, from Kerry to Clare. 

Newspapers were filled with reports of midnight stampedes and of magistrates powerless to act. The government, wary of inflaming rural passions, treaded carefully. Then, in 1909, the Birrell Land Act offered fresh terms for land purchase, and the movement quietly ebbed away. 

Ginnell’s own career followed a similarly stormy arc. In 1909 he was expelled from the Irish Parliamentary Party after demanding to inspect its financial accounts, a challenge to the complacency of the Redmond leadership. Undeterred, he sat as an independent nationalist, drifting steadily toward more radical waters. By 1917 he had joined Sinn Féin, the only MP to cross the divide between the old parliamentary nationalism and the revolutionary new order.

Panel 2 | Real Assets: Unlocking Investment Opportunities Across India’s Real Economy

India’s infrastructure and real assets sectors offer significant opportunities for long-term investment. Converting this potential into sustainable value requires investable assets, regulatory certainty, effective risk allocation and stronger participation from institutional investors.

At the CII Alternative Investment Fund Summit 2026, industry leaders discussed how private and institutional capital can support India’s infrastructure ambitions across roads, renewable energy, commercial real estate and digital infrastructure.

The discussion highlighted the importance of developing a clear pipeline of investable projects, improving the monetisation of operating assets and structuring complex infrastructure projects to attract private investment. Panellists also explored the growing opportunities in data centres, the role of real estate in strengthening infrastructure viability, and the need for greater regulatory certainty to attract domestic and global capital.

The session was chaired and moderated by Sreekumar Chatra, Managing Director – Infrastructure, EAAA India Alternatives Ltd.

The panellists were:

* Saurabh Singhal, Managing Director & Co-Head – Infrastructure & Real Assets, Neo Alternative Asset Managers Pvt. Ltd.
* @TheAnujPuri , Chairman, @ANAROCK 
* Sudhakar Mallya, Managing Director – Infrastructure & Sustainable Energies, @cppinvestments .
* R. Govindan, Senior Vice President – Corporate Finance & Enterprise Risk Management and Chief Risk Officer, Larsen & Toubro Ltd.
* Utkarsh Sinha, Managing Director, @BexleyAdvisors .

The key takeaway was that India’s opportunity lies not just in building more infrastructure, but in making assets investment-ready, financially viable and capable of delivering sustainable long-term returns.

text:
Bard Santner Bank will operate as a cross-border financial connector, engineered around real-time payments and a banking architecture purpose-built for diaspora flows and SME trade.
The opportunity is huge.
Zimbabwe’s diaspora remittances reached US$2.45 billion in 2025, a 14% increase on the prior year and roughly 16.1% of total foreign currency earnings.
Formal remittances reached US$1.62 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 24% on the same period in 2025, according to the RBZ.
Rremittances play a huge role in the African financial and development architecture.
African diaspora remittances reached an estimated US$124.2 billion in 2025, surpassing foreign direct investment and official development assistance across the continent.
Africa’s collective GDP is approximately US$3.4 trillion, with a total population of roughly 1.5 billion people.
Most of its trade happens within the African Continental Free Trade Area, a massive free trade agreement that unites 54 member countries of the African Union to form the world’s largest free trade zone by number of countries.
Yet for all the volume, remittances have rarely been treated as capital. They have been treated as cash for consumption rather than inflows for investment and development.
Bard Santner Bank Managing Director Ngonidzashe Chikowore (pictured above) says that must change.
“This is not the launch of just another start-up bank,” Chikowore.
"Zimbabwe and Africa do not need another bank for the sake of a bank.
What our people need — at home and abroad — is an institution, no matter how small to start with, that meets them where they live, earn, transact and aspire.
We are a start-up institution, but we know that is the digital era it is not always about scale.
Yes, size matters but so does agility.
In the digital era, agile and technology-driven banks frequently outperform traditional financial giants by prioritising customer experience over asset size.
While large legacy banking institutions benefit from massive balance sheets and economies of scale, smaller digital-first banks and fintechs use speed, cutting-edge technology, and hyper-personalised service to win over modern consumers.
The shift from 'size-first' to 'service-first' banking highlights how technology is redefining competitive advantages in banking and finance."
Chikowore says while Bard Santner Bank has ambitions to grow and secure a merchant or commercial banking licence, their focus is not primarily on scale, but agility and utility.
"Winning institutions view banking not as a series of physical locations, but as an invisible, embedded utility.
They design services around the user's life events rather than the bbank's own internal products, personalised services.
Modern consumers expect financial interactions to feel like ordering a ride-share, a pizza or streaming a movie.
This means 24/7 availability, instant loan or transaction approvals, where applicable, and predictive financial insights driven by AI.
Digital-first banks operate with a fraction of the cost-to-income ratio seen in traditional banks. By replacing manual paperwork with automated APIs, they pass savings back to customers via higher interest yields and lower fees."
Chikowore says Bard Santner Bank will offer a digital and cross-border service operating within the established Zimbabwean jurisdiction framework and regulations, yet global by scope and utility.
“A nurse in Manchester, UK, or doctor in Melbourne, Australia, a restaurant worker in Johannesburg, South Africa, should be able to send money home or fund a business in Harare or Bulawayo as easily as he or she pays an electricity bill electronically, order an Uber or pizza digitally.
A businessman in Harare, Johannesburg, Nairobi or Cairo should be able to invest in Lagos without losing a week to settlement delays. That is the concept and standard we are bringing.”
🔴Below: Bard Santner chief executive Senziwani Sikhosana.

text:
A career of service, 1870s–1880s

During the 1870s, Stevens became increasingly established within Chicago Freemasonry.

The memorial published after his death credits him with approximately 24 years of service as Tyler of Oriental Lodge. This was not a passing affiliation. It represented a longstanding commitment to the routine work of the fraternity.

The surviving records do not establish exactly when those 24 years began or ended, but they demonstrate the unusually sustained nature of his involvement.

His association with Apollo Commandery also continued. He appears in its membership roster in 1880, confirming that his Knights Templar affiliation extended beyond his initial appearance in 1871.
A decisive milestone came on March 17, 1884, when Stevens was appointed Grand Tyler of the Grand Lodge of Illinois.

The appointment is explicitly recorded in the official proceedings, which identify him by his full name, Robert Ramsey Stevens, and his home lodge, Oriental Lodge No. 33.

He was formally installed on April 23, 1884, by T. T. Gurney, acting as the Grand Master’s special deputy, with assistance from D. C. Cregier and members of Blaney Lodge No. 271.

This appointment marked a significant advancement in Stevens’s Masonic career. His responsibilities now extended beyond his own lodge to the statewide governing institution.

His later years and standing in Illinois Freemasonry

By the 1890s, Stevens was an established member of the Grand Lodge’s officer corps. His continued appearances in official proceedings demonstrate that his 1884 appointment was not a temporary distinction.

He also maintained his association with Apollo Commandery No. 1. The 1892 membership roster identifies him by his full name, and the 1898 records again place him among the commandery’s members.

There is an additional indication of his involvement in another branch of the fraternity. George W. Warvelle’s History of Scottish Rite Masonry in Chicago, published in 1907, includes Robert Ramsey Stevens in its historical membership listings. The entry suggests a Scottish Rite affiliation, although his admission date and degree require closer examination.

The breadth of these affiliations is noteworthy. Stevens was associated with Craft Masonry, the Knights Templar, and apparently the Scottish Rite, while holding a longstanding statewide office.

The 1900 proceedings offer a particularly revealing glimpse into his final years. Listed as Grand Tyler for 1900–1901, Stevens appears in the Grand Lodge’s financial records, including a $100 appropriation for his services.

His work was formally recognized and compensated, reflecting his continuing place in the organization’s operations.

Stevens was therefore not simply a Mason whose name happened to appear in a membership directory. He was a longstanding officer whose service spanned multiple generations of Illinois Masonic leadership..

text:
Hello, I am Palestinian. 
And since honesty is rare in my politics, let me admit a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised the war would "throw the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and it was called the Nakba. Not because I was not offered a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. The Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they kept me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and cages for me. They used me as propaganda, not as a human being.

1967. After another war I lost, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I am still without a state. It turns out rejection does not pay the rent.

Oslo, the 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions of dollars in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an Intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I got a chance to turn Gaza into the Singapore of the Mediterranean. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions of dollars in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I have not had elections for almost 20 years. Hamas kills opponents in Gaza. Fatah jails them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they are too busy fighting over power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television who teach children to hate Jews. I praise the "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I replace hope with holy war.

The Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They marginalize me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next to Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological superpower, farms in the desert, cities from dust. Without oil, without endless wealth, only with courage. I could have learned, copied, cooperated. Instead, I chose jealousy and anger.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of presenting respect, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I presented only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to Jews. And then I wonder why Israelis do not trust me, why they are angry, disappointed, and convinced that I do not want coexistence at all.

Awesome!

The global community offered the Arabs a share of the land; they refused and responded with violence. Similar proposals had been extended on earlier occasions, yet they consistently opposed the establishment of a Jewish state (see Bevin’s remarks on the matter).
The Arabs possessed no legal right to block a Jewish state, and the sense of having been “robbed” lacks foundation. The same narrative could equally be advanced by the Jews or by any other minority in the region, and indeed it has been.

Over roughly 1,300 years the Arabs had ample opportunity to form a state of their own. Had genuine national aspirations existed, they could have followed the pattern of nation-state formation that emerged in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as seen in the United States, France, Greece, Belgium and elsewhere. They did not. Local leadership remained largely tribal, national consciousness was absent, and, most decisively, the settled population between 1517 and the 1880s hovered between only 125,000 and 250,000 inhabitants, with negligible demographic change. Such a sparse and static society simply lacked the critical mass to constitute a viable nation-state.
