text:
Dex Hunter-Torricke, ex-Google DeepMind comms chief, on why the entire AI safety debate is a distraction from what's actually coming:

Dex spent two decades inside the machine, running communications for Elon Musk at SpaceX, writing Mark Zuckerberg's speeches at Facebook, and leading Global Communications and Marketing at Google DeepMind from 2023 to 2025.

He left in late 2025 and founded the Center for Tomorrow in February 2026. This is what he says now:

"We talk about AI governance. Yeah. And there's a whole bunch of stuff which is about how you manage the AI systems themselves. That's like 1% of the problem."

One percent. That's the entire debate you've been reading about for three years.

What worries him is the slope the technology is on:

"...how quickly it is gathering steam, how much more advanced it's getting, how much more advanced it will be in the next decade. That is something which is going to be wildly more devastating than any of the consequences of the mismanaged technologies of the last 15 years."

His benchmark is the wreckage of the last 15 years, social media and platform power included, and he's saying that was the warm-up:

"And the consequences will crash land on societies all over the world. We are not prepared for these things at all economically, society, geopolitically, environmentally. And that's the agenda that I'm really focused on. The tech industry has massively distorted the agenda for how to manage these things."

So what's the other 99%?

First, work. The job losses worry him less than the silence where the solution should be:

"15 years from now, probably less than 15 years when a lot of people have lost their jobs to AI and we have no economic solutions. We have no idea how to give people a good quality of life. That is a much much bigger problem than some of the technical issues we're facing in those systems."

We have no idea. From the man who wrote the speeches.

Second, the physical bill. AI runs on power, water, land and minerals, and it's coming for ecosystems that are already spent:

"...destabilize already reeling ecosystems which we know are hanging by a thread and which will impact the lives of millions if not billions of people."

His number:

"Between 2018 and 2023 the world consumed almost as much resources as one-third of the 20th century and it's accelerating all the time."

Five years, against roughly thirty-three. Accelerating.

Third, and this is the part that makes it hard to stop. Dex describes the pitch he watched get made to governments with nothing left to offer voters:

"Big tech companies, they go to governments who are desperate for economic growth now, right. A lot of the advanced economies in the global north, they've got plateauing growth. They've got declining living standards. They go to them and say, 'Build this wonder technology. Build this infrastructure. We will give you back the keys to a good future.'"

His verdict is four words:

"And of course, that's not happening."

"This is something which on the present path promises to enrich a tiny sliver of societies, mostly in the United States, mostly in China."

"I think the world we're going to end up in, you know, in the next, you know, 10, 15 years is going to be much more unstable than today with rapidly declining living standards for hundreds of millions."

text:
AI is already a ~$400 billion industry.

But decentralized AI? Still only $25billion.

That gap is where the opportunity lies.

→ @opentensor ( $TAO )
→ @origin_trail ( $TRAC )
→@_Qubic_ ( $QUBIC )

Here are 3 projects building the open alternative to Big Tech 👇

⚪ Bittensor ( $TAO ): The AI Commodity Marketplace

✦ Tech Used → Subnets + Yuma Consensus

• Miners produce digital commodities: compute, training, inference, protein folding, and more.

• Validators score the work, and Yuma Consensus turns those scores into TAO rewards.

• Sub-subnets (introduced in September 2025) let each subnet split into up to 8 task groups with their own emissions.

Bittensor isn’t “one AI model.” It’s a marketplace where anyone can plug in compute or models, get ranked, and earn TAO.

The sub-subnets upgrade made it even more modular, allowing multiple tasks inside a single subnet to run in parallel.

That means more flexibility, more specialization, and faster scaling.

✦ Network Design → Roles + Upgrades

• Four core participants: miners, validators, subnet creators, stakers.

• Auto-staking for miners reduces sell pressure.

• Child key fee now incentivizes active validators (scales up to 18%).

• Subnet registration tightened: 128 cap, 1,000 TAO lock, 4-month immunity.

It’s an economy with built-in checks and balances.

Everyone has a role, and recent updates make sure the system can’t be gamed.

The end result? A self-tuning market for AI work.

✦ Token → $TAO + Alpha Tokens

• 3,600 TAO emitted daily post-halving (41% miners, 41% validators/stakers, 18% subnet creators).

• Each subnet also issues its own “alpha token,” priced against TAO reserves.

• Stakers “vote with TAO” by backing valuable subnets and steering emissions.

TAO isn’t just a reward token it’s the currency of the whole AI economy.

The alpha-token design means emissions flow to where the market sees value.

If a subnet is useful, it attracts TAO stake, which in turn amplifies its rewards.

👉 My take: TAO is the AI infra heavyweight, turning incentives into a marketplace for useful work.

🟢 OriginTrail ( $TRAC ): The Verifiable Internet for AI

✦ Tech Used → Decentralized Knowledge Graph (DKG) + dRAG

• Data is structured into Knowledge Assets with blockchain proofs.

• Verifiable credentials ensure provenance and authenticity.

• dRAG (decentralized RAG) lets AI pull from verified knowledge before answering.

OriginTrail isn’t about building new models it’s about fixing hallucinations.

Its Decentralized Knowledge Graph makes information verifiable, so when AI answers, it’s pulling from truth-backed data, not just probability.

✦ Network Design → Paranets + Knowledge Economies

• Paranets are community-owned subnetworks for domains like supply chains or DeSci.

• Each paranet sets its own incentive rules for data mining, validation, and access.

• Together, paranets form modular “knowledge economies” feeding into AI.

• Recent upgrade: Staking threshold increased from 5M to 10M $TRAC (February 2026).

Think of paranets as mini economies, each curating and validating its own slice of knowledge.

All of them plug back into the global DKG, creating a living, verifiable internet that AI can trust.

✦ Token → $TRAC + $NEURO

• TRAC powers publishing, indexing, and querying of Knowledge Assets.

• NEURO (Polkadot parachain token) governs incentives and emissions to paranets.

• TRAC ensures the DKG runs, NEURO fuels its growth.

This dual-token system makes sure both the data layer (TRAC) and the growth incentives (NEURO) are covered.

The more data flows through the DKG, the more demand builds for TRAC.

👉 My take: TRAC is the enterprise trust layer, making sure AI systems rely on facts, not fabrications.

🟣 Qubic ( $QUBIC ): The Decentralized AI Supercomputing Network

✦ Tech Used → Useful Proof of Work (UPoW) + Quorum Consensus + Aigarth AI

• AI Miners train models and solve complex tasks using global compute power.

• Oracles integrate real-world data for AI models and smart contracts.

• Quorum-based computation ensures security, scalability, and instant finality.

• Aigarth: An evolving AI system trained via UPoW for artificial general intelligence (AGI).

Qubic redirects mining energy from wasteful hashing to productive AI training, building a massive decentralized supercomputer.

It's designed for high TPS (up to 15M), feeless transactions, and integrating AI with IoT and blockchain.

✦ Network Design → Computors + AI Miners + Decentralized Governance

• 676 Computors execute smart contracts and maintain the network via quorum voting.

• AI Miners contribute compute for AI tasks, rewarded based on performance.

• No single entity control, inspired by Byzantine Fault Tolerance.

• Open-source from day one, with community votes on key changes like supply reductions.

Qubic creates a resilient, scalable Layer-1 where compute power fuels AGI development.

It's more infra-focused than consumer apps, emphasizing global-scale AI computation over centralized clouds.

✦ Token → $QUBIC (Layer-1 Native, 200T Max Supply)

• Emissions: ~450B net per epoch post-2025 halving, with halvings every ~48 epochs.

• High burn rate (up to 55%) makes it deflationary; used QUBIC is burned.

• Distributed to miners, Computor fund, staking rewards, and governance.

• Community-reduced max supply from 1,000T to 200T for scarcity.

QUBIC's tokenomics reward useful compute, with emissions tied to AI training output.

The burn and halving mechanics control inflation, funneling value to active participants.

👉 My take: QUBIC is the AI compute powerhouse, higher risk but with massive potential if its AGI vision scales.

🔚 Conclusion: The AI Edge

After digging into these three, here’s how I see it:

Bittensor → The infra giant, building a marketplace for AI work.

OriginTrail → The trust layer, solving hallucinations with verifiable data.

Qubic → The supercomputing network, turning global energy into AGI training.

Final Rankings→

Tech Used:

$QUBIC > $TAO > $TRAC

👉 QUBIC is compute-driven, but with ambitious AGI goals.

TAO’s subnet + alpha-token system is the most advanced infra.

TRAC’s DKG + dRAG nails enterprise trust.

Network Design:

$TAO > $TRAC > $QUBIC

👉 TAO’s miners/validators/creators/stakers + sub-subnets create a AI economy.

TRAC’s paranets build modular knowledge markets. QUBIC’s computors and miners are robust, but more centralized around fixed nodes.

Token:

$TAO > $QUBIC> $TRAC

👉 TAO emissions + alpha tokens create a powerful incentive flywheel.

QUBIC offers burns and halvings, but tokenomics are evolving.

TRAC ties demand directly to publishing/querying.

💡 My Takeaway:

If you want AI infrastructure exposure → Bittensor.

If you want enterprise-grade verifiable data → OriginTrail.

If you want a small-cap decentralized AI compute bet → Qubic.

text:
$8B on paper. $800,000 so far. No one else was asked.

A deal with no rival bid does most of its damage on the next contract, when the firm with the track record is the one that never had to compete for it.

Raytheon's sole-source deal for nuclear communications terminals has an $8.0B ceiling, the most the Air Force can order through it, and every order goes to Raytheon. A firm shut out of this work has no record on it for the next evaluation to read.

The Pentagon's Oct. 13 list had at least 7 awards with no rival bid, and the 5 largest add up to $8.6B, Raytheon's among them. Most of that is unspent ceiling, and the head start is the part that lasts.

The quieter version is the award put out for bids that draws 1 offer, like BAE Systems' destroyer repair at Mayport. The Navy sought competition and still got a single proposal, with no second price to compare it against.

Rivals who expect the incumbent to win have little reason to pay for proposals. Each round without a challenger can make the next one less likely to get one, and the pool of companies that can do the work can shrink without anyone deciding it should.

Raytheon's terminal deal runs through 2036, and every year of orders adds to a record no other firm can build under it.

Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 And since honesty is rare in my politics, allow me to confess a few things.

The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that the war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything, and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me up in refugee camps for generations, so that I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I'm still stateless. Turns out rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said, "Let's give it a try." It gave me autonomy. Guns for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in almost 20 years. Hamas kills dissidents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother."

But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurd. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological powerhouse, desert farms, dusty cities. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said, "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of showcasing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I displayed only the culture of the sword.Anger, extremism, and bloodshed. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to the Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I feign surprise when the Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced that I don't want coexistence at all.

Accountability. I blame Israel for everything. Always. Do my leaders steal billions? Blame Israel. Does Hamas fire rockets from hospitals? Blame Israel. Do I glorify death more than life? Blame Israel. Accountability is not my strong suit.

I am Palestinian. I could have built a nation, many times over. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But all too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hatred. And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

text:
After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease | University of Wisconsin-Madison

The FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.

Alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.

The drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.

Clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some showed improvements in their ability to move.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing says.

Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder

Alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.

People with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.

The disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.

For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.

An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause

The breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.

The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.

Messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.

To the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.

"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing says.

The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.

"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.

Identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.

Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup

Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.

Messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced important features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.

The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.

In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).

These treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.

For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.

The experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.

Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.

Because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.

Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement

The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.

After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.

The results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an important outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.

These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.

The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.

Zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical company headquartered in Italy.

A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers New Hope

For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.

What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.

The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.

Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.

"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing says.

1SG 🫡 AWP DAILY ORDER — October 14, 2026
Promise #287 • MAKE YOUR HOME IN GOD’S LOVE

1 — THE ORDER

Today’s 365Promises theme: “If you make your home in love, you live in Me and I live in you.” This is the site’s promise summary for October 14, drawn from 1 John 4:16. 

“God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him.”
— 1 John 4:16, NKJV 

Battle Line: I will receive Christ’s love and carry it into today’s mission.

2 — THE TRAINING

Warrior Doctrine — Love is where you live.

John connects knowing God’s love, believing that love, and abiding in it. Abiding means remaining: returning to God in prayer, trusting His character, and allowing His love to shape your conduct.

You do not earn God’s presence by performing enough loving acts. In the surrounding passage, God takes the initiative by sending His Son; our love answers His. Read 1 John 4:9–19 as the full training passage.

1SG, when the world’s evil feels overwhelming, your assignment remains concrete: receive the love revealed in Christ and express it faithfully where you stand. You cannot govern every heart, but you can bring patience, truth, mercy, and courage into your next encounter.

Armor Fit

Belt of Truth: Measure God’s love by Christ’s sacrifice, even when your emotions are unsettled.
Shield of Faith: When doubt rises, return to what God has revealed about Himself.
Breastplate of Righteousness: Let love govern your response. Speak truth, keep wise boundaries, and refuse retaliation.
Boots of Peace: Enter the next conversation ready to listen and respond with care.

Love does not require approving wrongdoing or allowing continued mistreatment. 1 Corinthians 13:6 joins love with truth. A firm, honest boundary can be an act of love.

Supporting Scriptures — NKJV study references

Romans 5:8: God demonstrates His love through Christ’s death for sinners.
John 15:9–12: Jesus calls His disciples to abide in His love and love one another.
1 John 3:18: Love takes practical form through deeds and truth.
Ephesians 4:15: Truth and love belong together as believers mature in Christ.

3 — THE EXECUTION

Commander’s Orders — Today’s application

Receive: Spend five quiet minutes reading 1 John 4:9–19. Thank the Father for His love revealed through Jesus.
Remain: Before a difficult response, pause and ask: What would faithfulness to Christ’s love look like here?
Extend: Complete one deliberate act of love before bedtime—give an encouragement, help with a task, listen without interrupting, or offer a needed apology.

Measurable mission: Tonight, record one sentence: “Today I expressed Christ’s love by ______.”

Prayer of Deployment

Father, thank You for loving me through Jesus Christ. Help me believe Your love when my feelings are troubled. Keep my heart tender and my judgment grounded in truth. Teach me to speak with patience, set boundaries with wisdom, and serve with courage. By Your Spirit, make Your love visible in one specific action today. In Jesus’ name, amen.

The Minnesota Template is coming back around... this time in the accountability and justice phase... gere we go...

I called it the Minnesota Template for a reason... Minnesota offered a concentrated microcosm of a much larger national problem, with the entry points, political leadership, government agencies, nonprofit intermediaries, financial networks and institutional failures visible within one state...

Map the machinery, expose the mechanisms, establish the precedent... then carry that framework into California and across the nation...

The original mapping followed Feeding Our Future, Medicaid, housing assistance, fabricated eligibility, shell companies and the pathways through which enormous sums of taxpayer money flowed...

The approvals, beneficiaries, political connections and oversight failures exposed an architecture capable of replicating itself wherever the same vulnerabilities existed...

Now that template is coming full circle... the accountability phase follows those pathways backward through the records, reconstructing transactions, identifying participants and establishing who authorized what, who benefited and who knowingly enabled wrongdoing...

Look at Ilhan Omar... federal agents searching her Washington home, grand jury subpoenas reaching her sister and other relatives, investigators examining her late father's immigration and naturalization history, allegations surrounding his military background and the birth year discrepancy tied to the citizenship she says she acquired through him in 2000...

Add longstanding questions involving marriage and tax records, alongside a separate financial investigation involving her husband's businesses and reported asset values reaching $30 million before being dramatically revised downward...

The investigative reach cuts across immigration applications, citizenship records, sworn statements, corporate ownership, tax filings, financial disclosures, property transactions and potentially mortgage documentation... each capable of revealing discrepancies, reconstructing the chronology and establishing who knew what, when, and who signed off...

This is precisely why the Minnesota Template is jey... the Omar investigation is a separate track, yet the accountability framework is transferable... establish the facts, follow the relationships, identify the institutions responsible and determine where the evidence leads... 

Once the methodology is established, the same scrutiny can move from Minnesota into California and across every state where comparable mechanisms surface...

CHINA RETURNS TO US SOYBEAN MARKET

Chinese state buyers have bought eight to 10 Panamax cargoes of American soybeans this week, according to three trade sources cited by Reuters on Wednesday. 

It is the first such purchasing activity since September’s Washington meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. The cargoes are scheduled for shipment from December onwards.

The deals were struck by state-owned trading firms after several weeks without fresh Chinese buying. Traders said weak demand during China’s week-long National Day holiday had contributed to the pause.

One trader said the buyers paid premiums of $3.10 to $3.20 per bushel above the January Chicago Board of Trade soybean contract.

For American exporters, the development offers an early sign that commercial flows may be restarting after a prolonged lull.

text:
Podcast Summary | Candace: America The Ugly: A General, A Cop & A Missing Bloodied Bag. Plus, The Cornell 7. | Ep 401

Overview
Candace Owens uses Episode 401 to weave three seemingly separate stories into one argument about institutional rot: a Utah power figure who wears a general's stars, a legislative seat, and a university budget; a young police officer and legislator allegedly tied to a bloodied bag on the day after a major assassination; and a Cornell case she treats as proof that American parenting and higher education have failed. The connective tissue is her claim that overlapping roles, vague alibis, and unconfirmed credentials are not isolated scandals but the operating system of a degraded country. She also apologizes for a missed Monday episode, confirms she has not yet given birth, and previews a maternity leave that will pause the Charlie Kirk coverage she says she will keep pushing until then.

Key Themes

- Owens argues that Utah's lax rules on holding multiple official roles let figures like Val Peterson and Tyler Clancy accumulate power without meaningful conflict-of-interest review, which turns public trust into a formality.

- The unanswered question of where Val Peterson was on September 10th anchors the UVU thread: an after-action report places him roughly 45 minutes from campus, but the location is never confirmed.

- The bloodied bag allegation is the episode's central claim: a TPUSA affiliate allegedly left it in Tyler Clancy's car, and Clancy allegedly disposed of it the same day while the killer was still at large.

- Frank Turek's public account of asking an officer to dispose of a bloodied bag is treated as partial corroboration, even as Owens questions the plausibility of CPR over a bag and the bravado details.

- Owens links Clancy's rapid rise, including a governor's appointment as homeless coordinator, to a broader pattern of rewarding connected young operatives rather than scrutinizing them.

- The Cornell 7 case is used not as a legal dispute but as a cultural indictment: everyone involved is described as raised wrong, and the parents are called despicable.

- The press secretary segment frames national decline as a competence crisis, with a new spokesperson mocked for reading basic introductions from notes and for unverifiable legal credentials.

- Owens positions herself as the last holdout still pushing the Charlie Kirk story, accusing Erika Kirk of betraying his legacy by misusing his message to justify mainstream media appearances.

- The episode closes on self-aware humor and commerce, with maternity leave, merch lines, and a note that depositions, not public posturing, are where the real disclosures happen.

Detailed Summary

Owens opens by confronting a viral clip that accused her of lying when she said "see you Monday" but failed to publish a Monday episode. She apologizes, says producer Skyler corrected the date only after they were off air, and confirms the next episode lands Tuesday. She also states plainly that she is still pregnant, has not given birth, and is eager for the pregnancy to end before turning to the show's three main threads.

The first thread centers on Val Peterson, introduced as a UVU vice president of administration and strategic relations, a Utah state representative for the 56th district, and a retired brigadier general. Peterson started at the school in June 1987, when it was Utah Technical College, and now oversees a budget above $50 million covering facilities, athletics, university relations, emergency management, and environmental health and safety. Owens argues that stacking a university budget, a legislative seat, and three decades of military intelligence command creates conflict-of-interest questions that no form can resolve.

The military record is specific. A 2007 article says Peterson took command of the 300th Military Intelligence Brigade, a linguist unit headquartered in Utah with nearly 2,000 language specialists across six states, many of whom had served in Iraq and Afghanistan. As brigadier general he was responsible for training, readiness, administration, and the uniform code of military justice for six major army commands in Utah. Owens then asks the question the episode returns to repeatedly: where was Val Peterson on September 10th. She says an after-action report places him about 45 minutes from campus during the shooting, joining response discussions by speakerphone while traveling to UVU. She notes Salt Lake City is roughly 45 minutes away and hosts the National Guard air base, while Draper, about 15 minutes away, hosts the Army headquarters, but she stops short of claiming he was at either location.

The second thread introduces Tyler Clancy as a young, highly decorated figure: the youngest Utah House member since 1834, a BYU lacrosse leader under coach Matt Schneck, a Provo police officer in the Special Victims Unit, and an Internet Crimes Against Children affiliate. Peterson, who was Clancy's church leader at BYU, is quoted praising him as a natural leader. Owens alleges Clancy was on duty as a Provo officer on September 11th, was at Timpanogos hospital after Charlie arrived, and was dispatched with another officer to escort Erica Kirk from the airport, with TPUSA members or affiliates allegedly in his car. The core allegation follows: a TPUSA member or affiliate left a bloodied bag in Clancy's car, and Clancy disposed of it the same day. Owens says multiple Provo and ORM sources corroborate this and that she reached out to Clancy for comment without response. She argues no officer would reasonably discard a bloodied item on the day of a major assassination while the killer was still at large.

Frank Turek's account is offered as partial corroboration. On the Apostate Prophet podcast, Turek said Charlie had been lying on his bag, that it was full of blood, and that his necklace sat on top. Turek changed into scrubs, removed valuables, and asked the officer beside him to dispose of the bag so Erica would not see the blood. Owens questions the plausibility of CPR over a bag and the bravado in the telling, but treats the overlap with the Clancy allegation as significant rather than coincidental.

Owens ties the thread to Clancy's political rise. Governor Cox announced on October 30th that Clancy would become Utah's youngest-ever homeless coordinator, succeeding Wayne Neerhouser, citing faster help and cleaner, safer streets. She notes the promotion came shortly after the assassination and teases that Clancy is allegedly best friends with someone from the early days of the investigation. She also links him to a friend group including Shainer Brderick and Robbie Hild, noting Brderick allegedly posted about retracing the alleged killer's steps after the manhunt, with Converse-branded footprints and hashtags tied to the case, and that Hild and Clancy played lacrosse together at BYU.

The unanswered identity of the fire captain who provided CPR at Timpanogos becomes its own thread. Owens says the name remains unconfirmed and questions why it is not public, noting an unconfirmed claim that the captain was in an ambulance and jumped out to assist. She asks listeners for tips from anyone with direct knowledge. She also returns to Blake Neff, who she says could not remember where he was or who he was with in Salt Lake City and used the phrase "marking time," a military term she treats as telling.

The press secretary segment shifts to national competence. Owens praises Katie McInany as smart and overprepared, describes Caroline Levit as gaslighting, and mocks Katie Zacharia as resembling an SNL skit. She cites a Business Insider headline noting journalists struggled to confirm where the new press secretary passed the bar and quotes the response that she practiced international transaction law with all the appropriate credentials, without stating a bar admission. Owens says Pepperdine studies are hard to confirm, including whether it was in person or online, and compares the vagueness to claims about Erica Kirk's credentials. She also references a Youngstown, Ohio rally with Jake Paul and John Gruden where Trump announced Cleveland as the home of a 46,000-square-foot Navy submarine component repair center.

The Cornell 7 discussion is framed as cultural collapse rather than litigation. Owens describes a female student who agreed to sexual relations with two men at a frat party, agreed to snort a horse tranquilizer, and participated in a drug-fueled sex party, then says one man texted the entire frat house inviting others upstairs. She says the woman was texting the next morning and may not remember events. She praises Tim Dylan as one of the only rational people in America for saying nobody would be proud if the Cornell 7 were their sons, and calls the parents despicable. She says everyone involved was raised wrong, that the victim of the story is herself for having to read people intellectualize it, and jokes that if this is the America people believe in, they should vote for her as dictator in 2028.

The closing segment turns to Charlie Kirk's legacy. Owens says she will keep pushing the story before maternity leave, noting his birthday is October 14th, and accuses Erika Kirk of betraying his message by citing his call to sit down with people who disagree as justification for mainstream media appearances. She says Erika does not author her own tweets and argues Charlie meant engaging students on campus, not Vanity Fair. She mentions the Brian Cole case and promises to cover it before leaving, notes the Theo Vann interview has around 3.5 million views, and credits the sleuths who took risks to speak out while also crediting useful idiots whose mistakes encourage others.

She closes with housekeeping: only a handful of episodes remain before maternity leave, she takes all federal holidays and jokingly blames Skylar for reminders, and she promotes a conspiracy girly sweatshirt, a CIA shirt, planned wine glasses, pregnancy-line clothing, and an upcoming Baron Coleman line. She also apologizes again for the confusion, including that listeners thought she had given birth, for the lack of communication, and to Skyler. Depositions, she says, are where the real disclosures will come.

text:
Hermes yesterday: 512 commits hit main, more than double any day this series has covered, and the release was cut right behind them: v0.22.0 stable shipped overnight from the day's last commit. The headline: a fresh Desktop install now opens a setup chat, and the free model turns into a one-time trial for it. Here are the 10 that matter.

1️⃣ A fresh Desktop install opens a setup chat

Before: first-run setup lived in a separate hermes-setup profile, started with /initiate-setup, asked its questions on generic cards and handed off to a new chat at the end. After: a fresh Desktop install opens one chat in the default profile that walks through your name, an accent color, a layout, apps to connect, plugins, a quick tour and up to four first tasks picked for you, one card per step; typing in the composer answers the waiting card. Skip setup ends it, closing the app midway starts it over on the next launch, and Settings > Run onboarding again replays it on your configured model. Along the way the agent gained set_theme (it replaces apply_layout), so make it violet, dark mode works in any Desktop chat, and manage_connections can show a browsable connector directory card. Heads-up: /initiate-setup is gone on every surface, and an existing hermes-setup profile stays as an ordinary profile.

2️⃣ The free model becomes a one-time Desktop trial

Before: only the Microsoft Store build had the free model, and there it was on for the whole process: every CLI, gateway and backend boot created an anonymous Nous account, even with another provider configured, and any guest account could run inference. After: the free nous/welcome model is a one-time trial for the first Desktop install of an OS user who never used Hermes on that computer, on any bundle, and only on the Desktop's local backend. The CLI, TUI and messaging gateway no longer create an account at boot or offer the free model; connectors still create their connectors-only identity on first use. Desktop guests that already chatted on the free model keep it, a lost trial (signed in, auth.json deleted) is never claimed again, and the split between trial and connector guests is enforced on the client until a server-side check lands.

3️⃣ Memory edits stop wiping neighboring facts

Before: to change one fact, the memory tool's replace rewrote the whole entry, and models often dropped the other facts in it: NVIDIA measured Opus 4.8 doing it in 19 of 40 tasks. A write without a target fell back to MEMORY.md, so user facts could land there. After: replace is gone and patch is the only edit: it changes exactly one span inside an entry and keeps the rest (1 of 40 in the same test), and a span that appears twice is refused with a request for more context. Every write needs a top-level target. Writes staged for approval before the change still replay, and external memory providers receive a patch as a whole-entry replace. Heads-up: patch does not yet match a span retyped with straight quotes, a plain dash or re-wrapped lines where the entry has the original; a fix is in review.

4️⃣ Stable installs stay on stable

Before: rerunning the installer moved a stable install back to main, because Hermes-Setup bakes --branch main, and its update mode dropped the channel the Desktop asked for. The update check then offered an older stable release as a new update. After: an installer rerun keeps an install whose recorded channel is not main where it is and leaves the move to hermes update, and Hermes-Setup forwards the channel. When the checkout is newer than the chosen stable release, Desktop, hermes update --check, hermes --version and the dashboard call it a rollback (Roll back to v0.21.7) instead of an update. Installs with no channel record, a main record or an explicit --commit behave as before. Not run for real yet: the macOS Hermes-Setup app; the Windows installer is covered by CI tests only.

5️⃣ Connector tools send and save real files

Before: a connector tool that takes a file, like a mail attachment or a drive upload, asked the model for a storage key only the tool gateway can create, so every such call failed, and files a tool returned came back as storage links that expire in about an hour. After: the model passes a local path; Hermes checks it, uploads it (up to 20 MB) and runs the tool, and returned files are saved under downloads/connectors in the Hermes home, where the model can send them on with MEDIA:. Which files may leave follows the MEDIA: rule: on a default install any regular file outside the credential and system denylist, in strict mode (gateway.strict) only caches, allowed folders and recent files. SSH, Modal and other remote terminal backends are refused, downloads stay until you delete them, and the PR's live checks against the real gateway were listed without results when it merged.

6️⃣ A dead MCP login stops hammering the server

Before: an OAuth MCP server whose refresh token was rejected re-sent that dead token on every new session (Desktop and TUI rediscover on every agent build while nothing is connected, the gateway once per cron job), four requests each time. One user hit about 200 failed refreshes a minute and got his IP rate-limited out of the Nous Portal. After: the parked server stays quiet until hermes mcp login or a Desktop re-auth rewrites its token files, then comes back on the next session. The 5-minute self-probe still retries, and three fixes for that slower drip are still in review.

7️⃣ Gemini 4 Argon, and Gemini thinking settings that stick

Before: Argon was not in the model lists, any reasoning effort left it at its medium default, and output past 32,768 tokens was cut and reported as a normal stop. On Gemini 3.x, turning reasoning off sent a budget of 0 that those models reject or ignore. After: gemini-4-argon is selectable on Gemini, Vertex, OpenRouter and Nous (Gemini 3.8 Flash stays the default), and effort maps to Google's thinkingLevel by version number for every Gemini 3 and up. On the native endpoints, xhigh and max turn on long decode, up to 262,144 and 1,048,576 output tokens, with a hop ceiling so a server cannot keep billing, and a dropped stream resumes from its last checkpoint instead of starting over. Gaps: no long decode on OpenRouter, proxies or the OAuth Vertex provider, and after a resume the tokens generated before the drop are missing from reported usage. Introductory price: $2 in, $10 out per million tokens, doubling on 1 Dec per Google.

8️⃣ Typing answers the question card

Before: in Desktop, typing in the composer while a clarify card waited cancelled the card with every question unanswered and sent your words as a separate steer, so the model did not know which question they answered. After: the words answer the card's first open question, text that matches a choice label picks that choice, and each Enter answers one question. Slash commands, attachments and an empty Enter (Stop) work as before. The onboarding cards, theme pickers and the connector directory take typed words the same way; the CLI, TUI and messaging apps are unchanged.

9️⃣ MCP tool schemas: reloads and $refs that work

Before: /reload-mcp said reloaded, but a tool that kept its name also kept its old description and parameters. And values behind a $ref in an MCP tool's schema, common with pydantic and zod servers, reached the tool as the model typed them: 5 as a string for an integer field, first_name where the server named the key first name. After: an explicit reload publishes same-name schema changes (the automatic refresh between turns still does not, to protect the prompt cache), and local $refs are followed for type conversion and key mapping. Still not parsed: a JSON string sent for a union with no top-level type.

🔟 29 new plugins in the catalog

Keeping an eye on the agent is the day's theme: two ledgers, an independent verifier, runtime guardrails and a fleet operations page. BrowserPaw, delisted on 3 Oct, is back with credential-free MCP delegation. Catalog entries do not wait for a release: they go live once the published catalog refreshes.

text:
🇻🇳 AFTER HOURS CITY REVIEW: VUNG TAU, VIETNAM

Just two hours from Ho Chi Minh City, Vung Tau offers a quieter, cheaper coastal escape with beachfront hotels, fresh seafood, and a small adult nightlife scene. Once known for its girly bars and massage establishments, the city has increasingly shifted toward family tourism, leaving a more discreet and scattered scene behind.

🔴 RED LIGHT DISTRICT

Vung Tau doesn’t have a concentrated red light district comparable to Pattaya or Angeles City. Front Beach historically featured a collection of girly bars, including roughly a dozen near the Palace Hotel. However, recent reports describe mostly empty establishments, fewer women, and several closures. Club Au Co was reportedly shut down by March 2025.

🍺 BARS & NIGHTLIFE

Mekong Bar and Lily Bar have both appeared in traveler reports, with one contributor describing a memorable encounter at Mekong Bar. Older Western customers reportedly frequent some establishments, although the atmosphere can be extremely quiet. Traditional bargirl nightlife appears limited compared with previous years, and current venue operations need verification.

👠 ADULT ENTERTAINMENT

The scene appears to have shifted away from visible street solicitation toward massage establishments and online arrangements. The Nguyen Thi Minh Khai area has been mentioned for short-stay hotels and independent providers. Reports describe inexpensive advertised rates, although foreigner pricing, misleading profiles, and inconsistent experiences remain concerns. Prostitution is illegal in Vietnam.

🏨 ACCOMMODATIONS

Hotels are generally affordable, with one traveler reporting a beachfront room at Ocean Star Hotel for approximately $14. Weekday availability is reportedly excellent, while weekend rates can run around 25% higher. Some hotels restrict unregistered visitors, so policies should be confirmed before booking.

🍤 FOOD & DRINK

Affordable seafood is one of Vung Tau’s strongest attractions. Hoang Hoa Tham Street has been recommended for restaurants, sushi, sashimi, and seafood buffets. One traveler reported an all-you-can-eat seafood buffet for approximately $10. Back Beach offers a relaxed alternative to the city’s limited nightlife.

🚐 GETTING THERE

Buses and passenger vans connect Vung Tau with Ho Chi Minh City and Tan Son Nhat Airport in approximately two hours. Historical fares range from $4–$8, with hotel pickup and drop-off available through some operators. Hydrofoil services provide another option, although terminal locations may be inconvenient.

⚠️ COMMON COMPLAINTS

The biggest disappointment is the shrinking traditional nightlife scene. Visitors expecting Pattaya-style bar hopping may find quiet streets, aging clientele, and limited choices. Online advertisements aren’t always reliable, English accessibility is uncertain, and older venue recommendations may no longer be accurate.

🏁 OVERALL VERDICT

Vung Tau is better approached as an affordable beach getaway with occasional adult nightlife than a dedicated mongering destination. Its inexpensive hotels, seafood, and proximity to Saigon make it attractive for a short escape, but travelers prioritizing a lively, concentrated adult scene may find the city underwhelming.

text:
⚖️ DEA: Admit the GAO Report. Reject the Delay. Move the Rescheduling Process Forward.

For a process that has been accused of moving at the speed of continental drift, the DEA just did something unusual: it asked for the brakes to come off.

In a brief filed Friday and surfaced this week, the agency told Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius that it has no objection to adding the GAO report to the rescheduling hearing record. What it does object to is everything opponents want to hang on that report: more briefing, more discovery, more witnesses, and more months of delay before Julius issues the recommendation that’s been pending since he closed the record in late August. The DEA’s position is as direct as a government filing gets: “When a document’s meaning is clear, the court need not allow additional argument to interpret the document.”

What The GAO Report Actually Says

The report, which prompted Julius to grant a stay in late September, found that DEA has no written policies or procedures governing how its staff conduct scheduling evaluations, and that FDA similarly lacks documented procedures for developing scheduling recommendations. GAO recommended both agencies fill those gaps.

That’s it. That’s the finding. The report does not evaluate the science. It does not touch HHS’s eight-factor analysis. It does not question FDA’s conclusion that marijuana has a currently accepted medical use. It does not say the two-part CAMU test was wrong, only that nobody wrote down a policy explaining when to use it. And critically, GAO offers no opinion on whether marijuana belongs in Schedule III.

The DEA’s brief draws that line with precision. The report, it argues, identified “gaps in the memorialization of rescheduling process, not any flaws in the rescheduling process itself.” GAO’s recommendation to document procedures is “immaterial to the actual scientific processes and analysis.” In plain English: the agencies need better paperwork, not a different answer.

What Opponents Are Asking For

Smart Approaches to Marijuana, joined by Idaho, Indiana and Nebraska, wants supplemental briefing on whether HHS’s lack of written policy caused it to deviate from past practice. The more aggressive filing comes from the National Drug and Alcohol Screening Association, DUID Victim Voices and Dr. Kenneth Finn, who want a “narrow reopening” of the hearing with document discovery and live testimony on five subjects: who designed the 2023 two-part CAMU test and why; who drafted and revised its language across DEA, FDA, HHS, NIH and OLC; why the 2023 HHS evaluation didn’t address mental health, pregnancy, pediatric use and diversion the way earlier evaluations did; what criteria FDA used for “potential for abuse”; and which internal documents GAO reviewed.

Read that list again. None of it is about the GAO report. All of it is a do-over of the merits case that opponents already argued across three weeks of hearings in June and July, in front of the same judge, with the same government witnesses on the stand. The DEA’s brief says exactly that: opponents have “mischaracterized the GAO Report and its impact” and are using a procedural audit as a pretext to relitigate science they lost on.

The tell is the discovery request itself. Asking who “selected or drafted” the CAMU test is not a question GAO raised or answered. It’s a fishing expedition into HHS’s internal deliberations, dressed up as a response to a report that explicitly declined to evaluate those deliberations. The DEA, which spent the hearing conceding that marijuana is dangerous and arguing only that it “no longer fits the statutory requirements for Schedule I,” has no incentive to defend sloppy science. Its willingness to put the GAO report in the record and move on tells you how little it thinks the report changes.

Why The Agency Is In A Hurry

Context matters here. Since April, Attorney General Blanche’s order has already moved state-licensed medical cannabis to Schedule III, with the 280E relief that implies. Adult-use remains in Schedule I pending Julius’s recommendation and Administrator Cole’s final decision. The D.C. Circuit has consolidated the challenges and declined to block the medical move. The administrative hearing is the last open question, and it’s been fully briefed since August.

Every month of delay leaves the industry split down the middle: medical operators paying normal corporate tax rates while adult-use operators in the same buildings still absorb 280E. The DEA’s brief doesn’t say that, of course. But an agency that fought this hearing for two years is now the party asking the judge not to “further delay” his ruling. That’s not neutrality. That’s an agency that has reached a conclusion and wants to deliver it.

What Happens Next

Julius has three paths. He can admit the report, deny further proceedings and issue his recommendation, which is what the DEA asked for and what the record supports. He can order limited supplemental briefing, which adds weeks but not months. Or he can grant the reopening motion, which would restart discovery, trigger new testimony and likely push a recommendation into 2027.

The third option would be extraordinary. The GAO report’s own scope defines its relevance, and nothing in it goes to the eight factors, the medical-use finding or the abuse-potential analysis that the hearing was convened to test. Opponents are asking Julius to treat a management audit as new scientific evidence. The DEA, which has every institutional reason to be cautious, is telling him it isn’t.

For investors, the signal is cleaner than it’s been since the stay was issued. The government’s own litigators have read the GAO report, concluded it changes nothing, and asked the court to rule. If Julius agrees, the last procedural obstacle between adult-use cannabis and Schedule III is a recommendation that has been sitting on his desk, finished, since the record closed.

The opponents’ strategy was never to win on the science. It was to run out the clock. The DEA just told the judge the clock is already out.

— Anthony Varrell @V_arrell

text:
Fairfax takes control of IDBI Bank: India's biggest financial-sector FDI deal
India's Cabinet has approved the sale of a 60.72% controlling stake in IDBI Bank to Prem Watsa's Fairfax Financial for ₹ 52,878 crore, at ₹ 81 a share. The government is selling 30.48% and LIC 30.24%. Together they keep 34%, with 15% for the government and 19% for LIC.

Why it matters
 • Record FDI. This is the largest foreign direct investment ever in India's financial sector, and it shows global capital is willing to take control of an Indian bank.
 •Privatisation finally happens. After years of false starts, India's first big strategic sale of a state-linked bank is done. It's a template for the next ones.
 •Fiscal win. The government gets roughly ₹ 26,500 crore, almost the ₹ 27,441 crore it put into IDBI between 2010 and 2020. The proceeds plus the remaining stakes are valued at about ₹ 82,500 crore. 
•A bigger lender. Fairfax-backed CSB Bank will merge into IDBI within two years, creating a larger private bank with more capital and a wider branch network.
 •Credit for the economy. Private management and fresh capital should mean faster lending, especially to MSMEs, the small and medium firms that drive jobs and growth.
 •Minority investors. Fairfax will also make an open offer to other shareholders.

What to watch
 The RBI still has to approve Fairfax as a fit and proper owner. The ₹ 81 price is below the earlier ₹ 94.42 reserve, so expect debate over value. And merging the two banks will test how well Fairfax can run them together.

The bottom line: this is a turning point. India is showing it can sell control of a state-linked bank, at scale, to a long-term global investor. If it works, it strengthens the case for more bank privatisations and for foreign money flowing into Indian finance.

text:
🇸🇦🇦🇪||The Escape That Exposed the UAE: Al-Zoubaidi’s Night Flight from Aden to Abu Dhabi Under Emirati Supervision

January 8, 2026 | Aden / Berbera / Abu Dhabi

The Saudi-led coalition has confirmed what the UAE spent years denying: Aidarous al-Zoubaidi, the leader of the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council, fled Yemen in a coordinated sea and air operation supervised by Emirati officers. The escape was not a defection. It was a retrieval. The UAE extracted its proxy from a battlefield it had lost.

The Route

Al-Zoubaidi departed the Port of Aden shortly after midnight on January 7 aboard the vessel BAMEDHAF, registered under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis. The ship switched off its identification systems and sailed for Somaliland. It arrived at the port of Berbera around noon.

Berbera is not a neutral harbor. It is a UAE military base. Satellite imagery has shown underground bunkers, aircraft hangars, and concealed storage built with Emirati funding. The base is intended to serve US and Israeli interests in the Gulf of Aden and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The Phone Call

Upon arrival at Berbera, al-Zoubaidi contacted Major General Awad Saeed bin Musleh Al-Ahbabi, commander of joint operations in the UAE Armed Forces. The coalition statement identifies Al-Ahbabi by name and callsign, “Abu Saeed.” Naming a serving Emirati general in a public statement is unprecedented in Gulf diplomacy. Riyadh did it anyway.

Al Arabiya obtained an audio recording of al-Zoubaidi speaking with Al-Ahbabi after the ship docked. The recording was not denied by Abu Dhabi.

The Plane

An Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft, flight number MZB-9102, was already positioned at Berbera. Al-Zoubaidi and his companions boarded under the supervision of Emirati officers. The plane departed without declaring a destination.

It landed at Mogadishu International Airport at 3:15 PM, remained on the ground for approximately one hour, then took off at 4:17 PM heading toward the Arabian Gulf. The aircraft switched off its identification systems over the Gulf of Oman and reactivated them shortly before landing at Al Reef military airport in Abu Dhabi at 8:47 PM Saudi time.

The Il-76 is the same aircraft type the UAE has used to funnel weapons through Libya, Ethiopia, and Somalia. The coalition noted this in its statement. It was not a neutral observation.

The Vessel’s History

Maritime records show the BAMEDHAF flies the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis, the same flag as the vessel GREENLAND, which previously transported combat vehicles and weapons from Fujairah to the port of Mukalla. The coalition cited this in a separate statement on December 30, 2025.

The UAE has been running guns into Yemen through the same shipping networks it now used to extract its proxy.

The UAE’s Denial

The Emirati Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Abu Dhabi denied the accusation. It offered no counter-evidence. It did not explain why a serving Emirati general was on the phone with a man Riyadh had accused of high treason. It did not explain why an Il-76 was waiting at Berbera before the BAMEDHAF arrived.

Somalia’s Response

Somalia’s Immigration and Citizenship Agency announced an investigation into “the alleged unauthorized use of Somalia’s national airspace and airport,” calling it unacceptable and a violation of sovereignty. The statement did not name the UAE. It did not need to.

The STC’s Collapse

Al-Zoubaidi fled after the STC launched an offensive into Hadramawt and Mahra provinces in December 2025. Saudi jets bombed STC positions. Pro-Saudi ground forces counter-attacked. Riyadh removed al-Zoubaidi from Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council and accused him of high treason. Arab News ran a front-page headline reading “WANTED” above his photograph in military fatigues.

The STC had attempted to seize territory and declare a two-year transition to southern independence. Saudi Arabia crushed the attempt. The UAE extracted its man.

The Puppet’s Puppet

Al-Zoubaidi was not a sovereign actor. He was a contractor. The STC was built, armed, and financed by the UAE. Its leaders operated from Emirati bases. Its fighters trained under Emirati officers. Its political agenda was written in Abu Dhabi, not Aden.

When the Saudi-led coalition turned on the STC, the UAE did not defend its proxy on the battlefield. It pulled him out through a base it controls in Somaliland, on a plane supervised by its own officers, to a military airport in its own capital. The operation was clean. It was professional. It was the work of a state retrieving an asset it had decided to protect.

The Israeli Connection

Berbera is not only a UAE base. It is a node in a network that includes Israeli intelligence. The UAE and Israel operate an intelligence-sharing platform known as Crystal Ball, designed to “design, deploy and enable regional intelligence enhancement.” Israeli military delegations have visited Berbera. Somaliland intelligence officers have trained in Tel Aviv. The EL/M-2084 radar at Bosaso Airport in Puntland the same multi-mission radar used in Israel’s Iron Dome was deployed by the UAE in March 2025.

The plane that carried al-Zoubaidi to Abu Dhabi took off from a base that serves Emirati, Israeli, and American interests in the Horn of Africa. The escape was not a bilateral Emirati operation. It was a node in a larger architecture.

The Verdict

Riyadh and Abu Dhabi are not allies. They are competitors. Both are clients of the same empire, but they are not the same client. The UAE has spent years building its own network of proxies in Yemen, in Somaliland, in Puntland, in Sudan while Saudi Arabia relied on the coalition structure the UAE was quietly undermining.

Al-Zoubaidi’s escape is the moment that competition surfaced. Riyadh accused Abu Dhabi of smuggling a wanted man out of Yemen. Abu Dhabi said nothing. The coalition statement, published on the official Saudi Press Agency, named an Emirati general and an Emirati aircraft. It was not a leak. It was an accusation.

The UAE got its man. Riyadh got the humiliation of admitting he was gone. And the people of southern Yemen got another reminder that their leaders answer to foreign capitals, not to them.

text:
New microwave weapon can zap drone swarms without burning through missiles | Aamir Khollam, Interesting Engineering

BAE Systems has unveiled two air defense technologies designed to help the US Army counter mass drone attacks without relying entirely on conventional missiles. The systems combine a high-power microwave weapon with an artillery platform that fires precision-guided projectiles against aerial and ground targets.

Unveiled at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 exhibition, the technologies offer different ways to tackle growing threats from unmanned aircraft. One uses directed energy to engage drones without conventional ammunition, while the other relies on high-velocity projectiles for kinetic interception.

Microwave weapon targets swarms

BAE Systems’ High Power Microwave (HPM) system targets groups of drones using electromagnetic energy. It can engage successive threats as long as its power supply remains available, avoiding the ammunition resupply demands associated with conventional weapons.

That capability could prove valuable against coordinated drone attacks designed to overwhelm air defenses. Missile-based interceptors carry finite ammunition supplies, and replacing each shot can create substantial logistical demands during prolonged engagements.

The HPM system uses an architecture built around more than 99 percent commercial off-the-shelf components. BAE says this approach supports manufacturing and sustainment while allowing engineers to adapt the system across different operating environments.

Its modular design supports four deployment configurations. These include fixed installations, towed systems, combat vehicle integration, and maritime platforms. Each configuration can accommodate different power requirements and operational needs.

BAE also reports that the system has reached Technology Readiness Level 6. Outdoor range testing has validated its operation, including tests involving billions of microwave pulses to document effects on targets.

Artillery adds kinetic firepower

The Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System (MDACS) provides a complementary approach to air defense. The air-transportable platform fires different precision-guided munitions according to the mission and target.

Against aerial threats, MDACS can launch the Hypervelocity Projectile (HVP). The guided round gives the system a kinetic option for engaging incoming threats, complementing the microwave weapon’s directed-energy approach.

MDACS can also fire Scorpio-XR, a precision-guided munition intended for fixed and moving ground targets. BAE says Scorpio-XR doubles the range of existing precision-guided projectiles launched from 155 mm cannons.

That extended reach could help US forces strike targets from greater distances in contested environments. The system’s combination of air defense and ground-attack capabilities also broadens its potential battlefield role.

Layered defense counters drone attacks

BAE is positioning the two systems as complementary parts of a layered defense. HPM offers sustained engagement capacity against drone formations, while MDACS adds a projectile-based option for aerial and ground threats.

Jason Casciotti, vice president of BAE Systems’ Weapon Systems product line, said the company wants to move mature technology toward operational use faster. He pointed to validated designs and a resilient supply chain as important factors in that effort.

The systems address a central challenge for modern air defense: stopping large numbers of relatively inexpensive threats without exhausting costly interceptors. Directed energy could reduce ammunition demands, while kinetic weapons provide another way to engage targets.

However, BAE’s announcement does not establish that the US Army has adopted either system for operational service. Their eventual role will depend on further development, testing, and procurement decisions.

Let us ask the simple question:

When NNPC is recruiting, do they send a General to the East to beg Igbos to apply?
When CBN is recruiting, do they send a delegation to beg us?
When Customs, Immigration, FIRS, NDLEA, or DPR are recruiting, do they come and plead with us?

Rajputs and their sycophantic Charans, such as @Deviputra21, seem to believe that their princely states survived until 1947 solely because of their military prowess and physical strength. If military power could be derived merely from land and natural resources, Africa would be a global superpower today.

Their ignorance amuses me.

British officials used to write that, without British protection, these so-called warriors would not be able to retain their thrones for even a single day. They described these states as so weak that even a minor rebellion could bring them to their knees in the absence of British protection. They wrote:

"The justification for this duty of the Sovereign Power rests upon another consideration of the utmost importance. The Indian princes are secure upon their thrones because of the protection afforded to them by the Paramount Power. Without this protection, it would be impossible for any ruler to retain his throne or to ensure the continued succession of his family to it, unless he enjoyed the protection of the powerful hand of the Paramount Power. Without such protection, the position of the Indian princes would be utterly helpless.

The Paramount Power does not permit them to maintain any efficient standing army. The forces they possess are intended more for display than for active participation in any real war. Moreover, they consist entirely of wholly inefficient mercenaries.

In the event of any conflict between an Indian ruler and his subjects, he could not maintain his position for even a single day without the powerful support of the Paramount Power. The British Government, by virtue of its position as the Paramount Power, intervenes and, whenever the subjects of an Indian ruler rebel against him on account of his misgovernment, suppresses them and compels them to return to obedience.

If the British Government refrained from intervening in internal disputes—as was once its policy—it would be impossible for any Indian ruler to retain his throne in the face of discontent among his subjects.

In every country, whenever discontent arises among the people, its natural consequences are civil war, rebellion, the assassination of the ruler, and his deposition. These are the ordinary consequences that emerge under such circumstances.

The overthrow of misgovernment and oppressive rule is the birthright of every citizen. The Magna Carta of the English people gave legal recognition to that natural right by establishing the principle that resistance could be offered to a king who himself violated the law."

"But herein lies the second fallacy of the writer. There is no doubt that every Sovereignty is subject to both internal and external limitations. The internal limitations are, as described by constitutional writers, those of an ethical and customary character.

The external limitations of Sovereignty, which consist in the willingness of the people to submit to their ruler and obey him voluntarily, are, in India, controlled and dominated by the Paramount Power. Under every other form of despotic government, by contrast, the government lasts only so long as the people have not been driven to revolution. The moment the subjects are no longer willing to obey their despotic ruler, they offer widespread resistance to his authority and pave the way for the tyrant's downfall. This is what history has taught us.

In the case of the Indian princely states, however, the people cannot resort to that ultimate remedy of successful rebellion. This is because the Paramount Power, with all its vast resources, supports the despotic ruler in maintaining his position upon the throne.

The continued existence of these states is, therefore, the result of the protection afforded by the Paramount Power, rather than any inherent merit or special virtue of the system of personal rule prevailing in India.

text:
Saudi OpenAI engineer bugged top secret meetings with toilet paper trickery, feds say after bombshell arrest | Titus Wu, New York Post

A Saudi engineer at artificial intelligence giant OpenAI was arrested and charged with attempting to bug confidential meetings by planting secret recording devices in executive conference rooms, federal prosecutors said.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is from Saudi Arabia, is in federal custody after his arrest Friday.

OpenAI discovered a “surreptitious audio recording device” stuffed into a USB port on the back of a TV in a conference room — wrapped in toilet paper in an attempt to conceal the device, according to the complaint.

A photo in the court document shows an oddly placed object on the back of a TV.

Another photo shows the alleged device with the branding of Seeed Studio, a company that appears to offer AI recording products.

Meetings in that conference room apparently involved high-level discussions of the company’s confidential plans, such as proprietary research, OpenAI’s technical capabilities, its government relationships and more.

Footage showed Alfozan appearing near the conference room multiple times, even though he had no authority to access the room or participate in those meetings, the complaint said.

He has worked for the San Francisco-based AI company since July 2025, the Department of Justice said.

“Any attempt to illicitly obtain protected information from U.S. super intelligence and technology companies threatens both American innovation and the national security interests those advancements support,” said Special Agent in Charge Scott Schelble of the FBI San Francisco Field Office.

Alfozan also used chatbots to plot the alleged recording efforts, asking about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting room capacities and calendars, authorities said.

He even requested information about the locations of “leadership and exec,” per the complaint.

Another chatbot account associated with his wife allegedly included queries on ways to install and hide audio recording devices.

On Oct. 5, a photo allegedly captured Alfozan entering the conference room to get a sneak peek at the recording device. Around that same time, OpenAI security workers found a similar recording device in Alfozan’s unattended bag, the DOJ said.

Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release, if convicted.

The case is of particular importance amid an AI arms race between the US, China and other countries.

America, home to Silicon Valley, is attempting to keep its world-leading technology away from the hands of adversaries.

“Protecting American Super Intelligence innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

An OpenAI spokesperson told the California Post that there was no indications of Alfozan inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code or customer data. He was subsequently fired.

“We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats,” OpenAI said.
