text:
The Price of Being Our Friend: What Ukraine Has Lost

After more than four and a half years of full-scale war, Ukraine is still standing. But the cost in lives, land and money is hard to imagine.

In February 2022, Russia launched an invasion of Ukraine. Many experts thought the capital, Kyiv, would fall in a few days. It did not. Today, in October 2026, Ukraine is still fighting, and peace talks are back on the table.

But survival has come at a terrible price. The biggest loss is not buildings or money. It is people.

How Many Ukrainian Soldiers Have Been Killed and Wounded?

Nobody knows the exact number. Ukraine treats its losses as a military secret. Russia makes Ukraine's losses sound bigger than they are. So we have to rely on estimates, and they vary a lot.

•  Ukraine's official count: In February 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky said 55,000 soldiers had officially been killed, plus a "large number" missing.
•  Independent estimates: A July 2026 report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a respected Washington think tank, estimated 525,000 to 625,000 Ukrainian soldiers killed, wounded or missing through June 2026.
•  Deaths: Retired U.S. General Christopher Cavoli, the former top NATO commander, estimated in July 2026 that about 150,000 Ukrainians have been killed.
•  Missing: More than 90,000 people, mostly soldiers, are on Ukraine's official missing list. Some are prisoners of war. Many are believed dead.
A fair middle estimate is 100,000 to 150,000 Ukrainian soldiers dead and roughly half a million total casualties. Civilians have suffered too. The United Nations counts more than 17,000 Ukrainian civilians killed and almost 54,000 injured.

It seems Russia has lost far more troops, likely more than 1.2 million killed and wounded. But Russia has more than three times as many people as Ukraine. It can absorb losses that Ukraine cannot.

Has Ukraine Expanded the Draft?

Yes, step by step. As losses grew, Ukraine kept widening the net.

•  2022: At the start of the war, men ages 27 to 60 could be drafted. All men ages 18 to 60 were banned from leaving the country.
•  April 2024: Ukraine lowered the draft age from 27 to 25. It also ended a "limited fitness" category that had kept some men with health issues out of service and required men to update their military records.
•  February 2025: Ukraine launched "Contract 18-24," a voluntary program for younger men. Recruits are offered about 1 million hryvnias (roughly $24,000) for one year of service, plus a year off from the draft afterward. Few young people have signed up.
•  August 2025: In a surprise move, Ukraine let men ages 18 to 22 leave the country. A Ukrainian minister later cited EU data showing about 400,000 young men under 23 had left for Europe.
•  2026: Military leaders are discussing a stop to drafting men over 50 or 55. Lowering the draft age below 25 is not being considered.
The U.S. and other allies have pushed Ukraine to draft 18-year-olds. Zelensky has said no. His reason is simple: if the youngest generation dies at the front, no one will be left to rebuild the country. Meanwhile, many draft-age men are hiding or have paid bribes to escape.
What Percentage of the Population Has Been Lost?
This is where the numbers get truly alarming. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, Ukraine had more than 50 million people. By early 2022, it had about 43 million.

In late 2024, the United Nations estimated Ukraine had lost about 8 million people since the full-scale invasion began. That left roughly 35 million. Some 2026 estimates put the number closer to 32 million. That means Ukraine has lost somewhere between one-fifth and one-quarter of its people since 2022.

Most of those people did not die. They left. About 6.7 million Ukrainians became refugees, mostly women and children now living in Europe. Millions more live under Russian occupation. And Ukraine's birth rate has fallen to about one child per woman, one of the lowest in the world. A country needs about 2.1 children per woman just to keep its population steady.

The longer the war lasts, the less likely refugees are to come home. Kids are growing up in Poland and Germany, making new lives.

How Much Land Has Been Lost?

Russia now controls about 19 to 20 percent of Ukraine. That is roughly 45,700 square miles, about the size of Pennsylvania. This includes Crimea, which Russia seized in 2014, and parts of the east it grabbed that same year. About 12 percent of Ukraine has been taken since the full-scale invasion in 2022.

The occupied land includes nearly all of the Luhansk region, most of the Donetsk region, a strip of coastline linking Russia to Crimea, and Europe's largest nuclear power plant.

But the front lines are moving slowly now. In 2026, Russia has gained only about 0.3 percent of Ukraine's land so far. In September, Ukraine even took back some ground. Both sides are stuck in a costly standoff.

What Has the War Cost Ukraine?

In February 2026, the World Bank, the United Nations, the European Union and Ukraine's government released a joint estimate of the damage through the end of 2025:

•  Physical damage: $195 billion in homes, roads, power plants and other things destroyed.
•  Economic losses: $667 billion in lost business, trade and income.
•  Cost to rebuild: About $588 billion over the next ten years. That is nearly three times the size of Ukraine's entire yearly economy.

Those numbers are already out of date. Russia has kept bombing Ukraine's power grid, leaving millions in the cold and dark through the winter. And no dollar figure captures hundreds of thousands of wounded veterans or children who lost parents.

What Is the Best Outcome Possible Now?

Peace talks are moving again. In early October, U.S. envoys met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami. A plan reported by The Washington Post would freeze the fighting along the current front line. But Russia has rejected a short ceasefire, and a recent "energy truce" broke down within days.

Given Ukraine's shrinking army and population, winning back all its land by force looks very unlikely. Most analysts now describe the best realistic outcome like this:

•  A ceasefire along current lines. The fighting stops roughly where it is now. Ukraine does not legally accept Russia's claim to the occupied land, leaving the door open to get it back peacefully someday.
•  Real security guarantees. Western partners make firm commitments so Russia cannot rest, rearm and attack again in a few years. Without this, a ceasefire may only be a pause.
•  EU membership and rebuilding money. A clear path into the European Union, plus large reconstruction funds, gives Ukraine an economy worth coming home to.
•  Bringing people home. Prisoners, deported children and refugees return.
In that outcome, Ukraine would remain free and independent on about 80 percent of its land, tied firmly to the West. That is not the victory Ukrainians hoped for in 2022. But it would mean Russia failed at what some of us insist was its main goal: ending Ukraine as an independent country.

The Deal Ukraine Walked Away From in 2022

This is not the first time Ukraine has faced a deal like this. In March and April 2022, just weeks into the invasion, Ukrainian and Russian negotiators met in Istanbul and worked on a draft peace treaty. According to drafts reported by The Wall Street Journal and others:

•  No NATO. Ukraine would stay permanently neutral and never join NATO but could still seek to join the EU.
•  A smaller army. Ukraine's army would be capped. Kyiv offered 250,000 troops. Moscow wanted just 85,000.
•  Land. Russia would keep control of Crimea, with its final status talked over for years. The fate of the eastern Donbas was left for Putin and Zelensky to settle in person.
•  Guarantees. The U.S., Britain, France, China and Russia itself would promise to protect Ukraine.

The talks fell apart. In April 2022, British Prime Minister Boris Johnson made a surprise visit to Kyiv. A Ukrainian news outlet, Ukrainska Pravda, reported in May 2022 that his message was that the West would not back a deal with Putin and that Ukraine should keep fighting. Ukraine's lead negotiator, David Arakhamia, said in 2023 that Johnson told them not to sign anything and to "just fight." Johnson denies he blocked a deal. Arakhamia also said Ukraine did not trust Russia to keep its word, and that Western partners could only give advice. Other things clearly mattered too: the discovery of Russian atrocities in Bucha, Russia's push for an army too small to defend Ukraine, and big gaps that were never closed.

Still, comparing then and now is painful:

•  Land: Before the 2022 invasion, Russia held about 7 to 8 percent of Ukraine (mostly Crimea and part of the Donbas). Today it holds about 20 percent.
•  People: Most of Ukraine's estimated half-million military casualties, and most of its population loss, came after Istanbul.
•  What Ukraine gained: Ukraine now has the EU path it would have kept in 2022, but stronger Western backing and a far larger, battle-hardened army. Ukraine's own peace plan reportedly calls for keeping an army of 800,000.
•  What did not change: NATO membership is off the table in both deals. Ukraine never got it either way.

Whether the 2022 deal would have held is a fair question. Russia had already broken earlier agreements, and critics say the Istanbul terms would have left Ukraine too weak to resist a second invasion. But on land and lives alone, Ukraine's position today is clearly worse than it was in April 2022.

Not everyone agrees on what Ukraine should do now. Some argue it should hold out because Russia is straining too, and a frozen line rewards invasion. Others warn each extra month costs people Ukraine may never replace.

The Bottom Line

Ukraine can rebuild bridges and power plants. What is much harder to replace is people. The soldiers who died, the young men who left and the children who were never born will shape Ukraine for generations.

Whatever peace finally looks like, its real test will be simple: Will Ukrainians come home? Will there be anything to come home to?

4. How a durable peace could be structured
US–Ukraine–Europe common negotiating position
Negotiations with Russia
Verified energy and civilian-infrastructure truce
Broader ceasefire and monitoring
Security guarantees, reconstruction and conditional sanctions relief
Illustrative diplomatic sequence, not an agreed or announced peace plan.
5. Why October 18 could matter more than November 3
According to Reuters, Trump faces an October 18 deadline under US legislation to impose additional sanctions targeting Russian energy or invoke a national-interest waiver. This creates an immediate policy decision ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. 
The decision would send an important signal:
Additional sanctions would increase economic pressure on Moscow.
A waiver could preserve flexibility for diplomatic incentives but attract criticism if Russia offers no reciprocal concessions.
A conditional approach could link sanctions relief to independently verified ceasefire compliance.
6. What this means for Greece and Europe
Greece has several direct interests in a settlement: lower geopolitical risk in the Black Sea, more predictable shipping and insurance costs, improved European energy security, and reduced pressure on defense and public finances.
However, an end to fighting would not automatically normalize oil, gas or electricity prices, particularly while the Middle East crisis continues.
European governments would also need to decide how to finance Ukraine's reconstruction and support its long-term security without weakening NATO's deterrence posture.
7. Strategic outlook through March 2027
The indicators worth watching are whether Moscow accepts renewed talks, whether attacks on energy infrastructure actually stop, whether Washington maintains intelligence cooperation with Kyiv, and whether the US and Europe agree on credible security guarantees.
My central assessment: The United States can be a decisive facilitator of a negotiated end to the war, but diplomatic incentives alone cannot establish peace. A durable settlement depends on verifiable commitments, Ukrainian consent and credible consequences for violations.
The critical distinction is between ending the fighting and ending the conditions that could cause the war to resume.

text:
Yesterday, The Washington Post published an opinion piece by David Ignatius  It is essentially being called a leak of the American negotiating team's "peace plan." If that is true, I'm having a sense of déjà vu. It feels as though President Trump’s negotiators didn't even bother to come up with anything on their own and simply asked Russians to bail them out with ideas for the peace plan.

I tried to find at least some differences from what Russia has been demanding for years, but I couldn't find any.

President Trump's team is proposing that Ukraine give up the territories seized by Moscow. From Kushner and Witkoff's perspective, this is what a compromise looks like. The only thing that's hard to understand is where exactly the compromise is.

The EU is in shock over how two negotiating geniuses agreed to reshape the European security architecture as if they are the ones actually calling the shots there.

In 2008-2009, Moscow was pushing for a treaty that would allow it to control the security decisions of European states. In 2021, it demanded a limit on NATO expansion and a rollback of the Alliance's military presence to its 1997 levels.

Now the American team is including agreements between Europe and Russia on Russia's "security concerns" in its proposals to end the war. Truly, why didn't anyone think of this before?!

Now, about guarantees... I’m just tired... This is like an endless Budapest Memorandum...

But I think I’ve figured out where Russia's compromise is: in exchange for territorial concessions from Ukraine and the restructuring of European security, Russia will generously agree to Ukraine stopping its strikes on Russian oil refineries, while Europe gets hooked on gas again.

And Russia still needs to be persuaded to agree to all this. Here, Kushner and Witkoff propose appeasing Putin by lifting sanctions. I think that’s not enough. They should have also offered Moscow compensation for losses.

Ukraine's reconstruction is being used as an argument in favor of territorial concessions. Investment, along with the participation of the World Bank and BlackRock, is supposed to make the deal more attractive to Kyiv. Seems like someone is missing here - Gazprom, the Rotenberg brothers... Who else?

Seriously, though, it’s all depressing. It’s clear that Ukraine and Europe are being treated here not just as fools, but as some kind of pie that it’s time to divide.

If we're going to be this cynical, I'd like to ask the brilliant American team - what part of this pie is left for the United States? Right now it looks like just the wrapper.

Reports about the possible sale of Lukoil's international assets, worth approximately $20 billion, mention investors linked to business partners of Kushner and Witkoff.

Russian television is filled with such loud laughter and mockery of the American president that only someone completely isolated from reality could fail to hear it.

text:
Maci 💋 My POV
October 14, 2026 
Breckenridge, Colorado

Good morning, everyone! ☕❤️

It's almost 7 a.m., I'm sitting here with my coffee, and I have a complaint.

WHERE IS MY SNOW?! 

Seriously. We came to the mountains. It's COLD. The forecast keeps teasing me, and I'm beginning to take this personally. 

Yesterday was supposed to be our beautiful snowy day.

I was awake early, watching the clouds gather over the mountains. Everything looked promising. The temperature was dropping, the sky was getting darker, and I was practically vibrating with excitement.

Then it rained.

RAIN!

I looked at Edgar like he'd personally arranged this disappointment.

He suggested I take it up with God.

Very funny, handsome. 

Then the clouds parted, the sun came out, and that was the end of winter.

By then we'd all surrendered to a lazy morning.

I think we needed one.

---

I spent a couple of hours editing Edgar’s book, SEEN, which used to be called Irresistible Temptress. There’s a particular scene I’ve been trying to get right, and I finally had some uninterrupted time to work on the wording.

You’d think knowing the people it’s based on would make my job easier.

It does not.

Writing is not simple.

---

Edgar and Jenny were nearby, going through notes from his medical presentation.

I loved listening to them.

They weren't just reviewing the questions the investors had asked. Edgar wanted Jenny to understand WHY each person had asked them.

Was someone worried about the science? The financial risk? Regulatory approval? Or were they testing how well Edgar and his team understood the limitations?

At one point Edgar asked Jenny what she thought one particularly skeptical physician was actually concerned about.

She considered it for a moment, then gave him an answer that made him smile.

I could tell he was pleased.

Jenny is becoming very good at anticipating what he needs, and she's confident enough to disagree when she thinks there's something he's overlooking.

I like that about her. ❤️

Meanwhile, Mia and Jack had discovered the extraordinary pleasure of having absolutely nothing to accomplish.

They talked, wandered around the cabin, spent some time in the hot tub, and generally enjoyed being together.

Those two are ridiculously cute.

---

After lunch, I announced that I wanted to go higher into the mountains.

Much higher.

If the snow wasn't coming to me, I was going to find it.

Edgar found a route that would take us to around 12,000 feet, where we could park and hike farther.

All five of us went.

And can I just say something?

Edgar had changed into a sweatshirt and put on a baseball cap backward.

Oh, my.

I don't know what it is about that look, but I LOVE it.

We started hiking, and the views became more spectacular with every bit of elevation.

Breckenridge looked tiny below us. The mountains seemed to go on forever, with dark green forests, patches of golden aspens, and snow clinging to the higher slopes.

By the time we approached 13,500 feet, we were moving considerably slower.

I exercise. I'm in good shape.

My lungs didn't receive that information. 

We took our time, rested, and enjoyed the scenery.

Mia was fascinated by everything. Jack was taking pictures. Jenny kept looking back toward the valley, amazed at how far we'd climbed.

I stood beside Edgar for a while, tucked under his arm, looking out across the mountains.

I wish I could have put that view in my pocket.

Then the wind changed.

Clouds were moving across the peaks, and the temperature dropped quickly.

Edgar looked toward the incoming weather.

"We should start down."

I knew he was right.

And then...

Something touched my cheek.

A tiny, beautiful, WHITE snowflake.

I stopped.

Another floated past my face.

SNOW!!!

I was so excited I actually stuck out my tongue.

YES, I DID! 

I'm 24 years old, ex medicine student, and perfectly capable of behaving like a five-year-old when the occasion deserves it.

AND THIS DID! ❄️❤️

Mia started laughing and joined me.

Jenny was laughing at both of us.

Edgar shook his head, smiling.

I caught a snowflake on my tongue!

My first snow of the season!

The wind was picking up, and those clouds were beginning to look considerably less friendly.

So we headed down before the mountain decided to give us more excitement than we'd asked for.

By the time we reached the vehicle, heated seats sounded like one of mankind's greatest achievements.

Back at the cabin, Mia and Jack announced they were cooking dinner.

For EVERYONE.

They wanted to thank us for the hospitality and support we'd been giving them.

I told them that was incredibly sweet, but unnecessary. I love cooking, and I've been fortunate enough to learn from some wonderful professional chefs.

Mia wasn't interested in my objections.

Apparently, she and Jack had a plan.

Then they kicked us out of the kitchen.

ME!

Out of the kitchen!

I offered to help.

No.

Supervise?

Absolutely not.

Jenny suggested we should respect the chefs' wishes.

Traitor. 

So Edgar, Jenny, and I changed into swimsuits and went out to the hot tub.

Cold mountain air, deliciously warm water, and a view I could stare at for hours.

We settled in while Jenny told us something funny about the day's hike.

Every so often we could hear Mia and Jack moving around inside.

At one point something fell.

Then Jack laughed.

Then Mia said something that sounded suspiciously like an instruction.

I considered investigating.

Edgar pulled me a little closer.

"Leave them alone."

Eventually Mia appeared and informed us dinner was almost ready.

There was one more requirement.

We had to dress up.

For dinner.

In our cabin.

She was completely serious.

I loved it. ❤️

And when we came downstairs, I understood.

They'd set the table beautifully. Candles, flowers, folded napkins, everything arranged with so much care.

Mia looked terribly proud.

Jack was pretending he hadn't put nearly as much effort into it as she had.

I'm not convinced.

They served us a wonderful dinner, followed by a dessert.

It was a wonderful dinner!!

I congratulated our chefs.

Jack said complaints weren't permitted at his establishment.

Mia rolled her eyes.

I laughed so hard. 

We stayed at the table long after dessert, talking about the hike, teasing each other, and discussing what we wanted to do next.

I looked around and realized how much I love these people.

Not because anyone was doing something extraordinary.

Mia was talking with her hands. Jack kept making her laugh. Jenny was listening to Edgar explain something, and he was so relaxed, enjoying everyone's company.

I wanted Spencer there.

She would have loved the dinner. And I know how much it would have meant to her to see Mia and Jack doing something so thoughtful.

I miss you, Queen. ❤️

Before bed, I looked outside one last time.

No snow.

Not one little flake.

I'd received my allowance for the day.

And now it's Wednesday morning.

I'm sitting here with my coffee, watching the sky again.

I think the weather is being unreasonable.

WHERE IS MY SNOW?! ❄️😂

Happy Wednesday, everyone!

- Maci 💋❤️

But at least I got some snow.

text:
Brazil's 25 October runoff will decide the president. Brazil's fight against PCC and Comando Vermelho will also be decided by governors, financial regulators and border partners.

First round: Flávio Bolsonaro 47.03%, Lula 45.16% (TSE). Security is central, and the two campaigns offer different toolkits. Per ACLED's 6 October analysis, Lula emphasizes financial investigations, intelligence-led operations, federal coordination and arms and ammunition controls. Bolsonaro proposes new maximum-security prisons, harsher sentences and a lower age of criminal responsibility. They also split on foreign alignment: Bolsonaro backs the U.S. terrorist designation of PCC and CV and pledges to join the Shield of the Americas; Lula opposes the terrorist label, citing intervention risk, and has rejected the Shield while supporting cross-border cooperation.

In Washington, the designation question is settled: State named CV and PCC Specially Designated Global Terrorists on 28 May 2026, with FTO status effective 5 June.

The network: ACLED tracks CV expanding along the northern corridor that links the Amazon and the tri-border with Colombia and Peru to Brazil's ports, and PCC operating abroad through Paraguay and increasingly Bolivia.

The money is domestic and sophisticated. Operação Carbono Oculto (August 2025) traced a PCC-linked fuel scheme that moved at least R$52 billion since 2020 through formulators, distributors, stations and fintechs. Its second phase (May 2026) identified six more payment institutions with nearly R$26 billion in suspicious flows, found after fintechs became subject to bank-style reporting to Receita Federal from August 2025.

Federalism is the constraint. Governors run the state police that do most day-to-day policing. With 20 of 27 governorships decided in round one, and seven runoffs on 25 October, including Amazonas, Rio Grande do Norte and Rio de Janeiro, any federal plan needs a fragmented map to cooperate.

Practitioner question: whoever wins, is the bigger lever against PCC and CV a foreign designation, or Receita Federal data on payment institutions?

text:
🚨 BREAKING: Massachusetts sends first-in-the-nation letter asking sports betting operators about their use of AI

(First reported here that the @MassGamingComm would be looking into the matter)

Executive Director Dean Serpa is asking every licensed sports wagering operator asking how they use AI and machine learning in marketing and promotions. 

It follows a Sept 24 directive from MGC Chair Jordan Maynard to have staff dig into the issue.

Responses are due Nov 3. 

Participation is “voluntary,” and the MGC says answers will be kept confidential under state law and used to shape future AI policy. 

But when the MGC asked operators to "voluntarily" show up for a meeting about player limits and none of them showed, it triggered fury across the MGC.

If operators don't act, the MGC will simply move ahead without their input. When a regulator sends 8 sections of detailed questions to every operator, it’s a safe bet rules are coming.

The definition of “AI” is huge. It covers any algorithm, predictive model, automated decision-making, profiling, “personalization,” or “optimization” tool, whether fully automated or with a human in the loop. Calling it something else won’t get operators out of answering.

What the MGC wants to know:

📊 What data feeds the models. Betting frequency, wager size, deposits and withdrawals, net wins and losses, revenue generated by the patron, session length, VIP status, and response to past promos. The key question is whether patron losses are used as an input, and whether sudden jumps in betting, deposits, or losses affect who gets marketed to.

🎯 Who gets targeted. Do systems score and rank patrons by how likely they are to respond? Are customers segmented by predicted value or predicted spending? Does ML predict who will deposit, bet more, or come back to the app?

🎁 What offer they get, and how much. Can two patrons get different bonus bets, odds boosts, or deposit matches based on their behavior? Does the system set the dollar value of each offer?

⏰ When and how often. Does AI decide when to send a promo, including after someone stops betting or cuts back? Can it trigger offers off recent losses or deposits? Can it ramp up messaging frequency based on how a patron responds?

🧪 Behavioral optimization. Do operators A/B test promos to find what drives the most wagering? Is marketing tuned to predicted lifetime value, with “highly profitable” and “unprofitable” patrons treated differently? Are patrons with big recent losses treated differently from similar bettors?

The responsible gaming angle is the heart of it. Regulators are asking whether operators test their models for the risk of encouraging problem gambling. They also want to know whether risk indicators are used to cut off marketing, or whether the same signals (more losses, more frequent betting) can make someone more likely to get a promo. If operators say no, the MGC wants to know what controls prevent it. For vendor-supplied models, it wants to know what assurances the vendor gave.

Human oversight and explainability. Who in the company is ultimately responsible for AI use? Do humans review or override model decisions? And a pointed one: if a regulator asked why Patron A got Promotion X on a given date, could the operator show the data, model, and factors behind it? Operators are also asked whether they can tell what share of a patron’s promos were AI-influenced.

Why it matters: Massachusetts is signaling that the next frontier of sports betting oversight isn’t just ads and bonuses, but the algorithms deciding who sees them. Expect operators to scramble, and expect other states to watch closely.

text:
Vote No on Question 3 

Question 3 would replace Massachusetts party primaries with a single “all-party” or top two primary. Every candidate would appear on one ballot. Only the top two vote-getters would advance to November, even if they belong to the same party. This proposed change is a solution looking for a problem that does not exist, especially for unenrolled voters.
● Unenrolled voters already have the right to participate in Massachusetts primaries. They simply choose a Democratic or Republican ballot on primary day.
● They can vote in the race that matters most in their community without joining a party.
● Voters could be disenfranchised negatively impacting turnout and distorting the will of the people on ballot questions.
● Question 3 does not give unenrolled voters a new right. It takes away a system they already use and understand.
The proposed top two system would weaken parties and shrink real choice.
● Parties exist so voters can choose between distinct political philosophies. Question 3 removes their ability to nominate their own candidates to run in the general election.
● In a heavily partisan state, the two highest finishers would often both be of one party. Third party candidates and many independents would be shut out of the general election—the contest that draws the most voters.
● November ballots would offer less ideological diversity when turnout and attention are highest.
On May 4, 2026, The MA State House of Representatives - Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions- voted to TAKE NO ACTION on H.5003, Initiative Petition for a Law to Implement to All-Party State Primaries. TAKING NO ACTION ON A BILL LETS IT FAIL WITHOUT A RECORDED “NO” VOTE.  The majority opinion based their opinion on “administrative and fiscal implications of implementing the proposal at both the state and municipal levels, as well as concerns that all-party primaries may result in vote splitting, reduced party accountability, voter confusion, and strategic voting, often disadvantaging less-funded candidates and producing unpredictable or unrepresentative outcomes”

THE PROPOSED LAW THAT FAILED IS NOW QUESTION 3 ON THE GENERAL ELECTION BALLOT.

VOTE NO ON QUESTION 3

text:
Absolutely not.  

Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 And since honesty is rare in my politics, allow me to confess a few things.

The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that the war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything, and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me up in refugee camps for generations, so that I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I'm still stateless. Turns out rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said, "Let's give it a try." It gave me autonomy. Guns for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in almost 20 years. Hamas kills dissidents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother."

But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurd. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological powerhouse, desert farms, dusty cities. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said, "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of showcasing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I displayed only the culture of the sword.Anger, extremism, and bloodshed. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to the Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I feign surprise when the Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced that I don't want coexistence at all.

Accountability. I blame Israel for everything. Always. Do my leaders steal billions? Blame Israel. Does Hamas fire rockets from hospitals? Blame Israel. Do I glorify death more than life? Blame Israel. Accountability is not my strong suit.

I am Palestinian. I could have built a nation, many times over. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But all too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hatred. And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

text:
The best thing about hosting @MorningAnswer is the interaction I enjoy with so many intelligent people both who are guests as well as listeners like the one who wrote me this extraordinarily well-considered note below to share her informed perspective on the Cornell 7 case. I truly appreciate this Jane Doe's willingness to trust me with the sharing of her story.
+++

Your recent coverage of the Cornell seven case has inspired me to convey my thoughts on the subject. This could be due in part to the fact that at the end of October it’ll be 10 years ago when I was sexually assaulted in college. I was 21 when I was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house I often frequented.

I believe I was drugged at a bar prior to the encounter although I never received any sort of medical confirmation of that.

I went to a very small private liberal arts school in Illinois (less than 2,000 students) and Greek life was the primary social circle of the majority of the campus. I should preface this by saying I considered this fraternity my second home other than my own sorority. I was friends with all the men in that fraternity and it was regarded as a safe place to me. I also want to add that my college experience was rather atypical. I was an excellent student, held two on campus jobs in addition to my off-campus internship, and was actively involved in my sorority. When I wasn’t in class or at a sorority event, I was working on campus or at the courthouse, day and night. I was very type-A, your typical eldest daughter, very responsible, but popular. Think Elle Woods in Legally Blonde, but smarter. I was not reckless and I was the last person anyone would think would be victim of sexual assault. But nevertheless, it happened to me.

I never reported my assault to law enforcement for my own reasons, but I was working at the state's attorney's office in the county at the time and as an intern I didn’t want anyone to know what had happened.

The people in that office were my heroes at the time and I didn’t want those who eventually became my future co-workers to know the intimate details of my assault. Ultimately, I had worked in the system, I knew the law, and I couldn’t begin my legal career as a victim. At the time it was too difficult for me to pursue that avenue.

A year later I was diagnosed with PTSD and it was impacting my learning. I made the choice to report my assault, over a year after, only to the university. My only goal was to have some record of my story and to get help from the university so that I wouldn’t be placed in the same classes as this individual and we wouldn’t cross paths. We were in the same major and I was forced to interact with him in classes right after my assault. I never took serious issue with how the university handled my case, it was pretty standard and they offered me security escorts at night when I was working late.

As I reflect on this part of my life and wrestle with my own traumatic memories, I’m reminded of the one aspect that always remained significant to me.

Days after my assault when I eventually was able to get up the strength to tell my friends in the fraternity what happened, they kicked that member out of their organization immediately. I was told it was a unanimous chapter vote that took all of five minutes to resolve. No hesitation, no debate, no real adults involved. Just a chapter of honorable young men who were embarrassed to have offered membership to someone capable of rape. They issued a personal apology to me and the leadership of my sorority. I am forever grateful to those men and I never forgot the justice they provided to me.

While my thoughts on the Cornell case are mixed, there is one particular aspect of this case’s coverage and the public’s reaction that has bothered me deeply. That is the stigma that has exacerbated around Greek life and particularly fraternity men.

While my story is very different from Jane Doe’s there are common denominators that are unavoidable. The facts of her case are still in dispute, but the fraternity location is confirmed.

I’ve seen nothing but hate all over social media about fraternity men and that is simply not true. There are good men out there and many of them are in fraternities or were at one point in their young lives. My husband included. I cannot claim that all fraternity men make the best decisions, especially when alcohol is involved but the ones I knew were strong in their convictions, they embraced the values of their organization, (which are often overlooked by outsiders) and they did the right thing. They took matters into their own hands and made their environment a safer place to be for college women. I didn’t make demands or deny any of my own wrongdoing, I simply told my friends the truth and I was treated with the utmost respect. The white college man has become the villain of our society and that’s simply an inaccurate conclusion that the liberal media seems to believe is ok to perpetuate.

I may have been assaulted by a fraternity man but other fraternity men saved me. They believed me. While they couldn’t stop the assault, they did everything in their power to stop the stigma.

I’m not a celebrity. My story isn’t well known unless you happened to be on my campus in 2016 and were involved in Greek life. I suppose you could say I’m just another Jane Doe, but I don’t want to be associated with a media-driven story that’s gotten so out of control nobody knows whose side to believe. It gives all sexual assault survivors a bad name and ultimately confuses the younger generation about the significance of the law.

I went on to be president of my sorority and graduated with honors. I worked in criminal law for 9 years and saw sexual assault in many different shapes and forms. As disturbing as these Cornell allegations are, they are not unique. I suppose I felt compelled to share this because I wish my story was unique. I wish that sexual assault was a rare occurrence but that’s just not realistic.

I don’t think we can change college culture as it evolves into something we can no longer relate to, but we can teach our kids to do the right thing, act the right way, and behave as if all our decisions do actually impact the rest of our lives.

Before I left for college over 11 years ago, my uncle gave me some life rules to keep in my back pocket. Literally he lamented the note so I could keep it in my wallet.

One of those rules was to never do anything you wouldn’t discuss at the dinner table. As most of us know, dinner tables have become obsolete and kids barely talk to their parents now let alone share meals together like traditional families used to. But I wish parents today would instill similar ideas in their kids that would make them think twice before making some of the decisions we read about in the news.

As a younger adult, I can remember never wanting to embarrass my parents. As I watch today’s college students, I wonder if they are as paranoid about that rule as I was. If I had a son who was able to make the conscious decision that the fraternity brothers who helped me did, that is something I would certainly be proud to share at the dinner table.

Thank you for taking the time to read my story.

text:
Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery

Redwood will now recycle Rivian’s battery scrap and end-of-life packs as well as provide energy storage for its manufacturing plant 

IRVINE, Calif. — October 14, 2026 — American automaker Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) and energy technology company Redwood Materials today announced a major expansion of their partnership, establishing Redwood as one of Rivian's key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions—recycling Rivian’s production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, as well as providing stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. 
Through the partnership, Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage—deployed directly at Rivian's manufacturing facilities or at other locations—or to recycle it. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian's manufacturing operations. 

This new scope of the partnership builds on the existing work, announced in April 2026, that is deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker's manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. 

“Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition," said RJ Scaringe, Rivian Founder and CEO. "By partnering with JB and the Redwood team we're turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.”

"Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials," said JB Straubel, Redwood Materials Founder and CEO. "Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”

When EV batteries reach the end of their useful lives in vehicles, they often still have substantial useful energy capacity for second-life applications, such as stationary storage. Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease stress on the grid during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for the user, as well as the grid at large. During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, these packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with Rivian – and other – EV battery packs, Redwood's proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving. 

Once batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or where scrap is generated during manufacturing, they can be recycled. Redwood's advanced process is capable of recycling and recovering critical minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper at rates exceeding 95 percent, encouraging the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the United States. 

This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem—recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors. Rivian’s work with Redwood is a model for that approach: one partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery, built to move faster than the grid alone can.

text:
We all have our own understanding of the Fall, mine is slightly offensive, nothing in it is engrained in belief, it exists as a loose idea, but may offer a different perspective.  

If I placed a cat inside a box where it existed in a state both alive and dead, and I warned it not to search for a crack in the walls through which it could glimpse the outside observer, I would not be forbidding knowledge itself. The cat already knows there is an outside observer. It already knows there is a box. What I would be forbidding is the attempt to seize a perspective that was not yet its own.

Suppose the cat becomes curious. It is told that if it peers out and observes the present state of the observer, it will introduce entropy into the simulation, collapsing and inverting the system without the lid ever being opened. In that case, would its curiosity be a virtue?

At first glance, perhaps. We often praise curiosity because it is the engine of learning. But curiosity is not automatically virtuous. Curiosity directed toward understanding is one thing; curiosity motivated by the desire to bypass trust, to grasp prematurely what has not yet been given, is another entirely.

The cat's true test would not be whether it desired knowledge, but whether it trusted the one who designed the box.

This is why I think the Fall is often misunderstood.

Adam and Eve were not condemned because they wanted knowledge. Had knowledge itself been the problem, God would never have planted the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil in the garden. The tree was not an accident. It was not a mistake. It was not a temptation placed there merely to trap humanity. The tree existed because, in some sense, its fruit was always intended to be eaten.

Yet it was intended to be received, not seized.

If Adam and Eve had truly been seeking understanding, they would have sought first to understand God's purpose. They would have asked why the tree existed at all. Why plant it in the midst of the garden? Why forbid it for a time? Why make it accessible rather than hiding it beyond their reach?

The deeper question was never, "What knowledge does the tree contain?"

The deeper question was, "What is God trying to accomplish through it?"

Knowledge pursued through trust would have drawn them closer to God. Knowledge pursued through independence drew them away from Him.

The serpent's temptation was not simply, "You will know."

It was, "You will be as gods."

The promise behind the fruit was autonomy. It offered the possibility of obtaining through disobedience what God intended to give through relationship. The fruit became desirable because it appeared to provide a way to possess wisdom apart from God, rather than receiving wisdom from God.

In this view, the sin was not the gaining of knowledge but the manner in which it was gained.

The tree was planted to be eaten from, but only through the exercise of free will aligned with trust. Its purpose could only be fulfilled when humanity freely chose God's will over its own. Instead, Adam and Eve reached for the fruit in rejection of God's authority. They attempted to grasp the destination while abandoning the path by which God intended them to arrive there.

Like the cat searching for a hole in the box, they were not content to wait for the box to be opened. They sought to look beyond the boundary God had established, believing that what lay beyond could be possessed on their own terms.

Their curiosity was therefore not the innocent desire to understand. It was the desire to obtain what was promised without trusting the One who promised it.

And that, perhaps, is the true nature of the Fall: not a hunger for knowledge, but a refusal to receive knowledge as a gift from God when the proper time had come.

text:
If you're planning to vote Democrat, and you're doing it sincerely, because you genuinely want a fairer country, cheaper homes, better schools, and a future for your kids, this post is for you. I'm not here to insult you. I'm here to show you something nobody inside the system will ever tell you. Give me two minutes.

Why do people keep defending a system they know doesn't work?

You've seen it a hundred times. A program fails, its budget doubles, the problem gets worse, and the people in charge ask for more. Nobody inside seems surprised. That's because, for them, the system isn't failing. It's working exactly as designed. Just not for you.

To understand it, forget ideology. Follow the incentives.

A politician's horizon is the next election. Two years, four years, six at most. His reward comes from promising: free tuition, cancelled debt, guaranteed housing, a green transition paid for by someone else. The bill arrives in ten, twenty, thirty years. By then he's retired, writing his memoir, giving paid speeches. He collects the applause today. You pay the invoice tomorrow. Any system where the person who makes the promise never pays for breaking it will produce endless broken promises. That isn't a moral failure. It's a mathematical certainty.

A bureaucrat is rewarded for the size of his budget and his team, not for solving the problem. If he solves it, his department shrinks. If it gets worse, he asks for more money, and he usually gets it. Failure is literally funded.

Then add the mega-donors. Foundations like those of Bill Gates or George Soros spend billions shaping policy: global health priorities, criminal justice, education, elections. You don't need to imagine a secret meeting. That's the point. No conspiracy is required, only incentives. The foundations fund the causes, the politicians adopt them, the agencies execute them. And when it goes wrong, who pays? Not the foundation. Not the politician. The neighborhood where the policy was tested. The billionaire never lives inside his own experiment.

The Austrian economists understood this a century ago. Mises showed that a state can't allocate capital properly because it has no prices, no profit and loss, no signal telling it when it's wrong. Hayek showed that no planner can ever know what millions of people know. When an entrepreneur misallocates capital, he goes bankrupt. When a state does, it raises taxes, prints money, or borrows from your children. Error is never punished, so it never stops.

And that's where the cycle locks in. When capital is allocated by politics instead of markets, the most profitable skill is no longer building. It's lobbying. Getting close to the money. Writing the rule that crushes your competitor. Corruption stops being a bug and becomes the business model. Every round creates more people who depend on it and will defend it. That's why the system protects itself even when everyone knows it's broken. Too many livelihoods depend on the lie.

Meanwhile, Europe's fashionable economists offer the opposite diagnosis. Thomas Piketty and Gabriel Zucman tell us the problem is that the state doesn't take enough: more wealth taxes, more redistribution, more state. France has been running that experiment for fifty years. The result is one of the highest tax burdens in the developed world, record debt, and capital and talent leaving the country every year.

History shows how this movie ends. Debt piles up until it can no longer be repaid. Currencies get debased. Then comes the reset, and it is rarely peaceful. Rome debased its coins for generations before it collapsed. Weimar's hyperinflation came just before the darkest chapter of the 20th century. Empires that can't stop spending don't reform gently. They break.

We are approaching the end of that cycle. America now spends more on interest on its debt than on its military. Read that sentence twice.

The good news is that the ending isn't written yet. You can still choose builders over promisers. You can still demand that the people who make decisions live with their consequences. You can still ask for less state, not more.

Wake up. The people selling you the dream will never be the ones paying for it.

text:
Je n'ai jamais été aussi optimiste. Pas malgré le chaos actuel, mais grâce à lui.

Je vais vous expliquer pourquoi l'empire du mensonge construit par la gauche depuis cinquante ans va s'effondrer, et pourquoi ce n'est pas une opinion mais une question de physique.

Tout commence avec un mouvement né sur X il y a quelques années : l'effective accelerationism, ou e/acc.

Au départ, c'est une idée presque thermodynamique. L'univers a une tendance de fond : la matière s'organise pour capter et dissiper l'énergie de plus en plus efficacement. Une cellule fait ça. Une forêt fait ça. Une civilisation fait ça. Le marché, la technologie et le capital sont les formes les plus avancées de ce processus. Ce sont des machines à transformer l'énergie en intelligence, en abondance, en complexité.

La thèse e/acc est simple : il ne faut pas freiner cette dynamique, il faut l'embrasser. Plus d'énergie, plus de calcul, plus d'innovation, plus de croissance. Monter sur l'échelle de Kardashev au lieu de s'excuser d'exister. En face, il y a les « décels » : ceux qui veulent ralentir, réguler, taxer, interdire, culpabiliser. Ceux qui voient le progrès comme une menace à contenir plutôt qu'une force à libérer.

Mais il y a une dimension de l'accélération dont presque personne ne parle. L'accélération n'est pas seulement un moteur. C'est un filtre.

Pensez à n'importe quel organisme. Un corps humain en bonne santé peut courir. Il accélère, son cœur pompe plus fort, ses muscles consomment plus d'oxygène, et tout fonctionne parce que le système est bien conçu. Maintenant, prenez un corps malade. Des artères bouchées, un cœur fragile, des organes qui ne communiquent plus entre eux. Faites-le courir. Il ne va pas plus vite vers la santé. Il va plus vite vers l'infarctus.

L'accélération ne corrige pas les défauts d'un système. Elle les amplifie. Un système sain qui accélère devient plus fort. Un système dysfonctionnel qui accélère meurt plus vite.

Et c'est exactement ce qui est en train d'arriver au projet que je vais appeler par son nom : le projet globalo-socialiste. Celui porté par les démocrates américains, par la technostructure de Bruxelles, par les entités supranationales qui n'ont de comptes à rendre à personne, par un réseau d'ONG financées par l'argent public pour dicter la morale aux peuples qui les financent.

Regardez ce que ce projet a produit.

Des États obèses qui prélèvent plus de la moitié de la richesse produite et qui délivrent des services publics de plus en plus dégradés. Des écoles qui n'apprennent plus à lire mais qui apprennent à culpabiliser. Des hôpitaux à bout de souffle malgré des budgets records. Une immigration massive sans aucune exigence d'assimilation, présentée comme une chance par ceux qui n'en subissent jamais les conséquences. Une désindustrialisation organisée au nom d'une écologie punitive qui délocalise la pollution en Chine et l'emploi avec. Des normes, des normes, et encore des normes, jusqu'à ce qu'il devienne plus simple de créer une entreprise à Austin qu'à Lyon. Une justice qui excuse le coupable et soupçonne la victime. Une censure qui avance masquée sous le nom de « lutte contre la désinformation ». Et une jeunesse à qui l'on a expliqué que son pays, son histoire et sa civilisation étaient des crimes à expier.

Ce n'est pas un ensemble de bugs. C'est la conception elle-même.

Maintenant, changeons d'image. Voyez ce système comme un moteur.

Un bon moteur, c'est de la précision. Des pièces qui s'emboîtent, un minimum de frottements, une énergie qui se transforme en mouvement. Le marché libre, la propriété, la responsabilité individuelle, la monnaie saine : c'est ça, un moteur bien conçu. L'information circule par les prix, chaque erreur est sanctionnée, chaque bonne idée est récompensée.

Le moteur socialiste, lui, est mal conçu dès le départ. Il ne tourne pas sur la création de valeur mais sur sa redistribution. Il ne récompense pas la performance, il la taxe. Il ne laisse pas les erreurs mourir, il les subventionne. Résultat : ça frotte partout. Ça chauffe. Ça grince. Chaque pièce use la pièce d'à côté.

Et que font ceux qui pilotent ce moteur ? Au lieu de le reconcevoir, ils changent les pièces. En permanence. Une pièce cède, on en remet une neuve. Encore une. Encore une.

Ces pièces de rechange, vous les connaissez. Elles s'appellent la dette publique et la planche à billets.

La France a dépassé les 3 300 milliards d'euros de dette et n'a pas voté un budget à l'équilibre depuis le milieu des années 70. Les États-Unis ont franchi les 37 000 milliards de dollars. Les banques centrales ont maintenu des taux à zéro pendant des années, imprimé des montants que plus personne ne sait se représenter, et quand l'inflation est arrivée, elles ont fait semblant d'être surprises. Milton Friedman l'avait pourtant dit il y a cinquante ans : l'inflation est toujours et partout un phénomène monétaire.

Chaque crise, on rachète du temps avec de l'argent qui n'existe pas. Chaque problème structurel, on l'arrose de liquidités pour masquer le bruit du moteur. Mais les frottements sont toujours là. Ils s'accumulent. Et la facture des pièces de rechange finit par coûter plus cher que le moteur lui-même : la charge de la dette devient l'un des premiers postes de dépense de l'État français.

Pendant des décennies, ce moteur mal conçu a pu tourner à 3 000 tours par minute. Lentement. Bruyamment. Mais il tournait. Le monde allait assez doucement pour que le bricolage permanent suffise à masquer l'absurdité de la conception.

Et puis l'IA est arrivée.

L'intelligence artificielle, c'est l'accélération la plus brutale de l'histoire humaine. Ce qui prenait des années prend des mois. Ce qui prenait des mois prend des jours. Des entreprises de dix personnes font ce que faisaient des entreprises de mille. Le capital, les talents et les idées se déplacent à la vitesse de la lumière vers les endroits où ils sont bien traités.

L'IA vient de faire passer le moteur de 3 000 à 20 000 tours par minute.

Posez-vous la question qu'un ingénieur se poserait. Que se passe-t-il quand on fait monter à 20 000 tours un moteur mal conçu, rafistolé de partout, qui frotte à chaque rotation ?

Il explose.

Pas parce que quelqu'un l'a saboté. Parce que la physique ne négocie pas.

Et c'est exactement ce que nous voyons en ce moment, sous nos yeux.

L'insécurité qui gagne des villes entières qui étaient paisibles il y a vingt ans. Le conflit de Gaza importé dans nos rues et instrumentalisé par une gauche qui a troqué l'ouvrier contre le clientélisme communautaire. La misère qui revient dans un pays qui a pourtant un des taux de dépense publique les plus élevés au monde. Des classes moyennes qui travaillent et n'arrivent plus à se loger. Une France fracturée, où l'on parle désormais à voix haute de risque de guerre civile.

Ce ne sont pas des accidents. Ce ne sont pas des « crises » successives sans lien entre elles. Ce sont les pièces du moteur qui commencent à voler.

C'est la conséquence logique de cinquante ans de socialisme international : un système qui a détruit la responsabilité, la frontière, la monnaie, l'école et la fierté, et qui découvre qu'à haute vitesse, tout ce qui a été détruit ne peut plus être compensé par une ligne de dette supplémentaire.

Et c'est là que je deviens profondément optimiste.

Parce qu'une fois qu'on a compris ça, on comprend aussi que leur projet a une date de fin. Pas une date politique. Une date physique. Un système qui consomme plus qu'il ne produit, qui punit ceux qui créent et récompense ceux qui détruisent, qui finance son présent en hypothéquant l'avenir de ses enfants, ne peut pas durer indéfiniment. Il n'est pas soutenable par construction. L'IA ne fait qu'avancer l'échéance.

Le mensonge a besoin de lenteur pour survivre. Il a besoin que les conséquences arrivent assez tard pour qu'on puisse accuser quelqu'un d'autre. Dans un monde à 20 000 tours, les conséquences arrivent immédiatement. Le mensonge n'a plus le temps de se cacher.

Alors, que faire quand le moteur explose ? On en construit un nouveau. Et cette fois, on le conçoit correctement.

Écoutez Elon Musk. Un homme qui a reconstruit l'industrie spatiale, la voiture électrique et l'infrastructure satellite en partant d'un principe simple : revenir aux premiers principes. Ne pas demander « comment on a toujours fait », mais « qu'est-ce qui est physiquement vrai ». C'est exactement ce dont nos États ont besoin : arrêter de rafistoler et repartir de la base.

Écoutez Javier Milei. Un homme dont tout le monde se moquait, arrivé à la tête d'un pays ravagé par un siècle de péronisme, et qui a pris la tronçonneuse au sens propre. Ministères supprimés, dépenses coupées, inflation écrasée, excédent budgétaire retrouvé. Il a prouvé une chose que la gauche jurait impossible : on peut démonter le moteur socialiste et le peuple peut le soutenir.

Écoutez Milton Friedman. Relisez-le. Tout était déjà là. La monnaie, la liberté de choisir, la responsabilité, les effets pervers de l'intervention publique. Il disait que si l'on confiait le Sahara au gouvernement fédéral, il y aurait pénurie de sable en cinq ans. On a ri. On a confié le sable. On a eu la pénurie.

Revenez à une hiérarchie et au respect du beau. Une civilisation ne tient pas que sur des chiffres. Elle tient sur l'idée qu'il existe des choses supérieures à d'autres. Que l'excellence vaut mieux que la médiocrité. Que le mérite compte. Qu'une cathédrale est plus belle qu'un parking. Que transmettre est un devoir et pas une oppression. Le relativisme a été l'arme culturelle de ce projet. Le retour du beau, du vrai et de l'exigence en sera l'antidote.

Et enfin, faites le Nuremberg du communisme. Le nazisme a été jugé, documenté, enseigné, et il est devenu moralement indéfendable. Le communisme, avec ses dizaines de millions de morts, ses goulags, ses famines organisées et ses peuples réduits en esclavage, n'a jamais eu ce procès. On peut encore porter un t-shirt du Che dans une université sans que personne ne cille. Tant que ce procès historique et moral n'aura pas eu lieu, l'idéologie continuera de muter et de revenir sous de nouveaux noms. Il faut nommer les crimes, les enseigner, honorer les victimes, et rendre cette idéologie aussi infréquentable que celle qu'elle prétendait combattre.

Le monde qui vient sera plus rapide, plus exigeant et plus impitoyable avec les systèmes mal conçus. C'est une terrible nouvelle pour ceux qui ont vécu du mensonge.

Et c'est la meilleure nouvelle de notre génération pour tous ceux qui veulent construire.

Le moteur va exploser. À nous de dessiner le suivant.

text:
A possible operational consequence—but neither a straightforward nor a low-risk one. Volunteer stations depend on local people who can respond at short notice. If enough Portsmouth crew members decide that the personal cost—doxxing, public confrontations, and children being targeted at school—is too high, the station could remain short-staffed or offline for longer. The RNLI has already shown it will pause operations when crew safety is at risk: that was precisely why it suspended operations in September. Nearby stations at Hayling Island and Bembridge, independent Gosport, and Coastguard assets can take some calls for a time. That contingency is already in use.

A prolonged gap is a different matter. Portsmouth and Langstone Harbour sit on a busy stretch of water, surrounded by commercial traffic, ferries, leisure craft, and naval movements. Under maritime law, the Coastguard remains responsible for coordinating search and rescue; that responsibility does not disappear if local volunteers step back. But response times can lengthen, vital local knowledge can be lost, and neighbouring volunteer crews may have to take on more work. If the same landings continue in the area, those crews may come under the same pressure.

The RNLI’s own figures show that the vast majority of its launches are for ordinary coastal incidents, not Channel small boats. A thinner local service therefore affects everyone who uses these waters—not just those cases that have drawn hostility.

Not everyone shares that hostility, but many people still feel it. The council motion supporting the RNLI passed by a clear majority. At the same time, the abuse and protests have come mainly from a subset of violent activists and online campaigns—not from the wider resident population. Even so, that distinction offers little comfort to volunteers with families. People can, and do, step back.

But we should not accept a resulting coverage gap as the new normal. In a high-use area, it means reduced capacity managed through mutual aid—until the station is staffed again or the pattern of taskings putting it under pressure changes. The first depends on volunteers being willing to accept the risk; the second depends on decisions made well beyond Portsmouth.

text:
The Spa Town of Edipsos, Evia

On the northern coast of Evia, Edipsos has been attracting visitors to its thermal waters for centuries. It is one of Greece's best-known spa destinations, combining a traditional seaside town atmosphere with naturally heated springs.

The thermal waters emerge in various places around the area, including near the coastline, where warm water meets the sea. The result is a distinctive landscape that sets Edipsos apart from a typical beach resort.

There are several ways to enjoy a visit:
•  Explore the thermal spring areas along the coast.
•  Visit the town's historic spa buildings.
•  Walk along the waterfront promenade.
•  Enjoy cafés and tavernas by the sea.
•  Discover nearby beaches and coastal villages.
•  Take time to relax and enjoy the slower pace.

Edipsos has a long association with thermal bathing, and its spa culture has helped shape the town's identity. Visitors come for different reasons, from a relaxing break to an interest in the area's natural features and history.

The waterfront is a pleasant place to wander, particularly later in the day when the light softens and the town becomes more relaxed.

There is also plenty to enjoy beyond the springs. The surrounding northern Evia coastline offers opportunities for scenic drives, beach visits and discovering smaller settlements.

If you plan to experience the thermal waters, use designated bathing areas and follow local guidance, as natural spring temperatures can vary considerably.

Edipsos is not about racing from one attraction to another. It is about making time for yourself, enjoying the sea air and discovering a different side of Evia.

For anyone looking for a break with a little history and a slower rhythm, it makes a worthwhile addition to a trip around the island.

Have you visited the town of Edipsos in North Evia? We'd love to hear about your experience.

text:
I didn't leave Grant that day.

But I didn't pretend everything was fine either.

We agreed to marriage counseling, and Grant began working with a family counselor to establish a healthy relationship with Ethan.

The first time I met Ethan properly, we went to a small café in Old Town Scottsdale.

He arrived wearing a navy hoodie and carrying the same blue backpack I had seen in the basement.

He looked nervous.

“Hi,” he said quietly.

“Hi, Ethan.”

I smiled.

“Would you like a hot chocolate?”

He nodded.

We spent an hour talking about school, his favorite video games, and the kind of music he liked. I didn't ask him to call me anything special. I didn't pretend I could replace his mother.

I simply listened.

When we left, he hugged Grant before turning to me.

“Thank you for not hating me.”

I felt my throat tighten.

“Sweetheart, none of this is your fault.”

That evening, Grant and I sat together on our back porch.

“I know I hurt you,” he said. “I don't expect you to forget it.”

“Good. Because I'm not going to.”

He nodded.

“But I want to rebuild this marriage. And I want Ethan to know he can come home without feeling like he's destroying something.”

I took his hand.

“Then we have to stop treating honesty like a threat. If you had told me the truth eight months ago, we could have faced this together.”

“I know.”

“And Rosa?”

Grant had already called her to apologize and offered her job back. She declined, explaining that she had accepted another position, but she agreed to meet with us and clear the air.

A few months later, Ethan began spending weekends with us. We created a routine that worked for everyone, and Grant learned that being a father meant more than buying furniture or keeping promises in secret.

It meant showing up.

One Sunday morning, I found Ethan and Grant in the kitchen making pancakes. Flour covered the counter, the smoke alarm was going off, and both of them were laughing.

I stood in the doorway, smiling.

Grant noticed me.

“Don't judge us. We're professionals.”

Ethan grinned.

“Dad burned the first batch.”

I laughed so hard I had to sit down.

For the first time, our home felt different—not perfect, but honest.

I still had moments when I remembered the lies and wondered why Grant hadn't trusted me. We continued counseling, and rebuilding trust took time.

But I no longer saw Ethan as the secret that nearly destroyed my marriage.

I saw him as a boy who deserved a family willing to tell the truth.

Here's what I learned: sometimes the biggest betrayal isn't the secret itself. It's the belief that the people who love us cannot handle the truth.

And sometimes, the family you never planned becomes the family you cannot imagine living without.

Now tell me honestly:

If your husband hid a teenage child from you for months, would you forgive him after learning why or would keeping that kind of secret be an unforgivable betrayal?

text:
Tony Curtis’s widow remembered him as a kind, funny man who loved his fans. Less than a year later, his will would become the subject of a bitter family controversy.

On September 30, 2010, Jill Curtis spoke to reporters outside their Henderson, Nevada home, just one day after the legendary Hollywood actor died at 85.

She described a man who had spent his life entertaining audiences around the world, but who, in his final hours, was simply at home, surrounded by the people who loved him.

“He died peacefully here, surrounded by those who love him and have been caring for him,” she said.

Curtis had been in and out of the hospital for months. According to Jill, he suffered from COPD and serious lung problems linked to his years of smoking, even though he had quit roughly 30 years earlier.

His heart, she explained, had survived numerous health struggles throughout his life.

“But this time his heart was ready to go and be at peace.”

When asked what Curtis had been most proud of, Jill offered an unexpected answer: painting.

Although he had become one of Hollywood’s most recognizable stars, she said that becoming a movie star was what he had dreamed of since childhood.

“They don’t make people like Tony anymore,” she said.

She wanted him remembered as a kind, funny man who worked hard, had tremendous drive, and showed generosity to the people around him.

“I know Tony’s had some personal problems and things, but haven’t we all?” she told reporters. “And in the end his kindness and generosity and general spirit prevailed over everything.”

But after his death, another part of Curtis’s legacy would attract attention.

In 2011, details emerged that his will had explicitly excluded his children from inheriting his estate. The decision sparked controversy and added a complicated dimension to the story of a man whose public legacy was built on decades of Hollywood success.

His widow’s words outside their home had been about love, illness, and the man she wanted the world to remember. The later dispute over his estate raised a different question about what happens to a family’s relationships when a loved one’s final wishes become public.

Tony Curtis left behind an extraordinary film career, but his legacy would also be remembered through the deeply personal questions surrounding his final wishes.

Kimberly was close with her family and regularly stayed in contact. She had plans to move to California and hoped to pursue a career in medicine.

Shortly before disappearing, Kimberly learned she would receive a settlement of between $25,000 and $35,000 from a workplace injury lawsuit. She never collected the money and missed her final appointment with her lawyer.

Kimberly had also recently testified against two men in a drug trafficking case. Police had provided protection during the trial and offered to help her relocate. Whether her testimony was connected to her disappearance remains unknown.
