text:
[9 of 9] However, Age 65 all-cause mortality doesn’t tell you life expectancy; it merely gives the chance of dying at any time during one’s 65thyear, and that risk was 11% lower for vegetarians after adjusting for the other factors (https://t.co/JSMRQLg5YZ). That doesn’t give life expectancy—if 10% of vegetarians are dead at Age 65 and so are 10% of meat-eaters, that doesn’t mean the vegetarians might not live longer (or shorter) than the meat-eaters. The Malones acknowledge as much: “Nor does an 11 percent lower mortality hazard mean someone will live 11 percent longer.”

OTOH, the Malones write, “By age 85, vegetarians showed no statistically significant survival advantage, nor did vegans overall after adjustment for lifestyle differences.” [at Age 85—a distinction they omitted in their conclusions]. I’m not familiar enough with the study to know to what extent AHS-2 took into account how long a person was vegetarian (or vegan); by Age 85, much of the damage of bad diet may have already been done, so that if a person was vegan for the past 5 years it wouldn’t mean that everything they ate before 80 didn’t impact their health in a major way. But I asked AI (SI!), and according to Grok, AHS-2 did not differentiate based on how long one had been a vegetarian. https://t.co/JSMRQLg5YZ. Thus, the graph the Malones cited does not distinguish lifelong vegetarians from later switchers. I don’t know how big the respondent pool was that was lifelong vegetarian and Age 85, but it may have been too small a group to obtain statistically significant results. (I’m speculating; haven’t read the study). In any case, the AHS study itself argues that vegetarian diet reduces the risk of premature death so that one can reach the age of 85. That there was not much difference after 85 suggests to me that those carnivores making it to 85 ate healthier versions of a carnivorous diet or had good genes (statistically speaking) or good luck. It should not be interpreted to mean that just because there wasn’t a difference at 85, the hypothesis that vegetarian diet promotes longevity is false. (Note that Andrews et al. also reported a peak benefit to plant-based diet for longevity when looking at mid-late adult ages, whereas the difference had disappeared by Age 95.)

Longevity was not determined in AHS-2 (cited by the Malones) but was in AHS-1. “The well-known figures (vegetarian Adventist men living roughly 9.5 years longer and women 6.1 years longer than the California population of the time) come primarily from earlier California Adventist data (AHS-1 and related analyses), not from the recent AHS-2 mortality papers….Investigators continue to cite the earlier longevity advantages and note that the clearest mortality reductions at younger ages reduce premature deaths and thereby increase average longevity, even when the relative advantage fades at very advanced ages.” (https://t.co/ub7ZGQTp3C). The Malones completely overlooked this earlier finding.

Neither does mortality at 65 tell you about the quality of life. “Commentaries from the investigators repeatedly state that Adventists live longer and with better quality of life, and that the extra years tend to be relatively good quality. Lower rates of diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, and certain cardiovascular conditions among vegetarians are consistent with that interpretation.” (https://t.co/ub7ZGQTp3C). Again, no comments from the Malones on this.

The Malones’ comments on other confounders are fair. Also, the “what we eat with it” comments are on point. However, the same applies for vegetarians. Those eating a vegeburger on a white bun with French fries, manufactured sauces, sugar drinks, etc., have the same issues as those having all that with a hamburger. They are correct in pointing out the difference between highly processed vs. close-to-nature plant foods, as well as animal-based foods.

The Malones write, “There is no direct clinical evidence demonstrating that this dietary transformation would save 15 million lives, or that restricting red meat would independently extend human lifespan.” (bold in the original) True. But there never will be direct clinical evidence of that nature. One simply cannot do such a study. So while I agree with many of their criticisms that highlight the shortcomings of observational and survey studies, they can’t suggest a better alternative. It seems fair to me for them to argue that one shouldn’t therefore make wholesale changes in global food systems based on these uncertain models, but I think I’d give the models more credence when it comes to personal application since I do have to make a decision about what to eat and I can’t wait for a study that will never exist.

As for the climate change link, my understanding is that the chances of getting research funding and papers published in nearly any scientific discipline is significantly higher if one can associate it with climate change (or DEI!), or at least that was true under many governments/administrations, so it isn’t surprising that this link between diet and climate change would be emphasized. That doesn’t mean it was the primary motivation for the EAT-Lancet study or that its results are suspect. (I haven’t read it and don’t offer any endorsement or criticism).

The Malones’ criticism of the changes in public health policy being driven by this climate change-associated push for reduced meat consumption seems disconnected from their early comments about quality of diet (whatever the protein source). If that program were to be rolled back, the diet that would continue to be promoted and practiced would not be the Malones’ idealistic fresh meat, vegetables, etc., diet but for much of the population it would remain processed meat and too few vegetables, etc. I think they pulled a rhetorical bait-and-switch here (probably unintentionally).

I agree that governments shouldn’t be dictating dietary changes. I am for free choice, and that includes freedom to choose what one eats (within reason; I’m not a fan of cannibalism, for example!). I think if vegetarians force meat-eaters to give it up by exerting political force, there will be a backlash. (I already hate it that conservatives are attacking vegetarians a lot more; it is in response to the popularity of veganism among far-left radicals, not to mention climate change such as noted by the Malones, and other associations with leftist causes).

Overall, I think the Malones’ introductory graphs are unfortunate sources of confusion. However, the criticisms offered in the rest of the article are generally fair, and highlight the shortcomings of ecological or epidemiological approaches compared to an RCT. But a long-term RCT of human diet is simply not feasible. Therefore, careful analysis of ecological/epidemiological data is needed, and the work by Andrews et al. and the AHS study provide stronger support for a vegetarian diet than the Malone’s article suggests.

At the end of the article they return to another international comparison, Hong Kong vs. India, which is just a cherry-picked subset of their original analysis. All the comments relative to comparative wealth that I made relative to their global analysis applies to this one-on-one comparison. Why they returned to this I don’t know. But C.J. Andrews et al.’s more sophisticated analysis undermines their argument. In the Malone’s conclusions, they dropped the Age 85 qualification of the no survival advantage for vegans claim; that’s unfortunate, because that omission makes it a misleading statement (see above discussion).

Incidentally, Robert and Jill Malone were lacto-ovo vegetarians for 30 years, changing only around 2022 after health concerns (https://t.co/erSIriurSx). He lost 50 pounds after switching to an animal protein diet, cutting carbs, seed oils, added sugar, etc., and incorporating intermittent fasting. It is hardly surprising that one can be unfit on a lacto-ovo vegetarian diet. But it sounds to me like he went on the low-carb, high-protein diet that’s all the rage, without trying a healthier vegetarian diet. I.e., what would his health be like if he cut the processed foods, sugar, seed oils, practiced intermittent fasting, etc., on a vegetarian diet? I won’t knock what seems to work for him—good for him for making changes that have improved his health! But it is a mistake to conclude that his newfound dedication to a healthier diet implies that lacto-ovo vegetarian or vegan diets can’t be equally (or more) healthful. Some of their pushback against AHS-2, etc. reminds me of the enthusiasm of a new convert to their recently adopted religion; it helps that the religion is popular!

Robert

Certification is what makes Harvard expensive? 

I think Andreeson does not know what he’s talking about.

The UC system is ranked the best in the world. For California residents it is subsidized based on income, so families earning less than $100K get free tuition, and there’s a gradient for families earning more than that.

It has been that way for decades as the UC system got better and better.

“The government” allows NIMBYs to file appeals to stall construction projects. NIMBYs want that power and use it. They vote in local elections to keep that power.  YIMBYs need to educate voters and out-vote NIMBYs. 

Other ordinances, like fire-proofing, building to codes to make buildings safer during earthquakes, requiring landlords provide ACs if their buildings exceed 80 degrees inside, etc, are what separates the first world from the third world usually. 

Compare the death tolls of earthquakes in other countries to the outcomes of the quakes in 89 and 94 in SF & LA.

Insurance companies are not going to insure buildings that aren’t convincingly fire-proofed in California now. The government is trying to work out how to reassure them that the precautions being taken mean Altadena and the Palisades are going to be safer when they’re rebuilt — so they will be insured. (Thanks @BenAllenCA)

Technology can help with fire-proofing. I’m skeptical that this would happen broadly if governments didn’t require homes be insured, though.

California residents have known for decades they live in a fire-prone region. The government was not preventing them from fire-proofing their homes.

Yes, there are ways for government to accelerate housing construction. It should not take years to approve projects in California. The rezoning process in LA is purposefully obtuse. And voters here don’t understand the power of the city council or how anything works at the city level, which current city council members abuse to stay in power. (If this wasn’t true, you would fix it @mhdcd8)

You could say that technology could help voters rise up and pressure the government to fix its processes — as with social media. We’ve been doing that for 15 years, though, and LA hasn’t gotten better yet. Maybe technology needs decades, too? 🧐

And health care was more private 30 years ago. The ACA has bent the cost curve downwards, while forcing health insurance companies to offer mental health therapy. The ACA didn’t require dental and vision, so that’s still not covered. Somehow the government is not the problem there, but the solution.

And healthcare in numerous other countries is more managed by the state, and they get better outcomes for lower costs.

Technology can come up with cheaper ways to test blood and scan tissues and bones and conduct less invasive surgeries and so on. 

But so far the current system is still set up to grift, and it has little incentive to stop. Desperate people will pay their lives away to survive or keep loved ones alive, and they get exploited.

text:
At a house party in Virginia, I did not know anyone.

By the kitchen island stood a teenage boy in a stiff collared shirt, staring at a bowl of green avocado paste like it was his only friend on earth.

Every time someone reached for a chip, he moved two inches left to stay out of the way.

In my land, the sentry assigned to the provisions is the most trusted man in the camp.

I walked over and stood beside him.

"How is the supply holding?" I asked.

He blinked. "Uh. It's guacamole. My aunt made it."

"Does it require guarding?"

He looked at the loud room full of adults talking about mortgages. Then he looked at the bowl.

"The guy in the blue sweater double-dipped twice," he whispered.

"Unacceptable," I said. "We hold this corner."

We stood shoulder to shoulder for an hour. Whenever the blue sweater approached, I stepped half an inch forward and offered him a napkin until he retreated.

By 9:00, the boy was explaining the entire history of Star Wars to me while we ate the bottom half of the bowl ourselves.

His mother whispered "thank you" to me on my way out. Apparently he had not stayed at a party that long in three years.

Next month is his birthday. I am bringing the chips.

text:
As I said earlier:  neither. A complex man full of nuance and shaped by his times in ways he could not control.

Arguably the greatest general of his era, Lee was brilliant on the field and classy in defeat. He did the best job he could for Virginia, lost his fortune, and still loved America.

Yet he also fought for the wrong side and also prolonged the cruel institution of slavery.

Was he a good man who made a poor choice? I don’t know. If he had taken Lincoln’s offer and led the Union, I don’t know if the war would have lasted a single year with Lee in command. On the other hand, Lee likely didn’t want to war with his fellow Virginians. These were his neighbors, friends, and family. And he never could have gone home again if he had fought for the Union. He would have been a pariah in Virginia.

I think he was a man who made the wrong decision for honorable reasons. And I think he knew it later on.

But also find it difficult to judge a man asked to go to war with his friends and neighbors.

Lee shows us a decent man thrown into a chaotic era he never asked for. He tried to balance his emotions and faith, yet ultimately made the wrong choice.

Many of us do the same thing.

Lee teaches us that honor and decency alone don’t make us right any more than dishonor and immoral behavior makes our side wrong. Sometimes good Christian men make bad choices and godless atheists make good ones.

And sometimes honor binds us to defend our friends and family even when they are wrong.

It’s hard for any of us to walk in Lee’s shoes and judge his ultimate decision. That’s why his is a nuanced and complex legacy.

I think he’s proof that even good men can make bad decisions for good reasons. And that many of us today don’t understand the loyalty people had to their states and neighbors in the 1860s.
